Oxenfree is a dark, adventure game with many choices ahead.
This game is truly a work of art, in my opinion. The art style is definitely something that gives the game realness and you can relate to the characters in more than many ways.
There is lots of dialogue throughout Oxenfree, so be willing to pay attention to every word said, as it can reflect later on in your playthrough. This is something that may be annoying to others at some points as the characters interact a lot and could interrupt other parts of dialogue.
Your course of actions are shown throughout and it gives the plot of the game a real feeling to it.
Oxenfree is a game that keeps you enthralled and wanting more of the story. Most of the game, without the tasks you are given, is a scavengar hunt for clues that are connected to the plot.
There's so many different endings to this that you may want to play it a couple of other times to see what other achievements you can receive.
If you like mystery, thriller, adventure and ghosts, you should enjoy this amazing game.

Easily comparable to a sci-fi Dwarf Fortress Lite, and perfect for people who are interested in simulation/colony management games but find something like DF overwhelming or too dense to fully get into (or who want things like, y'know, graphics, sound, and the ability to use a mouse). And for fans of DF, RimWorld puts much more emphasis on the individual colonists, their relationships, their histories, and their abilities; whereas DF gives you too much info to process--everything down to physical description, favorite color, and complete psych profile--on all hundred-plus dorfs in your fort (most of whom are talentless migrants you never asked for, don't want, and couldn't care less about), RimWorld gives you a scant handful of colonists with unique backstories and skills, and you never know when someone else might be available to join the settlement (either voluntarily or...otherwise), so you'd better get cozy with your crew.
It's almost like the game tricks you into caring about your colonists when you know death lurks around every corner. Nobody joins your colony without you making some kind of choice as to whether you want them to, so every death feels way crueler than Urist McWaxworker getting smashed by a carp.
If you are into military/squad simulation then you will enjoy this.

I used to play Timeshock(on dos) with my father when I was growing up. Getting to play this table again is just incredible.
The visuals are pristine. Seriously, I hope others follow suit in the pre-rendered-to-layers graphical approach of this table, as the edge clarity, lighting, translucency, and detail surpass what's possible with real-time rendering as to be laughable. The physicality this yields the table is unmatched.
In terms of gameplay, this remains one of the most interesting, deep, and well crafted 'narrative' pinball tables ever made. The soundtrack aids this tremendously as well. There are few pinball tables that manage to create the experience of a dramatic journey, and Timeshock certainly does.
I own this on all its available platforms, play it in the can on my phone, play it in vertical-format on my PC now. (seriously, if your monitor can do portrait mode DO IT)
If you love pinball, buying this is a no-brainer. Worth every cent.

So here it is - the Ultra edition of Pro Pinball: Timeshock. If the differences aren't immediately apparent, remember that's only because the 1997 original was so far ahead of the curve. The lighting effects in this version have to be seen to be believed - static screnshots don't really do them justice. Every piece of wire, every screw, every element is lit up by the hundreds of lights on the table and you can see every one of them reflecting and reacting to what's going on, it's *beautiful*. You'd swear they'd mounted a camera on a physical table and filmed it (at very, very high resolution!)
The static camera is not an issue for me, although it's a pity there's only one choice of viewing angle and no cabinet mode (both allegedly to be added in future updates). Also, the physics are the same as the original version - not that the ball motion is especially bad, in fact not the worst on the market even 15 years later, but it would be nice to see some improvements in the state of the art.
Of course a lot of people will complain that there's only one table in the game, it's true, but Timeshock has the deepest and best ruleset of any pinball sim I've seen. Better that than twenty-five copy-paste games with cosmetic differences but near-identical gameplay. If you have even the least interest in Pinball there's no excuse for not giving Timeshock a go.

This is the definitive version of the definitive Pinball game.
Nothing compares to Pro Pinball in terms of good table design, realistic physics simulation and overall high-quality Pinball experience.
Timeshock was already great back in the day, and the new, remade version only makes it even better.
The graphics are amazing, and it feels just like a real Pinball table would, in a way other pinball simulators just can't emulate. You can really feel the attention to detail and the love for Pinball the Pro Pinball team have in every inch of the table. Just play any other pinball game out there and then play this one, and you'll know what I mean.
The design of the table itself is also fantastic. There is so much to do and to discover, that it feels like a real adventure, and it'll keep you playing for hours and hours. A bit on the difficult side, but that's part of the charm.
It's still in Early Access, so a few of the promised features are missign, specially some of the view angles and a decent interface for rebinding controls, but nothing that detracts from the main experience.
tl;dr - If you enjoy Pinball games, then this is a MUST BUY. It really doesn't get any better than that.

I have mixed feelings about this game.  It has a beautiful art style and its quite a joy to walk around the environments.
The voice acting (in parts) is superb and played by people who have voiced some telltale games, they really help bring the characters to live and make them quite believable however the game does have a tenancy to allow you as a player to cut off the characters talking by moving between environments which breaks the immersion a little.
Also when you are prompted to provide a response to a question the options sometimes fade quite quickly which is fine in some situations if a quick response is needed however if you give a response Alex just interrupts the person currently speaking and blurts out what she wants to say.  This is annoying.
I think the biggest gripe for me though was the slow pace of the story really didnt engage me, at first i was really excited to see what was happening however by the end i was quite bored.  This might be because i didnt play the game in a single sitting, instead i started it and then finished it a few weeks later.   This might have been different if i played and finished it in a shorter period of time.
Its not a long game though and the game does have a new game plus mode however i dont think i can bring myself to play it at this time.
I feel like im being overly critical of the game however i would still recommend playing it if you enjoy adventure story games.
Maybe just play it in one sitting or in a shorter period of time.

What can I say about Borderlands? I have played this game since release and am still playing it now. This is the first game that I have bought every DLC ever released and honestly believe that I had a bargain. They are not the equivalent of COD map packs or zombie modes, (even though when they came out they were a whole £1 cheaper than the COD equivalents!) what you get for the now tiny sum is an extension of a great game one which is a quarter of the playing time of the full game itself.
The original game? Every playthrough has resulted in something new besides the witty script writing which never seems to get old there are a HUGE selection of weaponry, class mods, shields, grenade mods character selection & customisation's. Ever expanding (yet not quite open worlds) ever increasing difficulty and a rewarding co-op experience. Yet another game I enjoy for the fact you make it your own and play it your way.

I have been aquainted with this game long ago, when I was actually reading gaming magazines.(lacking internet around that time) One thing that stuck to me recently is the sandbox combat that spices some situations, although the physics of of some situations makes it a bit awkward and sometimes it looks just too forced to even seem realistic.
Melee combat, however, is truly impressive. Making use of the smooth character movement(strafing, jumping, power strikes), you can perform effective combat manouvers and unpexpected turnouts makes it even more spectacular.( ex. that moment when you use a power strike on an Orc charging you and both of you cross swords, making it a click masher before it gets decieded who is disarmed).
The magic system could have used a bit more adaptability to the already flexible character tree that you can develop up to the epilogue of the game. However, magic itself serves as a very useful tool in some situations.( ex. unlocking the cells of prisoners with telekinesis so that the Necromancer doesn't see you and goes Darth Vader on your neck)
All in all, the game has quite decent a storyline, mood and visuals( especially for it's age) and I can honestly say that I have encountered only a few glitches. It may not cater to some modern gamers but those of you who are more old school will find this game quite pleasant and memorable experience.

Original: Don't underestimate the value of Pro Pinball series. Especially Timeshock. Even the original series still holds up excellently today -- amazing ball physics, rulesets, and audio. If you want this for cheaper, get the 3 tables -- Timeshock, Big Race USA, and Fantastic Journey -- for $6 each. You'll still support the developers who are making this game, but you'll ultimately be missing out on an even more realistic experience.
This version has been made even better than before. Pro Pinball is now more graphically enhanced, especially around dazzling light shows. It's still in Early Access (more features to come, as stated in the Store description), but this is a must-buy, even if the $15 price tag seems unsettling for just 1 table (Unlike companies that produce multitudes of tables, Pro Pinball treats its games as simulations that CLOSELY compare to the real thing, giving a more realistic experience). And yes, the remaining games will be remastered as well.

This game is okay, but in the end was not worth the wait in it's current state.
First of all, the Kickstarter for this game was a disaster. Their promise was that with the money earned by the Kickstarter, they would be able to speed up development. This was in the end of 2013. Yes, 2013. They promised it would be finished at the start of 2014. With barely any communication they just contineud to postpone the release without actually telling anyone about the progress of the game.
Next, the optimisation is very bad. The game might look pretty, but does not run well at all on any standard gaming pc. Also the angles of the tables are not changeble. And now the UI is actually on top of the table, the table looks very small and is not comfortable to play on (for me at least).
I hope they will still be able to improve and optimise performance of the game and also add the angles THE ORIGINAL GAME had. But with this slow progress, the game probably won't be out of 'early access' before 2020.

Edmund McMillen returns to the reflex - based, blood vessel-burstingly difficult sub-genre of platformers, bringing us another game in the vein of super meat boy.
The visuals are an unusual mix of grim and cartoonish. Think Meat Boy, but less bouncy: most areas have a colour palette of "black + grey + (another colour.)" The game isn't particularly nice to look at, to be quite honest, but it seems that this was intentional.
The soundtrack is from Ridiculon, the same person who made the music for Isaac: rebirth and its DLCs. It's decent enough overall; it fits the chaos of the "end of the world" theme well. With that said, some of the tracks, particularly those for the Hollows and Golgotha are just obnoxiously loud in pursuit of being "intense."
The core gameplay mechanics are very different from those in Meat Boy, but they work to create a similar gameplay experience. Ash, the player character, can jump variable heights based on how you press the button, jump to and from ledges for increased distance, but he can't freely wall jump. This single change leads to more inventive and engaging level design.
Each area also has its own fair share of unique enemies and stage objects, which make gameplay more advanced without alienating the player by changing the core mechanics. Overall, the level design is exceptionally good, giving each area its own unique feel.
The game has plentiful secret levels, most of which can be found through a secret exit to a main level. They aren't hard to find, but they don't need to be; they still feel satisfying to find. The secret levels themselves were designed by Tyler Glailel as opposed to McMillen, so they don't have the same level design genius to them, and a lot of them devolve into "go to the end and get back while being shot at by several enemies." they feel like something you'd find in Mario Maker: difficult but not due to good design.
Despite this, The End is Nigh is a fantastic game, and if you enjoyed Meat Boy or any such games you will probably love it.

-The Graphics-

-The Gameplay-
Being here for quite some time now, the game has REALLY taken a turn for the great, albeit a little slow, it is MUCH better than breezing through the game in 5 whole entire minutes, no; instead, YOU are getting many hours of trial, error, fun and commitment... -The Community-
Have you ever needed to grab a cup of sugar from a neighbor, you can do that in this game except with houses, coin, resources, you name it! Also a very scarce commodity that is little to none. (A friendly, bonded, neighborhood-like community)
-The Summary-
All in all, I think this game is rather spectacular and nothing short from a treat to fans of voxel games and MMO games alike. I do also want to remind those who are looking to purchase, you're messing around with nicotine-tier addiction, except this one can't be shaken so easily.

I have played this game since I was four years old. I have so many fond memories of playing Age of Kings (which we called the "red CD") with my brother and my father back in '99 and '00 and then the "blue CD" (the Conquerors expansion). I don't have any competitive experience but this is the only game I have always come back to.
When I learned in 2013 that they would release an HD edition compatible with the new and recent operating systems it was the happiest news I received for years and made up for some of the sorrow I still felt for the loss of our wonderful Ensemble Studios, the awesome people who brought this game to life, back in 2009.
It is a very solid RTS and I would still prefer it to any other I have played (AoE3, SC2, WoC, etc). And with the scenario editor you can create your own maps and shape them how ever you like (well you can't choose the shape, it will always be a square on the tip but you can choose whichever terrain and elevation you want). Plus you can publish your own maps or scenarios on the workshop and share them!
With the Rise of the Rajas expansion released recently, the game offers more civs than I ever dreamed possible. The campaigns (especially the first ones from Age of Kings and the Conquerors) are well-made and the voice acting is wonderful!
The game even offers a mini encyclopaedia on the Main Menu for both civs, mechanics, and history.
The game community is wonderful and I recommend you follow Resonance22, ZeroEmpires and Spirit of the Law (to name a few) on youtube for good insight on both in-depth analysis of mehanics and civs as well as upcoming community events, streams, expert gameplay and tournaments.
The developers have been slacking off the earlier part of 2016, leaving a buggy and relatively unstable game on the same patch for many months. Out-of-sync have been a common issue. But it seems they've gotten a thumb out and fixing stuff now in the autumn.
If you already own AoC on CD, you can play on voobly instead which is arguably more balanced and stable (but the average skill level is much higher and people are more competitive there in my experience and you will miss out on all the neat new expansions they're making now)

From a first-person-shooter to an open world adventure, this game quences your thirst for blood while supplying adventure with it's massively large maps. But because of the density of most large-scale battlefronts, it's easy for frames to drop pretty fast if you don't have a high-end computer. Though, luckily, Daybreak offers a squad system to be covert with friends; granting the ability to use things like squad beacons---an item used as a spawn point for squad or platoon members.
Another fathomable reason I apply PlanetSide 2 as one of my top FPS games is because it's
free to play. A player isn't pushed to a point where he's forced to needlessly spend money on Daybreak Cash or subscription like other games do. It's completely voluntary. I myself have actually gotten to level 75 before spending money on subscription or Daybreak Cash (if you deduce the friend-refferal codes and Daybreak gift codes).
Lastly, the game has quality; and most massively-multiplayer-online video games don't guarantee that for a fact. Unfortunately, even if you do have a top-of-the-line PC, you will experience framerate drops---unless you have at least 16 gigs of RAM---even then it's oblivious. My current computer is supplied with 32 gigs of ram and a 16 gigs supporting my GPU, and I still even see my frames drop ten or twenty (I play on the highest settings and usually get around 140-160 FPS).
Though the game has troubles with it's framerate sometimes, it's definitely worth the time to try.
From my perspective, I would give Daybreak a 8.7/10 for the good quality and hard work they've put into it even though it isn't one of those ridiculously popular games. As said before, PlanetSide 2 has a supportive, friendly community that are committed to helping it grow. I just hope to see you there one day~!

The story is amazing, the humor overflows bountifully, the environments are huge and fill me with a deep sense of desolation, the art is simple and beautiful, and the gameplay is as fluid as the original.
Walking through the abandoned ruins of old aperture is a treat in and of itself, but the puzzles are unlike anything any other game has ever given me. The solutions for many of the puzzles are the kind of thing that would pop into your head and then be ignored for being too stupid to work, which takes getting used to but is such a pleasure when you find out that it actually works. Crawling through the hulking dilapidated geodesic spheres filled with still-functioning 50-year old experiments that never saw the light of day evokes a profound sadness at what could have been, something that is very emotional without being particularly exposition-heavy. Despite the injection of humor, the story of Cave Johnson and his assistant is terribly tragic and I'd be lying if I said it didn't weigh heavily on me throughout the rest of the game. Sure, the puzzles are harder (by an order of magnitude, I'd say) than the original, but what really stuck with me was how immersive and vast the world is in comparison. It certainly helps that the "Half Life 2 Mod" aesthetic of the original portal has been replaced with custom UI development, because that was one thing I positively hated about the original.
Not since I completed World of Goo have I been so distraught at coming to the end of a game. Portal 2 is a complete all-around experience that I reckon will stick with me forever, and I wouldn't have it any other way. You're doing yourself a favor playing this game.

In terms of user experience when you're getting started, this is really very much "Early Access".
But the actual pinball table itself? Wow, it is an absolute work of art. The lighting, the effects, the physics - it's all spot on.
This feels like a real pinball table in a way most other video pinball just doesn't. Suddenly, as I began to play, I wished with all my heart that all of the tables on Farsight's "The Pinball Arcade" could be recreated by Barnstorm Games instead, to do those old beloved tables justice in a far more accurate preservation. Barnstorm Games' love for pinball is present in every minute detail. It's there in the travel of the ball. It's there in the gentle reflections of light. It's there in the click of the flipper. The ka-chunk of the targets.
Even the physics in the in-table video mode DMD game are better than I would expect from a pinball table!
If you love pinball, actual real pinball tables, try this game. Treat yourself! You will love it and it will love you back.
However, let me get back to details on what's so "my goodness this is so Early Access". When I first downloaded the game through Steam, I thought to myself "Oh, only ~700MB? That's pretty small!" - then I started it up and rather than letting me into the game and giving me an option to log in as a minor feature, the first thing I saw when I started up the game were some big ugly grey boxes, asking me to log in, or play as guest. I thought to myself "I kickstarted this, so I probably have a login somewhere...." - so I spent a good long while activating a forum account, retrieving a password, then activating that password. Then I logged in. Thankfully you only seem to need to do that once!
Then the next thing I see is a dialogue box telling me that it's downloading another ~500MB of data. Then it unpacks it. Then I'm in! So I go "hey, I wonder if logging in did anything special!" and click on Account. It looks like it did nothing special. So I click on the arrow to go "back", and it black screens so I need to exit the app entirely.
Then I decided to try playing the table. And it crashes out again. So I restart the game, and it works this time.
Now, there aren't any instructions for keys when you're looking at the table, nor on the pause menu, so I went through pressing all the keys on my keyboard to see if I could start a game. I didn't find it (fyi - you press the "S" key!) so I exited, then saw the instructions (and story!) under a little icon on the (mostly empty) main menu.
The actual table makes up for everything. But still - there's a lot of things they still need to do to make the overall experience of starting the application and getting into the game much better.

Easily comparable to a sci-fi Dwarf Fortress Lite, and perfect for people who are interested in simulation/colony management games but find something like DF overwhelming or too dense to fully get into (or who want things like, y'know, graphics, sound, and the ability to use a mouse). And for fans of DF, RimWorld puts much more emphasis on the individual colonists, their relationships, their histories, and their abilities; whereas DF gives you too much info to process--everything down to physical description, favorite color, and complete psych profile--on all hundred-plus dorfs in your fort (most of whom are talentless migrants you never asked for, don't want, and couldn't care less about), RimWorld gives you a scant handful of colonists with unique backstories and skills, and you never know when someone else might be available to join the settlement (either voluntarily or...otherwise), so you'd better get cozy with your crew.
It's almost like the game tricks you into caring about your colonists when you know death lurks around every corner. Nobody joins your colony without you making some kind of choice as to whether you want them to, so every death feels way crueler than Urist McWaxworker getting smashed by a carp.

This game really deserves a sequel or spiritual successor. The first person sword fighting is good, satisfying and possibly the best of its kind (haven't played Dishonored yet). There are some issues with hit detection, and Flurries (your main attack, but you'll probably be using power strikes most of the time) is pretty crap, but apart from that the melee combat is done pretty well and has a good sense of impact and physicality, whether you're blocking a strike with your shield or kicking an enemy. The RPG elements, which let you use magic and stealth as well, and environmental weapons (wall spikes, fires, flimsy wooden supports that can be broken to topple barrels and crates on enemies etc.) allow for different approaches to each battle. The platforming is also decent.
The game isn't perfect of course. Some sections of the game don't cater well to a specific build, boss fights are dull and in some cases (usually when they fly) annoying, and some of the enemy types aren't nearly as fun to fight as others. There have also been complaints about the plot, characters and voice acting, but I wasn't bothered by them.
Basically, if you're looking for good first person sword fighting and physics in a fantasy setting then Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is the game for you.

Keep in mind that I have limited experience when it comes to this game (played in the beta only), but I have been a long time moba player, so here goes nothing!
Strife is a solid entry level moba. Many of the characters are relatively simple, and nothing about it is overly complex. It manages to strip down a lot of the more confusing elements that other mobas have in an environment that feels fun. That being said, if you are looking for a replacement to LoL or DotA 2 then you will be disappointed. Towers rain powerful cannonballs down on you and essentially stop all forms of early to mid game tower diving, and their system that could best be compared to a runes/masteries system is combined with the shop all in a theoretical pay2win model. Granted, you could get past this model by simply playing tons of games in order to max out the items in game so your character will always win due to having the best items possible, but this just makes the game too unbalanced in my opinion. Games literally get decided by how smart you, your teammates, and the enemy are with upgrading items in the shop outside of actually playing the game.
Pro's:
Pretty graphics/world
Easy to get in to
Interesting item shop, while still being intuitive
Character variety (decent for a new game)
Short queue times (atleast in lower level play)
unique pets that allow for different tactics
Everyone gets a courier
Con's:
Theoretical pay2win model
Towers are either way too strong or characters by comparison are way too weak
Most games tend to go way into the late game, so don't expect fast wins
Conclusion:
Overall, I'd suggest this to people looking to get into moba's as this game is relatively easy to get in to and has a cool story/campaign mode to teach you almost everything that you need to know. I wouldn't suggest this for more veteran moba players as the game really feels too simple. If these issues have gotten or get fixed, then the game will actually be way better than what I saw in the beta.

TO ANYONE NEW WHO IS INTERESTED IN PLAYING PS2:
I've been playing for some time so I'll give you  a quick rundown.
(TL;DR at bottom)
Planetside 2 is an mmofps where three factions are at a constant conflict with eachother. The game features battles on an incredibly large scale and the battlefield is super dynamic. The main objective is to attack and defend numerous bases on the map to increase the chance of victory for your faction. The battlefield is always changing and communication is important. There are both ground vehicles and air vehicles, countless weapons to choose from (though you may have to work for some) and a large variety of appearance changes through micro-transactions.
The game itself has been around since 2012 but has aged beautifully. I'm a standing veteran of PlanetSide 1 and although I miss some aspects the first had that the second hasn't offered, this still doesn't change my opinion on the game.
The Factions:
Terran Republic(TR) are pretty much space commies as far as politics but are my preferred faction to play. Their colors are Red and Black
New Conglomerate(NC) are more like Freedom Fighters who scream Guerrilla Warfare. Their colors are Blue and Yellow
Vanu Sovereignty(VS) are the religious nutbags who prefer alien tech rather then human tech. They have laser guns and stuff and love to wear spandex. Their colors are Purple and Black.

Neat F2P Sci-Fi MMO FPS.
Original PlanetSide came out in 2003 and it was the first Sci-Fi MMO FPS (but not the first MMO FPS ever - that honour belongs to WW2 Online), inspired by such visionary titles like Starsiege: Tribes from 1998 which introduced large, open maps to Sci-Fi shooters, but adding novelities like vehicles, fractions with different equipment and a persistent online environment. It lasted pretty long too, that is until 2016 when the master server was eventually shut down.
PlanetSide 2, being the sequel, continues where the originator left, keeping the same core gameplay but adding new things. The visuals in the game might not be cutting-edge for modern standards anymore but they still hold up just fine and the art direction is fine too. Gameplay-wise, think of a really large Sci-Fi Battlefield with a few unique touches. Being a MMO, the outcome of battles will be determined regardless of your involvement, that is, whether you are playing or not.
The game's player base still is healthy and I recommend this title to everyone who is looking for a large-scale, persistent battle Sci-Fi combined arms shooter. Do make sure you meet the system requirements though, the game is not recommended to those with slow CPUs, low amounts of RAM and integrated graphics.

Like most folks who review Boundless, this recommendation comes with caveats:
I've never posted a review before, and I've put this off until now because, honestly, until update 112, I couldn't defend or justify a recommendation. This is not to say I wouldn't have recommended it before, just that it wouldn't have really helped anyone.
I've been "playing" Boundless for over a year. I started back when it was Oort Online and first released to Steam. From the beginning I saw the potential and fell in love with the "vision", rough as it was. I went to the dev sites and read their plans. I understood that they released it not so much as an "early access game" but rather as a means to support a really cool vision of a game... and I hoped I was right, that it would come to fruition. I have not been disappointed in my investment.
I believe the developers are taking the time to do this right. This isn't your typical "early access, get a deal on an almost ready game (Beta)". This was released to Steam when it was merely a prototype and a dream. It is now pre-alpha, and is starting to take shape.
The developers have steadily put out updates, and the team is continuing to grow. The game is steadily coalescing.
It is currently a beautiful building sandbox, with a few creatures, a spiffy inventory system, some crafting, one playable race (in first and third person) and lots of potential. I currently rarely see another player (except on the forums).
Basically, I'm saying "Yes, I paid a lot. Yes, it is really early and there isn't a ton of stuff to do yet... but I keep coming back to it. It is gorgeous. I've spent HOURS building. I LOVE the community and its quirky "spirit" and am anticipating EVERY "next update" to see what it holds. This in itself is an adventure, and I consider it well worth what I paid. If you'd like to experience the same, welcome aboard!"
But this isn't really a recommendation for a game is it? It is a recommendation for a community and an experience.
If you want to skip to the end... you live for PVP or PVE, want to experience an active RPG MMO, you'll probably be disappointed right now.

While this does provide tools for overclocking and tweaking your graphics card and monitor settings there are 2 reasons I cannot recommed this program.  Firstly the steam achievements encourage you to overclock your hardware to reach certain points to unlock achievements rather than encouraging safe overclocking practices. Secondly while using the tools to test overclocks on my monitor I discovered each time I tested an overclock setting Precision X was writing a new resolution profile into my monitor drivers with no way of removing it. *** PRE-ALPHA REVIEW ***
I'll admit, I first saw Boundless advertised as a new PS4 title, coming in 2016!  I immediately started looking to see what the current price of PS4's was... to my surprise, I found out that the game was in pre-alpha on PC... now, I normally steer relatively clear of early access stuff (even those that I've backed on Kickstarter)... but something about the look, feel and potential of Boundless made me want to buy it.
I'd played minecraft fairly extensively on and off for about 2 years, so I was expecting a game that at least met that calibre of enjoyment and content.  At first, I'll be honest, I was a little disappointed - maybe I was expecting the game to look like the demo video - but then I started getting lost in how visually brilliant it looks, even at this stage of development.  It's not minecraft... it may have gotten it's bare roots from minecraft, but Boundless has certainly evolved beyond that concept and started to carve a new path to become its own game, surrounded by its own lore and a very much involved community with which the developers interact constantly.
I was suitably impressed as the depth of field and the level of detail and other such graphical and gameplay differences that set this upcoming title apart. Yes, it does currently lack content, but you need to remember, this is a pre-alpha title... which now has the backing of Sony to also become a PS4 title in 2016, so development has been ramped up if anything.
If you're looking for a title that is ready to play, won't crash, and has a whole bunch of great content, you should probably steer clear for a little while (but add it to your wish list for later!), however, if you like being involved in an active, friendly community of both gamers and developers, where your comments will be taken on-board, coupled with playing a sandbox game that is taking shape around you and each update is a discovery of new and interesting things, you may want to take a look and see what it's all about... I'm glad I took the plunge, as I can't wait to see what the next update brings!

Features an interesting fluid simulation with a few proper ways to test it out, very low system requirements, runs smooth, and is difficult to even deliberately cause performance loss. Arcane Worlds is a unique indie game. It is basically a sandbox for you to mess around in, and it is quite a good sandbox. You have a variety of spells, ranging from waterfalls and volcanos to placing turrets and buildings. There is a mode where you need to collect resources to craft spells, but I have not tried it.
- This game has charming but fairly simplistic graphics. They are very beautiful and make for some epic screenshots. The flow of water and lava is mesmerising and the enemy design is fascinating. The visuals of Arcane Worlds are splendid and pleasing.
- The audio in this game is fairly basic. You have sounds for shooting your spells and enemies make noises. A fairly generic-sounding battle music plays when you engage in a fight with hostile creatures. The sound design isn't particularly good.
- Arcane Worlds doesn't feature much in terms of any meaningful gameplay. There are enemies you can kill which drop mana, which can be collected by special gatherers that float above a castle. There really is no point yet for mana gathering. However, the sandbox gameplay is really quite spectacular. The whole world can be deformed and sculpted, and this game also features impressive fluid physics. Carving out valleys and shooting a water source spell, and watching the water pour out and flow through the valley and eventually fill up, it something really special. I love good fluid physics and this game truly delivers. You can even make volcanoes pop up out of the ground anywhere you wish, and then they spew out lava and it's just magnificent.
- N/a
- This game runs fairly well and has adequate graphical settings. However, creating mass amounts of volcanoes at once severely decreases the FPS, but this isn't really an issue (unless you like to spam volcanoes everywhere!).
Arcane Worlds is a great little game that will give you hours of fun with the world-deforming spells. While lacking in gameplay, the sandbox kept me entertained for over 13 hours.
If you're looking for a fun sandbox reminiscent of Magic Carpet, then I highly suggest Arcane Worlds.

Okay, as much as I REALLY want to say that I hate the updates since I started playing years ago... it... works.
I actually find myself falling in love with it again.
Then...
I actually bought the lifetime premium.
I even used up the remaining cash on my FreeJam account to buy 24 crates for $10.
Now, of course this likely ruins my credibility completely, but perhaps having this perspective may help you decide whether to actually play this game as both a free-to-play, and to play via purchase.
So, let me begin...
==FREE-TO-PLAY==
So, you decide that you want to try this game out. You may also be someone who is unwilling, or is unable to spend real money on this game. What sort of milage can you get out of this game? In reality? It -really- depends. For one, your crates from doing matches will store half as much than a Premium player's would. You will also be severely handicapped when recycling parts you don't need, since, instead of getting 2/3ds of the block's price back in dust, you'll be getting about 1/6th's. As a result, it's barely feasible to use the recycling feature.
However...
Regardless of your level, if you can design (or, if you can take screenshots of a design on the Factory, reverse-engineer), a solid design... you will -easily- win dozens of blocks relatively quickly. If you play ranked, you will get at LEAST one Protonium crate per match if you win - you can get two if you also level up; every time you level up, you'll get a Protonium crate. Protonium crates are the best ones you can get, and they have a nearly guaranteed chance of at least two rare blocks in it, and, often, one epic. Roughly one in ten will have a Legendary block, which includes things like the Ion Distorter shotgun, and the Chain Shredder minigun, as well as the massive-scale mobility blocks like wheels and legs. The Legendary blocks, if you intend to not use them, have a very high recycling value.
Even if you don't get Legendary blocks, sometimes it's best to go with Epic or even Rare; Legendary blocks are often massive and have very high CPU requirements; often it's better to have a few Rare blocks to do the work of one Legendary weapon, since they are much smaller. As a great example, the absolutely terrifying Aeroflak anti-air weapons are huge weapons to start, but my main bot uses four Rare Aeroflaks, since two two Epics are too physically large to be practical.
As a side note, the Aeroflaks, in fact, only come in Rare and Epic qualities, meaning that they are easier to get than would otherwise be the case. This means that you can easily obtain the means to counter some of the most challenging opponents you'll face.
So, the ultimate question is, is this game playable as a free-to-play game? Yes. Is it pay-to-win? Not...exactly. Like a lot of games, Robocraft offers the means to speed up progression, but, ultimately, if you stick with it, you'll reach a point where you'll be able to get all the parts you need quite easily, by simply winning repeatedly. It doesn't hurt to ask for help from people who know a thing or two about bot design, or to buy a decent one off the Factory.
As a final, and a VERY important note: You can upload your designs onto the Factory. Any bot you upload, and gets purchased by another player, gives you 25% percent of the bot's value back to you. This amount stacks, so if your 100,000 dust bot gets purchased 10 times, you get 250,000 back! It's the best way to make up dust as a free player. Best of all - it's free to do so! At least... for now.
==PREMIUM PLAYER==
Okay, so you're wanting to actually pay for this game; you want to support the developers, or you want to get an edge on other players. Or, you're someone like me who LOVES to build things, and wants to be able to make up the parts quickly and easily, and to have the flexibility to get what you want.
If you want to spend money on this game, the biggest and most important upgrade you can do, is to buy the Lifetime premium. If you can't afford the Lifetime option, save up; even if you spend $5.00 for a few days of premium, that's $5.00 that could go toward permanently locking your account into Premium mode.
Premium is a very useful addition to your account; not only do you get to keep everything that drops from a crate (which means you get twice as much), but you get a 3x multiplier when recycling blocks (hence the aforementioned 2/3rds number). Between those two features, you'll have more than enough block income to be able to design what you want.
Though you can buy Protonium crates in the shop, do you really need to? My answer is, -maybe-? Considering how often I win Protonium crates (and, less often, Gold and Silver), it gives little advantage. I only did it because I had the cash sitting around from when they converted GC to real cash in my FreeJam account, and, though the parts I got were relatively useful, ultimately, I could have easily earned it from Battle Arena or League matches.
==FINAL VERDICT==
So, is this game worth the money? I would have to say, yes. Is this game worth playing as a free player? That is a tricky question to answer. If you have friends already playing this, and can give you a boost by buying a design of yours off of the Robot Factory, then definitely. It may even be worth grinding your way up with friends. If you're playing this on your own, though... it really depends on how much of a fan you are of building things, and how good of a designer you are. Your milage may vary.
If you're willing to pay for the lifetime Premium, though... it could either give you the flexibility you need to do what you want. Or, it may make the game TOO easy, and make you bored.
Ultimately, I hesitantly recommend this game. It's worth the download to -try-. But go in knowing that it's a game that is truly amazing when it works, but very aggrivating when it doesn't. I'm only leaving my rating negative, because I still believe it's too hard for new players. If they gave 15 days premium to new players, that would be fair in my eyes.

Oh boy...where do I start.
A few years ago, I was playing this game during early beta, and I absolutely loved it. It had a charm in its ability to bring people together with their creations, and throw them into head-to-head matches. Though it had its flaws, it was a very solid game.
I recently came back at the recommendation of a friend. I'm torn. On the one hand, the game play has become far more solid (though they got rid of megabots...shame!). On the other... what the hell?! This game is officially inaccessable to new players. Existing players (ESPECIALLY those such as myself after the crates system launched) have a MASSIVE advantage over new ones, for one reason, and one reason alone: The only way you can get blocks now, is by random drop. Those who already owned dozens of these blocks, get to keep them. This basically requires new players to buy blocks with real money, and that is a disgrade of epic proportions. Even as an experienced player, I had to melt dozens of blocks in order to get some of the Legendary blocks, which is a sacrifice that I'm wasn't sure if it was the right thing to do. Luckily, it worked out, but it hamstrung me for making alternative designs.
So, as an existing player, will I want to play this? Sure, on occasion. Do I recommend that new players pick this up? ABSOLUTELY NOT. Freejam has gone the way of OVERKILL Software, and has wanted to milk this game for all its worth. Don't let them. I plan to not spend another dime on this game again.
I will add a caveat, however; if you DO want to spend real money on this game, the prices I find are fairly reasonable; one, there is a lifetime premium option, that costs about the price between a B and a AAA game. As well, the crate prices are also fairly reasonable, considering what you get from them. And, finally, if you have Premium, the drop rates are decent - but only if you do well. But that's all I'll give them.

Short and sweet, it's Sega's spin on Mario Kart with their own intellectual properties. They take the tack of going through their whole game history through, from Golden Axe through Burning Rangers to Jet Set Radio the usual Sonic crew. The visuals are as crisp and clean as is expected from any modern Sonic game.
Some tracks fit better than others for the theme (really, what can you do with Golden Axe?) but the game is fun to play. There are the usual grand prix, time attack and battle modes as well as a smattering of others: Destroying a tank in Pursuit, drifting in designated zones in Drift, flying through rings in a Ring course, et cetera. While an enjoyable distraction, they all play second fiddle to the racing. The balance of items seems slightly off (the All-Star item is a monster) but strong racing usually wins the day and the AI driving does not appear to rubber-band aside from item frequency.
Overall, a solid title for Mario Karters and Sega fans in general.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a real gem of a game. This has been said many times before, but it really is nice to see the return of several old-school shooter characteristics. Dual-wielding guns, hunting for secrets, finding armor and health packs, planning routes around levels with a map instead of walking down continuous hallways broken up by firefights. I'd forgotten how fun these kinds of games can be.
A lot of games also tout a play-your-way format while having one thing in mind and punishing you for doing something different. TNO could have fallen into this trap and offered an action shooter with stealth elements reluctantly included, but the aforementioned open maps lend themselves for run-and-gun or stealth play. I appreciate this for the replay value alone.
In terms of shooting, you can't go wrong with this title. There is a nice selection of weapons, and upgrades along with skills add further options. Gunplay feels visceral, further compounded by large amounts of actual viscera. In the end, that's all this game had to do to accomplish its goal, and it does this well. Add in the future elements, and we're really in business now.

I first heard about this game from the James Recommends series by YouTube channel Extra Credits (which I will link to at the end of this reivew). The James Recommends video mentioned The Talos Principle to be "Portal's philosophical brother" and I can definitely say that such holds true. As you play through the game and read the various logs you find through terminals (mind you, there is a lot of reading that'll go through those), you will find a lot of different texts that will make you think quite a bit.
While the achievements for it might look like they require multiple playthroughs in order to get them, it is much easier than you think thanks to the ability to revert to a previous save that the game automatically saves for you. If it weren't for that, I probably wouldn't have gotten all the achievements in the game like I did.
All in all, I highly recommend this game if you'd like to enjoy a puzzle game that includes Philosophical aspects that make you think more about humanity and what we consider it to be.

I am giving this one a thumbs up since it is well done and succeeds at doing what it attempts to, but would probably not recommend it to most people.
I normally enjoy challenging games (loved Super Meat Boy, Cuphead, Dark Souls, etc); dying, learning what you did wrong, and then improving & eventually overcoming an obstacle really gives a sense of accomplishment.  The first 55-60% or so (judging from my completion %) gave me this feeling, but ultimately turned into more of a test of patience than I am willing to put up with. The game really isn’t about learning patterns and overcoming obstacles, but rather precision jump after precision jump and just grinding through it until you finally get that perfect run.  There are plenty of levels and bonus content, but there honestly isn’t much variety and all comes down to landing jumps with no margin of error, often in quick succession.
I consider myself to be above average at this type of game, but am starting to lose interest as the final 40% seems more like a grind rather than a fun challenge to overcome.  If you enjoy grinding through levels and/or have top tier mechanics at games like this, then absolutely play this one.  There is a ton of content and plenty of secrets/different paths to discover.  If you’re in the same boat as me then expect a fun game similar to Super Meat Boy for about five hours before it becomes too much.  Otherwise I would skip this one!

I just realized I haven't written a review for this game when I finished it.
It has been over a year, but every time The Talos Principle comes to my mind, I feel a deep warm feeling and the emotions this game gave me come back to me. Let me tell you, this game is something you will remember forever. It's not just an incredibly clever puzzle solver, this one comes with a beautiful and mature story which is delivered slowly and patiently, peace by peace. Design of the worlds accompanied with their soundtracks is just mesmerizing, the whole thing truly is a divine garden. Oftentimes, I could not help it but just had to stop and look all around me and enjoy the look and the peaceful music, or let the occasional phylosophical parts sink in. The story does not come with a twist, or a punchline. You will suspect what is it all about soon from the beginning, but that does not matter at all. The way this game delivers all it has to offer is what makes it perfect.
If something or someone tempts you to not buy The Talos Principle, be wise, do not let yourself be mislead by doubt, for it will bring end to the most enjoyable experience that awaits you. Let the feels enter you, let Elohim guide you through his garden. Seriously, whoever is reading this and considering purchase... I envy you. I wish I could erase the game from my mind and experience it again. I definitely will play it again some day, but it won't be as touching as for the first time.

At first the crafting system was tricky to understand however after a little experimenting I started to understand it. I can see how the discovery system will work and it is pretty cool. I still consulted websites for the more complex items, and I wanted to see what as all possible currently.
I started by building a house the most basic thing. I quickly discovered that it takes fair bit of work to build yourself a 8x8x5 cube to hide in. Initial reaction to this was this seems a bit grindy, but then again that based on the perspective of minecraft. MMO's usually do take a little more work than a multiplayer game. In hindsight I had a house about 4 hours, and I feel pretty proud of that little cube. I went caving next, and started to learn the ores and fuel system. This was a lot of fun. Getting lost in the caves and finding a way out was a little adventure in and of itself that feels quite rewarding. Something that I noticed hung me up was it is not really clear how to build or get the furnace to work, a small note when you hover over the item that says something like "It takes two pieces to make a furnace and this goes on top" would go a long way to helping a new player. They’re going to build one of them put it down and wonder why it doesn't work.
Next I started constructing the machines. I was able to figure out placing them easily. I like the crafting tree and the way it progresses. I am not a big fan of the time delay component. I can see how it adds to the game but it feels so artificial. I have already done the real work of locating this material and bringing it back to the location to do something with it. Making me wait to get the items just feels excessive, especially when coupled with things breaking so quickly.
I went exploring in the world last night and enjoyed the experience. The terrain was interesting and at times challenging. The area players are spawned felt like a nice little enclave once I got further out. I also found a settlement as I was walking back to my house and it was really exciting to find. There were some impressive builds in it, and I immediately began thinking about moving there. I also ran into a nice player on a quest to find the almighty gold. It was a nice interaction. I like the chat text font.
I am really happy to see how the core loop turned out. It feels like we have a winner.

I played one match, and that's all it takes to hate Strife. Nothing about it is revolutionary, just stitched together from other, better, mobas. The graphics look like they were taken from Disney/Pixar reject dumps, the voices are nauseatingly awful not to mention the actual lines. The characters are so grab bag generic that they may have actually been mary sue'd into creation. Item shop is minimal, crafting is abhorrent (12 elixirs in 60 minutes, on a victory, over 300 for a permanent recipe, you do the math). The tutorials treat you like a seven year old, and the match drags on and on and on. Towers can destroy you in a puny number of hits, and deal true damage (no way to mitigate/reduce it). The action is far from 'non-stop' since most of your time will be spent retreating behind a tower to wait for the absolutely pointless 'out of combat regeneration' or you can slowly channel a recall and then walk all the way back up a lane. The buffed allies (ripped from Smite's siege minions) are made of glass against enemy heroes. None of the heroes are unique, versatile, or powerful in any way at all, period. The battles are not epic, they are prolonged. Allow me to clarify on this, I can play LoL and have a 30 minute match packed with 'epicness' or it can take 3 hours and be equally epic. Or I can play strife for one or more hours and be bored to tears. This moba is crap. Unlocking all heroes means nothing when they all are terribly designed, implemented, and voiced equally across the board. Those that I played with were admittedly not toxic, if only because none of them said anything, and because teamwork was an illusion reserved only for bringing out the 'powerful' minions.

This game is very story centric, kinda in the same vain as the walking dead or life is strange.
Where do I begin here?  You start the game off as Alex, the main character who was invited to a party with her step brother.  Things go arwy and you need to go on and save the day.  Story does have a few twists, but nothing really mindblowing.
Pros
The art direction is great with hand drawn backgrounds with super colorful 3d character models.
The music is minimal, but conveys the mood fine. Voice acting is also superbly done.
Sound effects in the game are very distinct and always inform you on what is going on.
Your actions in game have consquences that affects in game events.  This of course means there is more replyability due to going back to see what you can do differently, and what different outcomes you can get.
Collectibles out there for all of you collectible junkies.
Cons
Pacing is a tad off,  I feel as if the game would have benefited from either fewer areas, or faster movement speed; it just takes a while to move from one place to the next.
While the interactions between the characters are great, the overarching story is a little bland.  At times, I found myself hardpressed to listen to what was going on.
Overall, I would give this game a thumbs up.  Not perfect, but defintely not a bad time.
If you love games like the walking dead and life is strange, I would recommend picking it up.  If you are unsure, pick it up when it's on sale.

With over 1k hours in the game I feel I can give a pretty good review on it. Overall, it's a good game. Very much worth the $0 you have to pay to play it. However, you will need a decent rig if you want to be able to run this properly. There ARE fights where there's hundreds of players fighting at the same time 1v1v1 since there's three factions. It can get Very demanding on your PC.
It's a HUGE grind. By huge, I mean i have 1,027 hours on record by the time of this review. And I haven't come close to unlocking all the upgrades to vehicles and infantry. This game requires you to pick your focus, and then channel all of your Certs (In game currency) towards that specific role. Afterwards, you branch out. So if you want Infantry play, pick your style (Heavy, Medic, Engineer, Light Assault, Recon) and spend your certs only in that role until you are comfortable with it. Then move on to either another infantry role or branch out to a specific vehicle.
NOT MENT TO PLAY SOLO. This is a massive game, with a grander scale of battle than Battlefield or Battlefront will ever offer. While yes, you can lone wolf the game and get moderate success. You will find the true beauty of the game was suppose to be played in a cooperate fashion. Join an Outfit, find a squad, get on Mic, and have fun. Some of my favorite gaming moments have come from Galaxy drops in a full Outfit Platoon with everyone coordinating together. Don't be afraid to reach out to players and make friends. The Main Battle tank is a two man vehicle, and a coordinated team will dominate other tanks who aren't talking to each other.
This is PLAY TO WIN. Not PAY TO WIN. Money isn't going to get you all the kills in this game. However, time already spent in it will. This isn't me saying "Because the dude has played more, he will outplay you more". No, the guy who has logged 1000 hours, will have accumulated more CERTS, and will have spent those Certs on upgrades. This could mean his Main Battle tank has a Reload speed of 2.1 seconds, when your MBT has a reload speed of 3 seconds. This is a huge advantage, not to mention upgraded gunner weapons, specialized main weapon, defensive certs etc etc. A player with more upgrades has a huge advantage over someone who doesn't. If you are new, find a more experienced player and stick with them. Use their vehicles until you can grind out the certs yourself. Lots of players Need and Love a dedicated gunner, become that and learn the ropes.
ZERGING, Oh...my...sweet...merciful god, the zerging. This ruins the game more than anything else. This is when you get outpopulated by the enemy on such a massive scale that there is literally nothing you can ever do about it. You and the other 20 people in base suddenly find yourself the 10% populating in the region. With the enemy sporting 90% dominance. Meaning they have more bodies on point than you have ammo in your gun. There is nothing you can do other than shake your head, pack your backs and go somewhere else. Re-deploying destroys a lot of maneuvering in this game. You will find yourself hopping from one base to the other in the form of self-suicides rather than just grabbing a vehicle and driving there.
Planetside 2 isn't perfect, but it's still a good game. And despite it's flaws, me and my friend have had soo much fun playing it together and trying different things. I very much recommend this game if you have a group of friends you play with that enjoy a good FPS. Even for the solo player you can join an Outfit and partcipate in coordinated strikes. You will find there are quite a few outfits that are quite dedicated.

Abyss Odyssey is a fantasy themed (Chilean mythos presumably), fighting focused side scroller game. There are also some rogue-like elements. Levels are procedurally generated. When you die, you lose your weapon but not your character progress. You gain xp, get powerfull, and try again.
Graphics, sounds and music are solid. Gameplay is a mixture of fighting and brawling games (more fighting games, less brawler games). If you like combo based fighting mechanisms, you may like it. Though except a modest amount of combos. If you get it right (continous combos and attack canceling), you may even love it.
I completed my first run on 3.2 hours in a single branch map (there are three branches), though the game is intented to be played multiple times by design. Hence the gameplay time may be multiplied depending on you.
If you are into this kind of game type, I would recommend it, at least on a sale.

While I only have about 6 hours playing the game as of writing this review, I can definitely say that as a game still in Alpha, it lives up to its hype and that its price is pretty fair.
Players will find themselves in squads of up to nine, fighting off enemy squads from attacking key map objectives, gaining control over enviornmental vantage points, and placing down mobile command centers. Each squad consists of essential roles like riflemen, marksmen, anti-vehicular and suppresive roles. Wolfenstein: The New Order is a real gem of a game. This has been said many times before, but it really is nice to see the return of several old-school shooter characteristics. Dual-wielding guns, hunting for secrets, finding armor and health packs, planning routes around levels with a map instead of walking down continuous hallways broken up by firefights. I'd forgotten how fun these kinds of games can be.
A lot of games also tout a play-your-way format while having one thing in mind and punishing you for doing something different. TNO could have fallen into this trap and offered an action shooter with stealth elements reluctantly included, but the aforementioned open maps lend themselves for run-and-gun or stealth play. I appreciate this for the replay value alone.
In terms of shooting, you can't go wrong with this title. There is a nice selection of weapons, and upgrades along with skills add further options. Gunplay feels visceral, further compounded by large amounts of actual viscera. In the end, that's all this game had to do to accomplish its goal, and it does this well. Add in the future elements, and we're really in business now.

Talos Principle:
Overall an exceptional game. From the creators of Serious Sam comes a first person (or third person over the shoulder) puzzle game.
Pros:
+ Great looking graphics
+ Difficult but still rewarding puzzles
+ Lots of ways to complete a puzzle
+ Different areas have different atmospheres, all the time being tied to the main feel of the game
+ Lots of different things to do at any given time, so getting stuck at a puzzle is not a problem
+ Deep, rich and rewarding story, but still easy to ignore if that is what you like.
+ Lots of hidden items and easter eggs, with some really rewarding hidden areas
+ Lots of references to Serious Sam all through the game although not in plain sight
+ Implements DirectX and Vulkan (although on my GTX 980 the Vulkan did worse in terms of FPS)
+ Main DLC is great
+ Different types of puzzles and mini games makes for a good mix
+ Moral and philosophical questions and dilemmas in story
+ Lots of different in-game achievements and goals apart from the main puzzles
+ Ambiance is good for relaxing puzzle solving
Cons:
- Some puzzles feel unsolvable, this leads to looking on the internet for the answer
- Some of the more advanced graphics settings did not save and kept reverting
- Base price is high if not on sale, for the average complete time
Specs: i5 4690K, GTX 980 4GB, 16 GB RAM, 1080p
I had all the settings maxed out with an average of 72fps (75Hz refresh rate). Vulkan had the FPS lower than DirectX, but with nVidia GPU that makes some sense.
Conclusion:
TL;DR:
Great game, great graphics, optimized well, lots to do, wait for sale.

The Talos Principle Review
"Let this be our covenant.  These worlds are yours and you are free to walk amongst them and subdue them."
And so it ends, but I (the character) have achieved eternal life.  Elohim, in his eternal grace, granted me eternal life.  I have proven myself worthy and conquered the puzzles.  I outsmarted the crafty snake that slithers among the gardens of Elohim.  Though I saw many peers fail and end dishonorably, it was through faith (and a walkthrough) that I solved the mysteries of the gardens.  I saw the work of Elohim, of which it is the work of Elohim to preserve.  His gardens are the physical manifestations of beauty and of his love for his children.  These worlds are yours to roam about freely and to observe the beauty of.  But only you must not enter the great tower of Elohim.
The Talos Principle is more than a puzzle game.  This will differ greatly for everyone who plays it (remember that a third of all the stars from heaven fell).  This was almost a spiritual experience for me.  I love seeing the scenery of this game, probably the most breathtaking areas from any game I've played.  And I don't mean graphically.  As you enter worlds to solve the puzzles you can also walk around and explore the mini hub-worlds.  There is much scenery to be seen (pyramids, ruins, statues, etc).
The puzzles are stupidly hard.  I'm amazed I share this planet with people who are brilliant enough to even construct these puzzles.  I can confidantly say I never would beat this game without a walkthrough.  If you're a bucket of bolts like I am, I suggest keeping a walkthough open or nearby as you're playing since you absolutely will need it.  As far as the puzzles themselves, seperate from their complexities, you will be completing tasks that you've probably done in other games.  You will need to activate switches, jam energy gates, leave objects on pressure plates (Zelda?), redirecting laser beams, etc.
In the end, the path is yours to take.  If you doubt Elohim you allow yourself room to be seduced by the snake (or in this case the MSdos Dr. Spaitso command prompt) you will stray from the path that Elohim provided, the path that will grant you eternal life (or in this case it resets the game).  I will conclude this review with a scripture from Matthew 7: 13-14:  "Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few."

I was very pleasantly surprised playing this game. It was just fun to play from start to finish, at about 7 hours. A perfect length with almost no padding or busy-work or anything that distracted from the game.
The artists had a vision, and delivered it graphically, musically, and through the dialogue. The soundtrack was great - right there with Bastion, Fez, FTL, and many other memorable ones.
A really great sci-fi, supernatural, suspenseful, psychological thriller, Basically an episode of The Twilight Zone, Outer Limits, or Black Mirror.

The lack of voiceover I didn't think would bother me; but it does seem really weird.
The HO scenes themselves are Ok, but there are great many objects where you need to 'do something else first.' That's fine, and often makes it more interesting. Here, though, the vast majority seem to be 'click on stuff until something opens or changes in some way.' Since you have absolutely no idea what is interactive, it comes down to random clicking on things. Nothing to do with observation or logic at all.
There are numerous slight errors or outright bugs which gradually add up to irritate. A crowbar is a 'wrecking bar' (maybe that's common usage? I'd never heard the term before). A 'clock' in a HO scene turns out to be a pocket watch. At one point I tried to use a bird I'd collected on a balcony. I was told 'That should be enough oil.' You are told to exploit the fact that an enemy is made of wood, but rather than use the pheonix you have with you, you have to go through a convoluted sequence to set termites on it. There have been loads of these little gripes already, and I've only visited about 1/5 of the scenes.
Oh, and the music? Not only repetative (hardly something new for a cheap HO game) but every so often there is a chime which sounds exactly a doorbell. I actually got up to answer the door twice before I decided to turn the music off.
So; it's a more-or-less passable HO with incredible attention to lack of detail. (I put it that way deliberately.)
I got it in a sale, and for a few pounds, it will probably be worth it if I can put up with the errors. If.
Edit: I couldn't. I got only a few scenes from the end, and suddenly nothing showed up on the map as 'to do'. Using a hint just brought up the map. Totally broken. I certainly won't be trying again. Total waste of 4 hours, all told. (Which I suppose is why I got it, but it was at least supposed to be a mostly enjoyable 4 hours.)

Oxenfree has many things to like and some things to dislike:
The story is mediocre BUT the execution is so good you will not really care about how the plot plays out.
The artstyle is beautiful and the pictures taken throughout by characters are very well made.
The soundtrack is used intelligently by the Devs for dramatic effect and is a nice calm flow while you explore Edwards Island however from what I have heard in game I am not sure that it would be worth buying seperatly.
Where Oxenfree truly shines, however, is in it's voice-acting and witty dialogue. If you don't like to listen to about 4 and a half hours (one run depending on speed and collectible hunting) of dialogue no matter how well written, the game is not for you as it's characters are truly what makes it worth it.
With it's various ups come its downs:
As the quote above shows, it is basically just a walking story with some interaction, however your interactions DO matter and the game features multiple endings.
When you are just walking and the characters are not talking the game feels very very empty.
There is a collectible or two in every section of the map (one called an anomaly marked by a pile of rocks
) and trekking back and forth to these spots outside of completing the story can be a bore due to the lack of character interaction.
The radio is a gimmick and during the story is well executed
however when using it to
tune into anomalies it just feels unescessary.
Overall if you enjoy character-heavy stories and aren't too bothered for actual "gameplay" then this is most definetly a must buy, however, if you are just interested in a fun experience then I would also recommend you play Oxenfree.
This game can be reacted to very differently by different people but in my personal oppinion Oxenfree is worthy of a 9 out of 10, it only misses one as it can be quite frustrating to trek across the island looking for anomalies

The latest big update included a much improved user experience, player models, expanded crafting, tool models, lighting fixes, expanded weather, etc. The game was already very beautiful and has only become more so.
With the recent announcement of support by Sony to make Boundless a PC and Playstation-only game, I'm excited to see where this team takes the game.

The game is still in development, so there isn’t much to do YET aside from build and explore which won’t amuse everyone.  Keeping that in mind, it's completely playable as it is. So far the building mechanics work great and everything is pretty much bug free. I have built a few biggish things now and haven’t run into any issues. The crafting interface is still somewhat new, so the system isn’t as smooth as it could be yet but it is coming along nicely and is still completely functional.
Variety -  There are some pretty incredible landscapes and everything is varied between worlds, from the color of the grass to the shape of the mountains. So if you ever wanted a glowing wizard tower on top of a giant spiral mountain with purple grass… well there’s probably already a perfect place for that. Everything is so damn pretty!
Updates - I have seen people complain about their frequency or speed but I don’t get it, I have been satisfied with the progress. Textures and lighting have been reworked, character models and creatures have been introduced, new tools and tweaks to building mechanics, a UI overhaul, and probably a lot more that I forgot. So while survival aspects and epic battles might be awhile, they have been creating a pretty solid foundation for everything in the meantime. Also - considering some of the recent announcements it appears things will only speed up from here.
Price - It is more than most EA games, but as the devs explained - “A higher price point attracts people who *really* want to try the game and participate in the development/community.”  This is probably a key reason the community has been so great, the cost itself is a deterrent for the undesireables. Even those that are waiting for more content to play are constantly giving feedback, sharing ideas, and helping shape the game. The forum is flooded with constructive suggestions rather than complaints coming from people who just bought an unfinished game because it was cheap, so good ideas might actually be heard!
I highly recommend this game, but only to a certain crowd (in its current state). If you just want to “buy a game” and aren’t interested in supporting development then you probably shouldn’t buy anything early access, but this one might still be worth checking out if you’re a builder.

It's been over a year since my first review and a lot has changed since then, so here's an update.
The graphics are beautiful even on the lower settings, and have been optimized to run fairly well. The game consists of exploring, mining, building, crafting, and trading so far, but there's a lot more to come. The player community is very welcoming and helpful, and the devs are very active with the community. It's a great game already and it's only in early access!
So here's what's been added since my initial review:
This is the biggest change in my opinion. Players can now craft their own portals to other planets. There are 12 planets total, with unique landscapes and creatures and varying difficulty levels. From each planet you can harvest different colors and types of blocks for building and resources for crafting. Once you've left the safety of the "Sanctum,"  you are free to explore those planets through the use of portals.
Players trade items with each other using the gold earned from leveling up. This combined with the addition of portals has really encouraged players to gather together and create settlements. Huge community builds are popping up, like Pixel Gate, Dragon's Watch, and Therka Market, which are not only massive and gorgeous, but also a great place to trade with other players to get resources from worlds you haven't visited yet.
Players can now protect their builds with beacons, and store items in their builds so that they can't be stolen. As a result, griefing has become nearly non-existant. Beacons also protect builds from world regeneration, a helpful mechanic that replenishes the resources on a planet. Beacon permissions allow multiple players to work on a build at the same time, making community builds possible and encouraging settlements. The settlement with the highest prestige rating becomes the planet's capital.
Machines allow for refining materials and more advanced crafting. More tools have been added as well, such as the chisel for building different shaped blocks, the slingbow for ranged combat, and the spanner for repairing machines.
With the addition of skills, players can improve their character's abilities to fit a role like miner, crafter, or hunter. The roles are not pre-determined, giving players the freedom to design their own roles.
Some things that are still to come are guilds, titans for boss raids, and more playable races and character customization. The devs are very active on the forums, constantly posting their progress and responding to feedback from the community. I have no reason to doubt that they will follow through on their promises and make a great, finished game.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a real gem of a game. This has been said many times before, but it really is nice to see the return of several old-school shooter characteristics. Dual-wielding guns, hunting for secrets, finding armor and health packs, planning routes around levels with a map instead of walking down continuous hallways broken up by firefights. I'd forgotten how fun these kinds of games can be.
A lot of games also tout a play-your-way format while having one thing in mind and punishing you for doing something different. TNO could have fallen into this trap and offered an action shooter with stealth elements reluctantly included, but the aforementioned open maps lend themselves for run-and-gun or stealth play. I appreciate this for the replay value alone.
In terms of shooting, you can't go wrong with this title. There is a nice selection of weapons, and upgrades along with skills add further options. Gunplay feels visceral, further compounded by large amounts of actual viscera. In the end, that's all this game had to do to accomplish its goal, and it does this well. Add in the future elements, and we're really in business now.

Wallpaper Engine also pauses when you go fullscreen on anything like webpage or a game (you can disable it if you wish).
Overall this is THE BEST software I have ever used on a computer. I'd HIGHLY recommend you pick it up right now! It's only $4 and the price will be raised (according to developer) once it leaves early access so hurry and buy it ASAP!

Moderate-length puzzle game that has a very Solomon's Key aesthetic to it except instead of Solomon you are a goat and have a mouse friend who occasionally sports a fancy hat that gives you magical powers.
Theres a number of different mechanics at play and the initial difficulty curve is gentle to introduce them, usually peaking toward the final room(s) in each area. Few puzzles rely on sheer timing, although many utilise automation as a timer or to flow you along. Certain elements of this can be confusing to begin with as its never especially clear what is going to affect what so it can be a little disheartening to need to learn through failure constantly.
I dont consider myself any sort of don regarding puzzle games, however I felt Escape Goat was a touch short. Most early rooms feel little more than filler -- the gentle difficulty I mentioned before -- and it is not until the final area does the game really make you stop and consider your actions. I cant accurately gauge whether I felt enjoyment more from solving the puzzles or simply going through the motions in order to progress.
That said, the post-game is where anyone who enjoys cracking toughies may find the most enjoyment. They kick the difficulty up to eleven, throw you on your knees and tell you to get to work. Theres also a level editor should you wish to exact such punishment upon others yourself.
All this with charming graphics for under a fiver? Its hard to deny.
