Oh, where to begin with this? I think I'll begin with what I believe the purpose of this software to be. EVGA marketed their proprietary PrecisionX 16 software as a means to overclock the GTX 1000 series of GPUs (something I never looked into until long after I installed it). That said, I have a 980 Ti in my personal system and the problems I've had with this software have been infuriating. Being an EVGA card, one would think that its very own software would be perfectly capable of taking the card further than any other third party OC utility, but to my dismay that was never the case. After starting up PrecisionX for the first time I tried setting the core at 1500 MHz, something that I was perfectly able to do on MSI Afterburner. Not so; In fact, after playing around  with the sliders for nearly 30 minutes I gave up. I wasn't even able to overclock the card ONE MEGAHERTZ above the factory clock. So clearly my configuration isn't optimal for this software. That, or there's a bug in the code that makes it incompatible with Maxwell series cards. I certainly wasn't using the software incorrectly or in a manner inconsistent with its advertising.
In summary, my experience with PrecisionX 16 has been infuriating and dismal. The only two positive remarks I can possibly formulate are that, first, you can customize your fan profile to your heart's content. Secondly, since the software never technically shuts off you're able to boost your gameplay time. Yes, Steam regards this as a game. I think that terminology was used more loosely than "halftime performance" at a football game. Thanks to PrecisionX I now have 60 extra hours to my name.
I couldn't take myself seriously by saying that I recommend this software. Maybe I'll change my tune when (if) the GTX 1080 Ti finds itself in my poorly manicured hands. But until then, back to Afterburner I go.

While Arcane Worlds makes for a decent proof of concept, it makes for a bad investment considering the infrequent updates. The last update was in March, which is semi-recent, but there were many months lapse between the previous update.
Arcane Worlds is a spiratul successor to Magic Carpet - it has the base mechanics of flight, mana gathering, castle building combat, and portal usage, but not too much else. After I finished the tutorial of the first world, I moved on to the second world which had enemies that I couldn't kill quick enough due ot a lack of mana with my fireball. I had to wait for the mana to recharge so I could finally build a castle to then collect dropped mana from birds I could kill. Of course, attacking the birds made a HUGE swarm of birds attack me, follow me across the entire map and kill me at least twice. They aren't hard to kill, but you have a slow-ish fireball that can be fired about 2 shots per second and takes up mana. You can't just pick up mana, but must have your....bear friends pick up mana by casting a claim mana spell on drops. Basically, I'd kill a dozen birds, try to survive and clumsily restore mana, then turn around and repeat at least 5 times. I didn't feel any satisfaction from the combat (since the monsters still wouldn't die after plenty of hits which are tough to land) and the map didn't appear to have any pick ups to advance. The game felt clearly unfinished and I lost all interest.
After reading reviews, updates, and comments, I get the impression that the developer sees this project as a "side hustle" - another way to earn some cash. This doesn't appear to be some primary project that is worked on a regular basis, and instead a way to get money and MAYBE be encouraged to actually work on the game regularly. What is worse is that the dev has started another game in early access for purchase while this game is NO WHERE NEAR FINISHED AS EXCLAIMED FROM THE DEV HIMSELF WHEN YOU START A NEW GAME. The icing on the cake is the Patreon page to support the development of their games.
Also, let me give you this excerpt when somebody sakd when the game will be finished:
Basically, a major problem with Early Access is that some devs don't see this as a way to make a solid product, but hope people will support them financially. Valve needs ot find a way to remove that mindset of early access devs.

In 1994, Bullfrog entertainment released Magic Carpet, a game where you flew about on, you guessed it, a magic carpet. The game became a cult classic, but besides the sequel Magic Carpet 2, no similar games were made. 20 years later, developer Ranmantaru games attempts to fill that void with a spiritual successor called Arcane Worlds.
As of now, only the framework of Arcane Worlds is done. Its only game mode throws you into a world with a small tutorial, where the basics of collecting mana and creating spells are explained. You then discover a portal, by which you can travel to other randomly generated planets. During these visits you collect treasures that serve as ingredients for creating new spells, that range from a simple lightning bolt to the ability to create an erupting volcano.
Having never played the original Magic Carpet, I had no real reference point, which means that I can’t compare it to the Bullfrog classic. What I can tell you however, is that the controls feel tight and responsive. Flying around is a breeze and more importantly, fun. Playing around with the various spells, slaying monsters and terraforming as you please, is also very entertaining. But after an hour or so you stumble upon the real problem of Arcane Worlds: that this entertainment doesn’t last forever.
After exploring a couple of planets, you’ve seen everything that Arcane Worlds currently offers. Shooting fireballs at flocks of birds becomes stale surprisingly quickly, and the terraforming is too rough around the edges to be fully enjoyed. The fact that the developer has put the development of the game on hold in favour of other projects, doesn’t help its case.
But then again, I’m not the target audience of Arcane Worlds. This project isn’t meant for people who weren’t even born when the original came out: it’s a love letter of one devoted fan, aimed at other, similarly dedicated fans of Magic Carpet. As of right now, I can only recommend Arcane Worlds to gamers who want to support the development of a HD version of Magic Carpet.  Otherwise, I’d recommend waiting until full release.

"Kicking Simulator"
I really dont know, what I should think about that game and I really dont know, what I should write about it.
Based on the Source Engine and Half Life 2, the Game places you into a medival fantasy setting, somehow based on the universe of Heroes of Might and Magic.
The story (if we can call this "something" a story) is a classic "slumbering evil is about to get awaken. Player is a unknown noname who will face incredible odds and become a true hero with hidden destiny. I think this is, how IGN would describe this game.
But well, lets talk about the story (maybe spoilers!):
You are some student of a wizard, discover an artifact, get a mission to hinder the dark forces from unleashing a great evil. Then, after a short intro session (which is quite a nice tutorial), you will get a mysterious female companion, who is bound to you and is only speaking in your head.
This is, where the game gets strange, somehow interesting, and crazy and throws tons of klischees at you.
Shortly after you are in the middle of a necro army, a cult that will fight evil with evil, your hidden destiny (which is totally silly) and a (total stupid) choice between two sides.
The game even have some decisions, you can make and has "4" endings. (kinda)
But dont expect a deep story. If the game were a parody of fantasy plots it would be a 20/10. Maybe it is a parody and I got it wrong. But the whole storyline throws so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t at you, that you go through 3 phases.
First you are enjoying it.
Then it annoys you.
At last you encountered so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, that it starts to be a real fun (like: At this point I will just lean back and smile).
The whole story has one good part, which is also its greatest flaw:
The two female characters. One a voice talking in your head, the other a young mage, not talking in your head, but is annoying, useless and always in your way. Because of the major plot around these two characters, the whole story seems to be a big funny stupid fanservice. Both characters seems to fight each other to get you, even if they will never meet in the whole game. Both are making you compliments, trying to get your attention and in the end, trying to get you to kill the other one.
While the the mage is an annoying little girl, the voice in your head is a well written, awesome voiced character, who is maybe the strongest and most enjoyable element of the game. While I hated every single second hearing the mage girl talking, I enjoyed every second of the other character, laughed about her dark jokes and couldnt do anything but liking her, even if she is "the evil one".
Within the game, you have the choice to rescue the mage, after she is captured and nearly fed to giant spiders, after that, she tries to get you cleaned from the voice in your head.
I rescued the mage and then tried both decisions...man, I never felt so guilty after killing the voice. It was (given the age of the game) one of the most touching scenes outside of a cutscene in a game.
Even after loading my game, I still felt guilty.
Well, in the end, siding with the woman in your head, you WILL have to face and kill the mage. It is not even a bossfight. It is a stupid girl, who is mad at you, and wont stand down, until you kill her.
Maybe the game want to teach you a lesson of life decisions and their consequences, I dont know.
The combat system is somewhat awesome and frustrating. You can block, do different strike attacks, sneak, use bow and magic. But the main part is your enviroment. Every object, you can move, you can use as a weapon. Pick it up, use telekenesis, kick it...you can do so many things, to make your environment your weapon. If you ever felt like it is a good idea to end a mountain fight by kicking your enemy of the cliff, this is your game.
But after enjoying your big playground for a few minutes, it will get really annoying after the first hour. Throwing objects will get boring, and a fight at the docks, ending a fight by kicking nearly every enemy into the water, because it is an insta kill, will make you question your life decisions.
Swordfight is unsatisfing because the enemy blocks every non power attack and on his side hits you every time, you lower your own block.
Magic feels even more static than in skyrim and looks over 5 years older than the game already is. Also it simply does no damage.
Ranged comat is flawless, which makes it a flaw. You could play the game with bow only, kicking your enemys out of melee range, camping on top of stairs and feel simply op.
Sneaking and dagger fighting feels somehow useless, because you have to put way to many skillpoints into it, but still after the first kill the survivors will start attacking you, even when they couldnt see you. Walking in sneak mode is one of the slowest movements I ever encountered in any game.
But my favourite were the bossfights. First looking really good, they mostly will turn into a confusing pseudo cutscene, where you senseless attacking the monster, until one of your followers tells you, what you really have to do.
Also I really dont get, how you are able to finish the final fight without any ranged attacks.
I really had to push myself to finish this game and Im not really happy about it. It is a game full of great ideas, which could have given the start to an age of medival FPS games, but was so poorly executed, that everyone forgot the game.
In the end, the only thing I remember clearly, is the funny voice of Xana (the voice in your head) and I think it is the best memory I can get from this game.
Last but not least I want to say: Making the mage girl your follower, making her killable and making her a story relevant character, so you will loose the game, if she dies, and then making her stupid as ♥♥♥♥, running into her death...I was terrified how much I enjoyed the moment, shutting her up for good. What a crazy game, making you go down the evil part, because the only good character makes your skin crawl.
(I had a lot of more things I could rant about, but it is irrelevant)

This is one of the biggest disappointments of my gaming career.
I've been a long time fellow of this game (since mid / end 2014) and it was really promising at the start. There have been community votes about the next features and the community was great. After some time that changed. At some point, community votes disappeared and the community filled with cringers. Everything the devs did is "great" and you could not say anything negative without a wall of hate against you.
(Only if you love, kids, hate and cringers ... than it's a good choice)
Even if I can not recommend this game anymore I like to be fair. There was a time (at the very beginning) when I loved this game and spent a lot of time playing it. At the end of 2014, there was a lot of active devs who develop a great game called "Oort Online". It was a game you'd like to play. You could ask the devs in the forum for the next things to happen or about some in-game things. It was an active communication. Also, this game should be released in 2015.
After some time (mid-/end-2015) things changed. The original game "Oort Online" got some invest from Sony (speculative - devs never talked about that in detail) or anybody else and we lost community votes - so the name changed to "Boundless". We, as the players lost all our possibilities to say what we want next, we lost a "free speech" possibility. Things changed and it was okay for most of the players.
Sometimes later (mid 2016) things changed again. The original planned release for 2015 was delayed because of "rebuilds" and other reasons. So the devs stopped responding to questions and everything negative got ignored. I had multiple questions in the original forum where the devs promised to answer and I did not get any answer within a year (this happened often over 2 years).
Sometimes later (end of 2016) things got even worst. The devs still did not have a clue about what to do with the game. I asked sometime about the plans for late game content but I got no answers. They also told me it's "bad" for games if the devs know what they want. (I still can not belive this answer)
More then sometimes later things got delayed even more. 2017 should be the year when Boundless should be released (2 years behind the schedule). It's now the end of 2017 and nothing is released. There are a lot of "promises" and a lot of things not released.
There are only ~35 players online every day (16.12.2017 - source SteamDB) and the devs don't care anymore about player opinions.
Do you like "Minecraft" like games without any RPG / MMO character? Do you like playing alone? Do you like getting ignored when you have good feedback or some ideas about the game? Do you like to press your LMB more than 3 hours without receiving anything? Do you like to wait more than 2 years longer than the original release date for a game to finish?
If you have any questions about Boundless you should at least have look in the forum. If your answer to some of the above questions was "no", you should avoid this game!
It is not worth the time or money. Maybe (and this a huge maybe) I'll give it a try again in some years.

Some people love lemonade, some people gag on it. I wouldn't recommend this game to everyone, but I'm not the target audience for it.
You can probably tell from the vids that the game is pretty, both visually and audibly. The story is interesting too, we're basically in a warlock's dream trying to fight our way to...wake him up or something. The characters are aware of their state of semi-existence. You can find pages from the warlock's journal as random drops to flesh out the story.
The game has shops with new weapons, enemies that drop items, treasure chests that require keys, checkpoints, multiple playable characters with their own quirks, a lot of familiar stuff. You fight your way through map after map, looking for the passage to the lower level until you get to the final floor.
There are just enough attack-moves available to keep combat interesting. You can attack in any direction, even in midair, you can block, parry, dodge, double-jump, grab and throw enemies, etc. There are a few unlockable special moves for each character, like Fireball or Slide Kick, and you can work them into your attacks for cool combos. This is the kind of game I wanted after playing Streets of Rage, a sword and sorcery beat-'em-up.
Here's the thing though, the controls during combat feel unresponsive because there's a delay between the time you press a button and the time the character executes an action. There can also be a delay after the action, so if you swing and miss you're gonna get rekt. It's incredibly frustrating when you know exactly what you want to do, and press the buttons, and your character is like, "Huh? You want me to swing downward onto that guy's head? Ok, hang on, first let me finish this tweet real qui- OW!"
There are these things called Cancel Points, they let you transition from move to move without the delays. To take an example from a guide in the Guides section, you could knock an enemy into the air, dash/dodge forward, immediately cancel it by jumping, assuming you have any Cancel Points, then continue attacking. Like, okay, why can't I just jump and keep attacking? Why do I have to go through this unintuitive cancel thing?
I imagine the slogging controls are meant to create tension or something, similar to Resident Evil games. Maybe they're intended to create a "challenge." No idea, but I like snappier controls for games like this. I almost want to compare the controls to those arcade games in movie theatres that are designed to get you killed so you keep pumping more quarters into it.
That said, just like anything else in life, you CAN get used to the timing and whatever, just depends if you're willing to spend the time adjusting to it.

If you think B.J. Blazkowicz was the kid who sat next to you in third grade and shot spitballs as Miss Brown then you might be right; just depends how old you are. He’s a hero now, by the way, a genuine Allied hero who lives for one thing and one thing only-- blasting noxious Nazis to smithereens. At least he was until his latest incarnation in Wolfenstein: The New Order, for he now comes along with real virtual feelings and even has, if you can believe it, a love affair with the sad, unforgettable nurse Anya Oliya. Their tender tale will bring a tear to your ears, eyes I mean!-- but those are not real tears; you’re a real virtual hero too are you not?
Heroes don’t cry, except in this magnificent spectacle of a game—one of the best first person shooters of all time but with a moving tale to tell as well. Not only Anya but Set Roth, the ingenious survivor of concentration camp hell, and Caroline Becker, the crippled but redoubtable leader of the Kreisau Circle resistance fighters, inspire admiration. There’s General Deathshead too, but wait! He’s the arch-villain and I, perhaps unlike you, will not spare a tear for him!
I’ve been asked by other gamers of redoubtable years (60+), if this a suitable game for “seasoned” players. I give an unqualified: “Heft that automatic, guys, and help to bring down the Wretched Reich!” There’s lots of blazing action and some acrobatic feats, like leaping out of airplanes, may require (if you’re acrophobic like me) a dozen tries, but the lower levels are not too hair-pulling but still hair-raising.
However if you play on the easier levels be prepared to be insulted when setting up the game. Seems some dork on the development team thought it would be funny to try and disparage those who paid hard cash for the game just so he can continue to be a dork. Ignore the slight and join the team that matters— B.J. Blazkowicz and Co.

The game can be quite hard and it can be a nuisance when you are about to exit the level when suddenly you died by some cause you didn't see. However, the game is the kind of hard that is challenging, rewarding and keeps you wanting for more instead of frustrating and the shortness of the levels help a lot. I only had to watch a guide for one of the levels. The music is also very charming and catchy, the controls (atleast with an Xbox 360 pad) are precise and the graphics and art are nice, even if there's not a lot of variety in the scenery except some small colors and detail changes.
I bought Escape Goat back when it was on sale by one buck, though I think the normal price tag justifies the sale, as it also includes a level editor and an extra set of REALLY hard levels made by users after you completed the main story. If you really like puzzle games and/or plataformers, and don't mind the shortness, you should check this game out. If you're still unsure, wait for a sale.

I first played Escape Goat on XBLI and instantly fell in love. It's a cute, but challenging puzzle platformer about a purple goat and a mouse with a sweet
magic hat who must escape from some jerk's diabolical prison. To do this, they must travel through nine different areas to rescue the magical, slumbering sheep within, and then conquer one final extra-long area for good measure.
Escape Goat has an interesting way about its levels. They're always shifting. Buttons and switches move blocks, barrels will roll, platforms move along tracks, and crates explode (usually in big chain reactions). Puzzles tend to involve trying to understand what will make what do what, and then making sure it all happens in the right order without getting yourself killed.
The actual movement can be a little floaty, but you quickly get used to it. It's not a game-ruiner. Block-wide openings require some precision to get through that may cause a few deaths when you're in a hurry or just unlucky with your dash timing. Still not a game-ruiner, but occasionally annoying.
There are enemies, but you can't kill them directly. You can often kill them indirectly, by using the environment creatively. In several spots, this can even gain you achievements. Which, by the way, aren't just your standard "congrats you beat another level!" fare. The majority of the achievements here are for completing levels in challenging ways. Many of these require you to do things that were clearly not intended when the game was originally released on XBLI, but which probably came to the dev's attention later on down the line. Barring a handful of annoying chievos, these add a good deal to the game, requiring you to think outside the box and push your skills to the limit.
On that note, the overall difficulty of the game is pretty good. You've got a few easy warm-up levels, and then quickly get into the thick of it. Towards the end, you'll be putting your platforming skills to the test. If it's still not tough enough for you, don't fret. Once you complete the game, a bonus mode unlocks with four worlds of extra-challenging levels. A warning pops up to tell you that the going's going to get tough when you start it. And it's not kidding. I'm sure not finishing that without a walkthrough anytime soon.
The game looks great! The dev understands the importance of color, something which pleases me greatly. There's a bit in the first Castlevania episode of Sequelitis about using colors that pop, and it's a lesson that I feel doesn't get taken to heart often enough. In Escape Goat, your goat is purple. Your mouse friend is orange. The environments use a variety of colors to keep your eyes focused. No slog through brownish grey ruins, here. I mean, there... there are some browns and greys. But you get what I'm saying.
Maybe it's just me, but I think the music here shines above all else. Which is only natural, as the dev was originally a video game composer before getting into design, as well. There's a unique sound to the music of Escape Goat that I really can't describe very well. They should have sent a musician. I don't know if it's an echoey sound or, I dunno. Reverb? Something. Makes for some mysterious melodies, though, I can tell you that. Give it a listen on
, if you like. If that sounds like something you'd like to hear in a game, then this is that game, and you know where the purchase button is!
The game contains a level creator, and you can play player-made levels by placing them into a certain folder on your computer. There's a stickied thread on EG's Discussions board that will tell you more.
It's pretty short at about 3 hours for the initial campaign, with potential time extensions in the forms of the bonus campaign and player-made levels. It's also pretty cheap at only $5, which seems like a pretty good trade off. I can safely recommend the game at that price. If you're on the fence, $1.24 during a sale is honestly about as much of a steal as a steal can be. If you're dissatisfied at that price (you won't be), then I just don't know what you're doing with your life.

This is nothing less than sheer enjoyment. The setting is a perfect combination of wild west frontier and off-world alien planet. It sets the scene for a myriad of goal based missions that though essentially based on the same mold you never get tired of going for.
There is a point when the missions do get repetitive, around the mid-point of my second play through, but the drop-in-drop-out save by location mechanism means you can play as much as you want and leave it, till your ready for the next time.
Where Borderlands really excels though is the unique character types available and their diverging skill sets. This means you can choose a character that suits your particular play style and further customize it, to your preferred killing style - NICE!
Singleplayer is great, but multiplayer is even better...  increasing the amount of fun to be had ten-fold! It also works seemlessly so you can switch between the two types with different characters.  Weapons-wise though the range is there, the best weapon you can get hold of is essentially the one you like best. This was perhaps the biggest disappointment for me. The range is there but the differences are so slight I didnt bother changing loadout too often.
Finally the DLC are all worth getting. Ive completed ZED Island and that was significant compared to the cost. Cant wait to try the others out. All in all worth the money and then some! Can't recommend this enough.

Having played Arcane Worlds since v0.19 I think every new build has brought something new to the table. Progress on the game might not be fast given that there is only one developer but it is certainly steady and v0.25 is almost like a different game to v0.19 now. One of the first major surprises for me was just how much better the randomly generated worlds looked after the generation code was revamped to build the worlds around the gameplay elements rather than the other way around. Before colours were mostly the same and random terrain was sort of thrown together. Now you will find pillars, lakes, valleys, forests and more with proper palettes that all fit together very well in making a believable and natural-looking random world. Couple those elements with terrain effecting spells like Fracture and Volcano you can actually have a lot of fun just terraforming worlds and customising them to your liking.
Spells are no longer found randomly on worlds like previous builds and instead you will find runes which you use on crafting worlds to create new spells. This gives you some early goals to work towards as different spells require different runes so you have to scavenge worlds for the rune types needed for the spells you want. Certain worlds will be easier to conquer if you have the right spells and certain puzzles might require a specific spell to solve.
A much-needed interactive tutorial has been added so anybody not already familiar with the old Magic Carpet games will now have the basic movement, combat and crafting mechanics explained to them. You don't get everything handed to you on a plate though so you still have to figure out what those circles are and what to do with them.
Several improvements to the map make locating items on worlds much more easily. Un-triggered circles are marked as are creatures and mana gatherers and there is a line back to your castle so navigating is much easier. In the universe map you can also check if you have missed anything on worlds you have visited which is pretty useful.
Difficulty has increased on v0.25 as your starting mana is now lower and you can't just rain fireball death on enemies right away so you have to fly more evasively until you have added some mana to your castle allowing you to sustain your fire rate for longer periods. Dark worlds are a new addition and whilst I don't want to ruin the surprise I will say that poorly prepared Wizards are going to have a bad time in these! One of my early criticisms of the game was that it was a little too easy and creatures offered no real threat to you which is now being addressed.
The game is also moddable which is fairly unusual for an alpha-build game. The scripts in the /gen/ folder are not only responsible for world generation but also the gameplay elements so there is a lot that can be done to tweak and customise the game. There isn't much in the way of documentation (or even comments) so the difficulty curve for modding is currently quite high but I expect this to change as the game develops further.
Arcane Worlds is a truly amazing experience for an alpha and I can't recommend it enough regardless of whether you ever played Magic Carpet or not.
I should point out that as the game is DRM-free many people (including myself) usually aren't logged into Steam when I play so the "played" hours count (3.5) is far from correct for me at least. I think I will have to change that!

Oxenfree is one of the few games I have played in the last decade that has left an impression on me long after I had finished playing it.  The thing that surprised me the most about it though, is that it also made the even smaller list of games that have left me with an emotional attachment to its characters.  Even after multiple playthroughs (some of them being in quick succession), the characters never got dull, and I wanted to know what became of them even after the game's epilogue (especially the ultimate fate of the main character).
However, all of this pales in comparison to another thing that this game has done; Oxenfree is the only game that I have played in over a decade that made me happy playing it. Underrated. A title that flew under the radar because of the Might and Magic name. Too different for traditional RPG fans but action-adventure fans weren't lured either, thinking it's probably just another RPG.
It also suffers because the intro is extremely dark and the combat, while not overly complicated, does have a bit of a learning curve.  I think the opening tutorial might have turned off a lot of players right out of the gate.  However, once the main story begins the atmosphere of the game changes completely and draws you in.
Fun melee action or combo'ing spells with melee.  Tons of environmental use like kicking bad guys off cliffs or dropping stuff on their heads.
It's pretty linear but done the right way, including varied environments and mini bosses, and it's all tightly coupled to the story so you don't feel like you're playing just another filler level that pads the running time.
Graphically the game is starting to look dated but required very high end hardware in its day to max out, so consequently still looks quite good on modern hardware.  At the usual $5 price these days it's definitely worth it.

I have over a 100 hours in on this game and come from playing DotA (original and all stars), LoL, and Dawngate.
Towers do hit hard at the start, but they are less aggressive than in LoL. If I have let all my minions die and stay in tower range the tower will attack me, as soon as one of my minions (aka brawlers) runs into tower range the tower will automatically switch back to my brawlers even if I did not leave the tower range. The only reason the tower will keep focus of you is if you stay in tower range after attacking a champion. In many games early on (around lvl 4) if you and your lane mate kill your lane opponents you can almost kill or kill the 1st tower by the time they get back to it if you have about 2 waves of brawlers built up when you kill them.
In mid to late game tanky dps can tank the towers (generators excluded) for a bit to let your team take them. I have back doored many towers because I could out dps it before it could kill me. The shields on the generators help give a team that had a bad game start a chance to come back so that the game is not automatically over if you lose a few tower early. Also the generators give huge bonus gold to your whole team if you kill them so the generators are supposed to be harder to kill. Also killing the generators make your main building easier to kill, so you are not supposed to be able to be able to super easy kill them...
In this game jungling is a shared responsibility between all 3 lanes. Also, since gold is shared between your team for last hitting, everyone is encouraged to last hit, including supports. The phases of the game are similar to cap vision/early gank/ farm, rotate into jungle/cap vision, back to lane, hopefully kill enemy on lane rotate to jungle after clearing lane, cap vision/rotate to allies lane to gank when able, focus on trying to kill baldir or cindara, take towers/cap vision, push, repeat in random order based on what the other team is doing. If it is boring it is because you are doing bad and are failing your team. Because of the way the gold mechanics work in this game your support characters can carry your team late game if built right since they are not item starved in order to feed gold to a possibly bad adc.
Summoner skills are replaced with a pet with a passive, passive/active, and active skill. The pets are balanced for different roles and or strategies. Many different pets are applicable for playing as adc, nuker, support, tank, or combination of the 4.
Wards are replaced with vision capturing pillars that give you site of part of the map. Vision is not based on how much gold you spend, but on whether you are doing your job of capping it when you are able and before trying to do things like gank, jungle, push tower, or take baldir/cindara.
Tired of players who won't buy boots because they want 6 slots for "good" items, well Strife solves that by giving a 7th slot that is only used for boots.
In strife when a player is DCed for a certain period of time or blatantly quits, all of the gold of their items is split between the remain 4 members.  Also, the gold that used to be split between 5 players is split between 4 players so if your team is good you can out farm the team of 5.  I have won many games that I was losing because of a really bad player that was feeding the other team because they rage quit and then our team started earning more gold since we were not giving some of our earned gold to the feeder.  The other team lost their free gold sack and we started earning more gold.  Game became more balanced so we had a chance to come back.
In Strife when you hit full build you can start spending your extra mony on tomes: health, mana, and power.  Each time you buy a tome it becomes a little more expensive to buy the next time.  The starting cost for a tome is 550g.
Most games unless they are pretty epic or completely stupid (really bad or VERY new players) last 30-45 minutes.
In League your progression is based on earning runes and points to spend on mysteries. In Strife you earn elixirs which you can spend to craft altered versions of items. When you alter a item you decide what components you use to make it. All items are made of 1-3 base components and the recipe requires item build points from 1-10. Some base components equal 1 build point, some are 5. You can't include more build points of components into an item than what the recipe calls for. Some recipes allow 1 build point of components and some allow up to 10 based on the strength of the recipe. If you craft a mana form of an item it will often be cheaper than the original item where as building a speed/power form of an item will be more expensive than the original item.
Crafting items lets you add an enchant on the item which can make it weaker but cheaper or strong and more expensive. Example one item can be enchanted to be about 700 gold less but it has 2x the cool down time, another item which was just released makes the item 750g more and kills you when the affect of the item expires after 9 seconds. If you put more powerful components into an item it makes it take longer to unlock during a match. If you put weaker components into an item you can earn it faster in a game. The end strength of the item in game is based on the stats of the components/recipe/enchant. The cost of the item is based on the cost of the components/recipe/enchant.
So... you can super customize your characters because you can craft dps items with lots of HP, or craft tank items with lots of attack speed/power, or craft support items with man/hp regen, or etc. I can customize the heroes in Strife more than I ever could in LoL or DawnGate (RIP) based on unlocking new crafted items. Also, you don't have to pick what items you build before the game starts. At any time during the game you can craft any of your unlocked item variants. I have had to craft tanky dps gear as a range with cc when the melee tank decided he was going to go pure dps. In LoL once your mastery is picked and the game starts you are stuck with what you have, in Strife you can adapt based on changing your build based on your unlocked items you choose to build.
Also, crafting items is not near as hard as what has been stated by many negative reviewers. The problem is they either want their customization for free with out time invested in the game or they don't understand how to earn elixirs.  You earn around 90 elixirs every time you level up (max account level is 70). You can earn free elixirs once a day by spinning the prize wheel. You earn elixirs for getting so many wins in a row or a certain period of time. You earn lots of elixirs by getting certain numbers of wins with different heroes which gives you a higher star level on the hero so people know how experienced you are with the hero. You also get elixirs for completing the starting story thing in the game. The very first item you craft in the game is free. It gives you a tutorial once you hit 360 elixirs showing you how to craft items during which the item you craft you get to keep for free.
SKINS! In Strife they let you earn skins for free! Now, yes, it takes a while, but at least you CAN earn skins for free if you sink in the time and don't want to spend any money. Each skin can have several color sets that range from 60-100 gems to buy. Then the usual cost for buying an entirely new skin is around 100. You can then buy new color pallets for the new skin which then costs around another 60-100 usually. You get one gem for every game you play whether you win, lose, or fight only bots.

This game is a compact, but rare jewel of a game!
The story unfolds slowly as everyone would suspect from a supernatural teeny thriller but keeps the player on edge, wanting to know more, dragging the protagonist ever deeper into the secrets of Edwards Island.
What is absolutely mindblowing, is the awesome voice acting for the characters. It is the driving element of the game, that let's the player get to know each and everyone of the group of teenagers who try to spend a night on the strange island. At the same time it's also the element that lets the player influence the relationships between those characters because in every dialogue the protagonist is given one to three answers to chose from. Also the pace of the dialogues come in very natural, discussionlike, and well... sometimes leave the player speechless, when some speechbubbles just disappear. Don't worry, that's soemtimes like in real life, you have to cut some annoying brabbling teenies short.
The graphics part is nice and very appropriate cartoon style in my opinion. But the animations are as similarly lifelike as are the dialogues. Even dialogues can be kept on while walking and navigating the different scenes, which shows where the focus of this game really lies: story and acting.
In fact that's what drew me in so deeply, I played the whole story through in only one session!
Well... that's not all... but I think you'd be spoilered deeply if I told you of the other surprises this game has to offer.
I'd say: AWESOME GAME!

Finally, a game that I have hundreds of hours in that I won't be voting down at the end of my time. Certainly Daybreak has done a number to try to ruin Planetside but, fortunately, their gross incompetence has allowed the game to be preserved, for the only thing that saves us from bureaucracy is its inefficiency.
Planetside 2 is a first person MMO/shooter, developed by Sony, and later sold to a small sticker and decal manufacturing company from San Diego. Within the game you can join the armies of one of three factions: spandex liberals, punk rock libertarians, or mecha-hitler. The game takes place on a choice of three and a half continents and, when you launch your character, you can select from deployment locations near the site of battle or at your faction's headquarters. From there, you can take a vehicle, take an aircraft, or simply travel on foot to the location of your choosing. The nature of the game is to capture counties on the continent and add them to your territory until the continent is fully locked down.
In my opinion, the most amazing part about this game is that you can be in, or travel through, any location in the game, whether you own it or not. You can sabotage enemy bases for upcoming attacks, restore your own base after previous attacks, repair and get ready for future ones, or simply travel through your own realm and experience what these places are like in times of peace. This kind of freedom to break out of the mold of small, confining maps in the Halo or Call of Duty style is both interesting and fascinating for me. I like having the ability to take the time and look around ability to take the time and look around almost as much as I like being in places that I'm not supposed to.
Naturally, as a shooter game, you have a variety of classes that should be familiar to you, or easy to understand: The heavy soldier class, the engineering and repair class, the light assault, as well as the superheavy MAX. But, by far, the infiltrator class is the most interesting in this game, simply because of the intrinsic nature of having an open map. You can explore enemy territory and take out enemy units getting ready to set out, stay hidden and provide support to a battle taking place below you, or covertly take out turrets and weapon stations, providing help in less flashy ways, staying hidden as an entire army rolls by you unaware. The simple availability to use stealth in order to provide a formidable advantage is only really possible in a game with such an open concept.
Vehicles and aircraft, as well as the max suit, are all generated by resources that accumulate over time from territories already conquered. It lends itself to be taken advantage of by steamrolling, but the important aspect is that it's generated by patience and strategy instead of real life currency. In fact, some of the most powerful weapons in the game are able to be acquired simply by using your own skill and wits. The most powerful sniper rifle can be acquired in about 20 hours of gameplay, and will stay with you forever. High class weapons for the engineer and the soldier have the same training time.
Even though it is a time-honored tradition to blame games like these for pay-to-win the advantages, most of the combat that takes place in the game is decided by numbers and the ability to aim down your sights. If you're doing poorly, you simply need more practice. The most effective aircraft pilots in the game use nothing more than free equipment and an incredible amount of skill for flying with a simple keyboard and mouse. I have an incredible amount of respect for that situation in the game, and it's surely what has allowed it to retain its popularity over such a long period of time.
Battles will look familiar after a while, for example, if you have a fight in a bio lab, you know what you're going to be in for. But even then, it's not wholly unpleasant to be in, and you can certainly stick to areas you know and like. Conflicts will still rely on individual strategy, unless they reach a critical mass and become a zerg rush, where you simply have to flee and live to fight another day.
In spite of its flaws, I would still rate this game highly and technically excellent with a mild disclaimer that it can be extremely stressful. My recommendation is positive.

Cars (2006) is an adaption/semi-sequel to the Disney movie of the same name. It's a mix between a Adventure game, a Collectathon game, and a Racing game.
Most of the game is spent driving around in the three Hubs getting from race to race, collecting points (which have a purpose, but will be explained later),
finding postcards, etc. Aside from the regular races, you can play minigames to earn more trophies. The trophies are used to access the Piston Cup races, which end each chapter (the game is split into five).
You can play the game using either the Keyboard or a gamepad if you have one. I personally don't have a compatible gamepad, so I just played the game with the Keyboard, but the controls aren't bad in my opinion. If you don't like the default setup you can always rebind the controls from the settings. While there are many skills you can use in the game, you'll likely only use the basics (drifting, two wheel driving, and boosting).
The game follows Lightning and Co. in the Piston Cup season after the first movie. There are cutscenes before every events, which keeps the story going. At some point Chick Hicks gets involved as well, which fuels (pun intended) the second half of the story. Chick pays off the Speeders (DJ, Boost, Wingo, and Snotrod) to steal Lightning's gear that he needs for the 4th Piston Cup race, which leads to a minigame involving them where you have to pull off the heist. You then get to play as Lightning in another minigame where you get the gear back. There's more stuff after involving the Radiator Springs GP from the first race, but the ending is predictable. If you're looking for Shakespeare, the game isn't for you. The story, however, does keep the player busy.
Another option you have aside from Story Mode is Arcade Mode, which lets you race on unlocked tracks and minigames with the characters of your choice. There's also a Versus Mode for those looking for multiplayer, but there's no online support. If you're interested in Arcade Mode, this is where the Points you collect everywhere in Story Mode come into play. You can use the Points to buy new Paint Jobs, Characters, concept art, videos, and trailers. There are plenty of points around, so unlocking these shouldn't be too much of a chore. But, if you want to dive in to Arcade Mode instantly, you can always use the Password screen to unlock everything from the start of the game.
If you scroll through the reviews, you'll see that there are many negative reviews pointing out the game's issues running on certain machines. A quick runthrough of the game's README file says "Cars only supports ATI or NVIDIA video cards" and "Cars does not support on board video cards. If you using a computer with the video chipset on the motherboard then you may experience and number of problems running the game. " Take these into consideration when buying the game. If you have problems launching or running the game, get a refund and you can get another game or get Cars Mater-national Championship (the game's sequel with prettier graphics, but far less content IMO). I personally had no issues running the game with my on board AMD card, aside from a few graphical hiccups.
In the end, I recommend this game to fans of the Cars series, or anyone who had this growing up and wishes they could play it again. Despite the graphical issues and the fact that it's a movie tie-in game, the game still holds up to me from the time I played this on the Gamecube in 2006. I'd say to wait until the game is $5 during a Steam Sale, as you get a ton more bang for your buck.

Borderlands is a futuristic action FPS with RPG elements and an open world environment to explore.  The game takes place on the planet Pandora.  You play as a vault hunter, drawn to the planet by dreams of unimaginable wealth said to be hidden in said vault.  Along the way you'll meet a colorful cast of characters that will help or hinder your progress.  As you gain levels, you can unlock skill trees that offer various stat and skill upgrades, depending on which of the four classes you play.
The game plays a bit like an MMORPG, with various quest hubs and optional quests that yield extra loot or experience.  One of the main draws of the game is the randomized loot.  You'll find all manner of guns, from simple pistols and revolvers, to rocket launchers and even alien technology.  Sometimes they even shoot fire, lighting, poison, or hell, maybe all three.
Graphically the game looks solid.  Although a majority of the game takes place in desert-themed environments, you'll find other locations such as a snowy mountain peak, crystal-lined caves, and in one of the available DLC, a swampy island filled with zombies!  The sound design is solid as well.  The story elements are rather sparse, mostly told through mission text, but this also makes the game easily replayable, with few cutscenes or scripted events to sit through.
The PC port is pretty shoddy.  The FOV is very low, giving things a very zoomed-in look.  There are very few graphics settings to tinker with, and most are simply toggled on or off without any more nuanced settings.  There are about 30 seconds of annoying, unskippable intro videos that play every time you start the game.  The interface was clearly designed with a controller in mind, with no effort made to adapt to a mouse-driven environment.  Generally though the game plays great with mouse+keyboard, or a controller.  I suggest looking up PC Gaming Wiki to find tweaks or work-arounds to various PC port issues.

I am on the fence on whether someone should buy and play this game or not. So I will list reasons for both:
To Play:
This is a definite buy if you love puzzle games like, as many have said, Portal. In fact, the whole game is about solving puzzles. You don't have a "portal gun," but instead you use many different objects to complete a puzzle. It is very relaxing, unless of course you get stuck, and a more laid back kind of game. There really isn't a story that plays out in front of you, rather it is a series of dialogue and reading that explains what is going on. So if you love puzzles, this game is another game for you.
To Not Play:
Like I said, get this game only if you "LOVE" solving puzzles. For me, I enjoyed Portal way more than this game due to the fact that I played Portal 2 with a friend. If this had co-op, it would have been amazing! But not being a huge puzzle guy, there were lots of moments where this game kind of became dull and I thought I would never finish it. This was a game I would force myself back to every couple of days just for the sake of completing it. It's enjoyable in small sessions, but not a game where I would binge play.
Overall:
If you love puzzles, get it. If you just "like" puzzles, then I think it's still worth playing every now and then when you want to feel smart. If you hate puzzles, then avoid this game because that's all you'll be doing here.

Once you get the major concept how to solve puzzles -it becomes a little bit boring: all puzzles are of the same kind and although some of them can take a bit of time -they still kind of easy and after a while you want to have something different.
All in all it is a good game, and it is worth to have it in your collection.

Ladies and gentlemen over the jury. After playing Escape Goat, I am not here to review a simple 2D puzzle platforming game. I am here to prove that this goat is a witch. Goats have long been known for their platforming prowess. They have always been able to scale tall mountains with ease. Like all goats, this one can dash forward to ram through breakable walls or extend a jump. Those are qualities that a normal goat possesses. This goat can double jump. There is no other goat that can jump in mid air.
The meager purple goat that you see before you has broken out of our deepest, darkest prison within only three hours. All with the aide of a cohort mouse that believe it or not, this goat talks to! Not only that, but the goat can command this mouse. The goat can send the mouse running in a straight line, scaling up walls, traversing ceilings and hitting switches. It can even get placed under a sleep spell where it rests wherever this foul witch goat places it! Making it useful to rest on 'weighted switches' that need a body to hold them down. This heathenish goat can even toss its unwilling partner in escape upward where it can then cling on the ceiling and walk forward. The mouse can be instantly summoned back by the simple will of the goat.
I would like to show the court evidence A. The magical hat I have just revealed allows the witch goat to change places with the mouse. Calling this hat magical is a farce! It isn't the hat that is magic, its the goat that makes the hat magic! The goat was able to have the mouse crawl through small areas and then teleport directly to them.
There were still things that the goat couldn't possibly use his mouse ally for. Wall mounted switches that only the goat could touch. These switches lead to a variety of things. Both bad that enabled platforms to help the goat escape and good that started machine like traps. Walls that moved, floors that shifted. All the goat had to do was exit out of each room's open door. If the door wasn't open, the goat managed to find keys that it used to unlock the door. Sometimes six keys in one room and this goat managed to collect them all!
Because of these talents, this magical goat may have escaped all 55+ rooms in this prison, but it cannot escape the arm of the law! This goat managed to escape its own cell block of five puzzling rooms. Then it made its way to the gathering place where it opened up new cell blocks. For every cell block the goat went through, it opened up two more cell blocks. It was able to go through each of the nine cell blocks consisting of five rooms each. All to rescue its sheep sisters from prison. After all that, the witch goat managed to escape nine final rooms of doom!
Each cell block is themed and had even more danger, but the goat make it look easy and fun! One cell block of five rooms featured ice blocks. Blocks too cold for its mouse friend. Blocks that the goat managed to ram and push. Another cell block had hollow blocks that the goat could travel through, but other blocks stacked on top of. Razorblades spinning around platforms couldn't stop the goat! Nor could death reapers that throw fireballs when they spot the goat. Nor could fire breathing wall mounted sentries!
Moving platforms, mechanized blocks, changing structures, rolling barrels that explode when lit on fire and walls that blew up when lit on fire. Nothing could stop this goat! How on this great Earth could one goat survive death like that? Well truth is, the goat never survived death. This goat is as fragile as your ordinary goat. Anything can kill it. Its magic that brought this goat back to life again and again! If the goat ever got trapped in a room. It could suicide, completely resetting the room. The rare times that the goat would fall into pits or be able to leave the room without exiting through the door, the goat respawned!
After all this, the goat thinks it can make a better prison. It can somehow make blue prints and escape from a prison of its own invention! Well witch goat, you may have escaped from the easy prison, but after you made your 3 hour escape look easy, there is another prison waiting for you more brutal than the first! The additional prison has 28 more rooms in 4 cell blocks. All without having to spend more taxpayer money.
I feel that I have proven my point your honor. We cannot have this goat walking among us in civilized society. May the good people of Steam find this goat guilty of being a witch and sentence it to prison!

I've played a lot of MOBA's out there looking for one with a good balance of well, everything. I believe I have finally found that in Strife. While the player base is still growing, match making seems much better than I've experienced in other games (LoL, HoN, HotS, Dota, Dota 2, and some lesser known ones.
The things that I believe make Strife stand out are:
- A  crafting systems that lets you customize and improve existing items so you can have tailored items for your style of gameplay. Crafting can also give an item an added passive ability.
- A pet system. In a close fight the pet you choose can make or break it. Lets of cool pets with abilities you can choose from.
-  Good community, especial for a MOBA. I've only had 1 negative encounter with a player in the short 43 hours I've played this game at the time of this review.
- Support players are able to get gold because kills give gold to all nearby players, not just the fastest attacking one (what some may think is skill).
- All heroes are free. There is nothing remotely Pay 2 Win about this game.
- Excellent UI and game design.
- Rapidly growing community.
- Able to broadcast games very easily if you so choose.
- Items offer active and passive traits that can be fairly unique compared to most MOBA's, or A-RTS'.
- Videos and gameplay tips available in game for many of the heroes, growing into all of them.
- Weekly updates and new stuff added often.
- A CAMPAIGN MODE!!!! They are building a campaign mode that is detailing the stories behind the heroes. Right now there is only one available and it is for the hero Bastion (think how to train your dragon guy), and it is very well done. As quite impressed with the story mode.
- BEST TUTORIAL OF ANY MOBA YET! The tutorial in this game is also a story mode for Caprice. It is fantastic. You can start playing this game with 0 experience in a moba, and do decently in your first bot game.
Overall it is just the best MOBA I have come across. Mind you I'm not some insanely intense competitive person that flips all the time. I'm a casual player who enjoys playing MOBA's casually. They do have tournaments a decent amount it seems as there is a number of player icons available for them. I would highly recommend this if you are a MOBA player, or are just bored and are looking for a good F2P game.

The Talos Principle is a rare gem, both sad and inspiring, and very moving. Polished to near perfection, it is like a sweet onion, with multiple layers of story and secrets, interweaved to create a cohesive whole that encourages players to think and leave no stone unturned in search of greater truth. The puzzles are almost universally easy and fun to solve, with a few exceptions that initially seem very hard but eventually turn out to be easy as well. Considering how many tools players have at their disposal, the puzzles are somewhat uninspired and repetitive and could have used more work, but this is only obvious in contrast to some of the more original problems that require smuggling tools between chambers or using some of the more rare equipment. In the end, this is a drop in the ocean of what is the most beautiful and intelligent game to come out in years, or maybe ever. The real puzzle is trying to find ways of climbing out of the test chamber and looking behind the curtain, and the ability to leave messages for future players to find is a neat touch that fits into the narrative and makes the game stand out from the rest. When everything turns to dust, this would be worth preserving for future generations. 10/10

So my recommendation comes with some good and some not-so-good:
First the good:
The concept is awesome. If this game meets all the promises made by the devs, it will be the best voxel game on the market. Period. Look at the concept art. Look at the dev pipeline. Multiple races and classes, magic weapons and items, giant roving baddies, and a full crafting and voxel building system! We're talking elements of Minecraft, WoW, and Shadow of the Colossus all in one game.
The graphics are great!
The interconnected portals are a good approach to a multiserver based game. Each server is it's own biome, so inter portal travel will be an important part of the game to acquire certain resources or blocks.
You have a freaking grappling hook!
They recently added a chisel tool for the creation of shaped blocks. The system before was confusing and clunky. The tool makes it an actual physical interaction that grounds shaped blocks into the lore of the game.
Backers get a say in the developement process through surveys about once a quarter.
Ok, now the not-so-good:
The asking price for the game is pretty high for the level of development it's at. I paid it, but I think the devs might get more backers if they made a couple of  pledge packages priced below the 35$ mark that still allowed access to the game. I think a lot of people are weary of paying a high cost for an incomplete game, especially with the risk of the devs abandoning the game.
There are NO models in the game except for 2-3 unanimated placeholder mobs and a torch; but no PC models (your toon is just an orange cude), tool models, or weapon models. Development on this game has been slow (none of the features I mentioned earier are actually IN the game yet) and while they release updates on regular basis, they are small (usually hotfixes) and don't really contain any major content changes.
As I said before, the graphics in the game are great, but nothing you can't get in MC with the right mods. Depth of field is way to shallow and I keep it turned off.
Not really much to do at this point. Crafting is basically non-existant and there's no real adventure element as of now. You can walk around, use your grappling hook, mine some blocks and if you're really patient, you can create some cool stuff like you've seen in the videos. But I personally can't stay on for more than 10-20 minutes or so. It's an MMO, but the multiple servers mean that the people who are online are spread pretty thin, so it's unlikely to encounter another player.
All in all, this game shows a lot of promise and if you're a patient and committed backer who is excited about the vision of the game, then pay the money and get a say in the process. If you're impatient and want a complete game,  then look elsewhere or mod the hell out of Minecraft. As for me, I believe the devs are working as best as they can on this very ambitous project and I'll continue to check in from time to time and hope the funding picks up enough for them to hire a few more people to speed up the process.

Even though this game is pre-alpha, it has a LOT going for it. It is incredibly promising, and quite fun even now.
Wonderstruck has laid the foundation for what has the potential for an extremely fun voxel MMO sandbox and RPG. Here's what gets me excited:
* The world generator can generate extremely varied terrain, and it's improving dramatically over time. The hosted worlds (servers) show off many biomes already.
* The voxel engine is quite flexible, with a mix of natural blocks, slopes, crafted blocks and all that. The game is already a creator's paradise (and the community has shown this!)
* The developers are very responsive, and the community is very welcoming. Every time the developers introduce a new mechanic, the community has a lot of fun with it. (For instance, bouncy blocks have led to all sorts of fun things)
* There is a grappling hook; and it is probably the most fun I have had with a movement mechanic in any game.
* The graphics are gorgeous. Seriously. Oort online is in a class of its own. It runs quite well, even with massive draw distances (due to a pretty unique approach to LoD)

to start with, the premise is interesting, albeit a bit vague especially in the beginning. and once you kick off the game, not too much is explained about the system, save for a few basic movements. you're not properly introduced to the function of 'capturing' enemies, nor using them, nor how it really works.
the combat is quite fun however, especially once you've leveled up a particular character and gained numerous skills in which you can configure, and try to string together some combos, but even so, after a few hours, it might get a bit repetitive for some.
levels are also almost meaningless in the game, as you could face off a low or high level enemy, and the only significance in it, is whether you can capture them or not. just as well, the 'mana' system is highly underused, as your mana is pretty much only utilized when you attempt to capture an enemy.
all in all, abyss odyssey actually feels like a game with a lot of potential waiting to happen, in many aspects, from the story, to a proper leveling and mana usage system, and even the captures, but it never properly materialized sadly. it doesnt make it a bad game, and it's still fairly fun as each run doesnt take too long to complete, but it feels fairly basic. perhaps one day the developers could evolve their ideas in a sequel.

This game is enjoyable. The art style is unique, the setting and story are for sure as well. Combat is neat, the gear system is good, enemies range from "just right" to "cheese ball" in terms of difficulty. It's a rewarding game for sure (clearing a floor feels good etc). My only gripe is the character's turn speed. The after playing a LOT of fighting games, beat 'em ups, and so on, the characters run / turn speed is just too damn slow. Granted you can get used to it, and I was starting to (resulting in less swearing at the screen while my character kept attacking the wrong direction due to the strange turn around input delay) but adapting to unresponsive game play isn't my bag. I wish there was a "meh" rather than a simple yes / no, or a star system, or ANYTHING else on Steam for ratings, because I'd rate it a solid neutral (rather than recommend it). All in all, if you really like precise combat? You're not going to find it here. If you enjoy a game with fun mechanics and enjoy rogue-likes and are willing to deal with some awkward controls to get your hands on something new? Grab it up. You likely won't regret it.

Looking for an extra challenge I decided to start a colony in the ice sheet biome.
3 unfortunate survivors land in the cold forbiding wasteland of the rimworld knwon as "Still Warmer than Russia". Mal was our hunter, cook and medic, she also took care of Cheetah; the colonies labradour retrivor. Princess was a pyromaniac that also had a knack for crafting and construction, last of all was Frank and he wasn't good at much but he was friendly and liked everyone. First couple days where rough as we tried to set up a base for when the temperature dropped, most of the resources came from mining and the few cargo drops.
8 days since crashlanding. When food was running low Mal went out to hunt a herd of muffalo, at first it was going well 4 of the 7 muffalo went down without a fight but the last three went manhunter and charged Mal. She was able to kill one and fataly injur the second but in its dying thralls the muffalo crushed Mals skull and she died instantly. This drove Cheetah into a rage and he attacked the last 2 Muffalo with no thought of his own safety. After a epic struggle Cheetah emerged victorious; wounded and sad he returned home; no longer mad with rage. In the next couple days temperture started dropping and the Muffalo's were prepared into enough meals for the rest of the year and warm clothes where made from the leather. Frank dug one grave behind the house and laid Mal's body in it.
26 days since crashlanding. All was looking up untill Princess decided to start a fire in her room despite the fact that it was already heated with an electric heater. Being a Pyromaniac she was unable to stop the flames from consuming her and she died leaving nothing but a pile of ashes. Frank dug two graves beside Mal's, he placed Princess' ashes in one. Looking at the one empty grave left he thought to himself who would bury his body when the time came... pushing the thought to the back of his mind he kept working. Frank, now alone with Cheetah, had to brave to cold forbiding winter with no help. However food was plentyful and the new geothermal power was heating the small house he lived in, as long as nothing went wrong he would be set until help arrived.
32 days since crashlanding. Frank goes out to gather some wood from a cargo drop, apon returning to the house he noticed some dirt tracked into the dining room. DIRT IN THE DINING ROOM! HOW COULD ONE LIVE LIKE THIS! It was to much for Frank, this was the last straw, and he broke; running outside in -40c wasteland he stripped of his clothes and yelled at the stars for the cruel reality he was forced to live in. Death came quickly and in the morning nothing could be seen but the fresh blanket of snow that buried the events of last night.
Cheetah lived warm and feed for the rest of the winter in the hut. Later another colonist joined that literally could do nothing but hunt and make art, his name was Min. A few days later a exotic trader came by and we were out of food so I sold Cheetah to preserve his life and let Min starve after buring Franks frozen body.

Looks and performs NOTHING like in the screenshots.
The screenshots and "game footage" were most likely created and rendered in another engine or 3D animating software.
The game looks and performs like it was written on the Half Life 1 engine, not what you would expect from an expensive, early access game.
The game is fun to play if you are willing to look past the shocking graphics and think of it as an "art style", if that's even possible... The gameplay is still relatively fun, if you can tell apart pixels of a tree from people hiding behind said tree...
The game looks nothing like the screenshots and performs like Half Life, there's nothing wrong with the controls and the actual gameplay, it just looks and sounds terrible. The game is in a good starting position, but nowhere near where it should be, especially with the misleading images and videos on the Steam store page.
Squad was.... admittadely fun for the few minutes I spent in a server with a friend, but the fun quickly ran out as the game turned from messing around to trying to actually play, which was impossible because of the terrible graphics.
This is something you would expect to find on a PS1, rather than a PC.
Moral of the story: Don't place misleading images and videos on your store page in the hopes that it will attract buyers.
Overall an OK game, if you look over the graphics and sound.

The short of it?
This is a great game! If you like kart racers, it's a must-buy.
The slowdown issue from the first Sonic racing game has been fixed (at least on my machine). The game runs really smoothly with all graphic options enabled and it looks really sweet. For the record, I have an Intel i7 2600K overclocked to 4.1 GHz, an XFX Radeon HD 6950 and 8 GB RAM. It's a shame the first Sonic kart game has slowdown issues or I'd recommend it, too. From what I've read, it mostly affects ATi video cards, but you don't know how much of an issue it's going to be until you buy the game. I have a fairly good system, so it's not a game breaker for me, but it can still be annoying.
For Sonic Racing, I recommend the XBOX Controller for Windows, which gives you good control and vibration feedback. If you don't already have it and can afford it, I recommend you buy it even if you don't buy the racing game. It's wonderful for the Batman games, Sonic Generations and the first Sonic kart game. I'm sure it would be awesome for a lot of other games as well. You can get a lot of console ports that look and play better on a computer with a decent computer monitor.
New in Racing Transformed PC:
1. Online multiplayer. I don't know how well this works because I haven't been able to try it. If you have this game, please challenge me so I can round out this review.
2. Four different ways to do stunts.
3. Coins for a slot machine that gives you extra goodies with which to start a race.
4. New triple boost method to start races
5. Racing on water and in the air!. This is a huge deal. It adds so much more to the game. It's fun to catch a wave, do a stunt and get a boost out of it.
6. Risk boosts. While flying, flip out of the way of objects just in time to receive a boost.
7. Much better AI. I'd say "easy" in the new game roughly equates to "hard" in the old game. Right now I'm only good enough to complete in B class (medium) and A class if it doesn't involve boats and flying. Those two elements are new and it's taking me awhile to master them.
8. All New Weapons. IMO, they should have kept the old ones and added a few new ones.
Other Cool Stuff.
Re-playability counts for a lot when it comes to video games and Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed scores high in that department. My mind is spinning already. Lots of new things to learn. Lots of new characters to unlock. Lots of new driving styles to unlock per character. Nicely done, Sega.
In the PC version, Team Fortress takes up one character slot. Pyro is the road man, Heavy is the boat man and Spy is the pilot. Sega used different voice actors than the ones we're used to, which, as I play more and more, is annoying as hell. It's even more annoying when I hear snatches that sound like the original actors. I'm so confused. Still, it's fun seeing our old friends racing. Maybe someone will come up with a way to use snatches of audio from Team Fortress to replace the sounds in Sonic Racing. One can hope, I suppose.
Football Manager and Shogun are also unique to PC version
What I miss from the first game:
1. Special character stunts. I wish they had kept the the 4-way directional flips and rolls for the second joystick and assigned a button for a special character stunt. They should have made it take as long as two rolls and given you a stage 2 boost (or something similar).
2. The horn. I imagine the horn could be annoying in multiplayer games, but I liked honking it to make characters do silly animations. I kind of miss the animations of both the special character stunts and horn honking.
3. Motorcycles. Seriously, Sega, why did you get rid of Shadow's cool ride? I miss it, man.
4. Pole position. In Grand Prix mode, your starting place in the field no longer depends on your placement in earlier races. You are always, ALWAYS at the back of the field. ACK! You made the game hard enough, Sega. Why make it harder? Was it laziness? Too hard to program a person's position in accordance with the average placement in races? You managed it in the first game. Why not in the second?

It's like a first-person Diablo with guns.  A mind-boggling number of guns, though many of them are similar.  Couple that with very humorous writing, some quite unique characters, and some excellent gun mechanics and you've got yourself a great game.  One of the best even.
The game has a pretty artistic semi-cel shaded art style that I don't particularly like, though it fits the tone of the game pretty well.  You can turn off the black outlines on objects with a mod which makes the game look a lot cleaner.  But for general graphical quality, the game is quite good.
Now the PC version is where the game lets us down.  The interface isn't really optimized for mouse navigation so some of the menus are a bit clunky.  The FOV is sickeningly low though it can be partially fixed with a mod.  There are also a few places where the game really could have used some optimization, especially in the DLC.
But problems aside, definitely one of the best games in recent years.  You will not regret buying it (unless you're a crazy person like the maniac on the banner.)

The Talos Principle is a rare gem, both sad and inspiring, and very moving. Polished to near perfection, it is like a sweet onion, with multiple layers of story and secrets, interweaved to create a cohesive whole that encourages players to think and leave no stone unturned in search of greater truth. The puzzles are almost universally easy and fun to solve, with a few exceptions that initially seem very hard but eventually turn out to be easy as well. Considering how many tools players have at their disposal, the puzzles are somewhat uninspired and repetitive and could have used more work, but this is only obvious in contrast to some of the more original problems that require smuggling tools between chambers or using some of the more rare equipment. In the end, this is a drop in the ocean of what is the most beautiful and intelligent game to come out in years, or maybe ever. The real puzzle is trying to find ways of climbing out of the test chamber and looking behind the curtain, and the ability to leave messages for future players to find is a neat touch that fits into the narrative and makes the game stand out from the rest. When everything turns to dust, this would be worth preserving for future generations. 10/10

Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is hands down one of the most entertaining games I have ever played in my life. To be honest, the story is lame, the levels are pretty linear, and after one or two playthroughs you aren't likely to find any new hiding spots for super-secret treasure(though there are quite a few of them).
But this game's combat makes up for all of its flaws, story or otherwise. I have never played a game with more engaging, interesting, or balanced combat than this one. It's the only reason I come back to this game, and as you can see from my logged hours, I have come back to this game time and time again.
The combat is fairly basic to begin with, you can hit things hard or not so hard, you can block with a shield or parry with a one-handed weapon, you can shoot enemies from far away with a bow. However, as you progress into the game and start earning skill points, combat very quickly becomes a deep experience. The game carries three classic releplaying game archetypes: the mage, the rogue, and the warrior. But the part that makes it so wonderful is the complete freedom you have to spend your skill points in any way you please. You can be sneaking up on your opponents wearing heavy armor and slinging fireballs if you want to.
Just play the game, that's really all there is to it. It's well worth the meager investment.

This game needs a lot more added to it before it's really going to be playable, but I'm really looking forward to what it will become. When the individual worlds become more unique and the array of creatures more numerous, when the collectable begin to have more of a point, I'll definitely be back into this game more often.
