New Review ( 16.03.2015 )..
I took another look at Arcane Worlds and it appears to be moving in the right direction. I played through quite a few levels until I encountered what seems like a game-breaking bug ( I am stuck in the world, none of the pedestals can be activated by movement, fire, or anything and no portal is available to leave the world ); while in early-access I can see something like this happening, but it should be far enough along where this doesn't happen..
Aside from the game-breaking bug, things are moving in the right direction so I look forward to revisiting this review once more in the near future.
Current Pros:
++ They're making progress with development and adding new features.
++ The world selection screen seems like a bonus which will make game-play more dynamic instead of being the same worlds each time ( extra bonus if procedurally generated ).
+ AI Creatures now attack you.
+ Able to cast "Claim Mana" spell so mana isn't automatically yours ( meaning it can be stolen when AI is added )
+ Able to create new spells with collected crystals instead of simply finding spells as in the original Magic Carpet ( Although I have yet to find a place to create spells in any of the maps; the tutorial said to do it at the alter, and I revisited the first map to try it and still had no luck so this will also be mentioned in cons )
Current Cons:
-- MAJOR: Game-Breaking Bug which leaves your only available save-game stuck in a world without being able to activate any alters, or portals, etc... ( I've tried everything, even burning the entire map )..
- Unable to create new spells outside of fireball from the tutorial, even after coming back to the original map and alter.
- Combat feels too easy.. ( Let me rephrase, while receiving "damage" is a "HUGE" event, you don't seem to be able to die or whatever... )
- Worlds seem quite small.
- World textures seem low-quality / worlds don't appear as detailed as the original Magic Carpet ( Bonus, I found my old CD of Magic Carpet 2, I'll see if I can get it running and upload screenshots or videos )...
- You can't see the carpet you're on.
- The levels are still repetitive.
- There are still no AI players.
- You can not expand your castle ( meaning you're stuck with one center "building" and a wall with 4 towers, one at each corner ).
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Original Review
As of right now I can't recommend it in good faith. While they claim it's a newer version of Magic Carpet ( I own Magic Carpet; and I have the original disks ), it's not quite the same. It is currently early access, so they'll be up for another review closer to release.
Magic carpet allowed you to fight an enemy, right from the ~second level. When you killed a creature, gold mana balls would drop down. You'd need to cast a spell on them to claim those mana balls as your own. Once you cast the spell ( Spam right clicking ), your hot-air-balloons would come pick them up. Enemy carpeteers could claim your mana if it wasn't picked up yet. If it was picked up ( if I recall correctly ) they could destroy the hot-air-balloon and take it. This was much more challenging that this game currently is.
I'd thought about making a clone of Magic Carpet for the longest time; but I didn't. Depending how this game turns out, I may create my own.
The water effect is not that great; monsters spawn in out of nowhere; you get the same spells over and over and over again; after playing for several hours ( on the pre-desura and pre-steam release ) I left the game, came back and it was fine. I tried loading the game and my save was gone. All spells, all levels, everything - albeit not much because it's still early access. Simply put, Strife is a slightly relaxed version of LoL with a bit of Dota/HoN mixed in and much fewer players. The main points of difference from LoL are:
* A lasthitting mechanic like in Dota, except that allied heroes share the income, so there's less of a competition for farm, but the flip side is that it's possible to mess up lasthits for allies.
* Significant health regeneration after not receiving damage for 10 seconds, meaning that players need to return to base less often, but it also makes harassment in lane less meaningful.
* No wards, but instead there's capturable towers that give vision (temporarily) like in Starcraft or HotS.
* All heroes are unlocked by default like in Dota.
* Instead of LoL's Summoner Spells, there's personal 'pets' that follow the player, give certain buffs and have a special ability. The pets need to be unlocked, and having access to more of them can give players an edge.
* Purchasable items can be upgraded outside of the game via "item crafting"; just like with the pet unlocks, players can get an advantage by grinding or paying for this, so there's a p2w element.
* Each player gets a free, personal and unkillable courier for delivering items.
* Instead of Roshan or Baron Nashor, there's two larger neutral camps that can be used to push a lane for a limited duration.
* There are special slots for boots so that players don't have to choose between having boots or having an extra regular item slot.
One of the most pronounced similarities to LoL is the cartoonish art style; even the user interface font is cartoonish, giving everything a somewhat childlike vibe.
* The game offers hotkey presets based on LoL/Dota/HoN, so players from other games don't have to relearn the keys or bother customizing them.
* Polished user interface; things like building items should be easy to pick up for beginners.
* Decent tutorial.
* Some significant glitches and bugs (half of the time most of the text in my game was unreadable because of missing letters), but this is to be expected from an early access game.
* A medium-sized hero pool, but the heroes are arguably quite bland and uninspired. Many heroes are very 'samey', and it's largely a generic mix of stuns/slows/nukes/skillshots, with some heroes having a slight twist.
* The items don't have too much impact, and the progression in general just seemed very limited, so the late game wasn't that different from the early or mid game. The matches often felt like they were dragging on for 30 minutes.
* Small player pool leads to more unbalanced matchups and longer queue times. This is not a problem with the game itself, but should be noted.
Strife is supposed to be the best game of the genre, somehow having less 'toxic' players while still being competitive, but also casual-friendly, but all these claims show is the hubris of the developer. In reality, the main appeal of Strife I can see is for the more casual players (which seems to be reflected in all the positive reviews of this game here stressing the casual aspect), but even in that case I'd rather recommend something like HotS because it has more original ideas and interesting gameplay, while still proving casual with things like even shorter average match length.
I seriously doubt that Strife will manage to beat even the 'dead' game that is HoN in popularity, because most of what Strife offers is just ripped off from other, better games, and S2 doesn't have the resources to generate the required hype to get a game that can't stand on its own merits going.

I like it, there are a lot of gameplay elements and UI features that tend to facilitate the experience. Among these things :
- the lane partners both get the gold when one of them last hit a minion.
- no wards : there are 4 pillars that you can activate in the forest to get visibility, but as a player who enjoys support champions, it allows me to focus on the battles rather than on ward management.
- the biggest mob in the forest, when killed, gives a huge ape that helps you push a lane. This is much better than a aegis/buff system.
- champion stats are REALLY simple.
- graphically cute and colorful. It's hard to get mad in a game this colorful. It really gives a "feel good" vibe. The char design is really really good, like LoL was in its early days.
- out of combat regen / free unkillable carrier : you don't have to go back to base often.
- the action is very readable. For real.
- the small things, like a popup that tells you that you can now afford the next item on your build (builds can be customized of course), or the radial-menu to explains (vocally) why you ping : "omw" / "be careful" / "enemy missing"
- all champions are unlocked right from the start. However you have to spend in-game currency to unlock the equivalent of "summoner spells".
- you can't communicate with your opponents in game.
The few cons  :
- the playerbase is small right now, it takes 2 - 5 minutes before finding a game. Which is okay as Strife is still in beta.
- there are no "complex item recipes". However you can change the recipes of the items via a crafting mechanism. I'm not a fan but it shows the devs are trying things.
As a conclusion, after about 10 hours of gameplay, I have to say I like it. I really think the devs made a goal to reduce the toxicity to a minimum, which is very refreshing.

The game itself is fun if you ignore everything about the fact that it's Half-Life, and play it solely for the action.
However, even that has its drawbacks.
While, yes, it was published in 1999, there are glitches within the game that are so frustratingly obvious to the developers that it makes me question as to whether or not they actually bothered to give the game a run through to find and fix these glitches.
One of the many I've encountered is just a literal 'Getting stuck' glitch. You'll get on an elevator, activate it, and the elevator simply won't move because your body has frozen in place and is stopping it from being able to, y'know, BE AN ELEVATOR.
Another is where you'll die randomly when activating certain machinery, such as the Star-Wars; A New Hope garbage compactor rip off, where upon activating it, if you try to move, you will just...Die. Out of the blue.
The lore as well, is an absolute insult to the Half-Life series. While Half-Life: Blueshift kept promise and stayed true to the series (But was disappointingly short), Opposing Force chooses to just throw in another batch of aliens into the mix. They are used as both the main 'Opposing force' to Opposing Force. The normal Xen aliens were practically thrown out the window, and are seldom used after the first few chapters (Minus headcrabs, Zombies and five Vortigaunts).
You'd believe that these new enemies would include the Black Mesa personnel that are terrified of being butchered by highly trained Marines who have difficulty spelling, right?
Nope.
The game has ALL of the facility staff that you meet as friendly as possible, all practically running around naked, and none of the scientists even bothering to wear a Hazardous Environment Suit (Which must have been very well available due to how many bodies of dead HEV Scientists you find within Xen) and attempting to fight you and your men.
What could you possibly replace the HECU with as the main human enemy within this horrid game?
Black Ops.
You read that right.
Black ops.
When originally, the Black Ops had only females whose relations with the HECU were unknown; Male Black Ops were added, practically being HECU that attack the HECU. Do they work as an Antagonist? Yes, they do, very well. However it simply doesn't make sense.
The HECU are advanced trained Marines that were sent into Black Mesa as a cleanup crew; The fact that they thought that  once a group as experienced as the HECU were unable to complete their job, that instead of just sending in another HECU Team to plant a nuke and extract, that they send in Black Ops to eliminate every NON-EXTRACTED HECU within Black Mesa, alongside all scientists, security officers and Aliens (Mind you, who ultimately fail at even successfully activating the bomb without the Gmans interference) is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
All in all;
It's a 'fun' action game with frustrating glitches and a horribly written story. Even the final boss fight is horrible.
My disappointment is immeasureable and my day is ruined.

It game is EPIC! The action is nonstop and everywhere. The intro video pretty much sums it up and wow they need to make a series because I have watched that clip way too many times now lol.
During prime time you'll have several battles with 200-300 players going on at the same time lasting for hours. You'll have 2 factions fighting each other and then the 3rd faction just pops out of nowhere with a massive armor colume and airdrops squads on your supply line. Pure chaotic joy!
Yes it can take a while to get use to the game and fast pace action. You'll get frustrated if you think you can just jump in and start killing without dying. Dying is a given, because you will die and die a lot lol, but don't get discourage by that as that is also how you'll learn to survive. When I first started, I tried to go straight into the big battles and I almost quit because I was frustrated from constantly dying but that was because I was clueless as to what I was doing or suppose to do. Such as guarding or taking objectives and capture points. I was running around like a headless chicken lol.
Join a small battle first to get an idea of what is going on and move up from there to the larger battles. There is a training area where you can practice with every weapon and shooting at targets. I advice you do that first and practice trigger control and spray technics; such as shooting 2-3 round bursts at a time or practicing close combat spray and pray.
Thankfully the best part of the game is what kept me playing and that happens to be the gaming community, as it is beyond amazing. There are many good Outfits that will teach you the basics and how to survive because the action can be very fast pace and strategic.
Very very helpful community and it doesn't matter what faction you're with, someone will answer your question if you ask in open channel. Such as asking which weapon to invest in first, what skills to invest in, etc. A lot of people just want to help others learn this game because honestly there isn't anything else like this out there. A great game that I enjoy. I remember playing this as a kid, and I was excited when I recently found out that it was available on Steam. This game has great races and mini-games. The controls can sometimes feel floaty and weird, but it is easy to get used to (I used a PS4 controller). The hub world, consisting of Radiator Springs, Ornament Valley, and Tailfin Pass, give you this sense of exploration. Not to mention you can hit npc cars in these hubs which can be very hilarious if you are doing this with someone watching you. You can choose a difficulty before starting Story Mode, which are Rookie, Pro, Champion, and another mode that is the most challenging that you need to unlock (I don't know how to unlock it or the name of it). The cutscenes have original voice actors. You can also get bonus content like characters (note: unlocked characters can't be used in Story Mode), paint jobs for characters, art, deleted cutscenes, and other videos, but you need to pay with points you receive in-game. The characters you unlock can only be used in Arcade and Multiplayer. Arcade is where you can choose a character and paint job and choose any mini-game or race that you have unlocked while playing in Story Mode. Multiplayer is basically just Arcade but with multiplayer. Multiplayer is split screen, and there is no online play. The only downfall is the sometimes floaty and weird controls that can take some getting used to and the difficulty that keeps on switching from easy to difficult, then back to easy and cycle repeats. Overall, it is a great game that anyone can enjoy, and I am more than happy to call it one of my favorite racing games.

DMOMM is a good game, that just misses the mark of been great. Let me start with the story. You take the role of Sareth – an orphan who is train by the wizard Fenring. Years goes by and finally our hero is tasked to deliver a crystal to another wizard named Menelag in the city of Stonehelm. But before you leave master Fenring summon a woman name Xana, who will be your guardian and she settle in Sareths head. When you're getting closer to the city you see people leaving because army of Necromancers are about to attack. And they do and Sareth saves the city … for now. After the battle you meet Leana, niece of Menelag and the wizard himself. Sareth goes to sleep and in the middle of the night he is attacked and here start your adventure. The story is the big minus of the game – it is so predictable. The other thing is the stealth. There is no point of using it, which is a shame, but game is design  around to fight, not to sneaking.
There is some rpg in DMOM and it's not deep. You earn skill points by doing tasks and you distribute them in three categories. There isn't big skill tree and some people won't like it, I personally don't mind that much. It would be better if the developer put little more variety in the skills.
The combat is what I like most. It's is somewhat repetitive, but awesome. At your disposal they are swords, bows, staffs, daggers, shields, magic all their pluses and minuses. When clicking the left mouse button you perform normal weak attack, but if you hold it you execute power strike, which do more damage and depending of your movement the animation is different.
While battling the enemies adrenaline meter is filling. When it's full you can kill enemy with one hit and it is gory. Lets not forget the mighty kick. In a lot of cases enemies will stand near a cliff, fire, spikes and you give them the boot it's instant death.
The magic spell are nothing new or exiting. You can freeze, shoot fireballs, lightnings. The most useful spell for me is Charm. There is nothing more satisfying of making group of enemies killing each other.
The level design is great. You will walk in to caves, island full with ruins, sewers, castles. Exploration is rewarded, they are a lot of hidden stuff.
There is a decent variety of enemies, but their design is generic. You will encounter humans, orcs, dragons, goblins, zombies, spiders, cyclops and the most annoying enemy – ghouls. Most of them has some weakness, but not the ghouls. They are just annoying.
The game is hard. If you walk right in front of more than two-three enemies, most likely you will die. Use the weaknesses, set some explosive traps.
Despite some shortcomings DMOMM is good game and I definitely recommended it.

I cannot count the amount of playthroughs I have done with this game, but to date one of the best RPG's ever made. The review scores really baffle me. While the story is generic and the voice acting sort of meh the combat and campaign are incredible. Imagine an RPG where skill progression doesnt just give you number increases, but tangible abilities, spells, moves and perks. Every encounter is like a battle arena sandbox with ledges, spikes, stairs, objects, oil jars, traps, and other things to exploit, you can play this game however you want, because xp (skill points) is awarded through progress rather than kill count, so stealth is viable. As you can see by my hours played, I can affirm to its play value, you'll want to try all the abilities in all sorts of combinations for sure.
All in all, its like oblivion/skyrim but linear and the combat is miles and away more fun (not a E.S. hater), and the perks and locals are far more fleshed out.
Pro tip: with all quests + or - side quests, you can get anywhere between 1 & 1/3rd to 1 & 2/3rds sections of perks filled between the 3 perk lanes (Warrior/combat, Magic, Stealth/misc.)

Well, call me crazy but I was never into the whole Sonic universe. Didn't watch the cartoons, play any other game on any platform or system. With that out of the way, after playing Sonc All-Stars Racing Transformed I'm inclined to find and try any other Sonic game on the market.
First thing's first. Graphics wise Sonic ASRT addopted a polished arcady look and it works very well for it. The character models, the cars, boats, planes are all just perfectly tuned to the environment and the style of the game. It's what the developers intended them to look like and they pulled it off perfectly. The world and all its elements are, and I say this rarely, flawless.
Now it comes down to what I consider to be the most important aspect. Some may disagree. I for one when I pick up a game I don't care about the graphics or the story. I look for one thing: a decent to great balance of graphics, story and gameplay. Rarely do games actually achieve it. Sonic ASRT has no story, the graphics are not what you would expect from a 2013 game but the gameplay it's where it shines. Simply put it's fast, chaotic fun, and I mean fast. Done right you'll be doing stunts that you'll end up asking yourself how in the world you pulled it off. Having great control over your vehicles is what makes it all possible. They all feel great once you get the hang of it. If you can't do it fast enough then just pray for a good pickup to decimate your opposition.
Turning to game modes Sonic ASRT features both online and local co-op for up to 10 players total and 4 local splitscreen. The races vary quite a lot, the PC version getting 5 game modes but quite a nice number of maps to race around in total mayhem.
Another plus for Sonic ASRT comes from its sound effects. The environment, vehicles, weapons and the soundtrack are just as balanced as the graphics. Nothing seems out of place.
What can I hold against a game that does all the above plus puts together the Heavy, Pyro and Spy from Team Fortress 2, Shogun from Total War Shogun, General WInter from Company of Heroes, Football Manager (Yes I mean it) with a whole bunch of other characters from all over the gaming industry? The only thing I can think of is the learning curve. The only real help you get from the game are the hints from the loading screens.
The verdict? Winning rarely felt this good. I would give it a 9/10 just because I don't believe in a 10.

This game really reminds me of mario vs. donkey kong: Unique puzzles involving manipulating the environment around you in an ordered and usually timed fashion in order to reach the goal. The exact timing of the puzzles create a great platforming challenge, as the actual window you may have to reach your goals can be very short and very difficult. Then there's the mouse, an NPC that you can send out to run along walls/ceilings, hit switches for you, and get into small places, this creates scenarios where you also have to aim the mouse with precise timing to complete your goal.
I really appreciate how there is no direct way to kill any of the enemies in this game, instead the focus is on dodging, sneaking, and distracting them. They're less enemies and more like elements of the puzzle that can hurt you, as many levels require baiting enemies to destroy blocks or hit switches. Then there's levels that basically amount to ridiculous rube-goldberg machines, and figuring out how they even work is half the fun and half the challenge.

This was the first game I purchased on Steam after watching a ton of FunWithGuru's easter egg videos. That being said I've beaten it at least four times. If you prefer a niche specific explanation here is a list of categories it falls under:
- Puzzle: The main point of this game is to solve a buttload of puzzles. Simple as that.
- Adventure/Walking Simulator: The multi-puzzle levels are mostly open to explore and the themes of the worlds create different atmospheres that give the game more mystery and depth.
- Philosophical: I've never really categorized a game as philosophical before, but the game is full of challenging, existential questions that you would never expect a game to do. This being said, don't think that the philosophy is thrown in there haphazardly. It's a major part of the storyline and is very well thought out.
Finally, the soundtrack. ♥♥♥♥. Damjan Mruvanic is not very well known in North America but he is definitely one of my biggest inspirations being a composer myself. You'll get emotionally attached to the music, hell, you'll get emotionally attached to this entire game; just prepare for that.

First impressions:
Arcane Worlds is essentially a sandbox. A fun one at that. The game consists of terrain alteration, nothing else.
Well, in this state, you really have no idea how this game will end up, considering it is still in early access. There aren't many features offered currently, which is a bit disappointing, but it is in early access after all. The game even offers you cheats via the pause menu. I enabled these after spending some time playing around with the base game. The cheats make Arcane Worlds a lot more fun. Sure, there's going to be some legit ways to unlock all of the spells offered, but it sure is fun to spam volcanoes all over the world.
I for one, spent all of my time screwing up the world beyond repair. I had volcanoes reach the clouds, then put waterfalls on the sides of them. I made a very, very deep pit that slowly filled with lava as I placed volcanoes around it. The whole world was a scorched, lava-filled mess by the time I was done with it. I should mention that there are entities in the game such as birds and these giant, smiling bears that serve no purpose, but as it stands, they don't really do much in terms of gameplay.
If you're looking for some quick fun, with no real goal in mind, then check out Arcane Worlds.

For anyone who can compare digital scars from seven long years of Super Meat Boy, this game will serve as fresh blood through tired skin. Don't be fooled by the lulling initial stages of instruction and training, you will soon be inches from your monitor screaming or weeping inconsolably after you manage to land perfectly on a tiny outcrop of spikes... again.
As expected from the developer, characters and setting are morbidly cutesy and the controls are ultra-taught and responsive. The true advancement of this game however, is just how well it manipulates you into a strange 'productive' state of anger. In a much more devious way than SMB, The End is Nigh spends time through the first few screens of a chapter training you in the necessary skills (and combinations of skills) needed to progress. It then finds ways of betraying that training in incrementally more irritating ways to slowly devastate you psychologically.
TL;DR - Psychologically devastating, highly recommended.

I wrote the original review of Boundless below quite a while ago when the game was called Oort Online. My thoughts towards the game have not changed, and in fact my excitement for it has only increased. I can not state enough how much I love Boundless (for the same reasons below; the community, developers, the beauty, etc.).
The game has come a long way since its release to the public a year ago (in-browser game without audio, crafting, models, etc.):

The negative reviews about slow development completely puzzle me. Let's keep in mind this is an in-house engine too!
Anyways, here's the original review!
---------ORIGINAL REVIEW-----------
Oort is probably one of my favourite games over the past couple of years, and not necessarily because of what's in the game at the moment. The community is fantastic and the Devs are like no other. The team are always active on twitter and the Oort forums and are an amazing group of people.
The game is beautiful. If you like vanilla minecraft, I can guarantee you'll like this at its current stage. I struggle to go back to minecraft because of how dated it feels. Of course Oort has some huge things to come that will set it apart from other voxel games (Titans, Character levelling, HEAPS MORE).
Before you purchase, make sure you find out what is currently in game and what is still a planned feature, and therefore you wont be dissapointed. Most of the negative reviews on here are because of that exact reason. Do your homework (Watch some YouTube videos, Twitch streams, etc.) before purchasing.
Oh and about the pricing, look at their website. This works like a kickstarter campaign, except over a year instead. Youre paying $35USD to BACK the game and get access to early alpha/alpha/beta. If you want the full 1.0 game you can buy it now at $15USD and play at launch, or wait and pay $25USD-ish at launch. It's a little bit pricey for some good reasons (40+ Worlds/Servers, keeping the community small and dedicated, etc.).
To finish off, YES I reccomend this game, it's incredibly beautiful, runs really well on most systems (Unlike shaders on minecraft), the community is just fantastic, and Wonderstruck are amazing.

I have one main word when it comes to this game: NOSTALGIA!!!!! No, seriously! This was one of my favorite Gamecube games growing up. Although I did grow up with the norm for these like Super Smash Bros. Melee and Super Mario Sunshine, I usually go unique and play games like this and MAN is this good! I remember a lot from when I was growing up and playing this again brung it all back! This is an open world game that is also a racing game. Think of the Crash Time series, but more for kids. In the game, you start a prologue race that takes place in Lightning McQueen's dream. As you probably guessed so far, this is based on the movie by Pixar (more specifically, it takes place after, and does it well) and I am not the type of person who are like, "Des gam ez bezd on moove, muzt suk," or something like that, and this game is further evidence. After Lightning's dream, you start the game for real, and you get so many options for play. You can do normal races, minigames, a side quest like thing where you collect stamps, and even Piston Cup races once you get enough Trophy points. In game, you can get regular points that act as a currency to buy things for the Arcade and 2 Player modes as well as some secrets.
Now I should go in detail. Normal races are just that, races. You go pass people, do jumps, find shortcuts, and use boosts once you get them. Minigames can be anything from Tractor Tipping, a stealth like game, or collecting tires with Luigi, where you collect tires. This game has variety so far, and we have one more mode to go, and that is the Piston Cup races. These are more like NASCAR races where you go in an oval at high speeds. In the middle of a Piston Cup race (only in Story Mode) you do a pitstop minigame where depending on the time, you can get a good speed boost, but the inputs can get confusing since they show the button number and not what the number is. Now, a good game can't be complete without some great music, and this game delivers! This game features old time music with modern twists (modern as in around 2006). Seriously, 2006 was the time for great video game music. Yes, even for Sonic 06. I mean, c'mon, you HAVE to admit the game at least had an awesome soundtrack. To make this soundtrack even more amazing, it even has licensed songs for it's style. I really recommend listening to the music on YouTube is you can or even buying the soundtrack that is licensed.
Now, I praised the game like crazy so far, but like everything, it has issues. First, the games graphics are based on the Gamecube graphics and not the XBOX360 graphics. That may be fine since it makes me more nostalgic, but this just seems weird. Also, this version seems to be emulated since there can be some graphical errors found, mostly in character's eyes and on certain textures. Like I said earlier, since the button's number is displayed and not the actual number, you can sometimes get confused, normally in minigames that don't use the normal controls that you mapped (in fact, when I started, the numbers confused me so much, I got my steering reversed, as in I somehow got my lefts confused with my rights. Don't ask). Also, the game is easy as heck. Once you get in first place, you basically won since you go too fast and end up like, 33 seconds ahead of 2nd. However, these are more minor things and the good HEAVILY outweighs the bad. I recommend this to everyone, especially people who grew up with the game on consoles. I got this from the Disney Mega Wave 2 (or whatever it's called) and it was worth it! This game is godlike and is perfect for racing game beginners and people who want a good local multiplayer experience.
Update/edit: I commented about the graphics that way because I did not fully scale them. When I made this, they were only at 800x640. Now that I fully scaled them and turned on the Anti-Aliasing (Whatever that is) I can say the game looks incredible fully upscaled.

Think Prison Architect meets Diet Caffeine-Free Dwarf Fortress.
It does what it does do extremely well.  The visuals give you a good sense of what you're looking at, the menus aren't too jumbled or confusing, and it really does avoid the inaccessibility problems of most colony and construction management sims.
However, it suffers from many of the same problems as Dwarf Fortress: namely, obtuse rules that you are forced to discover through a wiki rather than implied and emerging through gameplay and a frustrating lack of feedback as to why this or that isn't doing what you'd expect.  Some prime examples of this: Collapses due to lack of support for a roof you can't see or even know is there until too late, settlers dragging their feet to feed\treat the sick and injured, the sick and injured failing to stay in their beds despite all the work rules telling them to, and then of course back to back random events guaranteeing your death no matter what you do.
Now, while I know the Dwarf Fortress players out there will say as I often do that "losing is fun," the reality is that losing is only fun when you lose because of a known or reasonably inferrable problem.  Your tumultuous relationship with DF will punish you countless times for failures that it gave you no indication were incoming.  Rimworld unfortunately still does this from time to time, but FAR less often.
Overall this is a very good game.  It's obviously way easier to pick up - at the cost of some of the depth you might desire - but is definitely worth the week to month that you'll sink in to it.

To start: Normally, I add a header to these reviews, but since it often times made the review too long to submit, I've left it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: Well, the idea isn't terribly new. It's a puzzle-platformer with a retro aesthetic. Also, there really wasn't anything that really blew me away about the game. However, don't think that this game is bad because of that. It's actually a very solid game with excellent level design (with a few exceptions and another part that I'll talk about later). As far as the controls and mechanics go, this game keeps things rather simple. You are, as you might guess, a goat. You also have a mouse companion with you that you can use to distract the enemy (there's only one type of enemy, but that's okay; combat doesn't exist in this game) or send into narrow corridors to do various things. You can send out the mouse and call it back at any time, and there exists a power up in some levels that allows you to switch positions with the mouse.
The levels themselves do make a great deal of use of the mechanics and are very good about introducing concepts without tutorializing you to hell and back. While there are a few levels that don't feel like puzzles at all or are rather easily broken, I'd argue that about 90% of the levels are well thought out and cleverly designed. All in all, there's about 50 levels in the game, with the exception of the extra chapter that you probably shouldn't play.
This chapter is called All Intensive Purposes, and after one level I stopped playing it because of the immense bad taste just one level left in my mouth. That level was the first level of a chapter called Death Row, and it's pretty much an unfair piece of garbage. The problem comes from the fact that the event triggers for the level are invisible. Likewise, a lot of these triggers create unpredictable effects that can completely ruin your progress. Yes, there's even a pretty much unavoidable death trap at the end of the level that made me stop playing. There's a difference between difficult and unfair. Maybe there were better levels later on in the chapter, but after spending about 20 minutes trying to beat that level, only to be screwed over by an unavoidable death trap at the end. After how expertly crafted most of the main stages were, a level like that felt like an insult followed by a slap to the face.
Apart from that, though; the game itself is very fun and very enjoyable. It is a fairly short game, clocking in at just over two hours for the main stuff for me, but for quite a few very clever puzzles that actually feel rewarding to solve, $5 is a very good value. 8/10.
Story: You am goat leave prison fast much. Yeah, no point rating it.
Graphics: As mentioned earlier, this game goes for an 8-Bit aesthetic. The pixel art isn't exactly impressive, but it's not bad either. The animations are smooth, it's easy to differentiate between things, and it's pretty functional while not looking lazy or bland. For the technical aspects, the game launches with the option of fullscreen or windowed. The game fullscreened to my native resolution of 1080p without a hitch, so you probably shouldn't have many issues (if any at all). Overall, the graphics style isn't gonna blow anyone away, but the animations are good and the game works perfectly on a technical level. 3/5.
Sound: Pretty much just music to talk about here, and man oh man, does this game have a good soundtrack. Whoever Chainsaw is, ya did good. The only complaints I can make (and they're minor) is that the songs do get reused for a couple of sections and one of the songs loops weirdly. Other than that, this soundtrack is worth getting on its own merits. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 8/0/3/5; cumulative score of 8.0/10. Definitely a very solid game that is worth your time and $5.

Preliminary Review
As I've only put in one 3 hour session of this game, this is simply a preliminary review of my experience so far.
Pros:
- Mechanics: The game mechanics are quite interesting. Some might say 'ahead of it's time' others might say 'just plain wierd.' It isn't like a traditional RPG in a lot of ways, with no clear stats to manage. But there is gear and skills to choose from, and different ways to approach the games problems. All of those are quite solid, although the game doesn't do a very good job of telegraphing any of it, or explaining it. The underlying cake, while a bit old, is still reasonably tasty.
- Atmosphere: While visually dated, the tone of the game is fairly robust, with consistent motifs playing through with nods to old Might and Magic storylines. What this boils down to is the cream of the cake, which while basic, is still ok.
Cons:
- Graphics: Visually the game has not aged well. Compared to Half-Life 2 which also used the Source Engine, DM looks craptacular.
- Difficulty curve: The game throws you to the wolves quite quickly. Given the ways that the combat, stealth and magic are unusual, this learning curve can be quite sharp as not only is the player having to learn new systems for a game, they have to learn new systems FOR THE GENRE. Comparisons abound between DM and Skyrim, and while they are significantly different, what has made Skyrim remarkably successful is it's approachability - something that DM clearly lacks. On the flipside, the combat and mechanics as mentioned above do allow for a deeper experience than Skyrim, but it does require more work from the players part in order to get the full enjoyment from that experience.
Summary
If you're looking for a something quite different, and don't mind picking up something that is a little dated, give Dark Messiah a go.

Arcane Worlds takes up the same style of game play as the Magic Carpet series put out by BullFrog in 1994. It's not bullet holes and burn marks slapped up when you miss but burning trees and craters gouged out of the landscape. Even though the roster of spells is only about half filled the expectation is there; There is no problem that can't be solved with some magic.
The developer is doing everything right and I can't imagine early access on steam was an easy decision.  I have no doubts that single player will eventually become a fully realized spiritual successor to the Magic Carpet style of gameplay. The frustrating part of this is going to be waiting while the developer keeps up the same quality job implementing the rest of the game. Looking forward to each new update adding Spells or other game play features,  and since I am sure the Dev will be sick of it not going to compare Arcane Worlds to Magic Carpet again. Yes, its not the best game but if you want a game to challenge your puzzle solving skills its definitley worth playing.

The Talos Principle:
+ There's a huge number of puzzles in the Talos Principle (135 in total, more with DLC) and you'll unlock various items as you progress - cubes, connectors, jammers, fans, platforms and recordings (which create a 2nd copy of you temporarily). As the puzzles increase in difficulty, you'll need to use many items effectively and think outside the box to collect sigils and gold stars (for the gold star gates).
+ The story in the Talos Principle is outstanding. It's not one of those games where the plotline is immediately obvious. Without giving away any spoilers, you'll come across computer terminals with information about history, emails and more, which shed light upon your current situation. The Milton Library Assistant can be interacted with, a talkative PC program capable of complex conversation. Then there are QR codes, left behind by other Artificial Intelligence. Of course there is also the mysterious Elohim, a voice who speaks from the sky and attempts to guide your path - but for what purpose? By using all resources available, you can slowly piece together what exactly is happening, why and what you should do, although some things still remain elusive until the end.
+ Graphically the game is nice on ultra. I didn't try any setting less than that so I can't comment on low end aesthetics, but you ought to be buying this game for the awesome story and interesting puzzles anyway.
+ About 40 hours of content (75 with DLC) but this can differ greatly depending on your ability to solve the harder puzzles and how good you are at finding gold stars (should you choose to).
+ Beautiful collection of in-game music.
- Some of the tactics required for obtaining gold stars are deceptive and cheap. While this is a minority of gold stars, it still leaves you laughing at Croteam's pathetic trickery. For example, one particular star in World B featuring a Sphinx was so far-fetched it would only be discovered by pure chance. There's a clue that can be found to help, but once you find said clue nowhere does it state that it is connected to the location of the gold star, so it becomes utterly useless.
Overall Score: 9/10

As i was playing Don't Starve, my friend messaged me saying i would hate him (since i don't like people buying me things) and he had bought me Oort Online. When i opened up Oort it ran in a small window and opened another window asking me to register, i figured it would be some quickly thrown together windowed game. When i finished my registration it bloomed into full screen and i was welcomed with a server choosing screen after selecting to play. I never saw so much variety in a singe game before when it came to servers, i thought it only hosted in Australia and the UK at first, but then i saw the scroll down button (more like a page down button, something to consider for the devs). When i found a suitable server and i entered, i had to take a moment before actually learning the controls to take in the beautiful atmosphere. The vibrant, mixed layout of the sky! The squared off terrain was normal but i couldnt help but notice.. it looked more natural, upon closer looks i saw that the terain molded differently and some had slopes, complimenting the terrain! All around beautiful for terrain. Then, i looked to my inventory bar, a grappling hook immediately, very useful in further travels.
Aside from missing player models and no music heard ingame, this is a very well put together game, so far it looks like it could be in beta already if the devs loaded in the player textures right now. I can't wait to see what awaits me on Oort Online, i'd love to see the model ideas, maybe a choice between a male and female model and some customization of that character like clothing, from the art i've seen of the devs i can tell they're going to put forth a lot of effort!

Wow... This game is just fantastic. When I first got this, it was my piece of junk PS2 that had a really hard time reading discs, making it really hard to play for longer than an hour. But over 10 years later, with it on my computer, it's even better than I remember. Let's start with some positives:
The game is excellently designed. I never found one track that I deemed unfair or too difficult. Even the Piston Cup races were a ton of fun, and that's saying a lot for tracks that are just straightaways and then a left turn.
The free-roam is awesome. Seriously, I can drive around the HUB worlds for hours and not get bored.
Now onto some negatives:
Unfortunately, I can't say the same for the minigames. Some like Sheriff's Hot Pursuit, High Speed Heist, and Lightning Strikes Back are at best OK, but others like Tractor Tipping and Mater's Backwards Lesson get way too hard for their own good, and Doc's Lesson: Powerslide is just way too short. Also, Lizzie's Postcard Hunt is one of the worst scavenger hunts I've ever had to go through in a video game.
The control can be kind of awkward sometimes. I occasionally found myself just being flung against the wall for no reason, not turning as sharply as I wanted to even though I was powersliding, and it can just feel really slippery at times.
Now this is just a nitpick (and it might just be my computer), but a lot of the textures, mainly the eyelids on the characters (especially Mack), will start flickering at random. The framerate will just suddenly drop at random as well, but again, this might just be my computer.
Overall, Cars is a great racing game that definitely worth the £15, and even though it does have a lot of problems, I think you should try it if you haven't already.
My rating: 7.5/10

The game continues the tradition of objective oriented first-person shooter that began with Enemy Territory, through Quake Wars and Brink. There is a wide variety of mercs to choose from, all of which have the usual implicit classes such as soldier, engineer, medic... but each has their own take on the category, ranging from dedicated equipment, to mixes of combat and support roles.
Movement is really fluid, and is a MASSIVE improvement over Brink, which was sluggish and unresponsive. As a result, the pace of the game is really fast, and players are encouraged to jump around and make themselves as difficult to hit as possible. Combined with good melee skills, a player can fight their way out of a close combat situation to devestating effect.
If there is one complaint that I have, it's that there is a lack of deployables. They certainly exist, but nowhere near to the extent that players were able to litter the battlefield with turrets, radars and shields as they were able to do so in Quake Wars, which is by far my favorite multiplayer game of all time.
On the non-technical side, I have to complain about the community. While not particularly toxic, the people who play this game are really quick to stack teams, quit matches that don't go their way, and generally ignore team gameplay. It is not unusual to find yourself being the only one to press on objectives. I wish there was a way to incentivise players to be part of the team, rather than just picking their favorite merc (almost always a sniper class) and doing whatever they feel like. There are combat medics such as Phoenix, who can revive himself, but it is hard to find a player that will use these resources for the team, rather than just be an unkillable super soldier that relies on the enemy being unaware of the skills of the class.
The game is a fine product, but the community tends to be a letdown at times.

Escape Goat is a puzzle platformer about a goat in a magical prison trying to find a way out, and on the way rescuing sheep who is also trapped there. The puzzles often revolve around trying to find a way around strange machinery filled with buttons and switches, which fits pretty well and there is a lot of creative puzzle designs in place to the point where it is hard to explain it, you just have to see it for yourself. You also get a mouse companion who you can send out to climb walls to reach buttons you couldn't otherwise get to or to distract enemies, as well as teleport between characters in certain levels, which is a pretty fun mechanic.
The grapich and sound design is pretty charming, going for a retro style, but one that seems to be based on old PC games rather than NES games, which is a nice change of pace. The music is pretty catchy and cool, and the sound effects seem well done, though I wish the music would loop seemlessly instead of starting and stopping, like it is now it's a bit like listening to a song on loop on an MP3 player or something.
The controls are a bit stiff though, it's obviously made to be used with a controller, but my PS3 controller was not recognized with the game, I am unable to use a Xbox one and it is a PC game so I wish they had done a bit more to make it fun with a Keyboard, especially in the later levels which turns into a platform hell of borderline I Wanna Be That Guy proportions. The game is also a bit short, 2-3 hours to beat all levels, so be aware of that in case you wanna wait for a sale, though there is a level editor and some secrets to extend the playtime further thankfully.
All in all, if you have a Xbox controller and like puzzle platformers it's a pretty good game, just do be aware it's pretty frustrating sometimes if you play with a keyboard.

(8.5/10)  The name alone had me kind of wondering just what i was getting myself in to here.  Fortunately 2 minutes into playing I found myself drawn into an extremely slick 2d puzzle platformer with a great soundtrack.  The basic mechanic of jumping around and hitting some switches is complimented by a little mouse friend to help extend your 'reach' a bit.
Levels start out quite forving as they teach you the basic game mechanics and interactions with the mouse, but by the half way point start turning wuite fiendish and can require many, many, *many* attempts to get past.  By the end thye are sort of straddling that luck vs skill vs figuring out three way fight and sometimes you'll know what needs to be done, but it will take you dozens of lives before you manage to just slip between two death dealing traps in exactly the right way to continue.
On that note, one *warning* for people with more advanced gaming hardware.  It turns out that the timing of the game is not based on clocks/counters but rather on the frame pacing of the games draw engine.  For most people with 60hz displays, that won't matter much (though you can get a slight 'slowdown' if you set things to a 50hz euro sync rate instead).  Those of us with 144hz gaming panels though are in for a bit of a rough ride.
I hit a certain level where i was just physically incapable of timing jumps fast enough to 'work' and thought I must have the wrong idea of what the level needed, so I looked up a youtube walkthrough. Well wouldn't you know it, everything seemed to be moving way *way* slower for that guy, and he was speaking german... I put two and two together, rebooted the game with the display at 50hz not 144hz, and suddnly everything was literally moving 3x slower and those 'impossible' jump timings suddenly became quite easy.
(and to think i beat the first half of the game at 3x 144hz 'speed')
That resolved though I really did enjoy the game and would happily reccomend it to anyone who loves neo retro indie stuff with great soundtracks and great action puzzle platformer game play.

I very much enjoyed the Talos Principle!  Spectacularly beautiful graphic environments!  Decent backstory, though perhaps not as compelling as a Myst or Obduction.  If you like first person puzzle games, this is a great one!
Be aware that this is a very LARGE game!  (Worth the money!) I think I counted 165 puzzle 'areas' that need to be solved, plus another 27 puzzle gates to open (they're pretty quick and easy, though).  I actually spent over 80 hours over a couple months playing the game to get everything.  The puzzles themselves are clever, with the difficulty and variety of 'tools' used to solve them increasing as you progress.  Don't expect a great deal of variety - the puzzles are all of a similar nature, but some require some real out-of-the-box thinking to solve, particularly when trying to get the 'stars'.  As I'm not great at that, I had to get a few hints online to collect all of them.  The occasional Easter eggs throughout the game were always a fun surprise, though I'm sure I didn't find them all.
I ran into no bugs on my fairly powerful machine running Windows 10, I even ran it successfully on a 5-year old laptop running Windows 7.  It did run slower and noticeably dropped frames, but it worked just fine!  (For a couple of the puzzles that required good timing, I waited until I got back to my newer machine, as the smoother graphics helped.)
I would highly recommend this one to those who enjoy first person puzzlers!

I like to think of Escape Goat as "the little game that could". Launching first on the highly flawed and crowed Xbox Indie Game Market, it garnered a cult following that pushed it ahead of the seemingly endless shovelware that littered the platform, eventually making its way to Steam and even getting a sequel. Despite the acclaim, I've been sitting on the sidelines, still unconvinced by the unimpressive graphics and seemingly basic design. As is often the case though, my first impressions couldn't have been further from the truth, as Escape Goat more than lives up to its well deserved reputation.
Locked in a dungeon, you play as a magical goat with a magical mouse friend, on a journey to escape and bring with you the magical sheep who have been trapped for an eternity for crimes of witchcraft. To get to these sheep however you must first solve a series of puzzle rooms, the contents of which can be anything from harmless blocks to fire casting Reapers. Because of its nonlinear structure, there isn't any way for your abilities to grow overtime or otherwise have the game expand and evolve the further you get, but far from being a handicap the developer uses this potential limitation to craft remarkably consistent levels. There's no gradual rise in difficulty or sharp spikes later on, but instead a constant stream of challenging but not frustrating level designs that feel incredibly satisfying to complete.
You may only have less than a handful of moves and abilities, but the ways these can be applied to levels continues to broaden as different areas showcase various applications of them that never would have occurred to me to even try. It's this continual progression of what you think you can do without actually changing anything about your character that makes Escape Goat such a clever game to play. It rewards your own ingenuity without resorting to simply giving you a new mechanic to work with.
If you have yet to partake in the escape of Argus with your magical mouse friend, I'd advise you to delay no longer. Developer Magical Time Bean's Escape Goat is a truly impressive achievement and a joyous game to play, who's biggest flaw is it ends so soon (though perhaps it's for the best, as it completely negates the chance for filler). Despite its dated look it manages to feel fresh and innovative the whole way through, and you'd be fool to do as I did and wait so long to give it a chance.

Just to get this out of the way first: Strife is another game in the stream of similar games like League of Legends and Dota. Good? Got that out of the way? Now forget about those games and focus on Strife itself:
Pros:
-Very simple to understand
-Good tutorial
-Good community
-Nice graphics
-A decent AI practice system
-Good reporting system at end of match.
- matches can turn half way through. one mistake by a team can turn a winning streak to a losing one.
Neutral:
-Strategy and gameplay matter a lot to team structure. This means that if your character happens to find themself against certain other enemies then a skilled player will know who to face and who to run from. Even apparently OP characters can be beaten presuming the other team have the right character. This means it matters more about the combination of characters rather than individuals.
-being one short does not mean you have lost.
Cons:
-Low population servers. there are definate peak times and low times, sometimes getting a ranked game is tough. Luckily they have the practice games to help you play at low times. But you have to chose between quing for these (1min wait) or a ranked game (1-30min wait). It is a big gamble to queue for a ranked game if servers are not at least half full.
-There are obvious fake characters there just to cause your team to lose to their real owner (can report if you wait till end)
-if a person drops out of the game and chooses not to return then you are stuck one hand down till the end... no replacements. Your stats will be unchanged if you leave the game after they dropped, but that is a gamble as to whether you are leaving a potential win.
Conclusion:
This game looks fantastic, unfortunately it REALLY needs more players to keep it going well. This is not a fault of the game itself, it is competing against similar games in the same market, however the problem is significantly holding it back.

It's easily the best 2D platformer I've played in a long time.
Controls are tight, and platforming itself is changed dramatically in a way I personally liked from something like Super Meatboy by removing wall-jumping and adding the ability to hang off of ledges.
I felt oddly incentivised to collect all of the collectibles (barring ones received from the ridiculuous end-game challenges) which are put in each level in a place that requires some extra platforming to reach, and this is always a good thing.
The soundtrack is the co-star of the show as far as I'm concerned, with every piece being a remixed version of a classical song, like 'Flight of the Bumblebee' and 'In the Hall of the Mountain King'. The music fits the game so damned well and elevates it from a great platformer to a genuinely exciting and bombastic experience.
Get it if you like 2D platformers, classical music, Edmund McMillan, or challenging yourself with difficult gameplay.

Basically this is off-brand Super Meat Boy, except from the original creator. I didn't feel like it was as much fun as SMB, and most of the obvious design changes feel like downgrades. But it still is a solid game and worth playing if you're a genre fan.
Good points: Creative mechanics in some levels. High number of secret areas (though they don't feel particularly rewarding except the Future sections). One of the later levels (The Machine) makes very good use of the different level structure compared to SMB. Decent aesthetics. Tight controls and good level design.
Gripes compared to SMB: You can't warp to any room, just the start of an area. The soundtrack is just a bunch of public domain remixes instead of SMB's great original tracks. The deliberate limited color pallette makes it VERY hard to see things that can kill you, or the borders between what counts as floor and what counts as wall (both VERY bad things in this genre, especially since it's still true in the sections with limited lives). Any part with acid water comes down to frustrating button mashing. There's no alternate characters at all, so the only unlockables are more levels. No per-level speedrun timer or par time.

Abyss Odyseey is a good game, coming from an indie developer, from Chile, and this is reflected in the design of the enemies and in the mythology used in the game, specifically Mapuche mythology, this separate the game from the usual european enemies used by this kind of games ( goblins, trolls, demons, vampires etc), giving very interesting and original designs (pea♥♥♥♥♥ warriors, the voladora and even the unlockable character The Pincoya), the design is very detailed and with very good animations, with beautiful and detailed graphics, also the music is quite good.
-This game is a Metroidvania style game but the main focus is the combat mechanics, with a Smash Bros. like control configuration and a cancel mechanic a la Street fighter, the combat is solid and strategic, also you can capture any other enemies if you have a level required, adding an extra life and variety to the gameplay .
-The exploration side of the game is not exploited as the scenario is randomly generated, so there is no reason to do much exploration something very important in metroidvania games.
-The story is explained via a Journal, which you collect pages after killing some enemies, but this kind of narrative leave you feeling empty, also there is no a real ending in the abyss so if you are a completionist, you will feel incomplete.
In short with its original design, enemies, story and mythology and very solid combat, its a very recommended game, and only for that reason its worth the price, its a beautifuly weird game but may feel repetitive and the fact that is never ending may leave some people wanting a closure. After some time the game becomes very easy and there is no reason to keep playing it, but if you want to know other cultures mythologies and monsters this is a must.

Oxenfree is a cinematic story-driven thriller that crosses a Choose Your Own Adventure novel with a snarky teen cast reminiscent of a modernized Scooby Doo gang.
The gameplay is primarily driven through choices in dialog as Alex, the female protagonist of the game, in attempt to solve the mystery of a ghostly presence while also trying to keep your friends happy. The omission of overt violence is not missed, as the story includes plenty of subtler conflict with more realistic resolution and consequences. The aggregate of decisions made throughout the game also contributes to a unique ending, although I'm not sure how much the extra content would justify a second playthrough.
The voice actors all perform well and bring unique life to each character. At times the dialogue seems to ramble on a bit long, with some parts of the conversation more relevant to the plot than others. Even so, idle chat between characters contributes toward the overall success (or failure) of their friendship by the game's end.
Ghost stories aren't usually my thing, but I enjoyed the seamless gameplay and interactive storytelling that Oxenfree delivers.

Cons:
- Choosing an option often cuts off NPCs dialogue (which I wanted to hear), but waiting too long leaves the protagonist silent (also unwanted). - Characters move so slowly that exploration can be a slog
This is a well paced, masterful story bound to the player's hand that flows organically and with impact. Any player looking for a gameplay-light, story-heavy experience will find more than their money's worth here.

This game builds a terrific world in it's alt-1960 universe. Not just the Nazi-infestation, but the varied cast of characters you live and die with that form the backdrop of our hero's adventure. Great voice acting, terrific story. For me, it was an 11-hour nearly non-stop campaign that I had to see through to completion.
No multiplayer, but that's hardly an issue for me. This was well worth it.
PROS:
* Amazing alt-1960 story
* Stunning graphics -- some screenshots practially look like art.
* Wonderful soundtrack; subtle, but when it kicks in... damn.
* Game splits into two 'timelines' depending on a (very tough) early choice. This has a minor ripple effect throughout the rest of the game. Playthrough averages about 11 hours for one 'timeline'.
* Holy cow, this game visits almost every location you can imagine. I won't even spoil it.
CONS:
* Horrid texture and asset pop-in (like RAGE), but there are ways to minimize this that I won't get into. Google it.
* Additionally, textures sometimes do not load full-res. Or worse, some objects will render half with full quality, and the bottom half (for example) at low quality. Sometimes entire walls just stay low quality. And the compression artifacts stand out. (I did not try turning off texture compression in the graphics settings -- YMMV.)
* The game can sometimes be cheap by spawning in enemies behind you, even after you THINK you've cleared a room. This is incredibly unfair, but I found the best thing to do in those particular battles is to just try and RUN through and get to the marker.

I had always wished for Super meat boy 2. And while my first impression was that The End is nigh would offer a similiar experience, there's some aspects of the game that I'm not quite as fond of.
My biggest critique are the interconnected levels. I have no idea who thought that this would be a good idea in a game like this. It's not "hard", it's unnecessarily tedious, unfortunately. If you are a completionist, the game makes you replay the same (insanely hard and frustrating) levels over and over, and some tumours can only be accessed from one side of the map, meaning you have to start over at world-1 if you want to collect them all. This circumstance
leads me to not wanting to 100% the game like I did with SMB, as it, unfortunately, feels more like a chore at times. I honestly believe being able to warp to certain areas would definitely make the game a lot more fun to complete.
Second is the lack of pure, unadultered platforming in some of the levels. Sure, there are the cartridge levels (which are great), but some levels involve hoping the AI of some stupid enemy is behaving the way you need it to.
All in all, The end is Nigh is another great platformer by Team meat, but isn't quite able to live up to its predecessor. If you're a fan of SMB and other hard platformers, you should go ahead and play this anyway. Despite its flaws, it's still without a doubt one of the best platformers of recent times. The controls are tight and most of the level design is amazing.

People often like to compare this game to Super Meat Boy, and while it is a fair thing to do seeing as Edmund Mcmillen is responsible for the creation of them both I can assure you that The End is Nigh is it's own unique experience with lots of exploration, collecting and tough platforming to do. The controls are a lot tighter than it's cousin Super Meat Boy, in fact they're so good it makes SMB feel floaty and slippery after going back. The main quest is easy enough for the average platforming fan to complete but the bonus content is hard yet gripping enough to keep you playing after the 20th failure or so while still remaining fun. The soundtrack is amazing and is one of the very few times I have ever purchased a video game soundtrack and I am still listening to it even now even as I type this review.
TEiN does have one major flaw,  the colour scheme. while I am a huge fan of it in some areas it is quite difficult to distinguish hazards from safe terrain such as in The Future and some areas with visual effects such as The Hollows. Other than that however my experience with the game was a great one and would definitely recommend this to fans of the platforming genre or just hardcore Edmund Mcmillen fans. (such as myself) The End is Nigh is a very nice and sweet hidden gem of 2017 and I can definitely see myself coming back to it for another round sooner or later.

I very much enjoyed the Talos Principle!  Spectacularly beautiful graphic environments!  Decent backstory, though perhaps not as compelling as a Myst or Obduction.  If you like first person puzzle games, this is a great one!
Be aware that this is a very LARGE game!  (Worth the money!) I think I counted 165 puzzle 'areas' that need to be solved, plus another 27 puzzle gates to open (they're pretty quick and easy, though).  I actually spent over 80 hours over a couple months playing the game to get everything.  The puzzles themselves are clever, with the difficulty and variety of 'tools' used to solve them increasing as you progress.  Don't expect a great deal of variety - the puzzles are all of a similar nature, but some require some real out-of-the-box thinking to solve, particularly when trying to get the 'stars'.  As I'm not great at that, I had to get a few hints online to collect all of them.  The occasional Easter eggs throughout the game were always a fun surprise, though I'm sure I didn't find them all.
I ran into no bugs on my fairly powerful machine running Windows 10, I even ran it successfully on a 5-year old laptop running Windows 7.  It did run slower and noticeably dropped frames, but it worked just fine!  (For a couple of the puzzles that required good timing, I waited until I got back to my newer machine, as the smoother graphics helped.)
I would highly recommend this one to those who enjoy first person puzzlers!

It took me a little while to warm up to this game after spending a long time speedrunning Super Meat Boy. The soundtrack felt hit-or-miss, the platforming felt a little bit slower, and the lack of diversity in the gameplay felt a bit dull in comparison to the vast number of playable characters and bosses in SMB.
As I kept playing through, it all began to click. The End Is Nigh is a different experience than Super Meat Boy, yet equally rewarding as a tough-as-nails platformer. The movement in this game is slower yet still exceptionally tight, resulting in a platforming experience that requires more thoughtful decision-making than SMB, with about the same amount of precision. In effect, dying never feels particularly unfair in this game. Whereas I would sometimes call into question a death in Super Meat Boy, I feel like the mistakes that I make in The End Is Nigh are 100% on me. Even with the slower platforming, that adrenaline rush that comes with clearing a group of stages in a row is as intact as ever, which makes subsequent replays of TEIN a delight rather than a chore.
The story that the game tells is grittier, more mature, and funnier. Ash's bizarre optimism in the face of desperation is charming and poignant. The level environments support the storytelling by feeling like a more connected universe than Super Meat Boy, in part because of the immediate flow from one chapter into the next. You feel like you're taking Ash on a little adventure in this game.
As a byproduct of this connected, adventurers-welcome world, TEIN offers really no semblance of downtime, which makes speedrunning the game a nightmarish thrill ride. I've spent a couple hundred hours beating this game over and over and I still feel like I'm just getting started. I can't recommend TEIN enough for people who love to push their platforming skills to the outer limits -- you will find that this game will reward you in spades if you stick with it through the bitter end.

I've played this game enough to get a feel for it, so I wanted to share my opinion. *Note* This is a MOBA, that means it takes hours upon hours to truly understand and appreciate its depth, thus my take on the game is still rough around the edges
That said, I'd like to dispel some of the negative reviews that pop up in the "Helpful" reviews.
TL:DR
Try for yourself, the people posting bad reviews probably had one bad game and complain for the sake of complaining. Its free, so you won't lose anything by trying it! Strife is the player's MOBA
One person complained about the tower power and length of games. In my opinion, these are not cons. Towers are powerful, have large aggro sizes, and scale throughout the game. Is this bad? No and heres why.
*Towers are powerful to discourage kill-chasing, that is chasing another player who has low health into their tower area to get a kill. Why is this bad? Because Strife is not a game about kills, it is about objectives. You aren't playing to get a K/D, but to get a win, thus towers punish you for being greedy. Want to get around it? Destroy the tower first.
*Normally games take anywhere from 30-60 minutes on average. It depends on the game, the players involved, and team matchups. This is a MOBA. The standard is to have longish games. There are bot games which take 30 minutes roughly, but player games take a while to develop. I find this to be more personal preference than anything else, I don't mind having a long game, but this point wavers between pro and con because sometimes games drag on even though one team has the advantage. Don't make your decision based on this point
*This game features an innovative crafting system that requires an in-game resource obtained by playing. In my 25 hours, I have crafted exactly once. To me, it seems like the diference between crafted and normal items is simply what specilization the item has. You can add more health to that item, but you will need to give up mana regen. Overall seems balanced, and I'm sure high level players use enchantments (random modifiers) obsessivly, but I don't find it to be necessary nor pay-to-win
*A definite con for me is matchmaking. You choose what hero you want to play as and jump into a game matched with other people who have already picked their heros. That means you don't collaberate on team design, but get thrown into a team whether it is good or bad. On the bright side, you don't have to fight other players for the hero you have your heart set on playing
*Finally, Strife is an excellent MOBA that encourages good behavior, a trait modern MOBA's often fail to do resulting in bad (or Toxic) behavior that often ruins the game. Doesn't mean this toxic behavior doesn't happen, people leave, intentionally feed the other team, or just generally don't listen to their teammates, but Strife does a good job here and the community as a whole is praiseworthy. Once you get that perfect game, where the teams are evenly matched, team composition is good, your teammates are fun and play the objective, you will be hooked, I promise you.
*So try for yourself, it doesn't cost anything. Nobody forces you to pay in this game, and honestly most of the things you buy with the ingame currencies do not break the game by being OP, but instead allow you to further specilize your hero of choice. Want to do more lifesteal/quicker attacks? Craft a couple items and buy a new pet to do that. You pay for these things with currency earned (albiet slowly) by playing. Gems of course (premium currency) can be used, but mostly gems are used to buy cosmetic apparel for you and your pet, and you earn them at the rate of 1 per game. (Doing the math, it will take about 30 games to earn a new color for a hero, or 100 games for a new costume) There is still much to be done in this game, but much to love as well. As long as you play for fun, you will enjoy this game. If you are looking for a super-competative MOBA with perfectly balanced gameplay and clear-cut OP item choices, look elsewhere. Strife is the player's MOBA

SUMMARY
In short. I feel the game would be better if it had a single-player mode, or at least LAN or self-hosting of around 16 players. The world looks griefed already on some servers and it lacks a lot of features. I tried to enjoy it, but just couldn't push myself past 30 minutes.
Personally would suggest waiting for more progress.
CURRENT THOUGHTS (FULL)
I'm not really sure why this game has so many positive reviews when there really isn't much to do at all.
Thus far, I've put very little time into the game, literally 30 minutes by the time of writing and I'm bored. Very bored. I've taken 30 minutes to walk around and see a massive bunch of monstrosities that people call "creations" including the typical Minecraft 1 block wide towers to floating platforms and ugly as hell zigzag leaf platforms/roads from one mountain to another. I do not see the point in beautiful graphics if the world looks griefed already.
Building itself is, well, building. There is nothing revolutionary or new when it comes to building, other than a slope, but I don't much care for that. I can add that MC with a mod if I wanted slopes. The block types are also rather limited.
The features listed in the features list of the store page appear to currently be non-existent. Sure, the developer has stated below the feature list that "Many of these features are in development and not yet available in the Early Access version (pre-alpha). Follow updates on
to see what's coming next and when." Whilst this may be acceptable to some, I feel it is not enough. The website itself reveals no information about what is, and isn't in the game thus far and also goes into details about features that appear to not be in-game (judging from the lack of imagery, or rather, the overuse of concept art instead of in-game media.) If the features are not yet in the game, list them as such.
The graphics of Oort are great, yes. Very nice, we have shaders for Bloom lighting and Depth of field. The water reflects water too. That's real nice and all, but Minecraft did just fine with 16 pixel textures. The graphics alone should not sell the game. I get the impression this game has focused soley on graphics to date and just put a couple of placeable blocks in for good measure. The game lacks a lot.
The multiple servers listed do not tell of how many players are currently in the world, however, every single server today was listed as "quiet". I've also never seen a single player in game thus far. Is this dead already? Or has everyone left due to boredom? If so, why so many positive reviews? WHERE ARE THE PEOPLE?! Oh also, some of the servers I tried to join were down.
In my humble opinion, these games are far more successful when they're single-player and allow for self-hosting at minimum. I am not convinced that Oort will go far, despite how promising it may look, if it focuses solely on MMO. In my experience, people who truely enjoy building, and are good at it, dislike servers populated with poor quality builds and leaf towers. These groups would rather self-host and build freely without the mess on their horizon.
This will be Oort Online in 6-months
(but with shaders)
Would personally suggest waiting for a couple months worth of progress.
