First off, you need to think of this game, as a Pre-Alpha, and not a fully functioning game. I have read some negative reviews comparing the game with minecraft, or saying there are only placeholders for player characters, that there is no crafting etc. So straight away we can say this is not complete, and is not being sold as complete. That is a very important point to remember before you buy. So I am going to review this, as in its current state, and how that measures up to expectations.
I would recommend looking at all the videos, checking YouTube lets plays, and reading the developers site, and doing your research through the steam community. When you have done that, you will have a feel for how this game is at the moment, and what’s coming down the line. It will set your expectations, and if you decide then to jump in and join the community, you will almost certainly NOT be disappointed.
So with that in mind, I am about 5 hours in. I really like what the developer has done so far. The game engine is smooth, really nice to look at, and there is a lot to explore currently. There are lots of player creations you can find, mainly around the capital areas of each world. There are servers globally, East EU, West EU, the United States, and Australia. At the moment, the servers are very quiet, and that’s to be expected, as the player base grows.
There is a lot of work already done here, with the voxel engine, there is a basic blockset, and the minimap is now also in place. Crafting is unlocked, and is on the way. The worlds themselves seem very large, with a really nice day / night cycle, and amazing lighting effects. I have really enjoyed the few hours I have put in, and intend to put in a lot more. This game has huge potential, and as long as it continues to grow, it should be awesome.
One point is the comparison to minecraft. Sure there are similarities, but for one thing everyone exists in the same persistent universe. When the portal system is fully implemented, players will be able to "step" through to other worlds, and even create their own portals. Also the texture and lighting effects even at this early stage are much better than other voxel based games. the volumetric fog for example looks incredible. Its important to realise this is not minecraft, it is a crafting sandbox game, but there the similarity ends
I am realy excited about this game, it has incredible potential, and already has a rapidly growing player base. I would definitely recommend checking it out, if Early access is your thing.

This game will give you an experience like no other.
I did a lot of research on this game before I got it, mostly because I wanted to know how to play before getting in. The most important thing to know is that this is a team game before anything else. Communication is key. The importance of playing with your squad will make or break the game.
I think for someone who plays this for the first time, their first couple experiences will dictate how they will like it. For me my very first experience was entering into a server on a map that was huge. My squad didn't talk and were scattered everywhere but I knew that some squads were better than others so I didn't base the entire game on that one experience. The next game however I was in an amazing squad, the squad lead knew everything that he was doing and was barking orders in a way the squad could complete them and be effective at the same time. I remeber setting up an fob across the famous ammo hill. Which is a strong position on top of a hill top. He asked us to build a bunker with a 50.cal in it. He then told me to get in the punker and start firing on their position, while he was adjusting my fire with his binoculars. The rest of our squad and another squad went on to charge the hill. I remeber our squad leader just yelling from excitement when he saw that the burst of machine gun fire were shredding up the enemy postion while the bullets flew over our teams head. The immersion in this game is unparalleled.
The mechanics in this game go further than just following orders and shooting people. There are an asortment of different vehicles with different purposes. There is base building, which in turn you need suplies from your supply trucks. The meta in this game is great. It takes the best parts of realism from arma and the fun intense moments of battlefield and combines them.
I would highly recomend this game, however it's important to either youtube the basics or something before getting in on the action and it is a must to have a mic. The community is also great, but make sure your expectations of this game are set accordingly. I'm a pretty picky person when it comes to sound design, gameplay, and graphics, and while the sound and gameplay is spot on the graphics are particular. They are amazing in some areas but in some other areas its less so, such as trees or bushes. Its not a huge deal considering the explosions and weapons are just insanely well done.

Played this bloddy thing like 3 times, in 3 different styles, and I also got the extended port for Xbox360. After that much time playing this game, I can safely tell you, it's worth it on a sale. Here's why:
Ever wanted a game with a story as good as the first Half Life, that's as linear, but more RPG-Like? Then, this is your game. The only difference, is that the main character speaks, and you have legs as your crowbar.
Made with the source engine, the graphics of the game still look great today. The story, even though not being a f#cking master-piece, it's decent and entertaining, and the gameplay...Well, ♥♥♥♥ing love it.
You can be, whatever you want to be. You want to be like Havel from Dark Souls, a huge armored rock that slays everthing in one hit, but it's slow as progress with Half Life 3? Want to be a camping sniper who can trickshot someone in the balls in slow motion? Want to be the medieval Adan Jensen, and use stealth to the max, executing people from the back? Or just want to be Leonidas, and kick everyone on the balls, and throw them to the pits of hell? I'm not kidding, I did that already, even sended the video to a famous channel long time ago.
You also have offensive and defensive magic, and they're also fun to use...But I always end up taking stealth. The game has a few endings, and counting that this is as linear as modern FPS's (but with four times thework on the actual game), it's good!
The game also has multiplayer. Now, I don't know if the multiplayer comes already with the full game, or you buy it stand-alone, but sadly, it's almost dead. You have to understand, the game is really old...But there are still a few servers, most of them russian servers. The matches are team-based with 5 classes, mostly being the Spy-backstabbing-son-of-a-wh#re, the archer-sniping-MLG-kid, the SUPERIOR-REAL-SOVIET-DAMAGING-Black Mage, the White-Medic-Mage, and the generic Melee-HOLDMOUSE1TOWIN-Knight. (Please note, this review was written based off the 2 first hours of gameplay. I bought the game on sale for $10)
Edmund Mcmillen is easily one of my favorite game developers. Sure, he's had his slip-ups recently (I'm looking at you, Rebirth DLC) but he still makes some honestly good games. The main issue I believe the Rebith DLC had was just...how  unenthusiased he seemed for Binding of Isaac. I believe that had a huge detriment on the quality of those two DLCs.
But lord behold, we have a new IP from him! Unless this is a Time ♥♥♥♥ sequel. I'm honestly not quite sure.
The game I've been waiting for so so long. Or at least, was. The teasers on the Isaac devblog gave me absolute Meatboy blueball. I needed this game. It looked incredible. And only now am I buying it, a
late to it's release. And let me tell you, these first two hours have been an experience.
The intro to the game caught me pleasantly off guard, a... lovely introduction to the odd world. Essentially, the premise of the game is that...well, it's The End. The world is in shambles. Oh, but who cares about that! You're on a quest to build a friend out of tumours, and to play video games! Both IRl and in-game.
While the pallette could use a bit of work in some areas, I love the atmosphere of the game's world. It captures the gloomy, yet sort of non-serious mood. Edmund's classic artstyle is greatly shown off and modernized. It's simply beautiful to look at, with how smooth all the lines and little details are.
I believe it is important to note that
You can really tell Edmund put some elbow grease into making sure it wasn't too similar.
If you were a fan of the wall jumping, I have some bad news. It's dead. Kinda. So let's hope you like edge grabbing, similar to Spelunky's. One might think right off the bat that this removes the freedom of the game, and in some regards, yes, it does. It only allows you to walljump in certain areas, right? Whilst in Meatboy, if you wanted to scale a wall, the chips were yours. Well, with the way the levels are designed, I believe it fits this game perfectly. It makes secrets far more intricate to get to, and it really makes you think outside the box sometimes, with how you handle certain situations.
And, don't worry. There's plenty of platforming variations. Water, and springs are a couple of examples. Don't get TOO mad.~
Let's talk secrets for a second. Yeah, it's Edmund, what'dya expect? Of course it's gonna have tons of secrets. But, be warned. Getting to some of them can be a tad bit annoying. Sometimes requring you to do a series of overly-specific jumps and such, sometimes in a timed manner, to get to.
In terms of collectibles, say goodbye to Bandages, and say hello to Tumours. For almost every stage, there is a tumour to collect. Collect enough tumours, and you get access to challenge stages, which usually hold a catridge at the end, as well. The cartridges perform similarly to Meatboys; a series of levels that you must get through, only with a specific number of lives, or sometimes only one life! It sort of disappointed me to see multiple character unlocks not included, but I think this is a pretty okay solution to including in these challenge and retro levels. Rather than having to hunt down some absurdly hidden warpzone.
Now, some may disagree with me, but in my opinion, the most unique part about the game are the stages. And I'm not talking design; I'm talking how they're pieced together. For you see, there is no world map here, with levels to choose from. You go along the game by walking from one stage to the next. This opens up SO many possibilities for secrets to be placed, as well as alternate ways to handle platforming. And it really just fits the game's pace perfectly. Once again, Edmund trying to differentiate the game from Meatboy. I like it.
And if you're a sucker for kicking soundtracks, this is just the game. Each soundtrack fits almost perfectly with each scenario. I honestly don't see why Ridiculon gets so much shade thrown at them. They've made great music for both Isaac, and now this
Looks amazing and feels great.

Sometimes all you need is a name.  You come up with a clever pun - "Hmmm... Scapegoat... scape... escape... Escape Goat!" - and everything just flows from there.  It's risky to force inspiration by trying to design a game around a cute title, but in this case the result is surprisingly fun.

Escape Goat is exactly what it says on the tin.  You control a goat, and you have to solve puzzles to escape rooms.  The puzzles are of the "touch this switch to open the wall to grab the key" variety.  The retro graphical style reminds me of some early arcade games, and fits well with the gameplay.  I'm not a huge fan of the current trend of making everything look 8-bit, but it feels appropriate for this game.

There's not a lot of depth to be found here.  Your goat can move, jump, double jump, and ram things.  Early on you befriend a mouse who can climb walls and (on some levels) switch places with you.  Each room is a single non-scrolling screen, with switches placed here and there.  Sometimes there is a correct order you need to press the switches, in order to open the right wall to give you access to the next switch.  Sometimes you'll need your mouse companion to hold down one switch while you jump over to the next one, or you'll have to send the mouse through small openings to trigger switches you can't reach.  On some levels you face fire-throwing wizards, deadly traps, and other obstacles.  These hinderances can be exploited in your favor; for example, a well-dodged fireball can destroy a crate that was blocking your way.

The level design is great.  As a casual gamer I found the difficulty level to be just about right, though some of the levels took more than a few tries to figure out.  You usually have a choice of levels to play, so if you get stuck, you can always try a different set of levels for a while.  The game was designed to work best with a controller, but I used a keyboard and had no trouble.
Bottom line:  Escape Goat is not very involving, or very pretty, but it's a fun time-waster.

This is the only game I have ever refunded, if that tells you anything.
I'm usually a big fan of Edmund - I played SMB and both Binding of Isaac games a ton and thoroughly enjoyed them. I never minded the difficulty and actually enjoyed the sense of achievement that comes with it.
The difficulty here, though, is simply not enjoyable at all. For example, it wasn't until now that I fully appreciated the genius of how SMB would play back your cumulative deaths each time you died. That way, even in the midst of frustration, you could always either laugh at seeing that 90% of your deaths were a single jump at the beginning OR you could look at that other 10% and get a sense of progress. In this game, you will die, immediately respawn in an oddly jarring way and die again 2 seconds later.
Finally, I should note that, for the most part, my complaints are most relevant for the far more difficult extra levels. If you can be satisfied running through the standard levels without exploration or tackling the major challenges, you may be fine. However, if you're like me, you'll probably feel compelled to play through ALL the content and, if so, prepare for major disappointment and frustration.
In summary, Edmund once again delivers on the promise of a difficult platformers. The problem is, this time around, he forget to include any real sense of achievement or progress that made his other games bearable.

Oxenfree is a cinematic story-driven thriller that crosses a Choose Your Own Adventure novel with a snarky teen cast reminiscent of a modernized Scooby Doo gang.
The gameplay is primarily driven through choices in dialog as Alex, the female protagonist of the game, in attempt to solve the mystery of a ghostly presence while also trying to keep your friends happy. The omission of overt violence is not missed, as the story includes plenty of subtler conflict with more realistic resolution and consequences. The aggregate of decisions made throughout the game also contributes to a unique ending, although I'm not sure how much the extra content would justify a second playthrough.
The voice actors all perform well and bring unique life to each character. At times the dialogue seems to ramble on a bit long, with some parts of the conversation more relevant to the plot than others. Even so, idle chat between characters contributes toward the overall success (or failure) of their friendship by the game's end.
Ghost stories aren't usually my thing, but I enjoyed the seamless gameplay and interactive storytelling that Oxenfree delivers.

An emotional, thought provoking 2D walking simulator spinning an excellent story over light but competent gameplay.
Pros:
- Deep, well realized characters (mostly, one is just passable)
- Excellent voice acting, really bringing the story and characters to life. I was constantly reluctant to interrupt other's dialogue with my own
- Intriguing and thought provoking story, perfectly paced and woven masterfully
- Choices and their resulting impacts feel organic and honest
- Eye catching 2d art style and backgrounds
- Interesting collectables that add to the story; I was perfectly happy to spend an extra hour trekking about the world, looking for the ones I'd missed.
- The John Carpenter inspired melodies perfectly compliment the tone and feel of the game, great music
- The ending leaves you wanting more, with the definite draw of multiple playthroughs
Cons:
- Choosing an option often cuts off NPCs dialogue (which I wanted to hear), but waiting too long leaves the protagonist silent (also unwanted). By the end I had timing down where I could catch my option at the last moment, so I could have the best of both worlds. Just wish it didn't have to be that hard
- Characters move so slowly that exploration can be a slog
This is a well paced, masterful story bound to the player's hand that flows organically and with impact. Any player looking for a gameplay-light, story-heavy experience will find more than their money's worth here.
8/10

This review is for a very early version of the game and I shall update the review as major updates are introduced.
Oort online is one of the best games to come out of Early access for a long time. Although it pains me to do it I have to compare it to Minecraft in it's basic gameplay, that being voxal and building. However unlike Minecraft the look of the game is much what you would expect from a modern game. While that gives you a great explination of the basic resource gathering and construction mechanics it doesn't give you even a glimer into the way the game really works so I will try to.
The game is split into servers which are called 'Worlds' and each world is very unique in the way it looks and the types of resources you can find there in. While often players will have a 'Homeworld' to stay in to construct whatever massive building or impressive landscapes it is really intresting and one of the best single features of the games to explore the other worlds to find diffrent blocks for your buildings. However while wondering around a world of ice and snow and then a forest of sky touching trees is amazing in itself one of the best experiences is stumbling across other peoples constructions. I wondered around a world and found a stone bridge followed the bridge which was huge going from the top of a mountain held up by massive stone pillers coming out of a lake. At the end of the bridge I reach a massive days-to-build castle built in a cathedral style with massive glass windows and a huge hall lit with lanterns and a glass ceiling from which the sun streamed through at the right point of the day, the whole thing visable from miles around.
In one world you can find my Shinto Arch towering out of a watery world filled with lakes and mountains and at night the lanterns shimer, lighting it in the darkness.
That if only that makes Oort online not only beautiful for its stunning landscapes but for the buildings others build adding to the overal experience of the game and with the features being planned and readily worked on (Players are kept updates on the work being done which is great) makes Oort online a must buy game even in it's early state.
If you want to wait a bit longer for the game to have more of the freatures planned, add it to your wishlist but I would suggest buying the game right now and even if production stopped right now I would still get hours and hours of enjoyment out of the game easily.

One of the biggest concerns I see is that people think this is a minecraft clone. What no one really gets is that voxel building games have morphed into their own category of game. This game is similar to minecraft in that there are blocks, and you mine / craft / build with those blocks. That's about where the similarity ends. Legitimately great games like this one get canned all the time just because they're voxel games, and I for one hope this one makes it through. Minecraft was a great game, but it also had it's flaws. This game fixes a lot of the complaints I had about minecraft, and then goes on to implement some amazing and promising systems.
The movement in this game is stellar, and that coupled with the amazing ambient sounds and whooshing that you get when you move fast makesan immersive feel that is pretty awesome. The smoothness of flying through the air on a grapling hook is amazing. The customizability of the terrain is another great feature of this game. There's a lot more options for great landscapes than there were in minecraft's procedurally generated stuff. Overall oort is already a better game than minecraft and deserves to reach fruition.
This game has a strong group of devs working very hard and pushing out new updates rapidly (and it looks completely gorgeous). That, more than anything else, is why i chose to buy this game in early access. There's a really nice feel to the game right now, and the community is great, mostly because of how responsive and interactive the devs are. That is why i feel this game will be here to stay, and will reach it's final form (which will be glorious). Buying in now will give you the opportunity to help sculpt this game into something amazing (even better than it already is)!

All in all, it is already a great game to develop game-sense and teamwork, but one can fully enjoy the full option of the underlying framework when the official release is out. This game builds a terrific world in it's alt-1960 universe. Not just the Nazi-infestation, but the varied cast of characters you live and die with that form the backdrop of our hero's adventure. Great voice acting, terrific story. For me, it was an 11-hour nearly non-stop campaign that I had to see through to completion.
No multiplayer, but that's hardly an issue for me. This was well worth it.
PROS:
* Amazing alt-1960 story
* Stunning graphics -- some screenshots practially look like art.
* Wonderful soundtrack; subtle, but when it kicks in... damn.
* Game splits into two 'timelines' depending on a (very tough) early choice. This has a minor ripple effect throughout the rest of the game. Playthrough averages about 11 hours for one 'timeline'.
* Holy cow, this game visits almost every location you can imagine. I won't even spoil it.
CONS:
* Horrid texture and asset pop-in (like RAGE), but there are ways to minimize this that I won't get into. Google it.
* Additionally, textures sometimes do not load full-res. Or worse, some objects will render half with full quality, and the bottom half (for example) at low quality. Sometimes entire walls just stay low quality. And the compression artifacts stand out. (I did not try turning off texture compression in the graphics settings -- YMMV.)
* The game can sometimes be cheap by spawning in enemies behind you, even after you THINK you've cleared a room. This is incredibly unfair, but I found the best thing to do in those particular battles is to just try and RUN through and get to the marker.
4.5/5

I don't know who'd not buy the game. It's amazing. And of course, has Sonic and all of your favorite characters!
GENERAL:
Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed gives you 3 ways to play; alone, with people from all around the world, and at private party. And there's even more ways to play when you play solo. Giving you alot of hours to play for your amusement!
CONTENT:
You got 30+ characters in this platform. Yes, 30 characters, including the DLC and the unlockable characters from your favorite titles: Sonic, Super Monkey Ball, and so much more! And you can play with them on over 40 tracks. That's alot of combinations there. And it dosen't stop there, you get 5 gamemodes to play with, the combinations are HUGE here.
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is divine. It's like SEGA learned from it's mistakes from SEGA All Stars Racing ancestor and remade it into a more original creation. It's nothing like Mario Kart at all, where you must get OP items to win. If you play alone, you can progress through the game, collect and upgrade your characters! And some singleplayer portions are difficult. It's mechanics are also great. Don't like playing alone? Play online and show the world what you're made of!
WEAKNESSES AND CONCERNS:
There are problems with this game though, no matter how good it is. First being is that to win, you have to rely on one mechanic: Powerful boostings at a rapid rate. You'll never have a decent Time Attack record without a powerful character. I.E. Shadow with Dreamcast mod is one of them. But if you're skilled, you shouldn't have alot of problems with that.
Another concern about this is the server. Though the community is friendly, the servers you're gonna play in, will never be. As you're mixed with these new guys, and real MLG players, and some of them may have bad connection, causing an unbearable amount of crashing into walls and such. Even MLG players suffer from that.
Yet another concern is the aftermath, and I mean what happens now when you beat the game, although I like this game, I, at one point, abandoned it because of how usual it is. But I returned to it in a few months after.
One of my worries are also being about the tracks, although there's 42 tracks at most, the other 21 is  just mirrored.
Last one is about one of the mechanics: The Casino. Chances are in a race, you could get a crappy thing, but a really good one is actually rare. I.E. The useless Nitro is often, but the best ones, like Titanium Frame or Stunt Nitro is almost impossible.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
To be honest, I love the game, it has alot of potential. But I wish that the developers could realise it. But then again, they might be working on something that could beat this. You should get it at full price, but if you take the problems seriously, then maybe at 20-40% off. I give it a 8.9/10

Don't let the 'hours played' deceive, I've been a veteran of Rimworld since the days of Alpha 5, more than 2 years ago now. At the time Rimworld was a simple little game, there was no medical system, no pets, no social interactions or relationships, just a combat system and a bunch of things your little pawns could build and clean. And at the time, I had payed 40 dollars for this tiny game that I had only heard about from a lone gameplay video.
And I'll be damned if it wasn't the best 40 dollars I've ever spent.
Rimworld is a tale of constant improvement. Every update brings forth new mechanics and features that continue to amaze me months later, Tynan and his team silently working to deliver even more depth to an amazingly complex game. It's early access, sure, but Ludeon has gone and redefined what early access was all about in the first place. There's no panhandling or promises or strechgoals that are arbitrarily placed based on how many people buy this game, there's just updates, which substantial and unannounced. Tynan is taking the exact amount of time he needs to ensure that each installation is as inspired as the last, and that's something I can truly respect. The early access tag isn't here in an effort to drum up support and money for the studio, it's here so that as many people as possible can experience what a wonderful gem this game is.
And if the definition of 'gem' isn't a game in which your pyromaniac doctor can harvest a liver from a peg-legged fashion designer-turned-bandit, to pay for your chef's crippling drug addiction all whilst a nudist high school teacher struggles to fend off a swarm of giant mutant scarabs using a club made from solid gold, I don't know what is.

It's okay.  It's your standard shooter in terms of mechanics and weapons.  You've got the bulk of infantry weapons being auto-fire with all of those being only effective up to mid-range around 30-40m.  Some have less range and a generally higher fire rate for close quarters yet few, if any, have more range than previously mentioned.  Then there's your shotguns which have a max damage-producing range of about 20m unless you get slug ammo which increases the max by five to ten meters.  Overall, they fire reasonably fast and have reasonable accuracy for video game shotguns, these are the things you use to clear bunkers of enemies as you're in close.  Then there's the semi-auto and bolt action rifles, these are long to very-long ranges and are usually only used by the infiltrator(sniper) class.  Fairly-high to very-high damage, usually slowest of the weapons to fire and reload.
Overall, your standard shooter kits and options, nothing exciting.
Where the more interesting bits come is in the special ability each class has.  For instance, the heavy assault has a toggleable secondary overshield that can either absorb shots or reduce damage taken, the infiltrator can turn virtually invisible while crouching and not moving and remains fairly difficult to see while moving, the engineer can quickly repair vehicles, the medic can heal and revive team mates, the light assault has a jet pack, and the MAX is a big ol powered armor that's effective at combating air, infantry, and armor, though there are, of course, more effective options for air and armor.
You can build bases with defenses, fly a small variety of aircraft, and support with a small variety of armor including a main battle tank that's unique per faction, and other various light armors which all factions have that include things such as a light tank, a light turret-mounted jeep-like low-capacity transport, a 4-wheeled ATV, and a double-turreted lightly armored troop transport/spawner. Overall, despite any percieved armor you'll find everything pretty easy to explode with the right weapons and that the "right weapons" are pretty easy to come by, mobility and placing is your best defense (as always.)
While there are four contients to play on it's rather likely you'll only see one or two unless you play for an extended session beyond four hours.   Unlike how it used to be you can only play on one continent at a time and once that continent is won by a faction only one other continent ever unlocks.  Each continent gives a special and pretty decent bonus to whatever faction locked it down and locking a continent down can be done in multiple ways which we won't go through here.
Overall the combat is fast paced but impossibly repetitive, the repetitive nature becomes even more obvious if you aren't in the middle of a warzone and have even two seconds to stop and think.  There's no real winners or losers here, everything comes full circle eventually.  At some point it may be faction purple that has all the other continents on lockdown, at another point it may be faction blue, then another point it may be faction red.  It's less common to see the continents split, yet it does happen, however it's really rare to see it split where one faction has each locked down one continent.
The developers add things every once in a while, however, in general, they aren't things that the standard player will ever get to without pumping a few hundred or thousand hours into the game.  Experience for the standard player is 4 times up to 8 times LESS than a "member" player (even if you spend money on the game) and prices for microtransactions are actually INCREASED if you're not a member.  This means that the currency which unlocks things like new weapons or new class-specific items such as an engineer's turrets or buildable wall will take you a large amount of play sessions to even get close to unlocking, and that's if you play fairly long play sessions and are good enough to get these xp-earned currencies through both a large amount of kills and support.
Of course, the game cuts your XP the more you play, so don't play too much if you want rewarded for your time.  Events are pretty much only for members, discounts are only for members, virtually anything advertized is only for members.  You could spend thousands of dollars and still get treated by♥♥♥♥♥♥ 'cause if you aren't paying that sweet sub money Daybreak doesn't really care about you.  There's no premium which lessens the xp penalties or the like for people that spend money, there's only "♥♥♥♥ you, buy our sub" and "keep buying our sub."
There's a lot of ups and downs with this game, for your standard player you'll probably find it REALLY amusing and fun for the first couple of weeks at which point you'll either decide to member up or the fun will start to really wear off.  Membering up really is the only viable way of progressing and getting the weapons and options you want, after all.  Overall I wouldn't suggest playing this game just because it's been done a million times and what makes it unique isn't really impressive enough to warrant playing this over one of the newer more modern titles and, that is unless you're looking to get a shooter fix and don't have one that people are still playing and can't spend money on one, at which point you'll be able to shoot things just fine, but once that itch is scratched it's very unlikely you'll want to play again until that itch comes back.

Do you like to experience joy when you play games? Have you ever wanted to see your carefully designed civilization turn into a smoldering ruin because the guy handling explosives went on a psychotic rampage? Have you ever wanted to harvest the organs of a prisoner? Have you ever wanted to harvest the organs of a fellow colonist? Have you ever gotten really hungry and decided that the pet dog looked really appetizing? Do you like base-building games that are pretty much just amazing all around? If your answer to any of these questions is "yes", then I highly recommend RimWorld.  If you answered "no" to all of these questions, you are the reason why we can't have nice things.

Pros;
- Excellent voice acting work
- The art looks nice and is consistent
- The story keeps you guessing at what is real and maintains interest
- The characters are decently set up and have both strengths and weaknesses as people
- The conversation options liven things up a bit and keep you engaged

Cons;

- In the scope of things, it's pretty short

- Price is arguable- despite some incredible work, mostly because it lacks replayability and is short.
- Doesn't quite reach its potential in plot/character development, despite great foundation.
This game did not particularly strike much interest in me at first until I saw the first 10 minutes of gameplay, when I decided it would be interesting to check out. All in all, I think this title did have a lasting impression on me. While it doesn't quite grasp the heart and soul of teenage life, it does a pretty good job and between the voice acting and the character development, I was pretty invested in all of the characters even if I wanted to hate them (Clarissa). I have to comment again on the writing though, at times it really did feel unnatural, particularly Ren's dialogue has moments where it's extremely inorganic. Not all of the dialogue is like this, but it breaks immersion and investment when it does happen.
The gameplay is definitely not a key feature, it is essentially an interactive story. I'm really glad that there were varying chat options influencing conversation to break up what would have been monotonous walking. That said, the story didn't need to be an undertone for sophisticated gameplay, so I think this was a really good direction and was effective at delivering the story at a good pace, and keeping interest.
The sense of mystery was well presented, I feel like if even more focus was put into mystery and puzzle solving it really could have kicked this title up to top quality stuff. As is though, it does keep things interesting and keep you guessing at what is going on and what is/isn't real. The radio things with tuning into stuff and unlocking doors was interesting and unique, I feel as though it could have been fleshed out further.
Truthfully, I'd like to see a more fleshed out version of this game and I'd be happy to pay a matching price tag for that content. By the end, I really wanted to be more invested in the characters and know more about what had happened. A lot of their history gets hinted at or briefly mentioned. I'd like to see a longer game where those histories would go into higher detail, and characters would mingle and develop/destroy relationships with each other as the game progresses. The gameplay could be expanded on too, the scavenge hunts were too simplistic and the coded hints too obvious. If there were an extra layer of secrets to discover for those more clever and perceptive, this game would feel much more rewarding and worth exploring. I feel like the developers really have something going here that could be made into something much bigger and stronger of a title.
All in all, Oxenfree was a really well-presented short story of some teenagers going to an island for some fun and having a strange and sometimes scary adventure. I think it is worth checking out or at least picking it up on sale. The developers did a good job in just about every aspect, although there's some weakness in the writing and the game could have easily been twice as long with deeper story and greater mysteries/puzzles to become a truly competitive title.

This game is intense. I do not typically care for things designed to scare you. I first heard about this game when I was listening to a lot of game music, it is on Spotify, check it out. The soundscapes are very cool, they provide the perfect atmosphere for this crazy adventure. Audio is so important in the game. When the only choices you have involve what to say, everything you hear seems to become so much more important. All of the background art is so beautiful; the whole package is just so immersive.
This is a very standard adventure game, or so it feels. You don't really have to collect things and use them to solve your problems. In fact there were no "puzzles" where I couldn't immediately figure out what to do. Everything you need to interact with is clearly labeled as you walk up to it. There never a question of “where do I go now?” because your next objective is clearly marked on the map. That doesn’t mean this game is easy. There were a few times when I just didn’t know what to say, a few times when I just… couldn’t say. Once the incident happens on the island, things are slowly revealed to you, so slowly that when things start to go really wrong that you feel like you have gone crazy in real life. There were some times when I knew just what to say but the natural flow of conversation kept me from jumping in. There were times when I regretted what I said. And there was one time when I thought I remembered what I said, but then I couldn’t remember and started to freak out a little. But mostly the lives of these teenagers had me on the edge of my seat. I felt as if I could be on this crazy island with these kids on the verge of a mysterious danger. There were a couple of times when I actually stopped playing because my heart was beating so fast.
This game is very cool. It is a nice slow pace that builds up tension until you are just about to scream. Some of the pacing was off on the conversations, I ended up turning subtitles on because some of the dialog is halting and difficult to understand, but that made it worse because it created much longer pauses between speakers. This last part is pretty vague, you’ll probably be fine without subtitles, but once you get to the… things, you’ll understand. Or maybe you won’t and you’ll have to turn the subtitles on like I did.

All I can say for now (because it is still in its ver yearly stages) is that Oort Online is very beautiful and atmospheric. In this game, I feel adventurous and free. The mechanics so far are very fluid. If you want to support a good game, this is a great, solid choice.

It sounds like a winning blend to me. I’ve always found Arma a little over-encumbered with the fussiness of its many possibilities; the effort to account for a huge breadth of interaction undercuts the ease and finesse of any one experience. Meanwhile, recent Battlefield games – partly a victim of their own success – have veered further towards run-n-gun fun without the time or space for the articulation of strategy. Squad, I think, does a decent job of straddling the middle-ground, even though many features, like vehicles and reliably operable deployment interfaces, are yet to be implemented. Weapons behave with supposed realism (I wouldn’t know) but downed colleagues can be relatively easily revived. Strategy emerges from the game’s particular approach to squad-spawning: squad leaders have to build spawn points to ensure that your frontline is fed with a regular supply of new bodies. These dissolve when contested, preventing teams from simply dropping a gunman-spewing spawn-point on the enemy’s doorstep and meaning that the spawn points need to be placed with some considerable thought: close enough to the fray that they give your forces forward momentum, but not so close that any loss of ground will wipe them from the field. Of course, different squads will have to coordinate their strategies to good effect, pincering enemies or driving at a single point en masse.
Discounting the (not terribly instructive) training mode, there are three types of match. Advance and Secure, in which the two teams are engaged in a tug of war over a linear sequence of capture points, will be familiar to Battlefield players. It, like its analogue in Battlefield, runs on a ticket system, whereby the teams exhaust a finite number of respawns. Then there’s Insurgency, which sets one team on the hunt to destroy five weapons caches, the locations of which are only revealed as you kill enemies. The other team wins by either protecting these caches for the time limit or depleting the tickets of the opposing team. The final mode sees the US forces try to capture a number of locations in any order – which are then permanently in their possession. The defenders must dig in and try to outlast the assault.

After overclocking Intel® Pentium® Processor G3258, I thought I wouldn't be trying to overclock my GPU because of limited power supply (225w).
I went on and tried using EVGA PrecisionX 16 to overclock my GTX 750 Ti. First thing I did was to set its clock to 1500MHz (damn, they sure came up with pretty interesting and trivial achievements just for this overclocking utility). It obviously didn't turn out well, the screen froze and I had to restart my computer. After a lot of tinkering, tests, and restarts, I was able to come up with some decent overclocks (from 1241MHz to 1438MHz GPU boost clock and from 2750MHz to 3004MHz memory clock). I didn't have much time to test but the performance gains were noticeable, as I played TESV Skyrim and ETS2, drops in frame rate were reduced. I also got over 9% more 3DMark Firestrike
. All of these without changing voltages and with just turning the fan control to aggressive, temps never went over 60°C.
I believe the software works for anything Nvidia, it is easy to use. As was in the description, it can set GPU Clock Offsets, Memory Clock Offsets, Fan Speed, voltage, etc. The On-screen display is really neat and useful for
frame rate, clocks, memory usage, and temperature while in game. EVGA also has its own benchmark tool which can be connected to this utility.
As of writing, profile saving features for clocks and fan settings seems to be not working well so I might try and use the version which is available directly from the publisher's website. I'd still recommend that you try and use this utility if you don't already have any software to use for overclocking any Nvidia GPU (just proceed with caution as any damage done are likely to be irreversible and you'll only have yourself to blame).

The game felt really clunky and slow at first, but there's a combat mechanics guide made by one of the devs that turned the game on its head for me. It really changed how I felt about the game and it made it a whole lot more fun. I think if it was advertised as a rogue-like sidescrolling brawler, it'd have gotten more attention in its time, so as to get across the idea that it's unforgiving.
The game has a combo counter but it never goes very high, but it's actually quite nice that way. Each hit feels heavier and more satisfying, that even a 5 hit combo is something to be happy about. That said, there are 10+ hit combos but it takes a bit of work. The game feels clunky at first but there's a curve that needs to be passed, it seems.
It's like how people complained that Playstation All Stars (though it does have major flaws) was just a button-mashing mess when they couldn't even perform an AP Burst combo, so it became widespread that real combos weren't a thing you could really do.
After getting used to the game's mechanics it's really fun, but it's a shame that the story seems to take a back seat to everything else. I love the aesthetic and the characters and wish I knew more about them. There could have been so many layers of mystery and intrigue that it feels like a lost opportunity.
More enemy and level diversity would have been nice, too, even if it's enemies we couldn't transform into.
Anyways, I enjoy the game a lot. I wish it got a sequel that would do it justice, but pick this game up if you have the chance- maybe wait for a sale if you have to.

Complete and utter garbage in every aspect.
Let's start with simple things: moving. Moving around in this game is awful. It's like you're holding your character on a leash and pulling her around the screen. She will often refuse to turn around, pushing her back against a ledge instead of grabbing it, or swinging her rapier on the opposite direction that you meant her too. Jumping is a pain: you have a double jump but you have to hold the button as long as possible before hitting it a second time in order to reach the maximum height; even a couple frames less than that will make you miss most jumps. You do have a high jump, the command for which is down+jump, which is the same command you can use to jump down passable ledges. Have fun with that.
All enemies are the same: hp sponges that spend all their time turtling.
They read your inputs and react with frame-perfect precision to what you're doing.
Despite all that, the game still manages to be extremely simple and boring, since your grab attack never fails and is the only reliable way to damage enemies, bosses included.
Controls are redundant. You can attack in every direction with the right stick, or by hitting X and a direction on the left stick. This means that each character has four different attacks (neutral, forward, up, down), all of which are barely different and only serve to make you whiff most attacks.
You can dodge by holding block and tapping a direction, or by tapping the bumpers. Most enemies recover from whiffed attacks before you recover from your roll, though, especially considering that hitting the attack button after a roll results in YET ANOTHER pointless, slow attack that will whiff whenever it comes out and you don't expect it.
You can grab enemies by pushing B or by pushing X while blocking. Yes, you will whiff a grab when attempting a counter attack after blocking.
Despite all that redundancy, special moves are confined to Y + direction in much the same way as Smash Bros games. You have a stick, two bumpers, a trigger and a face button with redundant functions, and yet your most useful and customizable attacks require an awkward button combination to pull off. Control customization options are no help in this regard.
The roguelike elements are garbage, too. I was always finding the same crap over and over again - weapons meant for other characters I hadn't unlocked, merchants selling useless crap at ridiculous prices, and skill tree altars that grant you the marvelous ability to manage your damn skills.
All these things mixed together form an extremely luck-based experience: you have to hope that the AI will decide to not dodge your attack. You have to hope that you will find a weapon you can actually use. You have to hope you will find respawn tokens so you don't have to start from the beginning when you die.
A grueling slog that I wouldn't wish on my middle school bullies.

This is a dungeon crawler grinder and I haven't been so frustrated with a game in a long time. The way the game is, you really need to weigh the importance of your options and decisions. When you die, the game punishes you: you drop all of your items (including your weapon), and have to start over in the dungeon (the abyss), unless you use a camp token, which will allow you to respawn at a marked camp. However, camp tokens are expensive (I think the cheapest is 4,000 or so gold), and all of your items and your weapon will be gone. Which means any gold you spent on those items is wasted. Luckily, you get to keep the gold you earn, so I recommend grinding to level up your character to at least level 35 and to have a good 40,000-50,000 gold.
At times, the platforming is atrocious, which I think is more so the fault of the controls. The way the keyboard controls are is annoying. The controls aren't really explained, if not cryptic, I accidentally skipped the prologue and have no way to go back to it unless I restart the entire game (I think). Sometimes the controls get...confused? I'm not sure how to describe it, but I'll try to jump down, but instead jump up. Sometimes double jumping is a chore.
I didn't figure out how to Soul Capture (which is holding down your normal attack button and your special attack button at the same time i.e. left and right mouse buttons) until I was level 40 and about 10 hours into the game.
Battles can get repetitive and annoying. I think it would be nice to see the level of your enemies, as opposed to having to guess and then get killed and have to start all over. ESPECIALLY when it comes to Soul Capture-you cannot capture the soul of an enemy unless you are of an equal or greater level.
The inventory and menus can be annoying to navigate as well.
I think what really kept me going was the art. The character models, particularly the enemies, are very nice and modelled very well. The backgrounds and environments were also very well-put together artistically and the art direction in this game is solid. The consistency in the style and tone is quite nice, and the blend of Chilean culture and art nuveau was an interesting but overall good combination.
I did have a good laugh though-the mummy enemy design is directly based off a Harry Clarke illustration for the Edgar Allan Poe story, "Fall of the House of Usher". The demon Paganini is also based off a real person, Niccolo Paganini, and they were pretty accurate with his physical depiction (MUTTON CHOPS) although I feel the evil bad demon man cliche they have for him makes him an obnoxious character.
I think the developers were more focused on the art and story, and the gameplay suffers from it. It's not unplayable, persay, but there are a lot of small annoying issues that test your patience as a player. Overall, I think it's a relatively solid game that just needs more work on the gameplay mechanics, less vagueness on controls and maybe a bit more gameplay variety as well. I think the difficulty also really alientates and limits the games' audience.
If you can get past the flaws and issues, it's a nice game. Not amazing, but also not bad.

With fantastic music, levels with incredible contrast, and gameplay so amazingly well built, you would be missing out one of the greatest and most fun multiplayer port one could think of. For your own sake, and the sake of realising that high quality games still exists, you need this game more than you think.

As someone who has never played LoL or DOTA I feel that this game is a wonderful introduction into the MOBA genre. It has simple concepts that are easily graspible and the crafting, while some people view it as a waste of time, is still easy and kind of does something. A little bit. I for one celebrate their differences and commend the makers for trying (with relative success) to revolutionize the DOTA/LoL field.
Bottom line:
Strife is not a perfect game, but it has my thumbs up. It didn't take hours or even days to learn to play effectively and you have a wide variety of players to really fit your personal play style. This is an 2-D puzzle/platforming game that looks like it came from the SNES era of games. You are a goat trying to escape each room by solving the puzzles.  All you can do is jump, head-butt things or get some help from a little mouse who is also trying to escape. It's similar to the original Lode Runner or Montezuma's Revenge (or more recently Spelunky). The graphics look old school but the gameplay is really well done and the music is a lot of fun. They've also made it really easy to start over if you mess up one of the puzzles.
Since it was made for the XBox 360 it's got very good controller support but you could probably play it with the mouse and keyboard if you wanted. They've also got a Linux and Mac OS version too, which is pretty cool.
Definitely worth checking out if you're in the mood for some arcade fun.

Just a massive procedurally generated world, and nobody really knew what to expect from it. Oort has the same feel for me, its a massive world, i should say a massive collection of massive worlds. Each one looks distinctly different and im always intrigued to see what formations i might see over the next hill. Player population is sparse so it often times feel like i actually am an explorer, and the few player houses i find are the relics of a long lost age. For me i enjoy the simplicity, though i am eager for the new features to be added. I have faith in the developers, for what its worth, and i trust they will bring this project to fruition. That being said, i can tell this game has a long way to go. If you want to support a group of developers, and provide feedback, then by all means contribute to this project. If you'd rather play Oort online, then give it a while. At the moment, theres just not much to do. But that being said, there was never anyhting to do in minecraft(inf-dev) and it kept many of us hooked.

So after a few comments on my old review kept saying "this review is old and most of these features are out of date" I decided to take another look at Boundless. In short, my "old" review was still completely revelent besides 2 or 3 additions.
► WHAT'S NEW?
● GRAPHICS: Just before I quit playing Oort Online (Boundless' old title), the game had a texture swap that made it look a lot sharper at the cost of performance. It doesn't seem like they did anything for optimization from then to now which sucks because the already small community got a lot smaller when half of them couldn't run the game anymore.
● SERVERS: Still laggy and have you teleport around a lot. Careful not to fall off your build.
● COMMUNITY: Dead. This game has completely lost relevancy. Try looking up Boundless on YouTube.
● CRAFTING: Last time I played, the basic crafting system was being implemented. It wasn't bad, but when they put it in you went from spawning with a ton of blocks to spawning with nothing and having to craft your blocks. No change from then to now besides the menu looking better.
● COMBAT: "Enemy" creatures are new to me. You can fight them, but you just walk up to them and spam click until they die. They don't drop anything either, they only seem to increase the chances of being killed and losing all your blocks.
● MOVEMENT: Running around is still the same.. sticky. Mostly because of lag. I'm really surprised how hard the Grappling Hook was nerfed though. You used to be able to hang from a block and shoot another rope WHILE hanging, but now your character simply let's go and starts falling with a short delay before you can shoot another rope.
● RACES: I remember when "different playable races and perks" was all the devs talked about when I stopped playing. It was the next big feature they were working on and they even showed 3 different characters in a video that each played differently.
Like most indie games, these characters never saw the light of day. You can pick how you character looks now, but that's it.
● BUILDING: No improvements here. Building is worse then when I played because getting around takes longer (due to the nerfed grappling hook) and you have to craft all your blocks (you don't spawn with any).
Oort Online might be called Boundless now, but I still can't recommend it. Devs seemed to take all the money they earned so they could release the game on PS4. Maybe their publisher will push them to make a decent game.
I don't like putting out negative reviews, but really.. play SkySaga, Trove or Minecraft instead.

Drunk-Fu: Wasted Masters – PC
Drunk-Fu: Wasted Masters es un título de luchas que actualmente se encuentra en Early Access en la plataforma Steam y se publicó en fase Alpha el 7 de abril de 2017. Este juego es de tipo Bear ‘em up o Brawler, el cual debemos pelear contra otros jugadores (todos borrachos) para ver quien es el mejor.
El Juego
Somos un borracho y matón,  muy alcoholizado y nos ponen en escena dentro de un salón lleno de otros borrachines como nosotros. Se inicia una discusión que termina en un combate a puños; la única manera de salir victoriosos es dejarlos inconscientes a todos. A la hora de las partidas, Drunk-Fu: Wasted Masters nos permite utilizar varios objetos como un martillo, llave inglesa, bate, un banco y una palanca, además puede usar cosas pequeñas de los mapas tales como sillas, bancos entre otros con el fin de hacerle daño al contrincante.
Hay 3 modos de juego, Last Man Standing: Consiste en que todos los jugadores o bots deben golpearse, los que quedan noqueados serán eliminados así hasta que un ultimo hombre quede en pie  y será el ganador. Endless Mode: En este la lucha es infinita, pueden golpearse hasta que pierdan la razón pero unos segundos más tarde el enemigo se levantará, igualmente lo podemos hacer nosotros. Finalmente el Modo Swarm: en una sala con varios de jugadores pero sólo dos se encuentran luchando, cuando alguno de ellos caiga, inmediatamente otro podrá unirse al combate libre.
Multijugador
Actualmente (Alpha Pub 2017.4.12) no funciona el online, pero si puedes invitar a tus amigos en una partida hosteada o unirte un amigo tuyo; el modo competitivo local también funciona.
Editor de Personaje
Un aspecto muy positivo es esta opción, la cual nos permite modificar la apariencia de tu luchador alcohólico, se editar el color de piel desde lo más clara a la mas oscura,  también los artículos que lleven en la cabeza como gafas, gorras y mascaras y por ultimo su ropa como camisa, pantalones y zapatos.
Pros
El juego es muy divertido para jugar con amigos y familiares, ya que la forma en que se mueven golpean, etc, lo hace muy gracioso y se puede pasar horas jugando. También el atrás mencionado editor del personaje. Otro es que sus mapas están bien elaborados y decorados lo que hace un ambiente mas agradable para el gameplay.
Contras
Como si mencionó anteriormente, el multijugador parece no funcionar correctamente, además sus controles en teclado y mando son un poco complicados. La temática del juego es “tipos borrachos luchando”,  pero en realidad la “lucha” es muy pobre, debido a que tanto nustro personaje, como los demás jugadores se mueven de manera irregular, haciendo la jugabilidad muy lenta, provocando que se torne algo aburrido y repetitivo.
Conclusiones
En nuestra opinión al título le falta muchísimo por delante ya que es relativamente nuevo, pero creemos que posee mucho potencial que puede ser explotado en un futuro. Drunk-Fu: Wasted Masters es un juego desarrollado por el estudio independiente Rusto, tiene un precio de $4.99 en la tienda digital de Valve,También está disponible para Android y iOS.

The tutorial is much better than the hand holding that most city/base builder games give you when you start a new campaign. For those other games, you only have the choice of turning your tutorials on and off, while they nudge you in the direction they want you to go. In RimWorld, the tutorial only pops up when you come across an event that you haven't encountered before. And then it never shows up again, unless you want it to.
The gameplay flows very well. You begin with simple mechanics, and then as the game goes on, it becomes a more and more complex balancing issue. Rather than solving problems as they arise, RimWorld essentially forces you to prevent problems before they happen. This requires a lot of pre-planning, making sure to keep you on your toes.
You will face challenges such as weather conditions, sickness, and of course, the occasional enemy. Trade is an available option to you, and there are times when the game's "storyteller" will bring in a trade vessel at the desperate moment your colony is about to fall apart. The storyteller is a built-in mechanic which selects a series of events for you, and interlaces them into the gameplay seamlessly.
There are multiple difficulty options, and a further set of nuances which determine a situational difficulty level when you start the game. As you select your difficulty, you will also select an area on the world map for your colonists to land. The area can be a frigid tundra with little to no fertile soil, or even an arid desert which constantly gives your colonists heat stroke. Even further than this, your colony could be exposed to the open air, or safely tucked away inside a mountain.
Sound and graphics are decent for what they are. Everything is simple enough to the point where you can tell what is what, and then make a quick decision based on that.
The game does support mods, and many of the mods add levels upon levels of extended entertainment to the game. You can find the mods on RimWorld's forums.
I would recommend this game for people who enjoy city/base builders. There is a lot to offer.
I wouldn't recommend this game for people who don't like micromanagement or extended planning.

Quite an amazing game.
Such an ambitious story concept, and while it has some problems it actually tells a very interesting sci-fi story (but in a contemporary human context) and, as far as I was concerned, sticks the landing, woven through a fairly intense and lengthy puzzler.
The puzzles are very well crafted with a bunch of interesting mechanics that they make great use of.
I would say that some of the philosophical dialogue was a little frustrating because they want to explore some deep concepts, but the limits of the format meant that at times there were no 'pre cooked' responses that I felt was even close to what I wanted to express.  Given the limitations of how this was written/scripted this is not surprising, and I heartily commend them for trying - and for mostly succeeding at such an ambitious task.
My only other quibble is a technology one - something about the rendering/motion control was just a little motion-sickness inducing - not severely, but after a while playing I did get a touch of a headache/slight queasiness.  I don't get this often, so it was a bit surprising, and it might be something to do with my system etc.  Perhaps just take it in slightly smaller doses with frequent breaks.
Oh, and it's not particularly forgiving of making certain choices ... make sure you've done everything you want to do before you do certain things.  I had to replay most of the game because I wanted to see what the outcome might be at a particularly important point toward the end of the game.
The central puzzling game is great, the high concept story is impressively realized, and surprisingly moving in parts.
Thorougly recommended.

It's still in it's beta stages but it's not as early as it was a year ago when they only had 14 heroes.

The End is Nigh. It's an insanely difficult platformer just like Super Meat Boy, but it has one key difference: You can't wall jump! This defines the game, and is more fun than it sounds. Because the game centers around hanging on ledges and boost-jumping off of them.
Just like Super Meat Boy, precise controls aid you in your efforts to overcome ridiculous platforming challenges. However, it never overwhelms you with this absurd challenge at first. The game, for the most part, starts at a "moderate" difficulty then very slowly ramps up. Introducing you to harder and harder challenges that are perfectly doable. Even the most absurd platforming problems require subtle button presses and nuanced use of movement, in order to beat them.
The End is Nigh has more value than it seems. Not only does it have a ton of collectible and "adorable" tumors, which are more important than you think, the game has tons of other secrets to find. You'll spend quite a few hours searching for them, and you'll eventually get good enough to traverse the levels to find them all. The game really DOES have over 600 levels in total!
This game doesn't progress like a normal platforming game, such as Super Meat Boy, where you have to SELECT your individual levels. Each world can be selected from a map, but the individual levels within these worlds behave like one big long path. With forks in the road leading to goodies and secrets. You traverse between these worlds via teleporters. In fact, the entire game is one giant path that... almost looks like a pitchfork, due to 3 branching ways you can go.
Visually, the game looks quite good! The signature artstyle is here, with beautiful effects that look rather impressive despite the relatively primitive artstyle. In a way, this game is charming with its morbid atmosphere and sense of humor. There's something almost whimsical about the dark and bleak world of The End is Nigh. Technically, there doesn't seem to be anything wrong, and you have all the options you could want at your disposal, including solid video options.
What makes The End is Nigh so brilliant is that sheer satisfaction you get from beating tough segments. Just like in Edmund McMillen's amazing Super Meat Boy, beating the toughest challenges and secrets will give you a serious amount of "gamer cred". Whatever such a thing is even worth.
The only thing truly hampering this game is the difficulty. If you hate "rage platformers', please for the love of black blobs everywhere, just stay way. But if you're a masochist who gets sick pleasure out of being satisfied from beating tough platformers, this game is highly reccomended!

To appease the nit-pickers who'll complain about a review any more complex than a list of pros and cons, I'll keep this review short and simple.

-Rich Evans is a good voice actor.
-Jumping on enemies/projectiles is fun.
-The game has EXTREMELY basic physics; far less fun than what anyone would expect from a game made in 2017, let alone a game made by the same guy who made Super Meat Boy. Nothing makes it stand out aside from the fact that you can jump off of ledges, which isn't exactly anything worth writing home about.
-The second half of the game has lives, and resets your progress once you run out. Lives in a game like this aren't fun, they're just a lazy, tedious way to pad out the game's length. It doesn't make the game any harder, it just makes it more annoying.
-Said lives are based on the amount of tumors you've collected through the first half of the game, which is something you're never told, meaning that if you want more lives, you'll have to go back and play through any incomplete worlds all over again to collect them thanks to the lack of a level select system. Again, this doesn't add any difficulty, and merely pads out the game's length by forcing you to replay levels to reach the ones you missed.
-The game is ugly. Yes, I get it, the point is that the world is ugly because it's dead, but that doesn't really excuse the fact that every texture is just one solid color. It's boring to look at. Even Super Meat Boy's basic tile-based graphics were much, much better.
-No proper bosses. I'm aware that it's more of a personal thing, and that some people don't like bosses in platformer games, but still, a variety in gameplay would be nice.
-The soundtrack is just bland, generic remixes of public domain songs, with the rare inclusion of a unique song that still doesn't really manage to stand out from the drudge of generic remixes of In The Hall of the Mountain King and Flight of the Bumblebees.
-No level editor. Not that it needed a level editor, I guess, but it's hard to not compare this game to Super Meat Boy and be disappointed by how much it's lacking.
I can say without an ounce of hyperbole that this game feels like some quick flash game made for Newgrounds in the early 2000's. It just makes me wish I was playing Super Meat Boy; multiple characters, better level design, a level editor/in-game custom level prowser, actually fun gameplay, and so on.

Please note that even though I am giving this a positive overall, there is a lot of negative that comes with that.  Also, I have been playing MOBA's now for a long time and have over 5000 hours recorded on Dota 2 between my accounts and about 100 hours of Strife.
Strife is overall a very friendly MOBA and is pretty easy to pick up and learn.  The community is nice and in the many games I have played I have probably only ran in to 1-2 ragers.  If you hate the toxicity of most MOBA's out there, then this will be a breath of fresh air for you.
When you first open up Strife you are given a tutorial when you take control of a hero, (Caprice), and pretty much learn the basics of the game and a few things that differentiate Strife from the other MOBA's.  Even if you are a great MOBA player, I recommend running through the tutorial to learn some of the differences.  You can skip the tutorial if you prefer and play online right away.  The main menu is what you would expect in a MOBA with a few shortcut tabs to click on, it shows some of you profile information and some Strife news/updates that you can read.  Let's get into a few of the differences of Strife.
First of all there are Pets in Strife.  Each pet has 3 different functions to it that will help you in the game.  One of the function is an ability that is usually auto cast when the cooldown timer is reset and the other 2 abilities are usually passives with 1 having a cooldown timer and the other being a buff of sorts.  Lets take for instance a Pet that you can choose to be your starting pet, Pincer.  Pincer has an ability that you can use that will break away your crowd control or aggro and provide you with a 50% stun/slow reduction which is great for disengaging.  His 2nd ability is a passive called Breakout, that retaliates an enemy hero that attacks you with a 20 second cooldown.  So, every 20 seconds, if an enemy attacks you, then Pincer will auto attack them 1 time.  And his 3rd ability is Defense, which increases your Resistance by 20 and scales with your hero level in the game.  So Pincer is pretty much a great pet for tanky/initiating heroes and is just one example of the 11 current pets that Strife has to offer,  When you first start, you can choose between 1 of 3 pets....Pincer, Mystik, and Tortus.  You will unlock 1 of the others when you reach level 3 I believe, and then unlock the 3rd pet at level 6, so by the time you have played about 10 games or so you will have the 3 starting pets.  To unlock the other pets you need to save up your Seals, (an in game free currency that you get for completing matches, gaining profile levels, and completing some objectives).  It costs 3000 seals for each pet and does take a little grinding as a free player to get there, but before you know it you will have a nice selection of pets to choose from.
Another difference with Strife is their crafting system.  I have read a few reviews that just hate this system and its' "unfairness" for free players, but trust me, it is okay.  Crafting takes another free in-game currency called Elixers to use.  Pretty much all you do is choose the item you want to craft, change the components of the item to what you would like, and then choose the enchantment on the item that you like.  Most of the enchantments do add a minor buff to the item but they are in no way game changing buffs.  2% lifesteal might be nice, but its not going to win you the game.  When you first reach 360 Elixers to craft your item the game gives you a minor tutorial on crafting and lets you craft your first item for free and then immediately after lets you craft your first Elixer bought item.  There are also plenty of crafting guides on the Strife forums to help you from making a mistake.  Again, same as with the pets, it does take some time to have a nice stash of crafted items, but before you know it you will have plenty of items crafted.
Now some quicker reviews....
There is no teleporting unless you buy the Teleport Boots but you can only have 1 pair of boots and this means you can't have any of the other boots.
There is no creep blocking or creep denying.  This makes the game far less strategic that I would like because you can just auto attack and last hit with no worries about timing or anything.
With that being said the strategy in this game is just...well there hardly is any involved.  You pretty much just lane for most of the game and farm up until about mid-late game when you push.
There are 2 bosses on the map that provide bonuses.  Baldir provides gold and experience to all members of the team and on his 3rd team kill he will spawn 1 wave of minions in each lane that attack towers and heroes efficiently.  Cindara is a tougher boss but with spawn a beast called Krytos on the lane of your choosing and push that lane.  He does heavy damage to towers.  This concept is fine with me, except for the fact that the game tells you when these bosses respawn so a team can just directly dart for the boss and kill them if they have momentum.
There is no buy backs.  When you die you have to wait for the full respawn meaning no matter how much gold you have saved up if you lose a team fight towards the end of the game, even if you are winning, that could be game over.
Tower aggro is ridiculous and far too strong, especially in early game.  Enemy heroes can just camp by the tower and harrass or last hit with no worries.  Also, the towers, especially in mid lane, are too close together.  You can literally be standing between the two towers and pull both towers aggro at once.
There is tall grass spread out across the map that I like to refer to as "Pokemon Brush" because you can run in and hide from the enemy and be invisible until they run into the same brush.  This concept is okay to me as well except for the fact if you are chasing an enemy hero and they run into the brush, then your hero will automatically stop in his tracks and most likely lose the chase.
Movement speed and mobility in general is a joke in this game.  I believe just about every hero has the same starting movement speed and besides slight difference in the boots and there is 1 attack/movespeed item you have to have a movespeed pet or just run at the same speed as everyone else.  Far too often do I find myself chasing an enemy hero 1 hit away from dying and never being able to catch them...even with faster boots.
Beta game means not that many heroes to choose from right now....Some do need balancing still but for the most part it is okay.  Problem is...again with strategy....you pick your hero before even knowing who ur team picks or the other team picks and the same hero can be on both teams.  No thought process whatsoever here....just choose ur hero and hope for the best.
Again, I rushed a little bit at the end but an okay review.  Right now I play Strife still and enjoy it at times but it can be annoying as well.  I am hoping to stick it out and see what the Devs plan on doing with this great potential of a game they have.  Anyways, my final remark is to try the game out and see for yourself.  You can always uninstall and post a rage review on here =)
