The End Is Nigh is a adventure platformer game collaboration between Edmund McMillen and Tyler Glaiel where Edmund draws most of the art and Tyler writes most of the programing.
One of the first things that people talk about right away with this game is how it compares to Super Meat Boy. I haven't played much of Super Meat Boy, but I don't think it's a fair comparison because despite them both being platformers that Edmund helped to create, they offer very different playstyles to the player. Super Meat boy is fast and requires a lot more reflex than The End Is Nigh. Ash is less slippery than Meat Boy and doesn't have the wall jump. The few things that this game does have in common with Edmund's other platformer are Edmund's art style, high difficulty, Good controls, and a rocking soundtrack.
This game takes place after an unexplained apocalypse that destroyed the world leaving only most of Ash and a few other survivors alive. Ash is first seen playing a game cartridge before it breaks which causes him to start screaming "F♥CK" until he calms down. He decides that now is the time to go and "Make a friend" which involves gathering three parts and putting them together. In order to get those parts Ash has to leave his home and go out and explore the world.

Ash controls really well and feels nice to move around. At no point in this game did I ever feel like I didn't have full control of Ash's movement (
). Even in the water and in the air you can move Ash left and right or use the trigger to force him to fall faster. The control being good is important because in this game you are going to die
. Most of the time your goal is just simply to get to the other side of the stage without dying. You could also go after tumors but even then the goal is still to get them and then leave the stage. The kind of obstacles that Ash will face are spikes, lava, projectiles, and enemies. All of these of course kill Ash on contact. Dying just places you back where you entered the level and the levels in this game aren't very long so you only lose a few seconds of progress every time you die which encourages you to try again and again until you can finish it. Sometimes you will have to look before you leap and take a moment to think about how you're going to go through the stage before you start running in because you don't want to be stuck avoiding projectiles while you think of the next place you have to jump to. It feels very methodical because there are lots of times where you can only barely make a jump and you have to know
to pull it off before you actually pull it off.
Tumors are the collectable of this game. There is one in just about every level in every world with a total of 450 collectable tumors. Tumors are usually placed in spots that are harder to get to and add a bit of an extra challenge to the stage if you decide to bother collecting them. Collecting a tumor doesn't add it to your total tumor count right away since it requires that you exit the stage without dying or have to get the tumor again. It's not until about 3/4s into the game that tumors actually benefit you in anyway. Once
tumors will function as a life count and you will lose one life every time you die which will result in a game over that sends you back to the beginning of the world you lost your last life in. They are replenished as soon as you exit the worlds where this is active or when you use a warp point. If you collect a certain number of tumors you can find "Steven"s scattered throughout the game that allow you to see the future. There are four future levels and each one of them offers a special game cartridge when you finish it.
There is one hidden in every world. You can play these on Ash's TV and they're pretty much more of the main game but in low-bit and with challenges like collect all of the coins or complete it without using a continue. They offer bonus tumors if you finish them and you can get up to an additional 52 tumors which will push your save file completion over 100% if you already have the 450 tumors that are in the worlds.
Just as the steam tags imply this is an adventure platformer which means that there will be to at least some degree some exploration and platforming. Worlds are seperated into 16-20 "levels" with a warp point at the start of each world allowing you to travel to any previously visited warp points. I call them levels but each level is connected to the last and in some worlds you can skip some levels or you might have to come back to a level but from a different entry point in order to reach someplace that you couldn't get to before. The worlds themselves are also conncted to each other and will eventually come to a split where you can branch off into three different world pathways. This is in my opinion the biggest factor that seperates The End Is Nigh from Super Meat Boy- the open world. Each world contains secret areas with mega tumors that are worth five tumors each and cartridges. You can usually find secret areas by looking for a falling block, a lone ledge stub, fake walls, or a seemingly bottomless pit that doesn't seem like it belongs there. Most worlds also have locked doors which you require you to get a key from somewhere else and then return to that world once you have a spare key. Besides gathering collectables the secret areas also allow you to interact with more NPCs which can offer funny dialogue or a small bit of insight into the world.

Robocraft 31/50 (6 above average)
Customizability 10/10 (5 above average)
The customization in Robocraft is the defining factor of the game. Color is the only design feature you have to pay for, other wise you must build up in game money through a system of rewards and selling. You progressively gain more parts for your robot, and your options only expand from there. Building robots is simple and restrictions are in the quantity of parts you are placing, and the movement of some of the parts. All together the customization is limited by logic, and imagination is encouraged.
Encounters/Battles 6/10 (1 above average)
The battles in Robocraft are limited, one being a Capture The Base style battle, the other being Team Death Match, and lastly a randomized battle with randomized rules. If it were not for the unique robots and lack of class system in the game it would have scored much lower. The different weapons and forms of movement that robots have in the game are staples in the battles, and a certain strategy that comes with the weapon choices give the game a unique feel every battle.
Storyline/Storytelling 2/10 (3 below average)
There is a reason for the fighting, but if you didn't pay attention the first time the game began playing then you probably wouldn't remember you are fighting for Protium, a precious energy source.
Graphics/Design 8/10 (3 above average)
The use of basic and bold colors and textures give the game a very clean feel, and the simple landscape and many ways to go about navigating it are positively enjoyable. The game does lack defining graphics, but the simplicity allows for many people to be able to run the game.
Accessibility 5/10 (average)
The game is based on live battling, so if internet is an issue for anyone then this Robocraft would not be an adviseable game to download. It lacks offline game play, but does have the option of AI battling. Internet is required to start the game, but after that you could AI battle if internet speed was an issue.

Ah, Dark Messiah. A wonderful game! I had a lot of fun with this one.
Graphics:
Source engine. Sharp textures nice physics. There isn't much to say about it really. The graphics look fine and they are holding up well to this day. Oh there is one thing, you are able to see your own feet. I think this is important, it somehow adds a lot of "friction" to the world (think: Arx Fatalis)
Sound:
Okay. Has oomph. Little music in this game - which is a good thing (think: Dark Souls).
Story:
You are a hero on a quest to save some part of some world. I don't think there were any rats in a basement to kill, but there is a succubus manifested in your head that'll talk to you occasionally, resulting in some funnily greasy moments. It's nothing special all in all - but the succubus gives it a decent twist.
Gameplay:
This is where Messiah shines. Luckily - who gives a damn about graphics and story in an ego-fantasy-rpg-hackfest? Well, lay aside the rpg, there isn't much roleplaying to do apart from some character development. This character development will decide whether you'll be casting, shooting arrows or close combating your way through the world, and with the given physics and environmental dangers in level design this gives for some really awesome fights. I love the fights! I love the kick, i love the brutal finishing moves and i love the kick. Yea, you can kick people off high places in this game, and you'll never grow tired of that since there are about a million ledges to kick people, orcs and other monsters off of... of? The combat is awesome, like seriously. It's like Skyrim done right! It's fast paced, it's gritty, it's evil and it'll make you feel like a real Badass Dark Messiah of Might and Magic! You should get this game just because of that. That's it.
Start, and don't stop playing until you get to the Orc village. If you hold through until then, you will start loving the game. But yea, until then everything is weird. Combat mechanics feel odd and the game starts slow and boring.

Escape Goat by Magical Time Bean is a puzzle platformer stylized after the 8-bit Nintendo era. You play as a purple goat with strikingly green horns and golden eyes. Somehow this odd combination makes for a highly convincing and enjoyable character to play as, one which could even have been considered as iconic as Mario, if it had existed back in the day. Like many NES era games this is a title of few words, yet it does not need to say much for you to grow fond of this unconventional hero and push onward to rescue your trapped friends and escape the magical prison.
There are lots of good things to say about Escape Goat, but what really stands out are its incredibly tight controls, innovatively moderate to challenging puzzles, and a strong soundtrack that pulls it all together. You will find yourself ducking traps, avoiding pitfalls, dodging spinning blades, leaping over chasms, and avoiding the reaper's deadly burning gaze. The physics are simple and straight forward. Its easy to understand how each object works, but in combination they can make the room you were in become something completely different and reveal new paths and dangers.
With a dash that resembles a head-butt, the ability to double jump, and the unlikely companionship of a mouse, you will quickly find yourself solving puzzles and navigating tricky terrain with the ease and surefootedness of your mountain-faring kin. Afterwords if you are still feeling brave and want to really stretch your legs to see what you can do, then maybe its time to delve into the more difficult 'All Intensive Purposes' campaign. Be warned however, this is no place for sheep. Only the most agile, steel-hooved, and ninja-minded will truly earn the right to be called Escape Goat.

Abyss Odyssey is one of the best indie games I have played this year.
This game is a rogue-like 2d brawler with combat similar to the Smash Bros games set in an alternate universe 1890s Chile in which the dreams of a warlock have started physically manifest in the real world and threaten everyone's wellbeing. The story is actually very interesting. However most of it is told through notes you randomly find during gameplay and a few cut scenes. Animations and combat look and feel great. Also the visuals are some of the best I've seen from a 2d platformer. They aren't on Trine or Ori levels of greatness, but they are pretty damn good. There are 3 main playable characters each with a unique weapon and moveset complex enough that this game's combat system could have easily been made for a competitive fighting game. Not only that, you are also able to captures the souls of every enemy you defeat as long as your character's level is high enough. Then you can use those enemies, all of which also have their own unique and fun movesets.
For a rogue-like game, this game is actually very lenient. When you die you get the chance to continue as a soldier, which while obviously being weaker than your main character, is sufficient enough a lot of the time to last until you get to a respawn point for your character. If your soldier dies then it's truly gameover and you must restart from the beginning. When you die your character keeps all of his or her levels and gold though. As a casual player of rogue-likes I actually enjoyed this aspect because it means that every run, no matter how bad, lead to some progress. However after a while when your character gets to the higher levels and becomes somewhat rich, the game becomes a bit too easy in my opinion. Every single playthrough has a randomized map with different paths all eventually leading to the Warlock, aka the final boss. The Warlock is one of the most interesting boss designs I have seen in any video game. The idea is that as more people across the whole world beat the Warlock, all players will be contributing to the game's future content. Basically, whenever the Warlock is killed "x" number of times worldwide, the Warlock will gain a new ability for every player to experience. This is interesting because it means that people who play this game later actually get the "fuller" experience. That being said this game isn't that popular anymore so I doubt the Warlock will be changing anytime soon.
Enemy AI is generally quite good. I do suspect that the AI is cheating a bit in that it probably reads some of the player's inputs directly. However, I am fine with that because the AI doesn't actually feel unfair most of the time, rather it just gives a good challenge.
The game also supports local co-op and online/local pvp multiplayer (which is sadly dead)
So at this point you are probably wondering. If I am giving this game so much praise (which is does indeed deserve imo), who does this game currently have a ~50% mixed steam review rating? I can pinpoint one glaring flaw with the game which didn't really bother me all too much, but will definitely bother some. Simply when you are in the middle of a combo, you cannot break out of the animation until it is done or you get hit. This makes it somewhat frustrating when you are flailing away at the wrong side, open for the enemy to attack for several seconds. This will be a deal breaker for some. For me it was not.
Also other people seem to be complaining about the controls in general. Yes they don't feel extremely crisp like a triple a brawler. But on a 360 pad they felt fine for me after a little getting used to.
Replayability for this game is definitely high because it's a rogue-like. However, I think due to the nature of how the player will eventually snowball because of the permanent leveling system, this game has less replayability than most rogue-likes simply because eventually it will get too easy. There is a hard mode called nightmare mode tho.
If they just fixed the jump mechanic I'd be happy.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

As for the actual game mechanics themselves, it can feel clunky and awkward using some of the vehicles or heavy weaponry, even getting rifle rounds on target and range can be difficult. Part of that is intentional realism, but the game still has alot of bugs that they are working on ironing out.

Arkane Studios never was a well-known studio until their deal with Bethesda to make the critically acclaimed game; Dishonored. Before their rise to recognition. Arkane Studios made a semi-obscure game called Dark Messiah of Might & Magic.
Dark Messiah of Might & Magic, is the story about a young man named Sareth who has been trained his whole life by his mentor named Wizard Phenrig. In time he is finally given a task on helping his mentor Phenrig to find a sacred crystal called the Shantiri Crystal. After retrieving the Crystal, he's sent off by Phenrig to travel to the city of Stonehelm in which he's to deliver the crystal to another Wizard named Menelag, who is lord of Stonehelm. Though Sareth doesn't go alone and is given a spirit guide by Phenrig called Xana, who resides in Sareth mind.
DMOMAM (Dark Messiah of Might & Magic) story is possibly one of the worst stories a fantasy game could ever have. From the characters names, dialogue and boring and forgetful lore. DMOMAM doesn't seem to have any redeeming qualities in this field. Characters are usually shuffled in and out as quick as possible with very little backstory or personality to them. Many of the characters are more annoying than interesting. The spiritual guide; Xana is by far the most annoying out of the bunch as she literally talks in a sinister and almost hammy voice which is off putting beyond belief. The voice acting in the game is also terrible with chew-scenery attitudes and almost wooden performance from each character. Even if they were good it wouldn't have saved the goofy dialogue.
Though this may be the case for DMOMAM, what the game really shines on is its gameplay. DMOMAM's gameplay features a wide range of skills and traits for Sareth to choose from. This game is more fantasy RPG in skills than any other aspect. The game provides Stealth, Combat and magic as the main skills in which you can choose from. When specializing in one skill it can be very satisfying taking out enemies, like using a fireball to sizzle opponents alive, hack off a enemies head with sword, use the bow to take out targets from a distance and use Stealth to backstab your enemies silently. All is great fun and having the use of the kick mechanic can send enemies flying to their death onto spiked walls or off ledges. This is helped by the fact that the game engine that they use is the Source Engine. Which does good use with the physics and certain traps that are featured in the game.
DMOMAM does have some slip-ups with the combat though, sometimes the games hit detection glitches up, making you miss your opponents body, leaving you open to be hit. Because the game uses an actual character in first-person than a set of floating hands, it can be hard to navigate when climbing up stones and buildings in high places, leading you to a quick death. The stealth though good in some areas, is flawed in that it’s too easy to sneak and hide. The game uses an indicator which goes from 0-4 bars (0 being exposed, 4 being hidden), sometimes you'll be completely hidden even though you are out in board daylight which doesn't make any sense.
The graphics in the game are quite good and have aged well since the games release, with good physics and great lighting and textures, the game does holds up very well and helps with the immersion of the game. Art design of the world is quite boring when located in cities such as Stonehelm but at great when going through the mountains and dark caves. The sound design is quite weak when coming to certain sound especially from magic spells.
DMOMAM though is a game with tons of potential but a lot of things bring it down. It is a fun game though and will keep you entertained due to its RPG skills tree which will give you a decent amount of replay value.

Don't confuse this game with the other "Heroes of might and magic" games. This is a entierly new game. Everything from the universe to the genre is completly changed.
The game plays very much like Dishonored, as Arkane studios is the developer of both games. (*cough* also a bit like the recent theif 4 game as edios kind of ripped of about everything, and then dumbed it down*cough*). This means that you can play the game like you want to play it, you can go about any problem your own way, be it sneaking, backstabbing the crap out of everything, to just improvising and just throwing random props you find on the floor. Or maybe you go about it with magic or raw strength
This is NOT an open world rpg, and it does not try nor need to be. Much like dishonored the "maps" are open linear. It is a big, well designed map (that you will not find in any openworld game as it would take to much time to design), that has lots of thoughts behind it, with loads of variety. The levels can be explored and very often interacted with. I often find myself drifting around, looking for secrets, or new ways to kill enemies. "humm that 12 meters statue looks fragile, maybe i can destroy... OH GOD ITS FALLING RUN!!". Some parts inbetween levels are linear, be it jumping between rooftops in a frantic chase, it still feels authentic and as if it has a part in the game.
The niche of this game is the phisics. Be it kicking people into spikes, throwing barrels, kicking orcs of clips you name it. Combat is fluid, active and varied. The enviroment is a weapon that you will need to use. There are lots of diffrent weapons, with diffrent "enchantments". The combat is not only skill in the heat of battle but also choosing the right tool for the jobb, as using a firesword to hit a demon is not the greatest idea. in other words use logic when choosing weapons.
As far story goes, you are Sereath accompanied by Xana (the weird sarcastic woman stuck in your head), trying to find the skull of shadows, an ancient artifact, part of the legend fortelling the doom of mankind "something something".
The story is fairly predicteble, but nonetheless worth experiencing. It's not bad because even though the story is a classic cliche, it is well executed. Just dont expect a bioshock infinite.
This game remains to date, as one of my favorite games of all time. Good work arkane studios!

I really wanted to hate this game.  I waited for it to be cheap.  I even went to the local Wal_mart and played the Wii U version before even considering this version. For $7 or so, I felt it was worth a try if only to get the cards and waste time with my little brother.
Then, I played the game.  For starters, the announcer is a bit annoying but really hypes the game up so you always feel excited, even when you shouldn't be.  The character roster is amazing.  I even get Team Fortress 2 and JSRF characters!  Not to mention, I went ahead and bought the Metal Sonic DLC character while it was on sale, and that is now my favorite character in the game.  Half the roster is still locked, but I should be able to unlock characters through world tour mode just by spending the stars I earn from each event.
Overall, the game gets a 5/5 from me.  It is the closest thing to Mario Kart you can get without getting Mario Kart. Ha.  Seriously, though, it is a great game with great visuals, great characters and impressively deep gameplay.  There is a low bar to entry that should attract newbie racers, but the veterans can really sink their teeth into this.
Now, I know it's not fair to not mention the negatives, so here are a few:
1.  Announcer is absurdly annoying.
2.  Autosave system scares me with a "progress will be lost" warning every time I exit the game, even if the game isn't going to lose any data.
3.  Music is a little lame, and some characters would probably do better without vehicles.  Sonic, for example, can probably run faster than any of these cars move, his own car included, and no character really has any special gameplay mechanic.
4.  Some of the early challenges are actually very challenging and may scare away new players.

This game is Sega’s answer to Mario Kart, and it fills that role with style and flair.  It starts with a classic booster-and-power-up system (and impossibly long title), then arms itself to the teeth with tight curves, mid-air stunts, online multiplayer and two campaign modes with a wealth of activities. It’s quite fast-paced game, with drivers switching places and exchanging zany projectiles constantly. Speed boosts are frequent, since you aren't limited to using boosters on the road - turning sharply with the shoulder buttons can grant boosts of varying power levels, and boosts come as power-ups, too. The other game modes, found scattered throughout the World Tour, include Drift Challenge, Boost Challenge, Traffic Attack and Ring Race, among others.
One of SAAS's most interesting aspects is its gimmick: transforming vehicles. It's fun to have different ways to race, but the boat and plane modes, while faster than the vehicle's car form, are also harder to control... especially the boat, which is far too easy to turn. However, the unique quirks of the air and water phases (the plane's increased mobility, for instance) of the races and their respective vehicle forms  more than make up for the learning curve.
In short, this is no mere knockoff of its predecessors. Even if I raise an eyebrow and say "who?" every time I unlock a character, I really enjoy the game and recommend that you pick it up some time.
Also, that recommendation is nearly a command when the game's on sale. Just saying.

I'm mostly writing this to counter the negative reviews this is getting, which are very undeserved to me.
I'm not going to say too much about the aesthetics of this game, as it becomes clear with a single visit to this game's screenshot hub that they're brilliant. I love the character designs and level backgrounds so much. The soul capture mechanic is great as well, as you can literally capture the soul of any enemy in the game - as long as your level is high enough - and assume control over them, giving you an entirely different move set as well as an extra life, since your character doesn't die when the controlled creature dies. The roguelike elements in this aren't too strong because you keep your level and the gold you collected upon death, but the stages and loot are randomly generated.
What I do want to elaborate on, are the controls and combat. Most of the negative reviews mention solely that the combat is broken and the controls are bad, which to me really isn't the case. This will probably sound elitist, but I feel like anyone saying the combat is broken and cheap just hasn't gotten good enough at it, doesn't want to get good enough at it or has never played fighting games a lot. The combat just takes practice and getting used to, and I personally really like this combat and its learning curve. This game takes a lot of inspiration from the combat of Super Smash Bros., one of the most beloved fighting game franchises which also harbors a learning curve. How can people adore Smash but hate on this game's combat, when they're identical in quite some ways? It even has i-frame upgrades on specific attacks which can be used very tactfully and there is also a button to cancel your move/combo, which is one of the most important mechanics to master to do well in this game. Most of the negative comments on the combat and controls do come from people who have played the game for around one hour, maybe two tops. So that just makes my first points that much more valid.
I definitely also don't agree with people saying that button mashing is rewarded or that memorizing one or two overpowered combos will get you through the game, because I find myself playing very differently against different enemies. A specific powerful combo against one enemy could be horrible against another depending on what attacks they have and how quickly they can interrupt you and such, because they WILL take advantage of any openings in your attacks. Learning your enemy's attacks is probably even more important than learning your own attacks, just like in any decent fighting game.
This game definitely deserves a chance if you are up for taking your time to learn the game and not jumping in and complaining about it being bad, when it really is you not wanting to learn the mechanics.

I've greatly enjoyed "The End Is Nigh".  Like all of Edmunds games, it is blisteringly hard, but for the most part fair.  There are a few design choices I found questionable.  For example the Iron Cart Retro Levels (Denial, Anger, etc.) are a bit too unforgiving in their lack of lives.  And the obstacles in the bonus levels where you obtain those carts can be difficult to tell from the floor itself in some places.  And if you go for collecting everything, some of the jumps and manuevers you are expected to pull off can be downright infuriating, to the point where you don't feel any achievement in suceeding in those parts, just the hollowness that follows rage.  Still, those instances are few and far between, and the game more than makes up for it in atmosphere and music (seriously the music is amazing).
One final note: this is NOT Super Meat Boy 2.  While it shares some aspects, the core philosophy is entirely different.  SMB for the most part emphasized flying around the level, pulling off acrobatic stunts in order to obtain the fastest time.  The End Is Nigh is very much the opposite, in that it usually requires you to take your time and manuevere through tight spaces.  It is still fun, but in a very different way.  So if you are expecting SMB 2, you might be disappointed.

Basically it allows you to change existing item recipe components (say, from base items giving mana to base items giving attackspeed). The ways you can change the components are limited to keep the power level of the item in check and the item cost is adjusted depending on chosen components.
While I do believe that you can't really judge a moba game before playing for a few hundred hours, I've surprisingly enjoyed my few hours in this game. So I'd say it's worth checking out.

Bought this at most 3 days ago, writing this review as of 12.7 hours played and having beaten the main story with only 1 true ending left to get I feel I can give some decent insight.
This is similar to Super Meat Boy, there's no running and no wall jumping/sliding involved and your character doesn't gain new abilities as he goes, the game just makes you aware at certain points what combining buttons does and how your character can interact with the world.

The game does have a spike in difficulty, at points it is very mild and at others it does feel hard and like you don't want to do it as much, sometimes as a result of "how in the F am I supposed to do this!?" and sometimes it is because the enemy AI on a few particular enemies is too good, it feels that way but having gone through said levels again it was just me.
You have cartridges to collect in this, they're completely optional and beyond letting you play the old retro games and giving you bonus tumors for beating certain achievements they are not needed UNLESS you want the true ending. Sure that sounds like a deal breaker but honestly for how hard it'll be to get the true ending anyway you probably will be happy enough getting the normal 1 first.
I consider myself decent at platformers, despite my 12.7 hours (so far) I have died roughly 4K times and counting every time I boot it up. Will be nice to go for the under 200 deaths as I feel I have a good grasp of everything now and believe me there is plenty to keep you occupied if you wish.
Overall this game is a bargain and having paid full price I don't have any regrets, sitting at 20 ish achievements and tons left to do I feel this was worth the price I paid. A first-person hack n' slash RPG made by a bunch of people who had the balls to try something a bit different, and in my opinion succeeded for the most part. It won't hold your hand and you will start off under-powered and fighting uphill for a long while. However, this means that when you're hacking off heads left and right in the late-game and the characters comment on your growth in power, you actually understand what they mean.
The combat is one of the best parts of the game - the swordplay is fairly intuitive, the shield blocks effectively, and there's no weapon or armour degradation getting in the way of fun gameplay. Also, once you work out how to score a headshot with the bow, stealth attacks become fun and effective. Yes, there's a bit of kicking - kicking people off ledges or into spikes or down stairs, but I didn't feel I was oversaturated with this option and I felt that it aided me when I needed it.
It is, however, somewhat baffling that a game operating under the 'Might and Magic' umbrella railroads you into choosing the 'might' path over magic on more than one occasion. I feel sorry for the poor sod who threw all his experience points into spells, and then has to fight the orc warlord under the condition of 'no spells'. The fight is hard enough as it is without having to battle his 5 cronies at the same time while awkwardly switching from one spell to another as you can't equip more than one spell at a time.
Similarly, to utilise armours (of which there are 3 very specific types - warrior, stealth, and mage armours) the game forces you to level very specific traits up. Meaning that you are, once again, railroaded into making certain skill choices which makes you realise that the game would be the same if they'd simply asked you if you wanted to be a warrior, assassin or mage at the start and that the concept of organic skill choice in this game is mostly an illusion.
That said, I'm talking a lot about little niggly things - overall I had a lot of fun, and the game does allow a fair degree of freedom when it comes to your choices in the story, so I would highly recommend it, especially for a sale price.
PROS:
* Responsive and fun combat that utilises the environment well and genuinely provides a varied and free experience.
* The texture detail is quite good and I felt the Source engine was used to good effect.
* A story you can actually follow.
* The difficulty can be genuinely challenging, forcing you to think rather than just hack about.
CONS:
* Occasionally frustrating platforming elements.
* The characterisations of the women are grating, as they constantly fawn over you in what seems to be rather creepy wish-fulfillment for the developers.
* Those that like to be a jack-of-all-trades will be disadvantaged.
* The difficulty can be frustratingly punishing, resulting in multiple restarts because of tiny errors.

Yes, it's a retro-styled puzzle platformer. Dime a dozen, right? But look past that and what you have is a nearly flawless game. It never uses it's retro stylings as an excuse for bad design - like Doom, it feels like a game that not only lives up to modern standards but will have aged very well ten years from now.
The one-room level design is consistently clever and always uses it's different pieces in new and unexpected ways. The instant respawn means it's rarely frustrating, it's moderately challenging but easy to understand your many mistakes, and the controls are strong enough that 99% of your deaths are your fault.
On top of that, the soundtrack is catchy and memorable and even the sound design is very well done - the chime when you collect a key, for example, is so satisfying that I can hear it while I'm typing this. And although the graphics are simple, they'll grow on you as very charming in their own right - it looks so much better than most retro-styled games that the HD graphics in EG2 almost feel like a step down.
It's not perfect, of course. If you prefer games that last for dozens of hours, the basic game lasts only a few -  just long enough that it largely avoids getting gimmicky or repetitive. There are achievements, a set of obscenely brutal bonus levels, and custom level sets that can keep you playing for a long while, but none of them really live up to the original game.
Some of the levels are also less clever than others, particularly some of those in The Endless Machine that fall into the trap of trial and error puzzle design. Others rely far too much on reflexes, which doesn't suit this game particularly well - although the controls work well, your goat isn't really built for twitch platforming.
But, really, those are minor problems. When the game is great, it makes you remember why you fell in love with the genre in the first place  - and it's that great for nearly every minute you spend with it. It wasn't a recent obsession of mine for nothing!
It's a retro platformer that flows really well with a controller in your hands.

This game could not have been any more of a pleasure. I must admit that when I decided to purchase the game, there was a little bit of worry coming alongside my purchase, but once I began playing, all my worries were gone. Abyss Odyssey is a game perfect for anyone seeking a challenge. After playing the game for a while I began to try to dig into the combat system to just be impressed over and over again with how interesting it is.
The combat in this game has a similar feel to it as Smash Bros. Abyss Odyssey is not as loose at Smash, but the way you move and attack are similar. As you progress down deeper and fight you will level up your character and find alternate attacks you can equip to expand on your potential. Depending on what kind of skills you equip, you'll expand your combo potential and/or give yourself benifits such as more ranged attacks.
I feel the need to stress that if you're not interested in games that will push you and challenge you, this game is not for you. If you want a game that will reward you with feeling like you really accomplished something worthwhile, then you need this game in your library.
I don't like to rate games on a number scale because I don't believe that can be accurate, so I would rather inform you on what the game has to offer instead of trying to sell you on buying it regardless of your type of game.
The player type I would recommend this game to is one who desires a difficult game with high reward in term of accomplishment. A player who is more into disecting a game to play it at its fullest potential will enjoy this game. A player who is interested in jumping in and just fighting without interest in mastery of the game will not get as much out of the game.

It's one of the best programs to manage your Gpu overcloks and keep an eye on temps MHz etc.

This program is fine if you don't care to see your overlay at all times which to me is actually extremely important. I was actually using this until I noticed in H1Z1, it's impossible to display the overlay so there's no way to know what the status is of your overclock while in that specific game for example without running in windowed mode and actually looking on the EVGA PrecisionX 16 program itself.
I have no idea why there are achievements for a program as dangerous as this if put into the hands of someone uneducated in overclocking. It'll just encourage kids to destroy their parents' graphic cards or achievement hunters to damage their systems.
I use MSI Afterburner instead now because with that I'm able to see an overlay while inside of any game full screened, and it also allows you to display many more things inside your overlay such as your CPU temperature, RAM being used and many other things.
When you're testing a new overclock, it's good to monitor as many things as you can to see how it's affecting your other system components. This'll let you know whether you need to turn down some settings or upgrade your cooling systems even if for example your GPU is heating up your CPU due to bad ventilation.
My final conclusion is to just get MSI Afterburner if you're going to be doing anything past a mild overclock if just for monitoring sake. The amount of things you can monitor in the overlay on EVGA PrecisionX 16 are limited which will let you know less of what's really going on in your system.
So with that said, good luck on your system monitoring and overclocking endeavors!

I decided I had to play at least every character once before I made a review of this game. 34 hours later I still do recommend it. The funny thing is that I still haven't even really gotten into the pvp ladder, and I don't know that I even would until I am even more familiar with the characters that I liked and their nuances. With that said, here's what I've liked so far.
1. The combat is faster than some mobas that I've played, but not so fast that I get lost in the action.
2. The crafting system allows for a deeper customization of the characters.
3. If you don't want to pvp, you can play against bots and still get similar rewards.
4. The matchmaking allows for you to select the character -you- want to play, and then matches you acoordingly. (As opposed to some games where random people are responsible for the team composition, forcing some into roles they don't enjoy playing.)
I don't think this is a game for everyone, especially if you don't like pvp or working with a team. While I had an overall positive experience, there were a few things that I didn't care for, and it would be unfair if I didn't share those.
1. The respawn times were advertized as fast, and that really isn't the case.
2. The characters do not all appear to be well balanced. Some just seem to vastly outpreform others.
As a conclusion, I encourage anyone interested in pvp to give this a try. It's a free game that I felt was completely not pay to win [if you actually take the time to explore the characters vs bots, you will be able to complete an entire crafted gear set before you even play every character]. The worst that could really happen is you waste a little time, and you might find that you actually had fun doing it even if the game isn't for you.

I doubt many (or even any) remember Dark Messiah with the fondness I've got for it. It was one of few linear games that never actually felt linear. The environments were all diverse enough to feel fresh (the orc village in particular was fockin' AWESOME!) and there were enough enemies to make it feel varied as well, without ever feeling convoluted. You had complete and utter freedom over how to "train" your character, i.e. picking skills, and basically every single "build" in the game was viable if you knew how to use it.
Stealth was satisfying enough to warrant sneaking through entire levels at a time, and combat was also satisfying enough to go chopping off heads left 'n' right with your new +5 Earthfire Sword. Magic had a LOT of fun spells (chain lightning, anyone?) and very few uninteresting ones, the only real exception being Sanctuary, methinks. Hell, even Weaken was fun at times! Granted, mostly when the adrenaline was a-pumpin', but whatever. So, the inevitable question. What is my rating? Well, DM-M&M wasn't perfect, but I'll be damned if it didn't do exactly what it was meant to do: deliver one helluva story with some helluva gameplay! 8.6/10

Escape Goat is a puzzle platformer with a simple premise: you are a goat in prison with a mouse sidekick, and you should escape. I didn't expect to get in to this game as much as I did, but Escape Goat has some solid puzzles, the platforming is tough at times, and I ended up really enjoying it.
The story is basically non-existent. The music and sound are enjoyable. The graphics remind me of 16-bit-era PC games, and I think they look great. The game controls well on an X360 controller (didn't test keyboard).
This game is really very elegant. There are only a few things you can do: double jump, rush, and teleport (if you have the hat), and the mouse can do a handful of things by himself as he runs around. Similarly, the level design only uses a few elements to pull together some interesting and tough puzzles. The game isn't terribly hard (unless you play the bonus content), but it makes you earn your prison escape, and it feels satisfying when you do. I'm probably going to keep playing a bit longer to get a few more of the achievements that I missed the first time.
This game is a solid puzzle platformer, and if that sounds like something you enjoy, pick up Escape Goat. It's cheap, and for $5, this is a pretty good way to kill an afternoon.

Borderlands takes place on the desert planet of Pandora and opens with a monologue from one of the supporting characters. There is a myth that Pandora holds a mysterious vault, said to contain alien technology, wealth, fame, power and women. Nobody actually knows where 'The Vault' is and as many children grow up hearing about the stories of 'The Vault' they subsequently grow up to be 'Vault Hunters.' You are one of these Vault Hunters.
Borderlands' storyline is paper-thin and is somewhat cliché and uninteresting. The story is mainly told through a 'Guardian Angel' who appears throughout the game and guides you through it. I often felt confused as to why I was killing a certain person or why I was doing a certain job as there didn't seem to be much point in doing so. A lot of people will miss the storyline completely as they'll probably skip past through most of the text in which quests are actually described. The ending to the game also felt very weak and I was left feeling unsatisfied with what I'd accomplished during the questline.
As well as a lack of story, there is a lack of character development. This is a real shame because the inhabitants of Pandora, as well as the planet itself, all appear to be very unique and could've had very interesting personalities. Instead, they're almost lifeless and do nothing but stand in a select spot and may communicate to you once or twice through your comm device. Dr. Zed, for example, isn't allowed to "cut people no more" because he lost his licence. Well, why did he loose his licence? My intrigue with the characters was met with disappointment and I felt as though there was a huge amount of wasted potential to be had.
Though there is a lack of story to be had in Borderlands it luckily has a couple of saving graces. The first one of these graces is the gameplay itself. When Gearbox first started to advertise Borderlands they stated that it would have 'Bazillions of Guns.' Whilst Bazillion is in fact a fictitious number, there a huge amount of guns to be fired in Borderlands. Though the weapon types are the same that you've seen in every FPS you won't find a gun that has the same properties, nor the same look, as any other gun in the game. Though there is one characteristic that is carried in most, if not all, of the guns. They are very satisfying to shoot.
The art style of Borderlands is another saving grace of the game with a cell-shaded world that is not often seen in a game of this nature. There are also a number of unique looking creatures and enemies to be found as well as side characters. There are a few clipping issues that I noticed while playing but I forgave them due to the massive scope of the game and how beautifully rendered the world is. With that said, a little more variety in environments would've been nice. I understand that Pandora is predominantly a desert planet but I was a little tired of driving through dry, sandy landscapes.
Another unique thing about Borderlands is the style of the game itself. The developers call it an RPS (Role-Playing Shooter), and whilst the game is fairly light on the Role-Playing element, there are number of noticeable RPG elements that have been implemented into the game. There four classes to choose from, each with their own preferred choice of weapon as well as a skill tree which grows as your character grows in level. Enemies themselves also have levels and are resistant to certain kinds of attacks. It's an interesting crossover, and is successful in what it does although it does feel fairly light and I'd like to see these gameplay elements expanded in a sequel.
Whilst there may have been wasted potential surrounding the world of Pandora and its inhabitants, Borderland's unique blend of first-person shooter and role-playing mechanics has had me hooked for hours upon end and has quickly become one of my favourite titles. Simply put, Borderlands is borderline amazing.

So I've played this game for at least 1000 hours (ignore Steam, I had this game before it went fully over to Steam so my player account has tracked my time more accurately) and can I say I loved every second? No, like every FPS this will drive you up the wall with frustration. The game is far from perfect, hit detection is definitely dodgey at times, lag is definitely an issue (not a huge one, but definitely abused when possible by the pros), flying A2A is very difficult to get into, performance is terrible, and sometimes you just face completely unfair, overwheliming odds where you die again and again.
But I keep playing.
Because there is something infinitely satisfying about dropping C4 on tanks and infantry, knowing that the very frustration you felt when it happened to you is now what they feel too. When you chain the headshots on an enemy heavy an melt them before they can even react. When you completely outplay an enemy opponent. Mowing down 10 clueless enemies before they finally realise where you are.  The feeling of being part of a team that will fight no matter the odds against even when completely overwhelmed. This is what keeps me playing.
Are you going to enjoy this game at first? Probably not, you get thrown in at the deep end and you will die. A lot. But once you start figuring things out and something clicks, there is nothing quite like it. Sometimes the game will be unfair to you, whether you are the type of player who takes this in their stride or decides that they don't want anymore of it will decide how long you stick with this game.
At the end of the day, this game is free so if you have good internet I'd definitely say "Give it a go", but be prepared to die a lot. One final piece of advice would be: play with an outfit or friend(s) (preferably plural as the more the merrier) as this greatly enhances your experience.

Sitting at 99% completion on my main save file, I think it goes without saying I've enjoyed the game quite a bit. I like the level design and hunting down secrets. I've both adored and loathed the retro stages and I don't think I can leave this game unfinished, even if some of the iron man challenges are sure to give me a hard time.
While I recommend this game to any fans of SMB and difficult platformers, I think it's best to get some of the negative aspects out of the way early on.
The gameplay is quite self-explanatory. You jump, grab ledges and wall hooks and make your way from one screen to the next. While the controls are tight, grabbing some of the ledges feels like pixel hunting. If you miss, you hit a spike. Since most every jump has been "optimized" in a way that you can reach areas without too much hassle, this feels either like an oversight or artificially inflated difficulty.
Most screens have tumors as collectibles, and some of them make you go an extra mile before finishing the level. However, some of them are locked out of your reach if you enter the next screen, forcing you to replay several levels again. Once again, this falls under artificial gameplay inflation. And while on the topic of collectibles, if you grab one and exit the screen, you've obtained it. This means you can pick up a tumor, backtrack to the previous screen and THEN beat the stage. This makes some of the levels slightly more tolerable, but I find it slightly off-putting.
That's the bad out of the way. A lot of people have posted complaints about certain enemies being unpredictable (see: Thistle Fish) and therefore unfair, but that's simply not true. As far as I'm aware, there's a pattern to everything and if you haven't figured it out, that's on you. That doesn't mean some enemies and areas aren't relentlessly difficult, but they all have a discernible attack pattern. Well, maybe aside from the birds.
Just about everything else about this game I like. The controls are tight, there's no vsync delay, the soundtrack is a well-rendered heavy metal/8-bit mixture of classical pieces, the graphics look nice (and remind me of SMB on several occasions). Most rooms are enjoyable to play and hunting down secrets is mostly fun. The few abilities (such as dashing downwards) you have from the start are revealed as the game progresses, which means you'll probably miss out on something your first time through, but on subsequent playthroughs you know immediately how to utilize them. This is unlike metroidvania games where you hunt down abilities first and then return to previous areas. Personally I think it was a refreshing touch.
I suppose difficulty needs to be discussed. At frst I thought The End was more difficult than SMB. Having beaten the core game (and then some) I'm not too sure about that anymore. Some areas are relentless. Certain retro carts are a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and a half. And some secrets took me way more tries than I'd like to admit. But not once did I find myself wanting to throw my controller at a wall. Therefore I wouldn't call this an unreasonable difficult "masocore" game. But unless you're well-versed in platformers and like more difficult than average games, this might not be the game for you.
My 5 cents above are written at 29 hours of gameplay and a 99% savefile. Whether this game stands the test of time remains to be seen, but at any rate, it's definitely kept me entertained so far and I'm looking forward to beating it again.

So, here we are. Super Meat Boy 2! Oh wait...nevermind. It is in no way a sequel to Meat Boy nor related to it in any way. But, that is one of the reasons why i like this game.
On a graphical standpoint, levels have a simple but pretty interesting design, as well as detail.
Controls are pretty light and straightforward. However, the difficulty progression in the game seems to know no boundaries. By the time you reach The Future set of levels, everything changes. Difficulty basically jumps up a bunch and it keeps on getting harder, especially in secret areas. If you're somewhat familiar with game's mechanics - you more than likely won't end up looking at Game Over screen, since for some reason, your lives will have a limit from then on. Same applies to cart games. At least though, you can afford to take your time, which i appreciate.
As for the story, let's just say that a game such as this doesn't really need one, but it has its moments nevertheless. I am not a fan of Ash's background though, however, it doesn't affect experience.
In overall, game offers a lot of interesting and tricky levels for you to enjoy, secrets, as well as achievements. It is indeed a good challenge, even though it's frustrating from time to time and from a certain point in the game, most of it will be just trial and error.
To anyone who cares: if you value your sanity but still wanna try this game, i would recommend starting with Super Meat Boy, to get the idea of how the challenge is and how the difficulty would be progressing.

This game...it needs to win the underrated game of the universe award.  Apparently went it first released, it was hampered with bugs and over shadowed by games like Oblivion. It is a Source Engine based game that plays very much like a combination of Thief and Half Life controls/combat.  It uses chapters/missions similar to both of those games as well.  It isn't open world but that won't bother you because there is plenty of loot hidden in secret areas for you to find.  It also starts off a bit rough with a hard to understand story and uninteresting at the time, plus the combat is difficult until you get new skills/weapons.
The combat in this game is so well done, especially for a game this old.  Most people say that if Elder Scrolls had this combat, they would be the best games ever made.  You'll have so much fun kicking enemies into spikes, fire, off stairs and using the many types of weapons you find along the way.  You even get to forge a few weapons.  Once you get past the first few chapters the story and gameplay really get great. I highly suggest playing on Hard mode because it forces you to use the various methods of fighting within the environment well.  You can activate traps laced within rooms like cutting ropes on swining objects, throwing oil on the ground and lighting enemies on fire, etc.  This game was worth every penny and I can't wait to finish it.
Pros
- Brilliant Combat System (super fun)
- Variety of weapons to use and loot
- Challenging Difficulties
- Interesting Environments
- Great Inventory and Skill System
- Interactive Environments and Secrets
Cons
- Mission based
- Not Open World (plenty to explore though)
- Story is bland at times
- Steep learning curve
- Unbalanced beginning
- Slightly outdated and a few bugs remain (not the spiders)
Score 9/10

Ok, before people start bashing this game for the admittedly terrible voice acting and lame plot, consider what this game does. It is an action RPG that focuses on being smarter and more skilled than the NPCs. Sure, you could charge at an enemy and beat them to death with your sword; OR, you could shoot them with your bow, crush them with collapsable scaffolding, drop them down a pit, down some stairs, hit them with barrels, kick them into spikes, burn them, kick them into each other, or stab them in the back. The level up system is kinda lackluster, and does seem like it takes forever to get some useful skills. If you RPG damage sponges want a game that doesn't require much thought to play, by all means, don't buy this game. If you are looking for an RPG that challenges you on multiple levels and prefer gameplay to plot and VAs, give this a shot. A good plot does not make a bad game better, but a bad story doesn't hinder a good game.

Ah Borderlands, in a nutshell: The hit comically over-the-top Co-Op FPS Action RPG | Co-op Looter-Shooter with built-in "Your Mom's girl parts" jokes.
There are 4 Character Classes customised through 3 Skill Trees providing a good range for practically all play styles. Each class has one unique Action ability which can be further modified via class skills. As this is a shooter your arsenal of a bazillion dynamically generated guns with unique abilities play a larger role in the game so you don't miss the hotbar full of abilities you might have in other RPGs much. And you'll be using those guns to blast through a variety of enemies ranging from zany midget bandits to epic sized wild game creatures and beyond.
Borderlands is chaotic fun no matter the problems it has BUT it's definitely despite a couple of main issues which revolve around Over-leveling(*) and Damage Scaling(**) when co-oping with characters more than a few levels apart:
(*) ~ Because of the way the designers set mission difficulty (and the lack of difficulty scaling for missions & enemies) in
of the game, it's very easy to completely over-level your character making the majority of the game a cake walk even into the DLCs.
Basically you will become over-leveled relative to Borderlands' mission content if:
-You do a few too many sidequests - You'll over-level.
-You join another person's campaign, gain a few levels and return to your campaign - You're over-leveled.
-You always kill respawned enemies in the way to your next objectives - You'll probably over-level.
(**) ~ Your damage is
. So if for example you have a good gun with a damage stat capable of killing the target in a few shots but you are 5 levels lower than your target - Your damage will be scaled down so that the shots will barely hurt the enemy, any lower level and it gets even more unplayable very fast. If you are higher level you'll cut the enemy down in extra quick time because you'll get a damage boost.
That becomes super annoying when trying to get friends of different levels together in a game or if you end up joining a host/campaign which is +|- more than a few levels from your char's.
The issue with over-leveling/no-difficulty-scaling was kind-of addressed with the last DLC release which, after PlayThrough2 of the original Borderlands campaign, makes the content scale to your char's level .. but again, that only happens at the end of Borderlands' campaign PT2 when you have practically completed the original campaign twice and it is flat scaling.
To wrap up: Borderlands is great for some chaotic co-op looting & shooting with a light sense of humour, it has a few issues left in here and there from it's long prototyping & development phase over at Gear Box but it's still great fun to play.
Bring on Borderlands 2 which is looking great and has already shown that it's addressed many of the first's issues, but I really hope Gear Box have used some sort of Challenge Rating based scaling to prevent over-leveling and make it easier for people to freely play in any number of different matchs of different player levels using the same character.

Is Strife your standard MOBA?  Not really.  It follows the basic concept of 3 lane map and 5 vs 5 format.  After that it goes out of its way to separate from the norm.  Customization and flexiblity are its main features in the game.  As people play several games, they will gain gems, seals, and elixirs to purchase pets, character skins, and craft custom items.  Currently there are 30 different heroes to pick from.  Plenty of characters for people to play to their own style. Pets have different specialities (restore hp, mana, slows enemies, buffs units, and removes status effects) which helps heroes.  The mobile item animal carrier helps limits players from going back and forth to base during the game.  Also the ability to regenerate hp and mana after a few seconds out of battle allows players to regroup and continue the fight.
While the customizations are creative, it can also be a negative.  Not every player has enough currency to create items or buy pets.  This creates an unfair advantage during ranked play.  Another issue lies with strike system.  I understand the strike system is developed to punish leavers in the games, but the ability to reconnect to the match doesn't always work if a bug or lag spike occurs.  In addition, I don't think the strike system should apply with human players vs all AI mode because it is not a ranked match and people are playing causal.
Would I recommend this game?  Sure.  It is worth playing.  Keep an open mind while playing.

I give this game a mild thumbs up.  Personally, I see a game as a good value if I can get 1 hour of play time per dollar spent on the game.  I got the game during a steam sale for $10 and I finished the game in 18 hours.  So, for me, it was a good value.  I would be annoyed if I spent the retail $40 on this game.  There is not 40 hours of content in this game even if you went after all the stars (bonus challenges).  Also, there is no replay-ability in the game.  Once you finish the story, that's it.  There is no reason to play through all the puzzles again.
The best part of the game is the story.  I won't give any spoilers, but the game is thought provoking and relevant and it is what made me trudge through all the puzzles to find out what happens.  There was a great deal of development spent on the environments, visuals, audio, story, and even on the menus.  However, I wish the game play was more than just puzzles.  These puzzles became incredibly repetitive.  There could have been 2 games here.  One game strictly for these puzzles and one game for the story.  For me, the puzzles were a distraction to the story and it felt like they were just puzzles for puzzles-sake.  I would have rather seen the puzzles more Myst-like;  where they are more environment based.  For example, figuring out how to unlock a door, or lowering a bridge, or crossing a body of water.  For me, this would be more immersive game-play.  I love exploring a world and learning its lore.
On to the puzzles.... there are soooo many puzzles..... hey, we heard you like puzzles, so we gave you some puzzles with your order of puzzles to go with your appetizer and desert of puzzles.  Get it?  The whole game is puzzles.
There are 4 main areas of puzzles.  Area A, B, C, and the tower.  Areas A, B, and C each have 7 zones with 3-7 puzzles in each zone.  The goal of each puzzle is to gather a tetris-like shape that is used to unlock content.  The green shapes unlock areas A, B, and C, the red shapes unlock each floor of the tower, and the yellow shapes unlock tools for use in the zones.  To unlock the content you have to arrange the shapes to fill in a square or rectangle board (think tetris).  There are 5 tools, 3 zones, and 6 floors in the tower to unlock with the shapes.  There are also some bonus/extra areas that require this mechanic to unlock.
The main game play in each zone (and tower floors) centers around navigating a maze of energy doors, turrets, ledges, boxes, drones, and using environment manipulation with a double of yourself.  The puzzles are pretty cool and have some unique game mechanics.  However, there were some mechanics that were not obvious to me.  For example, I didn't know that you could set a box on top of a drone.  When new game mechanics are introduced, there should have been some clue as to their use.  Most were obvious, but some were really obscure. So, I had to use youtube videos to figure some of the mechanics out.
There are 3? endings to the game.  Since the only save feature is an auto-save (which happens frequently), you cannot load a previous save to be able to play an alternate ending.  This will require you to play the entire game 3 times (omg, who would do that?) or you can just watch the other endings on youtube like I did.
This game really should have been about the puzzles and not included the story.  Near the end, I gave mild effort to solve the puzzles and then went to youtube to find the solutions.  I really got tired of solving the puzzles and just wanted to learn what happened in the story.
TL;DR
A good story wrapped around a TON of puzzles that become repetitive.  Only worth $10.

Ah Borderlands, in a nutshell: The hit comically over-the-top Co-Op FPS Action RPG | Co-op Looter-Shooter with built-in "Your Mom's girl parts" jokes.
There are 4 Character Classes customised through 3 Skill Trees providing a good range for practically all play styles. Each class has one unique Action ability which can be further modified via class skills. As this is a shooter your arsenal of a bazillion dynamically generated guns with unique abilities play a larger role in the game so you don't miss the hotbar full of abilities you might have in other RPGs much. And you'll be using those guns to blast through a variety of enemies ranging from zany midget bandits to epic sized wild game creatures and beyond.
Borderlands is chaotic fun no matter the problems it has BUT it's definitely despite a couple of main issues which revolve around Over-leveling(*) and Damage Scaling(**) when co-oping with characters more than a few levels apart:
(*) ~ Because of the way the designers set mission difficulty (and the lack of difficulty scaling for missions & enemies) in
of the game, it's very easy to completely over-level your character making the majority of the game a cake walk even into the DLCs.
Basically you will become over-leveled relative to Borderlands' mission content if:
-You do a few too many sidequests - You'll over-level.
-You join another person's campaign, gain a few levels and return to your campaign - You're over-leveled.
-You always kill respawned enemies in the way to your next objectives - You'll probably over-level.
(**) ~ Your damage is
. So if for example you have a good gun with a damage stat capable of killing the target in a few shots but you are 5 levels lower than your target - Your damage will be scaled down so that the shots will barely hurt the enemy, any lower level and it gets even more unplayable very fast. If you are higher level you'll cut the enemy down in extra quick time because you'll get a damage boost.
That becomes super annoying when trying to get friends of different levels together in a game or if you end up joining a host/campaign which is +|- more than a few levels from your char's.
The issue with over-leveling/no-difficulty-scaling was kind-of addressed with the last DLC release which, after PlayThrough2 of the original Borderlands campaign, makes the content scale to your char's level .. but again, that only happens at the end of Borderlands' campaign PT2 when you have practically completed the original campaign twice and it is flat scaling.
To wrap up: Borderlands is great for some chaotic co-op looting & shooting with a light sense of humour, it has a few issues left in here and there from it's long prototyping & development phase over at Gear Box but it's still great fun to play.
Bring on Borderlands 2 which is looking great and has already shown that it's addressed many of the first's issues, but I really hope Gear Box have used some sort of Challenge Rating based scaling to prevent over-leveling and make it easier for people to freely play in any number of different matchs of different player levels using the same character.

You could see this game as a lane based tower defense game, but with each lane having it's own distinct unit types, or as a rock-paper-scissors tug of war game, where each time you see the enemy sending more units at you, you have to see if your current forces will handily beat it, or if not start building a counter to the enemy unit(s) now coming at you. Do it badly/slowly and they start beating up your base, do it well and you start to dominate all three lanes and kill everything as soon as it appears on screen. The lanes mostly fight against others in the same lane, but some units are designed to use dominance of one lane to give you a boost in another - like the bomber which is useless if you don't have aerial supremacy, but can be powerful at clearing zeppelins and ground forces if you do.
The base gameplay then works fine, and make an interesting lite-RTS style experience where you build units, upgrade your base to build more unit types, or research upgrades to existing units, all while fending off the enemy attacks. Unfortunately similar to RTS games each new level you start again from scratch, which has never been something I am keen on as it can makes levels fairly repetitive, especially later on when you have the same 15 techs to get as last time before getting a new 16th tech and finally get to do something a bit new.
Another issue in the game is some unit types aiming ability - most units fire straight ahead, but then bullets curve downwards, and no one ever learns to adjust for this and fires up slightly, meaning some units that seeming have long range actually can only hit things immediately in front of them, and some units are much more vulnerable and weak purely because they have some part of their design that drops "below the waterline" of where units shot in each lane.
There is a main campaign where you unlock new units as you go along, and there is a story to give it all background which was passable but no more, and missions have some variety of objectives - make a certain amount of resources, build a certain tech/upgrade/unit, kill a number of enemies, survive a certain time, etc.
There is also a survival mode where you can sit there and slowly the amount of enemy units sent against you increases and eventually overwhelms you, I can't say I played this mode much as it didn't really feel much different to playing any of the later levels of the game for the initial stages, then you wait around a while once you have all the techs/units/excess resources you can get for the enemy forces to ramp up, then eventually there is another interesting bit where they start to break through but you can hold on by making the right choices, but that tends to only last a few minutes before the enemy adds even more forces and then nothing you can do holds them back.
Overall it is fairly decent, a bit innovative in it's approach, nice to look at, but has a few flaws/frustrations that stop it really being something special.
