It's been two long years since Castle Crashers was released on Xbox Live Arcade, but PlayStation owners will finally get to see what the fuss was all about. Taking that long to port a game over to another console might seem crazy, but The Behemoth did its best to ease the pain by adding in some new features and including DLC packs that Xbox 360 owners had to pay for. Unfortunately, it seems like the PSN version also includes online problems, just like its former release.
Castle Crashers starts with a mysterious man snatching a large (and what I assume is also expensive) crystal and four lovely princesses from the King's throne. As one of the knights of the castle, it is your duty to retrieve the stolen goods and fair maidens. There's no dialogue, so you won't get more of a story than that unless you use your imagination. That's not a bad thing, though, especially for a brawler. If you're like me, you probably don't need an excuse to chop enemies up into little pieces.
The best part of Castle Crashers is exploring the world -- there are tons of levels that look and play completely differently. From slip-n-slide icy terrains to sandy deserts, it's clear that every area was crafted with care by the Behemoth's resident artist, Dan Paladin. His unique art style really brings the environments to life, and even the most ferocious monsters are still pretty cute. To counteract the adorableness of Paladin's creations, the game includes lots of potty humor and gore-filled battles.
The four starting knights wield magic powers that are differentiated by armor color -- Red has lightning, Green has poison, Orange has fire, and Blue has ice. Armed with magic and steel (or maybe a stick), you'll hack your way through mounds of enemies, gain experience points, and level up. As you progress, you'll garner more skill points to divide amongst four traits: Strength, Magic, Defense, and Agility. You can build up your character however you'd like, but that's not the only way you can customize.
On your quest to save the princesses you'll discover two other tools to help you: melee weaponry and animal orbs. You can find new weapons several ways; some will be obviously given to you and others you'll need to dig up or purchase at a store. Every weapon will affect your stats either positively or negatively. A regular sword might take away a point of Strength but add a point to your Agility, so you'll need to make the call on what traits are more important to you. The urge to find a better, cooler weapon never dies, so you can expect to search the many hidden crevices of the game until you find something that suites your style.
Animal orbs are probably my favorite thing in Castle Crashers because they're just so damn cute. There are 28 creatures (the two DLC animals from the Xbox 360 version are now included) scattered across the lands, and it's up to you to find them. Each animal provides a different boost and comes complete with an endearing name, so Meowburt the kitty increases your agility skill while Owlet the owl can retrieve food items for you. It's fun to battle with a small animal hovering around you, especially if it's Rammy the ram who will ram nearby enemies for you.
The Behemoth is known for making difficult games, most notably Alien Hominid, and that reputation stands true if you try and take on the campaign by yourself. Though it can be done, single-player assaults are more frustrating and less enjoyable than teaming up with other people. The biggest issue in trying to take on levels solo is that multiple enemies can assault you with ranged attacks, making it difficult to even stand up before being knocked down again. Since it's designed to be a cooperative game, it's hard to scold The Behemoth for making it incredibly difficult to conquer on your own. There's no "I" in team, after all.
Speaking of friends, you can crash castles with the favorite people on your friends list either locally or online. With local co-op mode, you can't sign into multiple accounts like you could in the Xbox 360 version; you can only split up the main PSN ID into quarters. Friends curious about the game can also drop-in and out from the map, but not in the middle of a level, so it's not truly drop-in, drop-out co-op. Despite that flaw, it is nice that you can mix up the local and online co-op modes, so if you and a buddy at your house want to pair up with some other people on your friends list, you can do that.
If you're lucky enough, you can successfully create private matches with your friends, but out of several people only one of my friends was able to host a match without getting an error. Dropping into quick matches, however, seemed to work just fine. While playing online, there was some noticeable lag, but it didn't actually interfere until the worst possible moment -- once I made it to last part of the final boss, the game I was in suddenly dropped. Curse you, wretched servers!!! I can only hope that a patch fixing these issues will become available for the PS3 faster than it did for the Xbox 360 version.
Since the game had to be re-coded for the PS3 anyway, The Behemoth added in some minor differences throughout the campaign along with some major re-hauls. The most noticeable change is that the former mode All You Can Quaff has been removed and replaced with Volleyball. True to real life volleyball, there are two four-person teams playing against each other. The only problem is it's really difficult to figure out if you're on the same plane as the ball, so expect to get scored on a lot until you get the hang of it.
Team Arena has also been updated to include teams. Now you can pair up for some two-on-two battles, or prove yourself against three other people. There's also an Insane Store that's unlocked once you've beaten the game on normal difficulty. All former DLC offerings and the popular Alien Hominid character are included, some are found in the Insane Store, while others have to be earned in different ways.
The Behemoth&#Array;s incredibly fun cooperative beat&#Array;em-up would&#Array;ve been pure brawler perfection if the multiplayer had launched in better form. It&#Array;s incredibly frustrating that it&#Array;s easier to play Castle Crashers with strangers than with your friends, but it&#Array;s still a great brawler that will soak up your time. Between unlocking new characters so you can level them up to finding all of the hidden weapons and animal orbs, there&#Array;s a lot to do in the campaign mode. If you never experienced the Xbox 360 version, or you happen to have more friends on your PSN list, Castle Crashers is a great game though you might want to wait for a multiplayer patch before investing.

Overall, this is a charming and well-done game where, in just one playthrough, you realize all the little choices you make each minute. Choices in this game feel like they have weight, even if they may ultimately not. I found myself haunted by my words from the beginning when, really, all I had been trying to do is be friendly and try to help. And, it should be noted, that the option to stay silent is there and I am actually really interested in a totally silent playthrough.
Depending on your view of these games, this will either be a great adventure or a boring walk through a storybook. The game does its best some of the time to alleviate these issues, but shoots itself in the foot in others. So, let me get to the big things that could sway your opinion.
1. Character banter: Let's not beat about the bush, the characters in this game are verbose. You will walk a few steps and we will begin an epic four-part saga into the latest developments of the lot and/or your psyche. You will also frequently listen to the witty banter of the characters, perhaps including yourself. I can see this being a serious draw for some and a serious headache for others. I liked the banter (and actually thought the writing was really well done) but even I was getting a little tied of feeling like I wanted to let these characters talk but still wanting to vocalize my thoughts so we didn't just go off and have more brownies or go try to kill demon people. And there were more than a few times where I felt like I missed something with a character or with a location because I happened to trigger plot progression before one of those actually finished.
2. Map length/navigation: This game is filled with picture-book-style locations that are beautiful to look at and occasionally a nightmare to navigate. My first playthrough was sort of a stumble-on-things-as-you-go run, but I didn't feel that tempted to go seek out secrets/alternative paths mostly because the paths are frustratingly long and we're frustratingly slow. At some point, I think it's legitimate to suggest that the developers made more long, winding paths that I have to do a dance at every hairpin turn because they wanted the game to last longer. I would have spents at least an hour less on this game if there were straight/swooping curved paths instead of zig-zagging paths.
3. Choices: This is inevitable with these sorts of choice-based games where you have to select an option from a list, but choices frequently felt like they took on a life of their own. There's nothing to suggest that "That's okay" is going to make me say "That's okay" honestly, sarcastically, or say it honestly, then proceed to insult the person I'm talking to so as to make them think I was saying it sarcastically.

Even being as old as it is, Dark Messiah still has, hands down, one of the best combat systems I have ever seen in a video game. Few other medieval fantasy games have the amount of fluidity and control over a character's actions as DM does. Your character takes into account whether you are moving quickly, what direction you have moved your mouse, and how long you have pressed the attack button in determining what attack will be done.
The physics in the game are great as well. Ever wanted to kill a horde of orcs by only throwing crates and barrels at them a la Donkey Kong style? In this game, you can! Ever wanted to mess around for a while watching Necromancers play slip and slide on ice traps you've laid down? In this game, you can! Want to fight dirty and kick an enemy  off a cliff? In this game, you can!
Other games such as Morrowind/Oblivion/Skyrim may have an open world with a more developed lore surrounding it, but they absolutely pale when it comes to their combat systems. Any person who has played Dark Messiah will agree.
On another note, this is still one of the few games in which you can enjoy a full view of your character's body when looking downwards. Games being made today still don't have this option, which is somewhat embarassing since this game had it implemented perfectly since 2006.
Lastly, this is one of the few games that genuinely feels as though you have actually taken down something massive and dangerous. The colossal size of some of the creatures, such as the wyverns and cyclops in this game, are genuinely huge, and require out-of-the-box strategizing to take down. For comparison's sake, I'll use Skyrim. I didn't love Super Meat Boy.  The game had its fun, rewarding levels here and there, but it was brought down by being too fast to react to anything, too slippery in the air for reliable jumps, and too full of hard-to-manage enemies and obstacles which made many levels feel more like luck than a test of skill.  A few of the boss fights relied solely on memorization, some challenges were excessively long with no checkpoints, the jump button didn't even always register, and I could spend half an hour getting a successful run of a stage and still not have done it fast enough for an A+ rank, which destroyed any interest I had in 100%ing the game.
The End is Nigh fixes every issue I had with Super Meat Boy.
This game has a moderately more relaxed pace, with far tighter, less variable movement.  The jump button is responsive every time and feels exactly the way it should.  There are no timers, and hanging on ledges is a suitable replacement for wall-jumping because it allows you to sit still and analyze the area methodically.  And you start out with your full moveset, but you learn how in-depth it is throughout the game.
Every screen is a checkpoint, and depending on how you enter an area, you'll have a different respawn point, making certain collectables more convenient and fair to obtain while still posing a challenge.  Most (but certainly not all) of this game's difficulty comes from the optional parts, which I consider to be very good design.
This game has no boss fights; it doesn't need any, because the environment is harsh enough.  What it does have are some tricky enemies to avoid (or use to your advantage), which are not always easy to deal with, but their patterns are reliable enough to manage.  The mechanics in this game also never seem to fall into the wretchedly physics-oriented hive that Super Meat Boy's air currents or repelling magnets did.
On top of all that, I'd even say TEiN has the better artwork, music, story, and characters.
The backgrounds are often monochromatic, fairly saturated cityscapes or skies against the silhouetted terrain our charming protagonist Ash explores.  Everything is slick and smooth, as opposed to strangely polygonal like much of Meat Boy's art.  There is more depth to be found in Ash's simple post-apocalyptic tale of woe and the odd little messages from the dead than there is in rescuing Bandage Girl from a fetus in a jar.  The music is comprised almost entirely of hardcore rock covers of famous classical music, which is frankly just a recipe for success.  It's the kind of soundtrack I want to listen to while I'm working to increase my productivity.
So far, I've completed 80% of the game and intend to see it through to the end.  It might not be as nigh as it seems.
Now, I've seen others say this game has no soul, and that it's somehow lazy.  But even in its world of skulls and corpses, there's a heartbeat.  This game is no less meticulously designed than anything Edmund has crafted, and I'd argue that it is his best work.

Age of Steel: Recharge is a tower defense game that is just plain good.
With polished pixel-styled graphics and easy to understand controls, the storyline in AoSR is compelling and the music aptly somber. Campaign mode is split into 3 Acts, with each completed stage unlocking it's Survival Mode.  It's a post-apocalyptic world and all the mod cons are here in the UI: You can turn screen shake on or off, adjust music and sound, and play in windowed mode.
What makes AoSR good is that it just feels good to play. Stages aren't a walkover, but won't leave you frustrated either. You can work out your strategy pretty quickly for each stage within an Act and work out better ways to complete it for replays. The mechanics are fundamentally tower defense in you (automatically) collect resources, choose what units to produce, make upgrades, and smash your opposition (uncannily referred to as The Opposition in the game, whilst you are The Alliance. Personally I always preferred Horde, but I digress). Each stage also offers an unique unit for the terrain and in some cases these become your main objective in creating them.
The graphics and sound lend themselves to creating a surreal atmosphere that become a little bit of a foundation for how easy it is to pick this game up, play a couple of stages, go off, come back - or play an entire Act in one sitting.
It's hard to find something to pick apart with this tower defense game. It's a good introduction to the genre if you have never really played one before, and aficionados will find appeal in the setting. Does it offer any buzz or unique feature to the genre? Not really. As you progress through the Acts, the pace does pick up, and at times you have to change tactic, but it doesn't have anything genre-defining. It's just a nice game to play.
And sometimes that's all you really need.
I'm giving the game a thumbs up based on it being a cmplete game, polished and enjoyable to play.
Is it overpriced for what it offers? Unfortunately, yes. It's something worth picking up on sale or in a bundle, but at its current price (~US$7) it is overzealous. It has replayability but not enough to warrant the price-tag.

This game is not worth $7.79. If you can get it as part of a bundle or at a drastic discount though, consider playing around with it for a bit.
It's a tower defense game, with the twist that most of your "towers" have to be manufactured at your base and then move into position. Your units aren't very sophisticated, they just move forward until they're in place, firing constantly whether the enemy is present or not.
The bullets are affected by gravity, and the units make no attempt to aim. The flyers try to compensate a little by jinking slightly up and down so that when you've got a few of them they expand the range where they can hit something, but it still kind of feels like your defense force is a bunch of simpletons.
There are three levels to the game. Ground level, where you can place turrets and tanks. Mid level, where you place air ships. And top level, where you send flyers and bombers. One big mistake the game designeers made was allowing you to advance your base to the point where it's flying and you no longer have to deal with the ground level. Several levels start out with your base in the air. Having to deal with only 2 levels simplifies the game and removes a lot of the challenge.
The final level, in fact, was incredibly boring. They introduced a new air ship called the Titan, which is the most powerful unit in the game. Then they gave me time to build 5 of them, as well as a bunch of flyers, and have them move into place before the enemy waves arrived. No ship was a threat to my mid level. I didn't even get to see them appear before they exploded in fireballs. I just had to sit around and watch my top level, occasionally replacing flyers that got killed and waiting an excruciatingly long time for the final boss to show up.
Even the final boss wasn't a threat. I didn't lose a single ship to fighting it. I lost half my ships when it finally exploded, but by then it didn't matter.
Some of the levels were challenging though, and I enjoyed the mental exercise of trying to figure out how to stagger my waves so that they arrive at a good time for maximum impact. The weird thing is, though, that the game doesn't let you replay any levels once you've completed them. Most games let you replay levels, and there's no reason this game shouldn't have that same option.
Some levels have a rain animation that places temporary "droplets" on your screen and distorts your view. That was annoying. It was also annoying when the ground shook from an explosion, because the game wouldn't let me click on anything - but that effect was at least kind of cool.
The English in the game is poorly translated, but often in entertaining ways so that kind of added to the charm of the game for me.
I enjoyed playing this game, so I'm going to recommend it. But I would suggest againist buying it at its full price.

This is easily one of the most fun, fulfilling puzzle games that I've played - rivaling the Portal series in both quality and scale. The entire experience is incredibly polished, and the universe it takes place in is hauntingly beautiful (akin to the Myst series; alone in a gorgeous but eerily-empty world.) The core game has about a hundred separate puzzles across dozens of levels, each of which has its own unique flair, and the story involves just enough player choice to give it replayability (something lacking in most puzzle-adventure games.) The game mechanics are relatively simple, but each puzzle mixes the various tools you gain access to in new and interesting ways. Some of the puzzles can be a bit nerve-wracking and involve split-second timing, but the vast majority are pretty relaxed and allow the player to solve them at their own pace. You can go through each puzzle in order, or jump around a bit provided that you've made enough progress to unlock the more difficult levels. Overall, the difficulty of the puzzles was reasonable - not so easy as to be boring, but not so brain-twistingly hard that it keeps you up at night.
On top of the well-balanced gameplay, the story was surprisingly deep for a puzzle game; I was reminded a bit of The Turing Test, another puzzle game, in its examination of what it means to be human vs. a machine, as well as some of the pseudo-religious elements of BioShock Infinite. The game opens with a lot of questions, which you begin to find answers to as you progress through the various levels. I found the story to be almost as rewarding as the gameplay itself, which is a rare quality in the puzzle-adventure genre. It's hard for me to find anything to complain about in The Talos Principle; even at its normal $40 price point, I'd consider it a good purchase. On sale, it's a must-buy. 9/10

Look past the brony humour, the dated comic stylings of Stephen Merchant and call backs to memes of 2007 and what do you find?
What we have here is a beta test for technology made for the new generation that never occurred; and let me tell you waiting for a third instalment feels like being an inanimate object floating through space waiting for your lithium battery to finally die out.
Life after Portal 2 can be compared to the death rattle of Cave Johnson and his last voice messages. The five stages of grief:
SHOCK & DENIAL- Holy Moses I’m a 30 year old man and Valve still hasn't made a third game for any series yet and these loose ends in these stories feel like an unpaid mortgage.
PAIN & GUILT- If only I stopped checking Google every four years to see if Gabe has hinted at releasing a new Half Life.
ANGER & BARGAINING- ♥♥♥♥ this! I'll check some mods.
"DEPRESSION", REFLECTION, LONELINESS- *Finds the string quartet version of the Portal credits music and remembers his youth*
ACCEPTANCE & HOPE- Well developers are into outsourcing  these days, perhaps Gabe can sell the licences of his games to Obsidan?
When life gives you lemons, you make lemonade. But what is one to do when life gives you two really engaging lemons and the rest of your ingredients for lemonade is still in the mail?
Portal was and always will be a strong beta test for a weapon that intended for use in the next Valve instalments. So the build up is there but much like the Matrix Trilogy you will find yourself confused and angry at where we are today.
Valve; if you are reading this, ♥♥♥♥♥ out your intellectual property to the bright eyed and bushy tailed programmers of tomorrow. Please.

This game was great, long ago. Now, it's no fun. I am biased, which I'll get into later.
There used to be tiers of blocks, which could be unlocked through the tech tree. I worked my way up, and found my favorite of all the "weapons" were the close range lasers that could heal teammates. I made a super-redundant craft using multiple tiers of rotors and weapons, with multiple spider legs, allowing the craft to take cover and heal from up walls and in the air. The redundancy allowed it to still function even after getting slammed by multiple enemies, and made it much easier to be a solo-healer.
But they ♥♥♥♥ed me over. There are no tiers. People self-regenerate. You can use multiple weapons meaning pretty much everybody and their mother made sure to include some form of anti-air, and my close-range healing-focused bot was ripe for the taking.
That's why I'm biased. I'm sure some DPS-heavy bots love the regen and single-tier, but for people like me who literally put all of their eggs into one basket, it sucks.

As time goes on I have become more patient and that patience is rewarded quite well in this game.
If you are looking for something else that you can't quite explain... Perhaps you liked CS long ago but find it too quick, or perhaps you like Insurgency but find the community not very friendly and the maps too small, or perhaps you have an Arma game sitting on your playlist but find it daunting to learn and complicated when playing... than perhaps Squad is for you. It takes some great ideas and implements them quite well.
Any criticism I have for this game are being addressed in future updates and I am looking forward to see where this game goes… Join me in this anticipation!

So, my review for this game is... it's a very unique game that bridges the military simulation of Arma, and The fast paced arcade shooter of say... Battlefield or Call of duty, much more like Battlefield due to Vehicles being in this game. Due to this game being in Alpha, things are subject to change.
The game relies heavily on communication between squads, with that being said, if you wish to be a team leader, you are required to have a mic. I myself just play as medic a majority of the time. weither or not I am good at it is up to you. If you do not have a mic, Do not let that discourage you from playing this game, just not as team leader.
In each squad there is classes that you can choose, Riflemen, Automatic Riflemen, Ranger, Sniper, Medic, ETC. I believe it is set up by the Squad leader, in said classes, you are given equipment based on your role, Rocket launchers, heavy machineguns, you name it and they might have it. There is currently no way to customize your weapons, like putting on attachments or "weapon skins"
There is details in the game that just wow me, Dust flying off of explosion, when you launch an RPG that the militia uses, there is a noticable backblast which I have found to be a very nice detail. Gunfire for me, anyways, tends to all sound the same. Regardless, gunfire is still very realistic sounding, and supression is very real.
You can play as four factions so far, Russia, United States Army, Insurgents, and Irregular Militia. I believe Russia and The United States can fight eachother on some maps.
Factions are choosen based on maps, Sometimes you get Russia and Innies, Sometimes Russia and Irregular Militia, and so fourth, I have yet to see Insurgents vs Irrgular Milita.
Vehicles. There is plenty of vehicles in the game, Technicals, Transports, Logistics and Firesupport. currently Fire support vehicles tend to have a .50 cal or rockets on them, I have yet too see rockets in use. They can be destroyed by Rockets armed troops as far as I have noted.
Gameplay is like a bit like Arma. Some things have been simplified, for example, maps "They are on G5" or so, you still have a compas on which you can say the bearings of the enemy "Enemy sighted,bearing 115" or so.
Multiplayer is as far as I can tell, hardcore, but still friendly to people learning how to play the game, I've met Japanese, French, English, Scottish, Russia, and I believe Arabic speaking peoples.
I rate this game a good 8/10

"Squad is a 50 vs 50 multiplayer first-person shooter that aims to capture combat realism through communication and teamplay. Major features include vehicle-based combined arms gameplay, large scale environments, base building, and integrated positional VoIP for proximity talking & radio." That's the description of the game, word for word. If some of these people who gave this game negative reviews actually read it before they opened their pockets, I'd take them more seriously, and they'd be $40 US dollars richer...
If you're looking for a new Call of Duty style arcade shooter, click away. If you love Battlefield, but want the next stage up, Squad's your option. If you love Arma and Red Orchestra, but want something fresh and new(ish), Squad's your option. It sits right in the middle. Squad is essentially an accesible immersive military simulator. I don't like the word "Realistic" becuase we will never, ever capture the true realism of War. It's not possible.
Being that this is early access, I can forgive the bugs and glitches, so we won't touch on them. But this game is up there with being one of my favorites for sure. It's a game where it's good with friends, but it's not required because your Squad mates ARE your friends (If you get a good Squad). I've had a few bad ones, for example Squad leaders that don't talk, and the kiddies who treat it like Call of Duty and think they're entitled to say what they want because they have "Squad Leader" next to their name. The community is really excellent, though. Squad has one of the best communities in my opinion, there's not been a lot of times where I've had a bad experiences with people being rude or insulting. Some people can be stern or come across as bossy but that just adds to the game's immersion, which I'll get to in a moment. If you're going to buy into this, chances are you'll feel welcome. Don't be scared to ask for help. This game is full of adults who are mature, and they won't deem you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you ask how to play! (Not saying that won't happen though :P).
I feel like immersion needs it's own para simply because it's breathraking. I'm not saying it's realistic but damn is it awesome. When explosions go off, it's not a pissy little PSSHHHHHHHHHH it's a BOOOOOFFFFFFFFFFFF. I do not recommend playing this at 100% volume unless you want to obliterate your Primary auditory cortex. Guns don't have a beefy pop, they have a death sounding crack, you fear all bullet noises, even if it's from your own barrel. The graphics aren't of triple A quality, but they are pretty damn good for something that it's Triple A. I'm fine with that because they really don't have to be. The sound itself kind of makes everything gel together nicely and give that scary atmosphere. It could be silence with the light breeze through the russian forest, then it would erupt with cracks of bullets, and the devastating grenade impacts.
The gameplay is fairly solid at the moment, again it's not triple A but with some refining and tweaking, we could have THE BEST FPS military simulator to date. There are a few changes I'd like to see, I think jumping needs to be comepletely re designed. I'd love a vaulting mechanic similar to Battlefield 1. It's really annoying to try and scale a wall or a fence because you really need to get it in a sweet spot for a successful scale. That being said I like how you also have a stamina bar for jumping. You can't jump too much otherwise you'll get too tired and won't be able to jump at all.
Vehicles have also been recently implemented, and for the most part they perform well. Steering is a little slidey, it kind of reminds me of the driving in GTA IV. I wish the vehicles would feel as though they are connected to the ground though. Other than that, they're pretty well balanced, and can be easily taken to town if your squad works as a team.
Don't get me wrong, Squad still has some work that needs done, and with how active the developers are, and how well they interact with the community, they can easily finish it by their mid 2017 deadline. Squad is one of the very few early access titles which deserve to be backed by the gaming community.

Squad is the answer for anyone looking to experience tactical fps warfare. I wouldn't advise playing without a mic as communication is vital.
The active and friendly developers are constantly working to improve the game as well as keeping the community up to date with those improvements.
The community is fantastic, with minimal trolls, hostility, etc. And 9 times out of ten you'll have a group of players all working together to execute orders from the squad leaders.
There is much fun to be had in this game, despite the emphasis around military simulation and intensity/focus. Ideal for people who enjoy military simulation! (Find a clan!)
------
PROS:
- big maps with a range of different terrain and types of compounds, buildings, rivers etc.
- a good variety of vehicles
- lots of different weapons
- base building
- the general community
- emphasis on teamwork
- active devs & updates
- tactical gameplay with -for the most part - mature people
- long, action packed games
- realism
- good keyboard mechanics and lay out

CONS:
- bad teamwork can result in an extremely frustrating game for obvious reasons
- the game isn't finished so there will be minor bugs from update to update although I've not really had any major issues so far
- on occasion, getting stuck with no where to spawn near the action can be annoying but that's usually your own teams fault for losing rallies and fobs! ;-)
- the insurgents / milita lack the scopes that the U.S, and I think also Russia,  have, which can be annoying on some maps, other times you don't notice as much though.
- despite the name, there is no function to squad up with friends prior to joining a server, which can make teaming up with people you know, or have met through the game quite difficult. however, recently as the games been getting more and more servers this hasn't been as bad of an issue and they are actually working on a "squad up" system for the menu.
- addictive (seriously...)
Conclusion:
I would highly recommend this game to you if you are looking for a tactically focused, large scale, online multiplayer military game that you can sink your teeth in to.
The game relies heavily on the community so this can make or break the experience but 99% of the time it is positive.
Squad looks like it's only going to get better with the addition of ieds, new factions, new maps, new weapons, possibly even tanks and - if Santa read my letter - aircraft.
For a game that isn't even finished, Squad really excels in delivering what it set out to do already and will continue to improve the experience as time goes on.

First off, the good.
The game is polished, with a neat pixel art style and an interesting 3-level battlefield.
Unfortunately, the actual gameplay leaves a lot to be desired.
Generally units can only attack units in their level on the battlefield, but the top level is the exception. There are fighter bombers that can attack everything and can do a lot of damage, so generally there isn't much reason to build anything else.
Projectiles fired by your units seem to miss more and have shorter range than what your enemy throws at you. I've had instances where I've had several upgraded units destroyed by one lower level enemy unit simply because it flew in slight above the firing arc of my units.
You only have one production queue for everything (building units and upgrading). Furthermore, the enemy can spawn multiple units at a time leaving you scrambling to get even a basic defense set up between upgrading to get the units you need and building stopgap defenses to deal with the enemies swarming you. There really aren't breaks between waves so once you get behind there's a good chance you've already lost the battle. I found myself with huge piles of money and because of the production queue issue I couldn't spend it as fast as I was earning it.
The game is quite short which is fine, but this means that the difficulty ramp is much steeper than it should have been. The later levels are insane with the number of units they throw at you and many times you have to already have built the correct defenses, there's no time to react.
Overall, with a rebalance and some new units (antiaircraft tanks for ground, helicopter gunships and AA ships for mid level for example) this could be an interesting game, but right now I can't really recommend it given the major gameplay issues.

Age of Steel: Recharge is a pretty standard tower/lane defense. Basically the entire game revolves around building land and air units, aswell as upgrading your base in order to defend yourself from waves of The Opposition’s troops. You are in charge of an allied mobile base and in each mission, the goal is to defend key areas to the Alliance in its fight against The Opposition.
The gameplay is pretty simple. There are three different types of Units, the first one moves on land and that’s where you got your tanks, turrets and walls. The second Unit type is in the water and on this lane the only thing that moves are ships. Finally the top lane is where jets and other aircraft move. Assuming it isn’t a bomber, a Unit cannot attack Units on another lane. This brings some strategy to the game, which makes you manage the amount of units you have on each lane and if you’re able to defend your base from that lane effectively.
Now, there is a few things I found weird about the game, such as the Steam overlay doesn’t work (Fraps framerate counter also appears not to work) and also that there is no way to check the objective for the mission you’re playing. The objective only displays at the beginning of the level I believe. That said, things like having the ability to queue multiple units for construction and clever hotkeys for building specific units are also not present, which I find rather odd, especially on a game like this.
I feel like the story is there just for the sake of it. The Opposition, the first non governmental army, wants to dominate the world and create a new society in order to achieve global peace and prosperity. On the other hand, the Alliance wants to free the world of The Opposition because they believe their campaign will eventually lead Earth to its demise. If you were looking for a rich setting, you probably won’t find it here.
To sum it all up, this is not a bad game, but it also isn’t a very good one, the features that are present do what they have to. If you’re looking for a time waster or something to play while you’re bored or in short periods of time, this might be the game for you. If you’re still unsure about it, get it on sale.

Highly addictive colony management sim that is difficult to put down once you get hooked. The term "emergent gameplay" gets thrown around a lot these days and most games don't get it right. RimWorld is an exception as it pretty much excels in this regard. All of your colonists come with a wide variety of traits, skills and personalities which makes for some very interesting and amusing scenarios as the game progresses. This is one of those games where each new game feels different and can lead to various outcomes (and it often includes the violent breakdown of your colony).
There are plenty of different difficulty settings to choose from. You could play it as a relaxing colony builder for example or gradually ramp up the difficulty and make life hell for the colonists. You'll have to keep your colonists well fed and taken care of by setting up production chains, defend them from extreme weather conditions, fend bandit and animal attacks as well as deal with their interpersonal issues. As a colony builder it offers you a lot of freedom over how you build and expand. It's extremely satisfying to build a well laid out and well-defended colony. The UI right now isn't the best but it isn't bad either. I'm sure it will be improved with further updates but the game is quite playable and fun.
RimWorld is mostly the work of one developer and it's remarkable in that aspect. It contains depth that's rarely found in big budget games with teams of hundreds of people. I am constantly blown away by the emergent scenarios it throws at you and none of that is scripted. One moment your colony may be running like a well-oiled machine, the next moment a single wild animal might start a chain of events that ultimately lead to it's complete breakdown. These failures never feel frustrating and you can always go back to a previous save (unless you're playing on permadeath).
The graphics are simple and might not look appealing at first but the game has a certain charm of it's own. You'll begin to appreciate the little details and effects on various actions and items. I personally feel like it's a great looking game and the visuals do grow on you. There's a lot to do in this game and it's impossible to cover all aspects in a few words. For example I haven't even touched upon the deep crafting, farming and work assignment mechanics.
Bottomline is - if you like management / sim games and love building stuff it doesn't get better than this. This is probably the best Early Access game I've bought and is definitely a case in favor of the medium.

This game is a cart racer similar to Mario Kart or Crash Team Racing. This game is pretty fun the way stages will change based on whatever lap you're on. The ground can shatter, the road can end going into an ocean... or you can launch off an air carrier and race in the middle of a massive dog fight.. it all depends on the stage. The changes are scripted and are the same each time but still it adds a fun dynamic to what otherwise would have been a standard kart racing game. Your kart can transform into a speed boat or a flying machine depending on what happens in the game. Winning is based more on how well you can handle your vehicle and how well you can drift-boost. You can also dodge attacks with speed boost making the game more skill based than luck based. Being farther in the back makes the chance of getting a greater item higher. Being in front however doesn't mean you'll be denied ultimate attacks. You have a chance of getting your ultimate "All-Star" item even in first place.
This game really did keep my attention for quite a while. I put about 30 hours into it playing the Grand Prix mode in easy, normal hard and expert. Trust me when I say this. "Normal" is the old Sonic Racing "Hard mode" Hard and expert mode will give you a run for your money. There is also a progression mode to earn stars and unlock characters and mods. They get very difficult if not impossible towards the end so proceed with caution.
This game is a total retro throwback to many of old segas games so many of the themes in the game have been remixed or improved upon with the exception of old stages from the previous Sonic Racing. My favorite themes in the game are the theme for Burning Depths and the theme for the Golden Axe level.
Overall this game is not too bad. Great visuals, nice background music, fun characters. It's a must have for any sonic fan and a 'try' for anyone who remotely likes cart racers. I'm sure you'll get at least some fun out of it.

Diablo 2 if it were a first person shooter.  What's not to like?  If you're a typical FPS player, keep in mind that with a cardboard gun and a low level character you wont be droppin' diesels with simply a single shot to the dome.  Borderlands don't play that.  You DO however.. do much more damage. So skill is not lost on this rpg/skill tree game.  Fun solo, more fun with a friend.  With the exception of Mad Moxxi's whatever whatever, it has good dlc.  Not much in the way of customization, plenty in the way your character plays.  There's a tanky melee damage soak who gets in their face and uses demolitions, a sniper who makes short work of anything with a soft spot (with a bit of skill), a jack of all trades support character who is a go-to-guy for enduring combat, and a stealth burst damage dps assassin.

I highly recommend this game. It has evolved into such a vast, complex game, with a community still healthy and thriving. This game offers hours upon hours of content, from campaigns to multiplayer. Intro:
Dark messiah does not feel like a linear adventure game with their backpack and level system. It's more like an FPS/RPG(I woudlnt say action rpg).
Longevity and difficulty:
It does not take too many hours to beat it, but it's worth it. Play at very hard and i bet you won't survive. I tried it on hard mode, but you still have to limit yourself if you want your hard mode to be challenging.
Limit yourself(a game is never too hard):
So if you want your hard to be hard, you should not unlock healself and do not use weapons that do exactly what a spell does unless you want to do a quick speedrun. At the very least, drop the ice bow and lighting shield.
Combat:
One of the best combat system. The enemies and the ai are strong and smart enough to beat you in a duel. so imagine when 2 of them jumps on you. This forces you to sneak first before you engage. It forces you to use you spells strategically to kill a couple before you jump on the last few of the room to kill. Thus, it forces you to use your environment and front kicking your opponent on a spike like a mortal kombat's fatality. Speaking of fatalities, you will most likely kill your opponent with a fatal blow and you must build up your meter for that like a super meter from street fighter.
Story:
Il say it now, don't play for the story. The immersion is there and everything, but the story is not that good. The ending is one of the worse.
Verdict: Buy the game. It's unique and this game probably influenced most first person slashing games after that. It was very unique when it came out in 2006 and it still feels that way.

What happens when you take spewer, give it gish's mechanics,throw it in the world of SMB, boil it in gamer's tears, and give it a pinch of salt? You get this game.
The end is nigh is a precision platformer that seems to be an extension of a lot of Ed's previous platformers. The comparisons to meat boy are inevitable so I'll address the elephant in the room.
-This game's overall look is similar to that of meat boy's, but it's more polished.
-Some of the enemies and hazards return in the form of something else.
-The dark world and warp zones return to some extent.
-The difficulty is up to par with meat boy
However, this game is by no means a sequel to super meat boy, and that's not what we should expect going into it imo.
-Ash's controls are tight, fast, and responsive.
-The areas are detailed and do a good job setting in the atmosphere.
-The soundtrack is fantastic, and definitely adds to the environment.
-Almost all collectibles are obtainable from the get go, which lessens the pain of backtracking.
-The level design is great
-This game favors exploration and keeping your eyes peeled for secrets, the room-to-room style of progression from most of ed's games is removed in favor of a gauntlet of levels.
-This game can challenge people of pretty much any skill level, the difficulty can surpass meat boy at times.
-this game does a good job of teaching you how it works.
-despite an extreme amount of deaths, (I have 6000+ after beating the full main game, not including nevermore). This game doesn't seem as rage inducing as meat boy, at least not until the
end game bonus content.
-Some of the jumps require almost pixel perfect accuracy and timing, which can result in trial and error.
-most of the enemies are
and can definitely hinder the experience, this can be lessened by paying attention to their patterns though.
-There are some really annoying hazards in this game as well, such as polluted air.
-Some of the collectibles are very poorly placed, but most of them are clever.
-There is a distinct lack of bosses in this game, which is a shame because there was more of a focus on enemies this time around. The climax is still pretty good though.
-sometimes the gripping mechanic can work against you.
-The story is nothing to write home about.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game and preferred it over super meat boy, I can reccomend this game to any precision platformer fan.

I first noticed this game because it was very similar to a gamejam game me and a couple of friends made for GGJ 2014. If you're interested in it, it's called "Manhattan".
I'm not ashamed to say, this game is a lot better than the game we made.
This game is what I would call a hidden crowd game. Basically, there is a crowd of non-player characters that look identical to the player characters, and it is the player's task to conduct an objective without being noticed by other players. This is primarily accomplished through careful movement and crowd navigation, in order to decieve opponents into thinking that you are an NPC.
In this particular game, the objective is to kill your opponents. This is done through moving up to the suspected player and attacking (by pressing X). This instantly kills them and awards you with one point.
This dynamic is made complicated by the different player classes available. At the beginning of each round, players anonymously choose a class, which comes with 2 unique abilites. One ability can be used once, the other can be used three times, but both interact with the gameplay in interesting ways.
Will you be a Warrior, who can cause a crowd of npcs to attack, or a Ranger, who can feign death by tricking an opponent into thinking they killed an NPC? A Rogue, who can clandestinely kill a player without making any noise or visual cue? Or a Wizard, who can teleport and polymorph foes. SQUAD is one of the few titles in the market that can at a glance make the internet look like a good place. Sure you will find the outliers in every case but most of my brief interaction within the game has been with genuinely good persons who want to share and help the lowest level players reach a level of proficiency and skill that they can shoot stuff but contribute to the teams functioning.
At its most basic, SQUAD is a tactical FPS borne out of Project Reality MOD scene. It bridges the gap between small scale intense games like INSURGENCY and the bombast of AAA titles like BattleField with the essence of mechanics that are only to be found in titles like ARMA without the complexity of the same. This means,
The visuals presented in game are rich and well detailed keeping in mind what OffWorld Industries is going for in this game, SQUAD is more focussed on the combat and not on small knick-knacks as of now, so interiors can feel bare and the lack of environmental damage deformation might turn some off but this is not that kind of a shooter.
Another point where the game excels is its soundscapes, guns, RPG's, vehicles and the accompanying orchestra of war has been beautifully done. Everything has a reverb to imply weight, weapons have a sharp firing sound accompanied by a follow on report which is something completely absent or muted in other shooters which gives a good sense of depth to the ongoing carnage that is being unleashed. All this accompanied by some of the most sombre OST work. Hats off you guys, you really nailed this out of the park.
This game is not feature complete so there are things that are being patched in almost on a weekly basis, new loadouts are being added, there is a small selection of vehicles (mostly focussed on transport and logistics) and the devs do not plan to add vehicles like fighter-bomber jets. As of v 0.8, the game runs pretty acceptably on my Core i5 4690
AMD RX480 while installed on a SSD. I have had a couple of CTD's but that is to be expected from a title that reads EARLY ACCESS.
As time goes on, I see the community of SQUAD being a perennialy small band of players without the capacity to mobolise the numbers you see from established shooter franchises but this is a good thing as this community in my interaction has shown itself to be made up of mature voices who are genuinely in the game for a good time and some serious fun.
Overall, if you are someone who wants to have a good time, with mature players and simply cannot access that in a modern military shooter franchise like BattleField please do check out SQUAD, if not via direct purchase, you can get into the action come next free weekend or discount run.
I would not recommend this game if you are into run-gun multi-players, arcade shooters or just want a casual match which lasts for ~10 minutes on average, every match is a significant time investment of an hour or so. This does not by any means imply you are a casual gamer but simply that you have a different set of criteria to enjoy in your games.

Disclosure of Potential Bias: I know the developers (I grew up two houses down from one of them!) and have seen the game (and played it) since its earliest iteration (all the way back to when the devs would throw a Codefest in the dorms at our uni and we would all hang out: playing games, coding stuff, plus eating hot pockets, chips, and walmart bakery cookies; ah, college life). /waves at Ocumens developers
TLDR: Cutthroat has a low barrier to entry (controls are easy), but has a high skill cap (git gud at pattern recognition) and even a metagame (better track the amount of times a warrior Riots, or if a mage has Soul-Swapped yet, and many more things) because the game forces you to be stealthy to be successful. You can play this game with your parents (or, if you're a parent, with your younger kids and your partner) and everyone can have fun within just a few rounds (you learn the controls very quickly).
I don't do to well with most party games (local multiplayer pvp games), but I've found Cutthroat to be a pleasant exception. The game relies much less on memorizing zillions of fighting combinations, rather, the controls are easy and quick to learn...the real challenge (and what makes it so fun) of Cutthroat is successfully differentiating between other players and a bunch of AI NPCs based soley on observing all characters' movements. There are no nameplates/name tags in Cutthroat so the first step you must take in game is to find your character based on how you're moving via your controller or your keyboard inputs, then, you must try to stay hidden from other players by mimicking the movement style of the many AI NPCs roaming around the map...all while trying to spot other players by looking for characters who are not moving in an AI-like manner. That's why Cutthroat is a local stealth-based pvp game...there are no character names so you have to get good at spotting movement patterns! If you make a bad guess and attack a suspicious character that turns out to be an AI NPC...guess what, you just revealed yourself to all the other players, but this can occasionally work to your advantage because you can identity other players by how they move in reaction to your action.  Imagine trying to move towards a player who just revealed their position by attacking (NPCs don't attack), but having to move in a deliberately stealthy manner (mimicking AI NPCs movement) so that that player and the other players don't spot you moving towards that player. Cutthroat has a very low barrier to entry, because the controls are easy, but has a high skill cap (which means you can play many many games with your friends and still not get bored...I've played many hours of rounds by this point and still haven't gotten bored of the game, because the skill cap is so high and there is a good stealthy metagame going on) since you must get very good at recognizing certain kinds of movement patterns, consciously move your character in a stealthy manner while also watching for other player characters, and deal with the special moves that each class has, plus deal with environmental features on some maps that shake things up. If you like playing games with other people primarily in person, or even online if you can't meet up in person (there is an online mode, but to set up a session you will need to be on voice comms with your friends since you have to tell them the name of the room you created as well as whether you are playing ranked or unranked; there is currently no game lobby setup), and enjoy stealthy games that are easy to get into but hard to master, then Cutthroat is a good game for you to play!

I feel like I have to preface this review by saying that I greatly enjoy tower defense games. Well, the good ones, anyway. I like the building aspect, difficulty progression, tactics, and that rewarding feeling when you survive the onslaught of enemies that come in overwhelming numbers. Even though tower defense games can seem deceptively simple by design, the various tactical nuances can provide some significant challenge. And just because these games are not overly complicated from a design standpoint, many games still miss that special something that makes the best tower defense games so addictive and enthralling.
Age of Steel: Recharge is not strictly a tower defense game, but it shares many design principles with the genre. Whereas most tower defense games are isometric or top-down, Age of Steel: Recharge looks like a 2D side-scroller at first glance. Except there’s no scrolling whatsoever, the camera remains fixed in every level. On the left side is your base. This is where you build units. You can also upgrade your base, which provides you with more units and/or unit upgrades. Every upgrade and every unit requires resources, which are provided by mining. This is an entirely automatic process, which I feel is a wasted opportunity to provide a more direct strategy.
The upgrade and unit menu is displayed below the ground surface. You can only research an upgrade or build a unit in any given moment. The amount of time needed to research a particular upgrade or build a unit that you require at that moment varies, which does require a bit of a tactical approach. You can build ground units, such as turrets and tanks, as well as air units, such as interceptors, bombers and ships. There are three planes of movement. Ground units obviously move on the surface, interceptors and bombers fly high whereas capital ships move somewhere in the middle. The enemy comes from the right side of the screen. Their units are a bit different, but overall they’re very similar. Controlling the sky is a big priority because bombers are devastating. Theirs will damage or destroy your ground units as well as bomb your base, whereas yours are very effective in clearing both ground units and ships.
Overall, the gameplay does provide a level of enjoyment, but the problem is that it’s much too simple. Once you find a strategy that works, it will work in almost every level. The game is also somewhat unbalanced. For example, the heavy jet is the only unit that can deal damage on all three planes of movement, which makes it seriously overpowered. You can just spam the enemy with heavy jets and they will destroy ground units and all air units. At the end of each level, the game will throw a boss at you. All of them are disappointingly weak. This is especially true regarding the last level, which is thoroughly anti-climactic in its entirety and the boss is a complete pushover.
Age of Steel: Recharge features a very nice 2D art style, with beautiful backdrops that vividly depict each setting. The units look best during night levels, with their little lights and everything and it’s a shame there aren’t more levels that take place during night-time. The music and sound effects are generally good. The soundtrack fits the overall theme and the explosions sound appropriate. The only thing that truly stands out, in a bad way, is what I assume is the sound of normal bullets. It kind of sounds like clapping, I can’t really explain it very well, but it simply sounds cheap and it does get annoying after a while. The interface could use some tweaking. When you mouse over an upgrade or unit in the menu, the description appears on the right side of the screen, on the battlefield, effectively obscuring your view of enemy units. And quite often it stays there even after you move the mouse.
The game features only two modes of play, campaign and survival. The campaign is rather short, it can be finished in about 3 hours. Unfortunately, the survival mode isn’t particularly noteworthy as it doesn’t provide the level of strategy needed for this type of game and thus gets stale pretty fast. The campaign does feature a short story, but I can’t tell you much about it as the text goes by so fast, it’s impossible to read everything. However, I was able to notice that the writing features rather broken English.
In the end, Age of Steel: Recharge did provide me with some enjoyment, but it needs work. In a lot of aspects, the game feels like a promising Early Access release, not a full, finished release. The core is good, but it needs balancing, tweaking and more content to live up to its potential.

It's basically like they took a lot of good things from all the other MOBA games out there, cross-bred them, & removed a bunch of the standard bull**** that comes with most MOBA games. It's simpler but still fun.
I've only had the game for about 2 days now & only played a few hours but I can honestly say that I enjoy it more than DOTA or LoL. It's not that DOTA or LoL are bad games. They're at the top of the MOBA genre for a reason. It's just that not having to tryhard every match & being able to just enjoy a more casual MOBA is more fun for me.
The bots in this game are much better than in DOTA or LoL IMO. They aren't as much of a cakewalk as the other games but aren't brokenly overpowered, so even if you have no friends to play it with or just want to try out a new hero you can without worrying much about letting your team down.
Graphics aren't as detailed as DOTA or even LoL but they are still solid for it being such a new game.
Sound is solid & the voice acting is just as good as any other MOBA game.
Gameplay is pretty standard for a MOBA. Lots of hotkeys & left & right clicking of the mouse.
One major differences are that you get a pet that gives you an active ability with a cooldown similar to the abilities like Flash, Ignite, or Teleport in LoL (some that I've personally used are health regen, mana regen, & debuff). Each per also has 2 passives. 1 passive seems to be constant while the other seems to be triggered when a specific action is performed or you are attacked & has a short cooldown (1 of them is 12 sec but they likely vary a bit based on strength).
Similar to DOTA you have a courier that delivers you items except in Strife the courier does not have to be bought & cannot be attacked by enemies. Unlike DOTA & LOL the item pool is smaller but there is a crafting feature where you can make custom items tailored to your liking. I've yet to dabble into this yet so I can't say if it is broken but from what I do know, the more potent the effects of an item is, the more gold it costs you to purchase & complete it, so it seems to be balanced as far as I can tell.
Just like DOTA & LoL there's no pay-to-win. All the heroes seem to be balanced quite well for the most part. Like DOTA you have access to all heroes automatically & only skin changes cost currency. But unlike in DOTA, you can get skins by saving up these gems. (It takes like 160 wins for a single skin but the defaults all look nice & the prices if you pay real money aren't any worse than the costs of LoL).
Similar to LoL there are 2 currencies available. 1 is like IP, the other is like RP. To unlock pets & skins quickly you can spend Strife's equivalent of "RP" which is gems. As mentioned above, you can get gems from winning games or buy them with real money. Skins are gem purchase only but new pets can be bought with the "IP" equivalent. I believe it is 3000 "IP" to buy 1 pet. Each pet has a base form & 2 varients that can be bought. The varients are strictly cosmetic & don't seem to give any advantage to my knowledge.
The pets also can be unlocked by leveling up your account (I've played only about 8 hrs & I'm level 8 already).
As of now I think there are 30 heroes available (I might be off by 1 or 2, I forgot to count the exact number since I 1st checked when I got the game)
Another really nice feature is the way the tutorial is presented. It is done in a seperate mode from the standard arena gameplay of the multiplayer. It is done like an actual single player game tutorial & is more like a RPG tutorial than a MOBA tutorial until you get to actual arena practice. The game also currently has a single episode of a single player mode featuring on of the heroes "Bastion". It has a story & plays similar to the tutorial & is a completely seperate style from the main arena PvP or bot matches. Upon completing the 1st chapter you can take a survey that asks you how you felt about the chapter & what you liked & would like to see improved/added in future episodes. I believe the developers plan on making many more chapters to come featuring many different heroes.
On to bugs. It's a fairly new game that is constantly updated & patched just like the other MOBA games out there. There seems to be a bug where the tutorial may crash. Just be patient (mine crashed twice but I got through it & it can be skipped if you think you can learn the controls/mechanics on your own). Another bug I've seen is the text in the menus will have letters missing. It isn't game breaking as you can still navigate into a match fairly easily. In my experience, playing & completing a match fixes the glitch upon returning to the home menu. I really haven't experienced much more than that. A little lag here & there but that's probably on my end. Nothing game breaking has happened so far.
Well now with all that out of the way on to the final point. IT'S FREE! Just like DOTA or LoL, it's free to play. So why not give it a shot? Especially if you've played DOTA and/or LoL.

Age of Empires II... what's not to like? This was my absolute favourite game in my early teens, even though - when I look back at those times - I sucked at the game and mostly played the excellent campaigns. Joan of Arc, Genghis Khan, Frederick Barbarossa, Saladin... I could still play through these campaigns while blindfolded.
Now that the game has been re-released in HD, I'm playing it in multiplayer, and it's great fun. It took me a while to learn the proper strategies, because if you want to survive in multiplayer, you have to be efficient - proper build orders, never stop building villagers, etc. The game requires a lot of skill to play and learning how to beat your opponent is very rewarding. There are just so many ways to approach this game, it offers a lot of variety.
About the game itself: it's a typical RTS where you build your base, harvest resources, and train an army to destroy your enemy's base. And it is very, very well-made, to this day one of the best titles in the genre, in my opinion. Most games start out in the Dark Age, where you have few buildings available and can only train weak militia units, and you "age up" to the Feudal Age, Castle Age, and finally Imperial Age, with each age unlocking new buildings, units, and technologies. Every playable civilization has its own unique bonuses, unique technologies and unique units. The British have the longbowman, for example, and the Teutons have the Teutonic Knight, a heavy infantry unit. While the tech tree is similar for each civ, they still play differently thanks to their unique units, techs and bonuses, although not as differently as in Starcraft or Age of Mythology.
If you're not into multiplayer and prefer singleplayer, don't worry: the campaigns are quite excellent, and AoE2 HD comes with the Conquerors expansion, so you have a large amount of campaigns to play through. William Wallace (a tutorial campaign), Joan of Arc, Saladin, Genghis Khan, Frederick Barbarossa, and in the expansion: Attila, El Cid, Montezuma, and a collection of historical battles. Mission goals in the campaigns are varied and it never feels repetitive, and some missions are very, very challenging, like the final mission of the Saladin campaign.
One minor note of complaint: the multiplayer sometimes has issues, but they've become a little better with the latest patch. Still, in large matches of 3v3 or 4v4 you will often experience lag, and sometimes you will even get out-of-sync errors, so beware. 1v1 matches work flawlessly though and I never had a problem in a 1v1 game. If you like team games, do keep this in mind though.
Overall, a thorougly recommended game. I enjoyed the heck out of this when I first played it in 1999 as a young teen, and I'm enjoying the heck out of it now in competitive multiplayer matches.

I am honestly unable to understand the mixed reception of this game.
Reading through some of the reviews I see many people complaining about "difficult controls" or "bad gameplay" which to my mind feel very unjustified since all gameplay elements are very thought through and serve a purpose.
If you actually take your time to look at the control scheme and how to play, you will realise that most negative reviews are just people who didn't spent a single minute of their time to even learn the basics not to mention the actual depth of this game.
You are able to:
✘ cancel attacks into special attacks, dodges, dodge-jumps, allowing for large combo strings
✘ short hop, fast fall and utilise the momentum of your airdodges, similiar to wavedashing in Super Smash Bros Melee
✘ switch characters mid-combo for further strings
It is true that you are unable to change directions mid-combo, but this just adds to the experience of having to make a commitment when attacking an enemy.
Given the fact that there is no collision detection for enemy or player models and and the actually viable AI of most opponents, like in many fighting games, positioning is very important and knowing when to attack and when not.
The missing collision detection also makes escaping easier when outnumbered or stuck in a tight spot, which you definately will be at times since enemies have their own unique moveset and never feel trivial (except slugs and spiders maybe).
As a huge Souls fan and supporter of the fighting game community i definitely recommend this unique piece of art.

A seriously impressive game from a single guy (plus some outsourcing). The goal of making Dwarf Fortress accessibility has been achieved, and though it lacks the deep simulation and ridiculous unplanned emergent stories from that (drunk cats), it surpasses them by making emergent stories the very core of the game. Then it makes it Sci-Fi with guns and an adverserial AI to challenge you when you prosper and assist when you falter, or vice versa.
I've followed this game for a while and it really deserves more attention that it has got. I can't stop playing it, there is always some goal or crisis that makes you forget the passing of time, and watching your little minions labour never gets old. This is a game about systems and how they all interact to create a believable simulation of a space colony. Nothing is dumbed down and works just like you think it would.
Combat is good with a cover system, different weapons with strengths and weaknesses, intricate body part damage calculations (does a bullet penetrate armor, miss the heart but nick the left lung? Now breathing is difficult and the lung is filling with fluid, if untreated it could cause unconciousness and infection!). Tech tree is extensive and rewarding (even better with mods). Multi-tiered production chains, interesting farming for food and drugs, procedurally generated art ala DF, pawns with believable traits and quirks, and a perfect difficulty curve that really matches whatever challenge you want (AI Storytellers is genius!)
And oh jesus the mods. There can't be enough and they all fit so perfectly I sometimes forget what is core and what is new. The simple graphics and understandable systems make it a natural fit.
And Tydan keeps adding huge new features that can't be done with modding and often. This game has no right to be early access with so many fully fleshed out features. I can't wait to see what makes it into "1.0"

RimWorld is one of those games that can treat you right one moment then sucker punch you the next - but what makes it so good for me is that it doesn't always. It has three storytellers with their own pattern, and those each have their own difficulty. If you want casual play, there's Phoebe Chillax on Basebuilder difficulty; mistakes are easy to recover from. Or you can also choose Randy Random on Extreme Permadeath for a real challenge - What happens is random and once it's done, it's done. Good luck surviving a huge raid on day 3. RimWorld gives a rather strong range of control of challenge right from the start.
The real fun is in the gameplay. You manage a colony (or a tribe) of 1-5 colonists, or pawns, and are tasked with their survival and the ultimate goal of building a ship to leave the planet. Defend them from raiders, killer robots, insect infestations, blights, eachother, and yourself. (We all get fed up with that
pawn eventually.) These pawns each have different traits, skills, and backstories that change how they function, like nudists, psychopaths, optimists, medieval lords, medieval slaves. Injuries also play a big role. A sick colonist will have to spend time in bed recovering or risk death, and a colonist can have their hand, arm, head (yikes!), organs, and more removed and that will affect them adversely. (Who needs a head anyway?) Not to mention that where you choose to build will affect growing seasons, clothes needed to survive, and diseases.
One final feature of RimWorld is the modding scene, and it is huge. A large variety of mods exist on the Steam Workshop and are a click or two away from being in your game, and even more unique mods await you in the Ludeon forums. Just like games like Skyrim, mods can make you spend yet another day managing those wacky pawns. The developer is also active and still polishing and adding more to the game, pushing it bit by bit to its final, grand form.
I didn't expect to love RimWorld as much as I did, and it was a bit of a hesitant buy. However, I fell in love with the game. I struggled to build my first functional colony. I waited on edge to see if my pawn would recover from disease. I felt unease from my first ancient danger. I swore when my pawn kept missing an easy shot. Every colony is a rollercoaster of emotions, and I love every second of it.

If you like story driven games and mystery, just get it without any thinking, you will like it.

I came into Oxenfree with my knowledge of Night School Studio's involvement with the Mr. Robot game, which is perhaps one of the best storytelling experiences I've ever had with a mobile game. Oxenfree however lived far and above past what I could have expected from Night School Studio.
If there's a mentality of how you should approach Oxenfree, it should be treated like a visual novel where your choices matters. I believe this is one of Oxenfree's strongest point, some of Oxenfree's seemingly irrelevant choices can severely affect the ending. Though once you've gotten into the New Game+, you'll start noticing the more irrelevant choices. While New Game+ is a fun way to indulge in a "Groundhog Day" loop fantasy, it can destroy some of your sense of agency in the game; and considering the theme of Oxenfree, could be taken as either a good thing or a bad thing.
Oxenfree is a coming-of-age story that is also a cosmic horror story, the two genres can feel like they're conflicting one another with the contrast of the optimistic nature in the former and the cynical nature in the latter. Though in the end, the focus is shifted more towards being a coming-of-age story, with all the Lovecraftian elements mostly in the background or saved up for the jumpscares. Being into Lovecraft horror myself, I feel a bit dissapointment with this. I really wish we could get more involved with the ghosts and the alternate dimensions, instead of just learning their origins and some minor interactions.
Speaking of the coming-of-age story, most of the characters are a bunch of teenagers. Put the two together and you may have what could feel either like the most relatable cast of characters or the most unlikeable cast of characters, come into the game expecting that these characters are just a bunch of sheltered teenagers whose conflicts are more on the simple and human side; and you may grow to find them likeable. Alex herself has become one of my favourite examples of a blank canvas video game protagonist along with Captain Martin Walker and Geralt of Rivia, Alex's personality isn't very defined; which leaves your interpretation, but enough things told about her to leave some sort on impression on you... or you can just play her like your standard silent protagonist, whatever floats your boat.
I've been rambling on about the story for the most part, which leads to the question of what about the gameplay itself? I normally don't consider this a mechanic, but the conversation system in Oxenfree is very much an essential mechanic for the game. The real-time nature of the conversation gives you that sense of urgency to answer as quick as you can, which once in a while will cause you to slip up. Unlike in The Walking Dead, in Oxenfree there are actual consequences for messing up a seemingly irrelevant conversation, so that sense of urgency and perhaps a bit of understanding of the characters can go a long way in netting you the possible best ending.
Back to the more traditional mechanics, Oxenfree has puzzle-solving with radios. I feel like this mechanic is there more for the sake of lore purposes instead of being its own thing. Solving radio puzzles aren't what I'd call exciting, as looking for the correct frequency can feel more like a chore; which gets even worst when you've upgraded your radio.
There's also the exploration in Oxenfree, which actually does affect your ending if you managed to understand the island's origins. The problem however, is that most of the exploration can only be done before the ending, and while this is a short game; it feels more like a way to pad the game a bit before it ends.
In the end, Oxenfree is a game that excels in interactive storytelling with its interesting lore and perhaps debatable characters, while not really giving much in terms of mechanics.

A great game that I can't believe is free.  I've been playing this game for 3 years and in that time it has undergone constant updates, renovations, and overhauls.  Whenever a major change happens people always whine and complain about it, but that is not because is was a bad change, it's just because they were used to the way it was before.  Then when you adapt and get familiar with the new features and mechanics you realize it was an improvement.  There are very few games I can say I have played for several hundred hours, and this is one of them.
This game offers:
-Tons of creative freedom.  It will awaken a designer deep down inside of you that you never even knew existed.  You may even spend more time designing your robots than actually playing with them, and you will love every second of it.  Some designs will totally fail in combat, but just keep building new ones and modifying the ones you have until you have a bot that fits your skills and playstyle.
-A variety of types of matches to play in and several maps to play on.  Different game types have different objectives and some bots are better suited to specific game types.  This offers more variety to the game to keep you interested.
-Tons of play styles.  Every bot is different and theirfore needs to be played different.
