I haven't played the game for long, but seeing how I have tons of experience with Mobas, and seeing how  I will continue to play it in the future for sure, I wanted to write an ACTUAL honest review that refutes these absurd pay2win claims from the so called "most helpful" review right now.
This will be somewhat long and indepth, but I will do my best to explain this game and what it is about and what you can expect.
Strife is your good old so called MOBA (Multiplayer Online Battle Arena). Just like in the main MOBAs DotA 2, League of Legends, and to some extent Heroes of the Storm, you take control of a hero trying to work together with 4 others to storm the enemies crux, a building inside their base, to win the game once it is destroyed. You do that by pushing along one of three lanes; the mid, bottom, and top lane, together with your brawlers (minions), destroy two turrets along the way, and destroy the generator to be able to attack the enemy crux. The generator is somewhat unique to strife, as destroying two or all three of them weakens the Crux considerably, making it easier to take out. Unlike in other games, destroying it does not make your minions stronger, but as mentioned, the Crux weaker.
Strife somewhat borrows a lot of elements from the top MOBAs right now, whether they are more or less well known. It has the out-of-combat regeneration of TOME, the cartoon style (although somewhat different) from LoL, the recipe and courier mechanic from DotA 2, the instant-queue-matching from HotS (pick a hero, be matched with others without being in some sort of champion select). It does introduce, however, a new mechanic called Pets. Before each battle you can choose from a wide variety of pets that you unlock for leveling up, seals (the ingame currency) or gems (real money currency). Every pet though can be purchased for both seals AND real money, so you are not locked off of choosing any pet you may want to save up for. These pets give you two passive bonuses and one active ability with a long cooldown, such as regenerating mana or health, or sliding in a direction. It is pretty cool if you ask me, and they have alternative skins too (purchasable with real money).
Strife is somewhere between casual and hardcore territory. As mentioned before, it does borrow the courier mechanic from DotA 2, but the courier can't die or be intercepted, or rerouted or otherwise controlled, it is simply a way of receiving items in lane. The heroes in Strife are wildly varied, you have your usual supports, bruisers, and burst mages, and hunters, but also some more interesting characters like Chester, a hero that attacks with chess figures and can create illusions and links between him and allies. Also, ALL the heroes are free, but skins and colour variations are obtainable with gems.
Strife allows you to craft items with elixir, an ingame currency you obtain from leveling up and winning, or gems. Essentially, you don't "craft" items, but you alter existing recipes. Let's say there is an item that gives you health and mana regeneration. You can give this item some more of that, or some additional power to make your attacks stronger. Now, claims of this being "pay2win" have been coming up, simply because you can purchase this with real money and thus have an advantage over other people. However, this is not true, and let me explain why.
After you have altered a recipe, you can also choose an enchantment which usually gives you a % bonus, like an additional 5 % power. These are different for EVERY item, which means you cant just alter your 6 build items and then have 30 % power over other people. They are really small bonuses, a little movement speed, 2 % health, and they MAKE YOUR ITEM MORE ExPENSIVE. Adding power, health regeneration or whatever, and putting an enchantment (you can also choose not to have an enchantment at all) make the ingame cost of the item RISE. Which means that essentially, whether you pay elixirs or gems to alter an item, it comes with the tradeoff of it COSTING MORE GOLD, for a really small bonus that wouldn't matter either way. It is like the rune system in League of Legends, just bound to items and with the negative of said item costing MORE after altering it.
It is a neat small system that gives you ingame bonuses for a tradeoff and allows you to truly customize the items you would build, however, just because you can buy this with gems doesn't make it pay2win - especially not since you get TONS of elixirs and can craft tons of items easily anyway, So, before saying it is pay2win, check the game out for yourself, and see.
Strife is neat. The animations are fluid, battling is fun, matches are generally over in less than 30 minutes. The heroes are wildly varied in how they work, and the voice acting of them is generally well done, if a little repetitive. Like, a LOT. Luckily, you can turn this off in the options, or make it less rare, which is a nice feature.
However, it is a beta and the game needs work. So far, it is a bit unoptimized, making my graphics card sweat when it can easily handle Dragon Age Inquisition on Ultra (but that may somehow also be my mistake). The first tutorial campaign has tons of logic issues (a pirate burning down her ship and leaving her crew hanging JUST to join a tournament? Alright...) But that is nitpicking. Also, the death of enemy heroes while playing could be a bit more impactful in visual and audio design, but it is hard to explain exactly what that means until you see it. And finally, it is impossible to look through all the heroes available in the game right now without actually going INTO a game and the hero select, but you can watch pets out of the game? Doesn't make sense, there should be an additional hero tab to watch these.
So far, I would recommend this game and give it an 8/10 on my personal scale. It still has its issues, obviously, but its fun, fast paced, and quick, and certainly feels, despite familiar mechanics, like a breath of fresh air in the MOBA scene, something I am very happy to see. The crafting mechanic is nice, but has only a minor effect and comes with a tradeoff  and other knacks that prevent it from being pay2win like others have claimed. It is free, so check it out yourself, and have a great day whatever you may be doing today :) Oh and also the campaign is great.

On top of the already-solid game, there are countless secret areas and hidden goodies, allowing for decent replay value. The atmosphere is bleak yet somewhat optimistic, with the tone being set by a lovely intro and retained by a beautiful art style and soundtrack. Every piece of music in the game is an alternate take on a classical piece (for instance, many cave areas play "In the Hall of the Mountain King". A nod to Manic Miner, perhaps?)

"How can you say that?" you might ask, knowing full well that Age of Empires 2 is an excellent game that is widely praised and regarded as a classic. Well, I'll explain.
Age of Empires 2, as a game, is a classic RTS game where you manage a Medieval Civilization, going from a tiny settlement to a sprawling empire. If you don't get invaded first that is. There is a massive focus on combat in this game, most games are decided on the battlefield, with players fielding massive armies against each other to knock out buildings, defences and eventually innocent civilians. But of course, these armies don't come out of nothing, you need to build up some money, gather food, collect wood for buildings and stone for castles. If you aren't familiar with Age of Empires 2, I suggest you look for reviews of that game.
Age of Empires 2 HD is a little different, and not always in a good way.
The upgrades from the original are primarily on the graphical side of things, the updating to a modern lobby-based multiplayer, better mod support and two expansions not originally made for the game. Make no mistake, these aren't all what they're cracked up to be and there's a few problems in this release.
As far as graphics are concerned, the game looks as nice as ever, with only the water reflections, the larger resolutions (which aren't easily adjustable) and a few changed in-game graphics, most of which are welcome additions. To call it HD is perhaps a stretch, but it is graphically superior to its original counterpart.
The modern lobby-based multiplayer is a welcome feature, theoretically allowing for easy and simple online play, without the need for third party clients like Voobly and Gameranger. In practice, the lobby system is very suspect to bugs, with crashes upon game launches occuring frequently and dropouts that halt the game halfway through happening somewhat less frequently. For all the unreliability in Voobly and Gameranger that this system could do away with, it is in many ways inferior, with these problems ocurring less often in either client.
Another couple of things that Voobly and Gameranger players would be able to avoid is the problems that actually happen in-game. Path-finding was never stellar in the original game, but many claim that it has been significantly degraded in this version. Not to mention that the actual game seems to typically run slower, with more log and with more connection problems than it does in Voobly and Gameranger under similar conditions.
The mod support is nice, but the amount of content for AoE2 that isn't on the Steam Workshop is gigantic, which leaves mostly classic and popular scenarios as well as an assortment of other bits and bobs to choose from. Your typical AoE2 player won't be missing out on much, but for those who want really specific things, they might have a hard time to get a hold of them.
And lastly, there's the two expansions. Opinion is divided about these; some say that the new African Kingdoms are extremely powerful, to the point of possibly being imbalanced. And The Forgotten Empires is perceived as being a slew of rather lacking civilizations that don't boast much power, but seem to have very little place in the game. Personally, I think that the African Kingdoms expansion adds a lot to the game and is very fun to play with, even if the new civilizations, particularly the Portugeuse can seem a little tough to play against. As for the Forgotten Empires, it's fun in much the same way, but the civilizations added seem too timid to really add all that much beyond a few interesting unique units and techs to open up a few more strategies than there used to be.
The bugs that make online play well under optimal for such a multiplayer focused game, not to mention one so old and a few of the gameplay problems make me really hesitate to recommend AoE2 HD, because these issues are extremely frustrating and can feel like a dealbreaker. But when the game works, it's as fun as the old AoE2 and sometimes even more so with the higher resolutions, the extra content and the new community. I can't blame you if these bugs get the better of you and you end up going back to Voobly though.

This is one of my favorite games ever, and arguably the one that has the best 1st person swordplay action to date, including The Elder Scroll series, Chivalry, War of the Roses and the like.
There's three basic classes: Warrior, Wizard and Thief. This sounds restrictive at first, but apart from the fact that you can play the entire game 3 times and get a totally different experience out of it every time depending on your class, you can also just distribute your level-up points in all three skill trees as you see fit and mix it up. Even for a warrior, it's pretty useful to be able to turn enemies against each other or to spot traps or hidden doors; Even for a mage, it's useful to do more damage with your staff or sneak around more effectively, and even for a thief/assassin, it's useful to be able to disarm enemies or create magic invisible fire traps.
The story is cool and intriguing with a couple of big optional choices and side missions that affect it, the locations beautiful and diverse (although the graphics are a little outdated, of course), exploration and sneaking fun and immersive, boss fights pretty unique and against several pretty BIG enemies, the RPG mechanics balanced and the fights badass and VERY satisfying - and this is the meat of the game.
You can disarm foes, dismember them, burn them, shrink them, zap them, freeze them, stealthkill them, kick them into spikes and fires or off cliffs or into other enemies and use the environement in all kinds of other creative ways (cut/shoot ropes to have large objects drop on or swing at enemies, or to collapse bridges or pillars to crush enemies, create fire arrows by simply holding an arrow into any fire, and shooting into oil puddles or at enemies directly - sometimes after you picked up an oil pot and threw it in their face for that extra-crispiness. You can of course use firespells for that, too.). The cool implementation of the environment into the combat always has you looking for opportunities at any location, which makes both planning fights from the shadows and thinking on your feet in hairy combat situations a lot of fun, and you feel like a proper badass after a huge fight that was so awesome that it could have been featured in a movie. This game makes you feel badass, and you feel like you EARNED to feel badass.
Enemies include humans, goblin and orcs (warriors, archers or wizards of all sorts), zombies and skeletons, quasi-dragons, spiders, trolls and more, and they often require different tactics.
Oh, and you get *SLIGHT SPOILER ALERT, SORT OF (because you can set "change form" in the key bindings anyway)* the ability to turn into an "Alien"-like demon form later on, which I hardly used, but well, if you're into that sort of thing...*END OF ZOMG SPOILER*
You'll also do a lot of freeclimbing with the ability to grab ledges and the use of chains and ropes (You get Thief-style rope arrows later on, too!).
All of this in 1st person, which is very immersive and simply works well, especially since you have full body awareness, meaning the model that exists in the world is also the one you see from your perspective - and it throws a shadow. You're not a camera on a stick with fake arms on the side, you're ♥♥♥♥ing IN there.
I was a bit disappointed in the MP back then because it was too fast for my taste (and in comparison to SP) and didn't have any objective maps - or co-op. No mods to speak of either, which is unbelievable for a somewhat unique gem like this, especially since it's a Source game.
Dark Messiah was made by Arkane, btw, who later made DisHonored. It is rather linear, so don't expect anything like Skyrim - but that's not a bad thing since Dark messiah is a different experience altogether, in a good way. It does have its flaws, but overall, it's a great experience.
Damn, I just wanted to write a sentence or two... Anyway, I just installed Dark Messiah again to play through it for the 7th time (I think), despite having some awesome new games I haven't played or finished yet. That should tell you how much I love this game. :)

If there is one that can be said, it would be that the older I get, the more I wish games went back to the way that they used to be. I'm not even sure if RPG Maker games can even be called a guilty pleasure anymore as I seek them out much more than I do most higher budgeted titles. There's something about them that just makes me want to dig out my old Ikea chair (which I would have to battle the cats for it) find my old CRT, hook up my SNES and play the afternoon away in front of an open window. Memories of a Vagabond covers that nostalgic feeling very well and adds new and interesting gameplay elements that had me happily going into the NG+.
Starting off Memories of a Vagabond puts players in the role of a Hero about to propose to the love of his life. Already at this point players have access to choices both for the Hero's actions and his words which starts things off much faster than a lengthily cutscene would and instead finds a proper balance of playing and watching. What I absolutely LOVED was that DarkElite showed me the controls both with a keyboard or with my 360 controller prior to first taking control. There was no guessing as to whether there were added controls or not. They also put one of the best possible features in. Turbo. Instead of adding a run button, it speeds up the entire game making certain scenes go a bit faster if it is not the first time. All of this leads up to the true start of the game where our Hero dies. Wait? What?
Memories of a Vagabond to some degree made me think a bit of a Souls game where death is not a permanent thing, but more of a learning experience. After the first story death, and all the following occurrences, whenever the player dies the Hero has a choice of classes that he can take. Players may take the same class or to go ahead and try another one with a total of four classes (Warrior, Assassin, Mage, Hunter) each with their own looks, skills and equipment possibilities. I'll be honest that while I tried out all the classes during the first selection process, I went through the entire game with the Hunter and only really started to class change during my NG+.
For those that may worry along the lines of "What if I don't die?" (Which dying does become less frequent as the game progresses… or just being more careful) there is a location that freely allows the player to change to another class without having to die. Eliminating the "game over" could have gone either way, but it made Memories of a Vagabond was made that much better by both not having players restart from the last game over and also eliminating the “What if I had taken the other class instead”. This really allowed for a much smoother experience and a lot less cringing if it had been a while since the last save.
Accompanying the awesome gameplay is well written dialog that spans from start to finish including my favorite insulting comeback ever “You have tiny wings!”. Each character feels like there own person from the various townspeople to the wandering monsters shouting out their challenge. What made these dialogs even better was the numerous times where the Hero could either insult back or say nothing at all. Sometimes the choices carried more weight than others which was a nice touch as not everything had to be a serious choice.
The only issue that I may have had overall... I'm still not sure if it was really all that big of a deal. Memories of a Vagabond is short for an RPG in which I clocked in somewhere around three and a half hours before going back in for that mentioned NG+. The reason I'm not sure if that's a big deal or not, is that it's fun and not only does it set out to do what it does well, but there never felt like there were long periods of senseless grinding which is generally what takes at least a good 10-20 hours in a 40 hour RPG. Along with the main story there are several side quests and a coliseum that can be taken on that also changes its challenges depending on the class being played. It should be noted that the coliseum is not a forgiving place as dying sends you back to the class selection. Most fights that may seem that require an extra boost to take on can be solved by either one quick level up, a bit more equipment, or acquiring another party member.
Memories of a Vagabond is an amazing game that even while short, offers enough to come back to with side quests that may not have been completed the first time around or the coliseum that I decided to truly tackle in my NG+.

Oxenfree is a game about a group of friends who travel to Edwards Island to have a night of stupid games and unsupervised drinking. This all takes a turn when they use a radio to tune into the frequency of the paranormal. What happens after is history.
Oxenfree introduces us to five different characters whom we can build or destroy relationships with as our main protagonist, Alexandra, or commonly referred to as Alex. Most of the characters have more than interesting backstories that we discover along the journey. The backstories help decide what our relations with all of the characters will be. Alex's personality is entirely decided by the player, so not much can be said about her. Alex comes to Edwards Island on a ferry along with Jonas, her new step-brother who she just met that night, as well as Ren, Alex's long-term bestfriend. Jonas is a "strapping young lad," as defined by Ren, who recently lost his mother. He is, for the majority of the game, your partner while traversing through Edwards Island, so you learn quite a bit about him all in one night. Keep in mind that your words and actions will bring out the truth in all of the characters' personalities and intentions. Ren is a spunky, pot-brownie addicted, fluffy haired, goofball that you can't help but love. Ren has a crush on Nona, another main character, and your actions throughout the game will determine whether they become a couple or keep their distance in the end. Nona is a shy girl who secretly also has a thing for Ren. You're only given one chance to pick Nona as your partner in the game which will allow you to learn more about her, but of course, you still won't know as much about her as Jonas or Ren. She is best friends with Clarissa. Clarissa is a snarky girl who especially has it out for Alex. This is because she ended up dating Michael, Alex's dead brother, and blames Alex for her death.
Last, we have Michael, Alex's brother who drowned around less than a year prior to the games events. Not much can be said about Michael,
Overall, the characters are bursting with their own unique personalities, but something just feels a liiiiittle bit off about all of them, like something is missing from their character's, other than that, they are absolutely some of the realest characters in a game that I've seen in a while. Oh, also, very solid voice acting.
As said previously, Oxenfree is about a group of juniors/seniors who travel to an island for a night of fun but they end up using a radio to tune into something beyond paranormal. I believe that Oxenfree should be experienced blindly. Go into it without knowing anything and you will for sure have a grand old time. If you want to play blindly, don't read ahead, for those of you who are dying to know, here you go.
Oxenfree allows players to walk around and explore and ineract with their surroundings. However, the main aspect of the game is the radio. The radio is used for multiple things, like learning about the island, talking to
opening doors and gates, finding anomalies through the stacked rocks, and listening to some relaxing music to distract you from the nightmare you're walking through. The radio is used by dialing/tuning it through different channels to pick up different frequencies to move forward. Eventuall y, you get an upgraded radio that allows more accessibility to certain things throughout the game. When traversing through the island, I found it to be rather tedious that there isn't a sprint action, Alex will speed up and slow down at random times, but I guess it's realistic considering you walk on slopes, stairs, and straight paths, and running on a few of those isn't exactly ideal. The most annoying thing about the game is the rock climbing. I'd give this point of the game a 9.5 if it weren't for the rock climbing. It takes up way too much time and your partners won't scale with you.
I wrote a lot more, but I'm nearly out of space, so to save space and time, let's just say that the soundtrack really is something that is worth listening to.

Not bad, not great but not bad. It's your usual Tower Defense-esque game, think Age of War with a good selection of units and plenty of fast paced enemies ready to bring your whole base crumbling down. It's simple, you build units and towers to hold back enemies while attempting to complete objectives. You can build buildings, upgrade units and unlock more units the more resources you obtain over time. There are some nice things like the graphics which is your usual low rez 16 bit that has become rather popular in indie games nowadays but there are also some rather annoying things like the ludicrously small unit cap or the fact that there even is a unit cap in a game like this. My final thoughts, I don't regret buying it, it's not bad if a bit overpriced. I think an even 5 bucks or 4.99 would be a more worthy pricetag of the current product because this isn't really anything you haven't seen before in a game like Age of War.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike by the Imperial Japanese Navy Air Service against the United States naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii Territory, on the morning of December 7, 1941. The attack, also known as the Battle of Pearl Harbor, led to the United States' entry into World War II. The Japanese military leadership referred to the attack as the Hawaii Operation and Operation AI, and as Operation Z during its planning.
Japan intended the attack as a preventive action to keep the U.S. Pacific Fleet from interfering with military actions they planned in Southeast Asia against overseas territories of the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and the United States. Over the next seven hours there were coordinated Japanese attacks on the U.S.-held Philippines, Guam and Wake Island and on the British Empire in Malaya, Singapore, and Hong Kong.
The attack commenced at 7:48 a.m. Hawaiian Time. The base was attacked by 353[15] Imperial Japanese fighter planes, bombers, and torpedo planes in two waves, launched from six aircraft carriers. All eight U.S. Navy battleships were damaged, with four sunk. All but the USS Arizona were later raised, and six were returned to service and went on to fight in the war. The Japanese also sank or damaged three cruisers, three destroyers, an anti-aircraft training ship,[nb 4] and one minelayer. 188 U.S. aircraft were destroyed; 2,403 Americans were killed and 1,178 others were wounded. Important base installations such as the power station, shipyard, maintenance, and fuel and torpedo storage facilities, as well as the submarine piers and headquarters building (also home of the intelligence section) were not attacked. Japanese losses were light: 29 aircraft and five midget submarines lost, and 64 servicemen killed. One Japanese sailor, Kazuo Sakamaki, was captured.
The surprise attack came as a profound shock to the American people and led directly to the American entry into World War II in both the Pacific and European theaters. The following day, December 8, the United States declared war on Japan,[18][19] and several days later, on December 11, Germany and Italy declared war on the U.S. The U.S. responded with a declaration of war against Germany and Italy. Domestic support for non-interventionism, which had been fading since the Fall of France in 1940, disappeared.
There were numerous historical precedents for unannounced military action by Japan, but the lack of any formal warning, particularly while negotiations were still apparently ongoing, led President Franklin D. Roosevelt to proclaim December 7, 1941, "a date which will live in infamy". Because the attack happened without a declaration of war and without explicit warning, the attack on Pearl Harbor was later judged in the Tokyo Trials to be a war crime.

This game is similar to tower defence games. The resource mining is automatic and you can use resources to buy defence units (turrets, tanks, planes) or to upgrade the units. Or you can upgrade the base to get different units and more upgrades.
This game plays on three floors, the ground (turrets and tanks and shield), the middle air (airships) and the top air (planes) and every floor has its own units. Generally each unit only fights against enemies on the same floor but there are bombers (defender and attacker) which drop bombs from the top to both other floors and there are air-defence turrets which can hit planes and airships.
The game play is fluent and interesting. You can only build one unit at a time and you are limited to 12 so you have to build wisely. But you can destroy misplaced or unused units. You cannot build while upgrading and the other way around, therefore you have to plan in advance.
Every level in the campaign plays about the same because the attackers are always the same and they always attack on the 3 floors. At the end of each level there will be a different enemy boss which is not very hard to beat.
On later level you will start with an upgraded base and get a special defence units which might be helpful against the enemy boss.
I like this game but the content does not justify the price.
The campaign is very short (about 3 hours) and the survival mode is boring because you start with a fully upgraded base and the enemies don't get harder.
Also it is not possible to replay the levels in the campaign. You could reset your progress in the game but be
: This does not only reset the campaign, it also resets the records of the survival mode and everything you might have unlocked. So there is no real replay value.

This program is -essential- for high-end GPU's.  I'm using it on a nVidia 980GTX card which very quickly overheats under load without this software.  The auto-scaling GPU frequency feature combined with the auto fan speed curve feature makes for a quiet, and less power-hungry machine for office work and movies.  However, this program can make a system unstable on high CPU load. IE: When I'm recompressing Blu Ray videos using Handbrake, my CPU load stays at 100% (AMD FX 9580 4.7ghz x8) and attempting to play games at ultra-high graphics settings, or too quickly starting or restarting multiple programs that use graphical hardware acceleration causes the graphics card to freeze up.  The CPU will continue to run, as does the hard-drive, but only a hard shutdown of the computer will restore functioning to the graphics card.  Continued updates from EVGA for this software, and updates from nVidia continue to improve the sensativity of this issue, but be careful if using other overclocked equipment in your machine.

As a huge fan of both Super Meat Boy as well as most of McMillan's games, this is an amazing game in my opinion, but I will add a warning to this review. If you do not like challenging games, don't get The End is Nigh, even if you do maybe watch a couple videos and see what you think. In my case, I bought it almost as soon as it came out without even remembering the game was being released. A freind and I played it for about four hours straight that night taking turns and trying our best to figure out the mechanics, and I have to say in my case I felt it was totally worth the price point, yes its challenging but if you push through the frustration and stress it can be very rewarding depending on who you are.
I will emphicize again that this game is not for those who want something easy, but then again most of Edmund's games don't necissarily fit the description of 'easy'. If you loved Super Meat Boy like I did when it came out, you will most likely enjoy this game, its not too similar to feel like a sequel but instead has its own ideas of challenging the player in a way that makes them want to do everything better. Everything from the mechanics to the soundtrack made me feel motivated to become better at the game's mechanics and intracacies, as simple as they may be.
For $15 I was expecting something I could master in 10 hours or so, but instead I got a game that I feel like I could play for a hundred hours and still feel like I could improve on certain things, and to me that makes this game one of the best platformers I've played in a very long time.
On a side note, I find this game much easier to play with a controller, I played through almost half of it without but as soon as I tried playing with a gamepad I can't even imagine playing it with a keyboard. That might just be me though, I know a lot of people prefer keyboard for games like this but I'm not one of them, jumping at specific angles is just much easier for me with a joystick.

+ Well done, cartoon art style

- Combat is shallow

- There is no wake up invulnerability after being knocked down, resulting in you being tossed about like a rag doll
- Almost all enemies aren't fun to fight:
-- Small mobs just spam abilities with no warning that constantly knock you down
-- Large brutes don't flinch, can't reliably be combo'd, frequently grab and throw you around, and hit like trucks
-- All bosses are terrible, frustrating, and tedious. A chore to fight against any of them
- The rpg aspects of this game are not well implemented, and feel like they were thrown in to pad out the game
-- A bad stat build results in the game slowing to a crawl
-- At higher levels it takes forever to get stat points
-- Generally turns the game into a grind fest
- The game technically is unpolished
-- Foreground elements can block onscreen gameplay
-- Your character's sprite layer must to be placed in front of an enemy's sprite layer for an attack to register
-- The character can get stuck on seemingly nothing if their sprite layer is behind an object's sprite layer
- Most weapons are useless, and have unintelligible stat point placements
- You can only carry a small number of health potions, making it impossible to brute force bosses or levels
- There is no difficulty options, so you can't run though the game on a easier difficulty, and then run through a harder difficulty with a higher level character
Overall, this is a mediocre beat em up with tacked on rpg elements, that turn an ok game into a grindy, frustrating, and tedious mess of a chore.

When I first saw this game it was on sale. I was really interested in buying it cuz I love milsim fps videogames, but I didn't buy it straight away. After some days the sales were over and I kept watching gameplays on Youtube of Squad. I bought it at full price, and I DO NOT REGRET IT.
This game is an Early Access, but they are patching it regularly, and omg, one of the best milsim fps I've ever played.
When you join a match you either join an existing squad (max members 9) or create a new one. Usually there are 4 squads per match. So far servers are up to 70-72 players. The EA is focused on infantry combat but recently they patched it and added some vehicles:
humvees;
logistic trucks: used to transport supplies to the FOB (forward operation base) in order to build fortifications, ammo boxes, etc;
BTRs;
pickups;
Ofc every faction got specific vehicles. So far there are 4 factions: a general Militia faction, US Army, Russian Army, Insurgents.
The game is really focused on teamwork. As I said, you gotta join a squad or create a new one. If you join an existing squad, you have to cooperate with your teammates and listen to your squad leader. The game ha got 3 different voice chats: One to talk to those close to you, another to talk via radio to your squad mates, and another one reserved for squad leaders to communicate between them and decide what to do to accomplish the mission.
It's real fun. Ofc it happens that some squad members just go rambo'ing around but they don't really last long. Teamwork is the key, I repeat it.
The optimization for my pc is good, but I don't know how it works with lower specs pcs, so i cannot give useful info regarding that.
Would I recommend this game? HELL YEAH.
Would I recommend this game if you wanna play solo / arcade? HELL NO. (If this is the case, don't even think about buying this game.)

Dark Messiah of Might and magic is a truly disappointing game. From the clunky controls to the frustratingly simple combat, the core game mechanics are boring, and the presentation is quite shabby to boot.
Graphics- While some of the game's graphics can look pretty good, the overall effects are very uneven. Especially the game's more open areas look absolutely atrocious in comparison to other source games, as low res textures and bad backdrops abound.
Sound- I found the sound design to be generic and not really anything special, although it did the job. The voice acting was pretty bad.
Gameplay- The hack and slash mechanics with magic mixed in work much better in other titles that mix these dynamics, but for some reason Dark Messiah features a terribly frustrating control scheme and nonsensical combat mechanics that often feature your character taking damage full seconds after the enemy blows have been deflected. Button mashing combined with circle strafing led me to the most success when playing this game. In short, the gameplay, enemy, weapon and skill systems are pretty generic and do not provide for a satisfying experience.
In addition to these concerns, the story is very very dull, providing no narrative flow or any kind of imperative to your actions.
Overall, I'd say Dark Messiah is a sad example of low-budget game development gone wrong.

Is it old/ out-dated? No, every day is a fresh experience. The very nature of this game means it's freeform/ sandbox so you can see and do different stuff every minute if you want. . But first let me give you my concise MOBA resume so you can see where I'm coming from.
- No input delay (hero turn-rate and stuff like that, that sluggish feeling you get trying to control your hero)
- More stable servers (I'm USW + USE)
- More proportionate in-game progression system (supports in Dota are always left in the dust and when the enemy team gets BKBs they can become quite worthless, in Strife they don't need to buy couriers or wards and they share gold with their lane partner)
- Much lower playerbase (Strife is still in beta)
- A bit of a progression to win sort of system (not a pay2win, the more you play the more you can craft different stuff that gives a little bit of an edge in the versatility department)
- Less mechanically oriented (for example there's no denying & less activatable items)
- All heroes are free from the start
- Less of a grind to fully play on equal footing (in League it takes forever to get level 30 let alone all the runes you need to play a fair range of heroes optimally)
- Again instead of wards there are pillars which give vision (sort of like in Starcraft) so you spend a lot less time running around placing wards and more time ganking and fighting.
- Obviously much smaller playerbase
- Strife has voice chat

platformer games!

With SMB you are taken out of the level when you finish it and you're plonked on the next level in the map select screen, and whilst I've nothing against that; after playing The End Is Nigh for a little over an hour and a half it's obvious to me how much I prefer it personally.
So hey, overall my first impressions of this have been fantastic. And having a quick peak at the achievements has made me eager to try to catch them all.. But something tells me it's going to be a long and painful journey...

I'm sad to say that it's a slower, duller, lazier and uglier version of Super Meat Boy. It's not horrible, it's just not as good.
First, the game just looks flat. McMillen's games always looked a bit simplistic but Super Meat Boy definitely had a wow-effect. The End is Nigh doesn't. It's just a monotonous gray&black palette and not a single spark of fun in the image. Remember how expressive and fun SMB or The Binding of Isaac look; that's what you won't find here.
It controls similarly to SMB but it's slower, and while SMB had an extremely fun core mechanic of sliding meat-physics, TEIN offers you... well, hanging on ledges. It even sounds boring. In addition to that there's also water, and water controls just feel clunky and off-putting.
In addition to that the game is just easy unless you're collecting tumors. Tumors are collectables, but not like patches in SMB, which were rare and exceedingly hard to get. Here tumors are on every screen (and every screen is basically a level) and unless you decide to get them you miss the whole point of the game. So basically instead of being a really hard game it forces you to go for additional objective so that you make it a hard game.
And worst of all, TEIN commits a sin of being monotonous. Where in SMB each level was a sort of a chess party at a million miles per hour, TEIN feels like you're just moving from a small puzzle to a small puzzle. And it many ways it is true because each level is now 1 screen, and most of them are the same size.
The only great thing about it is music. But it's not enough for me to not refund it. Sorry, Edmund, I'd rather go torture Isaac some more.

Having been a fan of previous McMillen games, I picked up The End is Nigh when it was first announcened. Now that I've beaten the game, I'm a touch torn on my feelings towards the game. Some of the design decisions work for me; others not so much.
What I liked:
+ The McMillen Astethic + Design
+ Environments/Worlds
+ Ash
+ The Past
+ Sound Design + Soundtrack
+ Value
What I didn't like:
- Controls are janky at times on controller (Ash seems to miss ledge grabs way more then with keyboard).
- Collectibles: I'm all for collectibles in games, but make them feel rewarding. Some of the carts in The Future are just a pain to get and all they unlock are harder platforming levels (having the major draw be achievements is just a waste imo; Isaac showers players with fun unlocks & Achievements)
- Levels: While I understand this is a precision platformer, some of the levels just get downright monotonous at times.
- Ash: Ash is seriously underutilized as a character. More Ash!
- The Future: Didn't really work for me. Felt kind of off.
Overall I enjoyed my time with The End is Nigh, but I'm not really itching to jump back into it. There are a few design decisions that didn't really work all that well for me. With that being said, I'm sure if you love platformers, this game will be really fun to you.

I very tentatively recommend this.
"How can you say that?" you might ask, knowing full well that Age of Empires 2 is an excellent game that is widely praised and regarded as a classic. Well, I'll explain.
Age of Empires 2, as a game, is a classic RTS game where you manage a Medieval Civilization, going from a tiny settlement to a sprawling empire. If you don't get invaded first that is. There is a massive focus on combat in this game, most games are decided on the battlefield, with players fielding massive armies against each other to knock out buildings, defences and eventually innocent civilians. But of course, these armies don't come out of nothing, you need to build up some money, gather food, collect wood for buildings and stone for castles. If you aren't familiar with Age of Empires 2, I suggest you look for reviews of that game.
Age of Empires 2 HD is a little different, and not always in a good way.
The upgrades from the original are primarily on the graphical side of things, the updating to a modern lobby-based multiplayer, better mod support and two expansions not originally made for the game. Make no mistake, these aren't all what they're cracked up to be and there's a few problems in this release.
As far as graphics are concerned, the game looks as nice as ever, with only the water reflections, the larger resolutions (which aren't easily adjustable) and a few changed in-game graphics, most of which are welcome additions. To call it HD is perhaps a stretch, but it is graphically superior to its original counterpart.
The modern lobby-based multiplayer is a welcome feature, theoretically allowing for easy and simple online play, without the need for third party clients like Voobly and Gameranger. In practice, the lobby system is very suspect to bugs, with crashes upon game launches occuring frequently and dropouts that halt the game halfway through happening somewhat less frequently. For all the unreliability in Voobly and Gameranger that this system could do away with, it is in many ways inferior, with these problems ocurring less often in either client.
Another couple of things that Voobly and Gameranger players would be able to avoid is the problems that actually happen in-game. Path-finding was never stellar in the original game, but many claim that it has been significantly degraded in this version. Not to mention that the actual game seems to typically run slower, with more log and with more connection problems than it does in Voobly and Gameranger under similar conditions.
The mod support is nice, but the amount of content for AoE2 that isn't on the Steam Workshop is gigantic, which leaves mostly classic and popular scenarios as well as an assortment of other bits and bobs to choose from. Your typical AoE2 player won't be missing out on much, but for those who want really specific things, they might have a hard time to get a hold of them.
And lastly, there's the two expansions. Opinion is divided about these; some say that the new African Kingdoms are extremely powerful, to the point of possibly being imbalanced. And The Forgotten Empires is perceived as being a slew of rather lacking civilizations that don't boast much power, but seem to have very little place in the game. Personally, I think that the African Kingdoms expansion adds a lot to the game and is very fun to play with, even if the new civilizations, particularly the Portugeuse can seem a little tough to play against. As for the Forgotten Empires, it's fun in much the same way, but the civilizations added seem too timid to really add all that much beyond a few interesting unique units and techs to open up a few more strategies than there used to be.
The bugs that make online play well under optimal for such a multiplayer focused game, not to mention one so old and a few of the gameplay problems make me really hesitate to recommend AoE2 HD, because these issues are extremely frustrating and can feel like a dealbreaker. But when the game works, it's as fun as the old AoE2 and sometimes even more so with the higher resolutions, the extra content and the new community. I can't blame you if these bugs get the better of you and you end up going back to Voobly though.

The End is Nigh is an arcade-y platformer that feels similar to Super Meat Boy (since Edmund McMillen partly designed both); but the main mechanic involves hanging from ledges/hooks to long jump, rather than being able to wall-jump anywhere. It can still can be played very quickly, and often the fastest path is the most efficient way to progress.
Each world consists of 20 or so screens that serve as individual challenges (with many secrets), and if you die you will instantly respawn wherever you came in from. The difficulty curve is well paced, but this game gets very difficult in its second act, so it may not be for everyone. I'm currently at 98% and I'll probably leave it at that, however there are many hidden challenges/achievements that I can still attempt to do, if I feel up to the intense trials.
The soundtrack was created by Ridiculon (who composed the OST to BOI: Rebirth), and it consists of short remixes of classical pieces that range from "Flight of the Bumblebee", "In the Hall of the Mountain King" and "Night on Bald Mountain". The soundtrack's repetition in each area will either drive you mad as you fail to make that one jump, or you may find yourself in tune with the game itself, pushing yourself forward just to hear the next song. I was in the latter camp, and I never found the music annoying enough to turn off, even after my hours of failed attempts in the later worlds.
Overall I really enjoyed my time with it; it never felt unfair and I never felt too frustrated outside of the cartridges, but I'm probably more patient/skilled than the average player. I may come back and try to beat the 4 cartridges I have left, but I'm satisfied with it at this point. My commendations to Tyler Glaiel and Edmund McMillen; the game feels great, it is fun and accessible, and still presents enough of a challenge for hardcore players who really want test their skills.

This game is unbelieveably awesome, well worth the asking price, a true diamond in the rough.
I purchased this game for my son and I to play. My initial impression of this game was that it was fairly standard fare, arcade cart game with a twist - transforming cars/boats/planes during a race. This opens up the game to some great variety but there is a secret lurking under what looks like a pretty straight forward game, more on that later.
Graphically the game is definitely nicer than the console versions. I had the pleasure of playing this on a friends PS3 and immediately noticed the 720p res and lower texter detail, the PC version is definitely a step up. In saying that though, the graphics are nothing special and the game is not particularly demanding, I had it running on a "mainstream" card, Radeon 7770 ($150NZD or $50USD), at max detail, 1080p with FXAA and did not experience any slowdown at all. Despite this, the environments and characters are beautifully realised and due to the nature of the game, the graphics are actually great and I can't see any room for improvement.
In the sound and music department the game is made well enough to include sounds and music that don't get annoying with one exception, the menu. It would be so great if you could just disable the menu music. The sounds from each of the characters is fitting and there are some nice gags in there from the likes of wreck it ralph and others that don't get tiresome during frequent playthroughs. Environmental sounds do the job nicely.
Finally, the real star on show is the game play. Multiplayer in this game is perhaps the most complete realisation of multiplayer ever conceived. The ability to play, not just 4 player split screen locally, but online at the same time is just amazing.
In single player, once you've had fun with the "hard" difficulty, and you feel like you've mastered the game, along comes "expert" which shows you that you are truely an ameteur and you must learn the finer points like boost levels, trick and drift boosts etc etc.
You can't win at expert, to truely succeed you need to learn all the tricks for extra speed which opens up a whole new world of skill based play.
I won't go in to any great detail here because the fantastic steam community have made some great guides on how to win at this amazing game.
I can't speak highly enough of this great game. It puts other cart racing games to shame and is a must have for any collection.

Brief overview:
The Game is Hard, Very unforgiving, You may feel like you have nothing compared to everybody else but Honestly you start off with the best overall guns and decent equipment for survival. Most of the game relies on your strategic battle sense - don't over commit for 1 kill, play support classes or play your part in a team, LISTEN to your Squad.
The grind for equipment is pretty long I can admit, there are 'Pay to Win' elements in the Game but honestly it's not a detrimental advantage. The Pay to win elements are: Implants and the ability to purchase weapons and attachments to save time and certs for other skills and abilities that are not purchasable by real world currency.
Overall Feeling:
I Love the Game, I have spent real world cash on saving time to buy things but at no point do I feel that I have an advantage. The feeling I have is that I saved the Grind for that particular item (Like GTA's Shark Cards).
The battles can be some of the most unique experiences you'll ever find on an online Game. I believe from what they announced, each continent can hold up to 2000 players, even in an MMORPG like World of Warcraft, you never see all/ more than 80% of the server in 1 area. when you login during the Prime time, you can more than likely get Good heated battles. After hours, when it's a little more quiet expect the world to feel dead - that is a downside you cannot avoid.
They have a Dev team that seems to be trying to improve the system of the game: New guns, New Continents, New Vehicles, Player-made Bases, tweeks and improvements to certain guns, etc.
I would say, it feels pretty fair. Even when you find yourself going against armor as infantry. Infantry needs to unlock certain weapons and items to counter vehicles but just like you imagine, Armor should be a threat and have the advantage. It is not an impossible advantage but don't expect to counter them with ease.
The enemy spawn camping the base when it's about to be captured so you cannot contest the point - This is by far one of my most favourite times of the match. You have plenty of chances to get easy kills on enemies over extending to keep you at spawn while you shoot through the shield. You have to play tactically - I know a lot of people will say 'but that's a cheap tactic', wrong! That is a tactic to win. When you plant the Bomb as T in CSGO, Are you meant to run around looking for kills or Guard the bomb, most likely camping waiting for a defuse attempt?
It's all tactics and you can best them by doing other things in the Game, Sunderers to spawn elsewhere, Vehicles from the closest neighboring point for Armor backup, there is a way to counter everything - Just depends on if you have decent teammates, your ability and the coordination to pull it off.
Try it out, it's best if you go in there with a friend so you can enjoy learning together and not let Squad commanders push you around if they start to be Anal.
Hope this review helped and gave you the Courage to Dive into the Huge download of the Game (another downside you can't avoid)

I'll start out by saying this game needs a good amount of work. However, it is a great game and I can see it getting much better. They have made up a concoction both similar too and completely different from the other MOBAs I've tried.
They do cater to the casual player, sometimes I think too casual, but there is still a very good amount of depth. The pet and crafting system add a ton of depth to the game and I can see it adding a lot to the replayability of the game as it fleshes out and I become more familiar with it. I do think that they should give new players a few extra free crafts however. They've done great things to eliminate toxicity and I like the gold and XP sharing, but they need to give more money for kills in order to support the fast play style this game seems to be meant for. The last thing I'll touch on is the art style. I know lots of people like the silly, kinda anime style, but I'd like to see something more serious. It's S2 though, so I'm sure there will be a ton of alts in the near future. Hopefully, they'll release some character models I like more.
In the end, this game is great and tons of fun, but it still has a long way to go. I would give it a 75-80 out of 100. I see it being a 90 in the near future though. They're still working things out and they have a hell of a base to build on. This is now my MOBA of choice, because I see the potential in it.

RimWorld is one of those games that can treat you right one moment then sucker punch you the next - but what makes it so good for me is that it doesn't always. It has three storytellers with their own pattern, and those each have their own difficulty. If you want casual play, there's Phoebe Chillax on Basebuilder difficulty; mistakes are easy to recover from. Or you can also choose Randy Random on Extreme Permadeath for a real challenge - What happens is random and once it's done, it's done. Good luck surviving a huge raid on day 3. RimWorld gives a rather strong range of control of challenge right from the start.
The real fun is in the gameplay. You manage a colony (or a tribe) of 1-5 colonists, or pawns, and are tasked with their survival and the ultimate goal of building a ship to leave the planet. Defend them from raiders, killer robots, insect infestations, blights, eachother, and yourself. (We all get fed up with that
pawn eventually.) These pawns each have different traits, skills, and backstories that change how they function, like nudists, psychopaths, optimists, medieval lords, medieval slaves. Injuries also play a big role. A sick colonist will have to spend time in bed recovering or risk death, and a colonist can have their hand, arm, head (yikes!), organs, and more removed and that will affect them adversely. (Who needs a head anyway?) Not to mention that where you choose to build will affect growing seasons, clothes needed to survive, and diseases.
One final feature of RimWorld is the modding scene, and it is huge. A large variety of mods exist on the Steam Workshop and are a click or two away from being in your game, and even more unique mods await you in the Ludeon forums. Just like games like Skyrim, mods can make you spend yet another day managing those wacky pawns. The developer is also active and still polishing and adding more to the game, pushing it bit by bit to its final, grand form.
I didn't expect to love RimWorld as much as I did, and it was a bit of a hesitant buy. However, I fell in love with the game. I struggled to build my first functional colony. I waited on edge to see if my pawn would recover from disease. I felt unease from my first ancient danger. I swore when my pawn kept missing an easy shot. Every colony is a rollercoaster of emotions, and I love every second of it.

Yes, it is early access, but holy heck is this a great game.  I've poured 36 hours into this game and I'm not even close to getting tired of it.  I've laughed, I've cried, I've save scummed.  It is a bit pricy for what it seems like at first, but totally worth every penny.

While I do recommend this game, it certainly has its share of pros and cons.  It's absolutely a blast to play, and it controls fantastically.  The only people I've heard complain about controls are people who play with the joystick ... don't do that ... it's a 2D platformers, use the d-pad ... that's what it's there for!
The music is a lot of fun, and the visuals are engaging, ranging from cutesy-macabre to hauntingly beautiful.  The levels are all deliberately made and offer appropriate challenge, and rewarding feelings for completing them.  And there are a LOT of them.
I think were the game falls flat is first, and least importantly, the writing.  The little blurbs the NPC's say are trite and cringingly "edgey" as if it's a collection of the worst quotes from a 15 year old on /r/atheism.  But I can get over that, since we all know Edmund has a hard-on for hating on/mocking Christianity.  But I think this goes hand-in-hand with my biggest complaint ... the game feels like it's got no heart.  At least in games like Super Meat Boy or 1001 Spikes it felt like there was a heart, or a certain joyfullness to them.  The End is Nigh is fun to play and I plan to chip away at it for as long as it takes to complete, but I don't look back on it with joy, and I don't anticipate playing it later the same way I do Super Meat Boy.  Games like Super Meat Boy and 1001 Spikes would always be in the back of my mind at work or whatever, when I was in the middle of them, but not so much The End is Nigh.  It just feels like a time-filler, kind of like a mobile game, in that I'll pick it up and play for an hour, then maybe forget about it for a few days and do it again.
Despite that it's a solid game, and definitely one for any platforming-junky.  I truly do like it, I just think it's missing a little something to send it over the edge and into greatness.  But don't take my word for it ... go and play it yourself!

I badly want to play this game to completion but cannot get myself to do it for a few reasons:
One: It's ♥♥♥♥ing difficult on just the normal difficulty... I cannot imagine the impossibility of completing it on the nightmare difficulty without dedicating hours to becoming skilled with the controls and the game mechanics; and I usually will just hop right into a game on one of the harder difficulties in seek of a challenge - I like challenge. What I don't like is seen in reason numero...
Two: THE GAME IS NOT COMPLETE. I enjoy the artistry, the music and the overall idea but besides the difficulty in itself the game has some faults that make it even harder. Such as the fact that gold might as well be useless since you cannot keep your weapons or inventory items after you die. This isn't all that bad though the fact alone will cause some apprehension while playing, especially since the controls are a bit difficult to get used to and in a lot of instances, players will find themselves faced against a multitude of highly-coordinated enemies who will need to be struck many-a-time before they die. This is enough of a challenge alone but if you're killed, you lose all of your items and you need to start from the beginning unless you buy a checkpoint coin...which inevitably ♥♥♥♥s you over as you start in the middle of the map with your default weapons.
Three: Once your main character dies, you're given an alternative soldier character with much less ability to defend himself than your main. This is fine as it encourages a player to revive their main. A HUGE issue is that the soldier cannot always reach the resurrection shrine in order to do so since he can only jump like two feet in the air and in a lot of cases cannot even get around the map himself which, in turn, forces a player to just let him die so that they can respawn with their main... with, do I dare say it again...the default weapons.
Overall I like the concept of the game but I think, like how any great story needs a proofread, this game should've been looked over a few times for any inconsistencies before it was released. I'm thankful I only bought it for a dollar.

This game is a roguelike but different to other roguelikes I've played. It's less about the randomness and more about the challenge of going floor after floor, getting what you need to survive. You effectively have infinite lives as long as you can return to an alter which isn't that hard. It almost feels like the experience of playing a fighitng game in arcade mode.
The controls take a little to get used to. If you take it like a brawler you will die and be frustrated by getting locked in animations that create openings for your enemy. The combat is about dashing in and dashing out, avoid the enemies attack and punish them then get back again. It's really fun once you get the hang of it. A lot of the negative reviews talk about clunky controls but that's not quite the case, I felt the same way until I had figured out the above style. But also note I played this with a controller. One thing that isn't explained well, you can dash by hitting the bumpers, this is extremely important.
You can finish the game with the starting items quite easily so finding them becomes less of a big deal, some items are extremely powerful though and help a great deal. The game could really use a sprint button for running long distances.

Memories of a Vagabond is a short RPG Maker turn based RPG game. You can play as one out of four classes which is switchable in the middle of the game. There are no game over in this game. However, when you die, you always "respawn" in the same place.
I think this story can be summed up in one sentence. The story mostly focuses on its short main story. Well, there are a few side quests which is completely standalone from the main story and doesn't have any story at all. The companions which follows the main characters doesn't really have a solid reason for following the MC, especially the one with the Mercenary class. There are almost no character development besides the MC, with an exception of a short story from the start with the bunny girl (which doesn't explained in detail and raises more questions). However, there are a few choices which can be made in game, which can resulting to different outcome: from the changing dialogue to a new companion addition to your party..
It seems that the sprites in this game are taken from more than one source because some sprite looks out of the place, such as the "big house door" and the characters sprite. Despite all that, the sprites still look awesome. I have to admit that the battle background scene looks weird compared to the awesome sprite though.
The UI in this game isn't appealing at all. I love how the dialogues are appearing and disappearing very fast, however, imo, the design can be polished more.
The mappings in this game are not the best one out there. The town is always following the "square land" format and the "dungeon" designs are poorly made. I hardly can call those dungeon at all because it's too straight forward.
Also, while i'm at it, sometimes, there are delays between screens.
The musics in this game flows well with the game, and i don't really have to say anything. It's not good but not bad either and i am enjoying it.
As i said before, you can choose between 4 classes (5, if you count the class in early game): Warrior, Mage, Bounty Hunter, and Assassin. However, the classes are not balanced. The warrior takes all the glory with its op double attack skill, which has a decent damage and low SP (MP in this game). The warrior, surprisingly, also has a quite high SP to spam the skill, while Bounty Hunter, written as "the balanced class of them all" in game, has a lower SP from warrior with its low attack. There are no SP recovery items for Mage, which makes the class to be relying on items or can only use spell a few times (note that it has a very low normal attack damage). Although the assassin has a stealing skill, it's useless in late game, as you can earn gold easily. The problem is, it also lack a low cost-high damaging skill.
If you think that the "mastery" skill which will unlock a particular skill to all class after using a certain skill a few times will help, you are mistaken. I have tried to master the Double Attack skill from Warrior. However, it unlock another skill instead, which allows you to attack all enemies instead of double attacking.
Although you can change classes in game, the level doesn't transfer to each other. The other class levels are depends on the highest companions you are with.

So I bought this on the Steam Autumn Sale, after seeing it recommended on various threads in reddit and elsewhere, expecting it to be somewhat similar to Arma 2 Free which was the last milsim game I've played.
I am happy to report that my initial impression was an understatement. Squad is better than Arma in the things that matter to me, which are pacing and teamwork. Perhaps it's because hardly anyone ever played arma 2 free, but I always felt alone even when I was together with other players.
In Squad even when you're half a kilometer away from your squad you'll never feel alone- your squad leader is pleading for you to rejoin the formation (sorry! I get distracted by enemy fire), your medic is soothing your downed squadmates with yells of "DON'T GIVE UP!", and occasionally a drunk fool calls people insane stuff while insisting he's sober.
...That last one I wouldn't mind seeing less of, but it was just the one time anyway and he was promptly kicked off the squad for being insubordinate. Which proves to me that Squad is a game worth playing, because unlike practically every other game I've played toxic behavior is self-moderated by players. Server admins rarely have to step in because everyone in the team is invested in communicating clearly and with a goal in mind.
The worst squads are the ones that are completely silent, and that's saying something because I normally dislike voice chat in other games.
If you want a game where you feel that your efforts in both words and actions are rewarded with victory (or a fun defeat), then this is the game for you.

I remember when I used to play this game loads and you could unlock loads of new items, unleash your creativity and build whatever you wanted, with out having to pay for anything.
Over time the game became alot more pay to win as more weapons and features were added which ruined the experience. Such as when the healing weapons where added there were loads of people playing support roles (including me) which really helped win games. Then an auto healing feature was added which made healers useess.
Then the ability to have multiple different types of weapons was added which made it less about filling a role eg: sniper, bomber, and more about how many weapons you could have.
At this point I uninstalled the game because it didn't feel like anyone could have a unique robot anymore, this along with the increasing pay to win features that were being added and all of the gimmicky new weapons and maps, which i personaly dislike compared to the old desert and mountainous maps which were more simplistic, and the new gamemode types which are very confusing, make the game feel overwhealming, confusing and boring.
Around half a year later I reinstalled the game with high hopes they had fixed alot of things and made the game alot easier to understand but as soon as i had got in a new feature of buying and selling blocks, weapons and items had been added in, after experimenting with it, I came to realise that system made no sense, relying on you to level up to be able to unlock 1 item (it was presented in a confusing spiral and it takes forever to level up).
Then i played a quick match. Everything seemed as it was before (When it was 1 life per round and which ever team lost all their players lost the game),  exept there was a time limit and a certain amount of points had to be reached and the whole team was spawn camped and we lost. I also couldn't help but notice I was a healer and couldn't heal my team (they would ethir auto heal or die before i could do anything) and I couldn't kill anyone... because all i had were heal guns, and their team had no healers. The maps were also alot smaller which made strategy much less important so there was no point in flanking or setting up an ambush, because the enemy team would be at your spawn with in half a minute.
After playing a few matches I uninstalled the game.
Now i have looked at the trailers for this game and now there are massive floating shields ridiculous maps, objective points to capture, what looks to be an orbital strike (0:43) and all about who ever has the biggest gun wins. The game seems to have drifted away from what it used to be. Relying on your team, relying the healer to keep you in the fight, relying on a bomber plane so sneak up onto their sniper and take them out so your team can stick together and win a fight. Different people filled different roles and you never knew what to expect in every game, at this point it just seemes like everyone does their own thing and there are no roles or strategies making every bot seem less unique
I just thought that I should share my opinion on the direction of the game and compare what it used to be to what it has become now. I know the entire game isn't going to revert back to its old ways just because some people that played the game when it first came out commented saying how they feel the game has gotten worse overtime. But I hope to give some insight onto what the game used to be to help people make up their mind on wether to get the game or not. And i have nothing wrong with anyone liking the game now, im sure people do like it.

A seriously impressive game from a single guy (plus some outsourcing). The goal of making Dwarf Fortress accessibility has been achieved, and though it lacks the deep simulation and ridiculous unplanned emergent stories from that (drunk cats), it surpasses them by making emergent stories the very core of the game. Then it makes it Sci-Fi with guns and an adverserial AI to challenge you when you prosper and assist when you falter, or vice versa.
I've followed this game for a while and it really deserves more attention that it has got. I can't stop playing it, there is always some goal or crisis that makes you forget the passing of time, and watching your little minions labour never gets old. This is a game about systems and how they all interact to create a believable simulation of a space colony. Nothing is dumbed down and works just like you think it would.
Combat is good with a cover system, different weapons with strengths and weaknesses, intricate body part damage calculations (does a bullet penetrate armor, miss the heart but nick the left lung? Now breathing is difficult and the lung is filling with fluid, if untreated it could cause unconciousness and infection!). Tech tree is extensive and rewarding (even better with mods). Multi-tiered production chains, interesting farming for food and drugs, procedurally generated art ala DF, pawns with believable traits and quirks, and a perfect difficulty curve that really matches whatever challenge you want (AI Storytellers is genius!)
And oh jesus the mods. There can't be enough and they all fit so perfectly I sometimes forget what is core and what is new. The simple graphics and understandable systems make it a natural fit.
And Tydan keeps adding huge new features that can't be done with modding and often. This game has no right to be early access with so many fully fleshed out features. I can't wait to see what makes it into "1.0"

You're Adrian Shephard, a 22 year old marine, or something army-ish. Okay so I'm not really sure what you are, but what's important is you're in HECU, a military.thing that exists to make sure the Black Mesa research facility is safe at all times. After being mysteriously bumped up to corporal (*coughGmancough*) the Black Mesa facility is invaded by aliens. Unbeknownst to Adrian, the HECU are under orders to "silence" the facility, meaning they have to kill everything in there, whether it be aliens or scientists, with their sights especially on someone called "Freeman" who has been killing all the HECU. A mysterious "Race X" is also appearing, a new race of aliens even more powerful than the originals.
The story is great. It ties in with the first Half-Life a lot, which is really neat while also including this sense of consistency. The game explains a lot of things from Half-Life, like why the black ops are there, and also makes the HECU become actual characters, as opposed to the mindless grunts they were in HL1. It's full of fun twists and turns as well as being just fun. One flaw, however, is that in HL1 you always had a set thing you were trying to do. Fire a rocket, find the lambda core, defeat the alien master, there was always something. Throughout a lot of OP4, Adrian is just wandering around mindlessly with no real goals and it makes you wonder why he doesn't try to leave instead of constantly going back inside Black Mesa.
The gameplay is the same mixture of shooting and exploration, just like in the original. The beginning first felt a little dull but then the game started to pick up. I especially liked the shooting at some parts, even though I hated one of the new alien enemies who in my opinion was just really annoying, an enemy which requires too much ammo to take down and does too much damage.
In this expansion you experience the story of Half-Life from the perspective of a soldier. You are going to Black Mesa, and your aircraft crashes. You wake up and don't know what is really going on and what the mission is.
The game itself is pretty hard for me to curate, because it all just feels and plays the same as the original game. (With the expansion having half the length of the original game.) The new features are some different weapons and enemies, both of which are creatively implemented. The only new feature that I didn't think was all that well executed was the nightvision goggles. They looked cool at first, but they sadly only really work in short distance.
This expansion takes place in Black Mesa for the most part, not much time is spent in alien dimensions. At the beginning, I had the feeling that the weapons were a little bit more balanced than in the original game. Because I found myself using the shotgun more often. Still there are some new weapons that I almost never used.
What I found special about Opposing Force is that I could see that Gearbox added some more humor in the expansion than what there was in the original Half-Life itself. I still have to say that the story in my opinion didn't really add too much to what we already knew from Half-Life, but it is still fun to see it from their perspective

It's a shame that the really very bad parts of the game make it impossible for me to recommend the game.
Visually it is fantastic, but game design wise the stupid decisions haunt the experience.
The game mechanics of the fighting are poorly introduced, the pacing of more difficult encounters feels random.
I get it that this is supposed to be a hard game and this was clear to me when I bought it.
But when a game has a steep learning curve, then a really annoyingly punishing system like the one in place is inexcusable:
You'll die (quite often in my case, because it was really hard for me to adapt to the unusually sluggish controls) and instead of respawning, you get replace by a soldier with even worse agility and abilities. This guy then needs to find a sparse statue to revive you (never found one) or if he dies as well, you'll start at the village and the descent begins again.
I'm voting this down because it is not only not a good game, but it is also saddening me how much potential has been wasted by ACE team once more.

With Worms Revolution being the first Worms game I actually sat down and played since the awesome Worms World Party, I was a bit sceptical at first because the little bit I saw from the 3D Worms Games in between didn´t really click with me.
This scepsis was enforced when I was greeted with the most clunky menu design I ever had to witness ... so much clicking and so confusing at the same time. Even when you got into it, it´s still a bit of a chore, escpecially in Online Play, wchich would really benefit in a better and more clear system to get games easily going.
This, however, is my only big grasp with WR since the remaining game turns out to be quite excellent. I quite enjoyed the new game mechanics as in the water and the physics objects, which give the game a really nice twist.
The weapons are awesome as usual with some cool new stuff, especially in the water department. The often critisised ninja rope has been changed a lot but once you got used to it it handles just fine, only different.
Also, the new worms classes, while they don´t feel that special at first, actually develop a lot of depth and strategy once you learn their uses. I also enjoyed the single player mode very much. The campaign is pretty challenging and the enemy AI has a near perfect hit rate sometimes, but this can always be overcome with the right strategies. In total with the DLCs there are over 70 missions, which is a lot and should keep busy for a while.
So all in all, I´d definately recommend WR. Make the menus better, and therefore have easier access to multiplayer matches and you are nearing the perfect worms experience.
