Memories of a Vagabond is a small RPGMaker game. That's about it. Aside from 2 or 3 aspects that I may like the game for, this seems to be 90% filler content. It's a functional RPG without a heart of its own. There isn't really an idea or a purpose for the story, and neither is there an interesting combat system.
It's unfortunate for me to start the review like this, but this is what I've felt during the whole experience.
First off, I got this game for free. I've seen it around in bundles and/or giveaways a few times, and decided to give it a go. I didn't go in with any expectations, but unfortunately, the game did nothing to win me over. It didn't do anything
either! It's just not interesting at all.
I beat it on Hard Mode in 5 hours.
As with every other RPG Maker game, the engine doesn't allow for resolution options, only Fullscreen on/off; when I go fullscreen, it screws the aspect ratio up, so I can either play with the screen displaced and low resolution, or in a tiny window.
Aside from that, I haven't had any technical issues.
I've read quite a few reviews on steam, and they're mostly positive, which I don't understand. I mean, JRPGs aren't all that common on PC, but Memories of a Vagabond does absolutely nothing to stand out or be a memorable experience...
However, I do respect the developer for supporting this game nicely. From what I've seen, he's been solving problems posted in the Community Hub, and is also launching a patch tomorrow.
Anyway, here's the review.
The
here are mostly standard. A few of the objects are pretty nicely designed, but there isn't much to say.
The combat effects look pretty smooth, which I appreciate, but it's nothing mind-blowing. The combat backgrounds have a different style, being seemingly hand-drawn (well, digitally, but you get the idea). They're fairly simple, but it gives the game a bit more personality.
There were also some graffities spread around. These were completely out of place, in this fantasy setting. I'm not sure if they're an inside reference or what, but it seems completely random to have these.
The
, as noted by other reviewers, is certainly the game's highlight. And I didn't even consider it
good, for the most part. It's fitting with the locations, but it's mostly orchestrated, which I don't think fits very well with these low-res games. But again, it's good, especially the one from the last Boss. That was certainly a well chosen song!
The
and
were, once again, standard. I've had a few interface issues, though. Those problems were caused mainly by some of the mechanics, so I'll right about it when I get there (1).
The
and
has probably been my least favorite aspect of this game. It just seems very amateur, the characters have nothing interesting about them (on the contrary, many of them seem very childish), and the story is also a very bland
scenario.
The game's tries to keep a more or less serious tone (no
serious, but serious), but then throws in some really out of place jokes.. I don't understand what it was trying to do, to be honest. There was a funny area near the last area, but again, it just came out of nowhere.
In here, you go through
-ish areas, and also have an
, to travel between them. The areas are pretty small (including the overworld).
There are no random encounters! You can always see the enemies walking around, so you can approach them at will, and when you're ready. I think that's good. Also, once you kill the enemies in the dungeons, they're dead and do not respawn. If you're having difficulty issues, you can grind a bit in the Overworld (a couple of levels make all the difference, and are quick to get).
Other than that, there are a few sidequests, with very minor rewards (both in terms of equipment and interesting events, they're completely filler).
There is also an
of sorts, where you battle increasingly difficult groups of enemies. I always like this idea in RPGs. However, the game doesn't take advantage of it at all. There's no adrenaline-pumping ambience to it or anything. You go in, fight, and get back out. At the end of each fight you'll get a pretty decent reward (in gold, items and equipment).
There's
with this, though.
I've only managed to finish 3 fights before the enemies got too strong for the point in the game. I could have endured it, maybe grinded a bit, and tried to keep going, but there was not point! After the third fight, I went and beat the final boss without any problem at all. I had the best equipment available (by simply buying it from shops) and yet, the arena's difficulty was already too high. Yet another elements that feels pointless and misused.
I suppose it was intended as an end-game thing, perhaps. Without an interesting combat system, however, I have no desire of trying it out.
As is to be expected, you can use a Basic Attack, Skill, or Item. Skills require mana to use, and can be normal attacks with an added bonus, or status ailments. The status ailments, however, are completely useless against basic enemies, and cannot be used against Bosses (or at least their hitting rate is reeeeally low), so there's a big portion of the combat rendered useless. Most of the time, you'll be going between strong attacks, AOE, and healing. There isn't any deep strategy to the combat. Battles usually take no more than 3 turns, with Bosses being the exception, just because of their amount of HP.
There are no phases, interesting skills, or anything of the sort. Everything is just as you've seen in every other JRPG. It does, once again, nothing to stand out.
There's one huge problem I have with it, though, that modern RPGs seem to have eliminated. That is how you have to manually heal and restore your HP after a fight. Most of recent RPGs take the route of each battle being self-contained. This way, you don't need to worry about the time between battles, and just wasting time buying and managing potions.
There's another design route that comes with this, and that's taking the random encounters out. With random encounters, it makes sense for you to be "permanently" damage, making the dungeons tense.
With a limited number of enemies, however, that stops working in the game's favor. Another possibility is making each battle almost like a puzzle. Each battle can be harder, but also far more interesting. Without the nuisance of having to buy and manage potions, you can have more difficult fights that bring you to the limit, without it being a problem. As it stands, it just ends up being a couple of conflicting design decisions that make the combat much worse.
There's also an element to the attack types (with Fire, Wind, Earth, Ice, etc. having weaknesses and strengths) but with the fights in the game, they're useless. The enemies don't really have an apparent type so that you can play with that in mind. It's mostly guess-work. But in the couple of hours of this game, there's no chance to use that strategically.
I'm sorry for being this harsh on a small game like this, especially when the developer cares for the game. If this was a first game, more like an experiement, then that's fine. It's functional, despite the many flaws, and everyone learns from mistakes.
Still, I can't recommend this, when there are so much better games out there. I didn't enjoy it at all, due to it lacking personality. There's nothing that the game's trying tell or do, unfortunately.

So, after rage quitting somewhere in my third NG+ attempt at Dark Souls, I've decided to go through my library, give all the games I've accumulated a fair shake. First up is Abyss Odyssey.
Full disclosure, I got Abyss Odyssey because it was thrown in with a humble bundle, and I am playing it with a mouse and keyboard. I am also realizing this is less than ideal. My initial intention with it was to beat it before settling on a full opinion of it. That very quickly became "give it five hours." That has now become "an hour and a half might be enough."
Abyss Odyssey isn't necessarily bad. It might even be good. Visually, it's actually pretty inviting - the setting is evocative and immersive, the full character illustrations are pretty neat. While the characters are very, very much broad strokes, that works for the setting. The narrative setting itself is also largely intriguing, as the player finds themselves delving into the dream of a slumbering warlock made reality in 1890's Chile. I can't call that anything but unique, especially with the character's confession that they too are a part of the dream. Between the visuals and the mysterious narrative context, Abyss Odyssey certainly motivates the player to explore.
Furthermore, exploration is a big part of the game, with the world changing each time you enter the abyss. Each time you can find new items and try a different approach into a new version of the dream. It's really a cool idea.
My problem arises with the actual gameplay mechanics. All of this setting and presentation is well and good, but it serves merely as a backdrop for the meat of the game, which is side scrolling brawler / fighting game in the style of the adventure mode for things like Street Fighter. So as the player moves sideways and up and down through the abyss they are confronted with mobs of different dream creatures, which drop keys and health and mana and what have you.
My personal inclination is to to say the mechanics are horribly clunky. The character moves very slowly and feels unresponsive. Constructing actual combos and meaingfully positioning yourself feels cumbersome. Now, people have said elsewhere that this is essentially the combat mode from Smash Bros, which I can see, and I am terrible at and do not enjoy. It is possible that this game is very fulfilling for someone who takes to this style of gameplay, but I do not. So overall my verdict on the gameplay is that it is horribly frustrating and ungratifying. My attempts to acclimate myself to the play style were so heavily thwarted in my short attempts at the game that I can't bring myself to go any further, even given how inviting the world is. Which is a shame.
So. A beautiful, intruiging game world. Massively clunky and frustrating fighting game mechanics pitting you against hyper responsive AI - though this hinges on my sucking at this game. A platformer utilizing unresponsive and clunky movement. This to me constitutes Abyss Odyssey.
Not necessarily bad. For someone who can make this game work, which I'm sure they're out there, it might even be a great game. But I am not that person.  I'll be surprised if I can force myself into a few more hours of gameplay on it.
If you can pick it up for cheap, give it a shot! Chances are you might like it. If you dig Smash Bros style combat, you might dig this too.

The main character really seemed to grow as I played, and I began noticing all of the options were becoming kinder and kinder as she confronted her past. Treat yourself at the next sale and pick this one up!

I’ve never written a review before, as I generally consider it a waste of time of my time, but wow this game was so ♥♥♥♥ing awesome I had to post something. To give you a little background, I’m a Fire Emblem fan through-and-through and I don't have time to play video games much anymore as I'm busy. When I saw this gem on the steam store though, I couldn't resist.
I ended up completing the game on the hardest difficulty and unlocking both of the endings. In my opinion, the game’s greatest strength is its small maps and smart AI. Instead of just throwing my strongest unit at the enemy, I had to you know, use tactics. Personally, I would suggest not playing it on the hardest difficulty, as a couple levels were super annoying. (I’m looking at you John. Your little assassin buddies are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.)
Story-wise, I really liked how the narrative progressed. I’m not going to give any spoilers, but it made the later chapters feel more impactful as you were emotionally connected to the characters. There wasn't that much dialogue, but it was always high-quality and relevant. Not the greatest but for the price you really have nothing to lose. I'm only on Scenario III but that should encompass the majority of gameplay features.
Pros:
-Does well to capture the gameplay of RPGs like Fire Emblem and Tear Ring Saga
-Plenty of slots for save files.
-Sprites are kind of nice
-Tutorial does its job
-Base Conversation feature
-Adjustable difficulty
Cons:
-Story, while reminiscent of Fire Emblem, does not feel compelling as a result of execution
-Love relationships is rushed
-In-combat talking can be unpredictable and you might miss a text if you hold fast-forward after your turn
-Some names could be better
-*Awful font spacing [EN]
-*Full Screen [F1] appears to be bug out when loading to a new map?
-*Not true 720p, the framerate in battle scenes are choppy
-Portrait cutouts have slight "haloing" around the edges
-Music leaves a lot to be desired, sound effects are generally weak
*Likely a limitation of the SRPG Engine
Story/Gameplay
The story is your typical enemy invades the hero's homeland and conquers the territory with bloodshed. Nothing too new but let's get to our first "issue." Emperor David catches my eye as an oddball name. While it does have old lore behind it I still find it phonetically weird and clashing a bit with some other names. The dialogue is much what you would expect. It has a slightly upgraded vocabulary (no more dastard) but the **writing is not convincing. Rather it's a bit reminiscent of shadow dragon, being based off a 1980s story, which wasn't very good. The love interest and dialogue was incredibly vague. Gave us no reason to like her and quite frankly it just negatively affected my opinion of both of them. Moreso her since our hero has some redeeming qualities.
The game plays like a tactical RPG, more accurately Fire Emblem. It's pretty faithful and it seems the majority of weapons/items have infinite durability. That being said I do feel the movement of all units should be reduced by one space, everyone seems to move a bit too far. The map sizes, thus far, haven't been large at all, maps would need to be 1.3x screen size to feel "normal."
The RNG is also unforgiving with weak character growths. Either it's close to some really old FE titles (Gaiden) or taking a page out of Berwick Saga. It'd also be great if we had more characters early on. Main character aside (who will get thrashed by magic) your units are rather squishy and I have to resort to forgotten/new strategies to work around it. The last time I recall having such an awful comp was in Radiant Dawn. The low growth rates don't make the characters anymore likable. A certain character got no stat raises for over half her level ups (6), pretty awful and none were defense stats either which she desparately needed.
Graphics and Sound
The graphics seem to use a lot of default SRPG assets which are well made in their own right. The sprites in the battle scene reminds me of better GBA FE combat sprites. Animation effects are appropriate. Unfortunately the battle scene looks as if the framerate has been reduced... likely isn't the case but it is needlessly choppy for some reason. The game window is about 720p but with the notable black borders the usable resolution is lower. The amount of black space is beyond overscan. Toggling full-screen (F1) seems to cause problems if I load into a new map. Lastly the outline of character portraits are a bit awkward. As if they were ripped from a white background instead of an alpha channel.
The audio is sorely lacking. The sound effects could use more oomph but are still serviceable. The music does not do the game any favors. Sometimes it's okay like the overworld theme but otherwise I dislike it.Most tracks seem amplified beyond normalized levels (introducing clipping) or added too much compression and then amplified. The classical music, while it makes sense, is rather off-putting. Feels too slow for the pace of battle and doesn't make the game any more immersive.
Conclusion
For $0.99 I didn't know what to expect. It's also a "full game" on version 0.25 [at the time of writing] so that doesn't make much sense either. Most of the issues I came across are related to execution rather than the actual idea itself. I'm playing on normal+, while I don't mind it being arguably difficult I think it's that way for the wrong reasons. Anyways you could consider this "Review" a preview of what the game has to offer.
**Delving into details would definitely bloat this otherwise lengthy "review"

This was a unique and charming horror/adventure game. However, it should be noted that it isn't the typical jump scare kind of game, which gives it that fresh feeling I haven't had in a while. The game does a great job of creating a atmosphere of uneasiness and dread with the help of its soundtrack. It's worth mentioning that the art direction and voice acting are fantastic as well.
This was a relatively short game as I finished it within 4 hours (but without finding all the extras). There is some replay value due to some consequences of your choices that are mutually exclusive. That being said, I didn't find the game to be a strong "choices matter" game since your choices, with the exception of a few, aren't significantly important to the outcome of the game. In the post-game, I found myself thinking "how did my choices lead to that?!" In a game that  claims to be choice-based, that makes the whole experience feel less satisfying than it otherwise would have.
I particularly didn't like the dialogue and movement mechanisms, which probably would have felt smoother with either a mouse or a controller (I used my laptop without a mouse). Also, I don't know if it was intentional, but the protagonist seemed to always interrupt others when I was genuinely interested in what other characters had to say next, and with the dialogue choices constrained to a time limit, I felt like I was always scrambling to respond. Overall, the controls didn't feel right. The radio tuning also took way too long without a mouse.
Despite my complaints, the game was enjoyable and I would recommend this game (especially if it's on sale).

If you liked the full game Half-Life, you will enjoy this expansion pack. In fact, if you're in any way a fan of first-person shooters you will probably like it. So yes, it's a great add-on which you will get several hours of fun out of, but I'll just go through a few problems which you might come across. Firstly, some of the sound design is a bit off. Considering how solidly-made the Steam version of Half-Life is, this bit was slightly disappointing. The character's footsteps on concrete sounded as though they were on wood. Confusing. Secondly, I encountered a bug about halfway to two-thirds of the game that got me stuck in the same spot in an elevator as it touched down, and this required a re-load. I got around this problem by moving around a bit as the lift approached its stop point. Finally, the tone of the game is sometimes a bit hard to swallow: even though Black Mesa was infested with aliens at this point, a fat security guard seemed completely oblivious and at ease, instead concentrating on trying to get a chocolate bar or something out of a vending machine...
Whatever. I still had about seven hours of top-class enjoyment out of Opposing Force. It has the trademark Half-Life great level design. The storyline, featuring a new protagonist, ties in well with the previous game. It's great that the game allows you to come across the paths of previous characters, like Freeman and the G-Man, etc. The overall difficulty is just as well-balanced as before, including the end boss battle, which is well-designed and requires a bit of strategy. And the ability to play a Marine and command some fellow troops is implemented really well. How the game manages to put you in the boots of who would have been an enemy in the original Half-Life whilst still making you sympathise with the character is very good. The story ties together with the previous one well.
So recommended for any Half-Life fan, and if you're new to the series, get the full game plus this - for the price you can't go far wrong.

Dirty bomb is a very good shooter that is fast-paced and complex. There are about 30 characters (called 'mercs') to play as; there is a slight p2w feel as you only get 2 at the beginning and the rest you have to buy with a. real money or b. a ridicoulous amount of ingame money. You basically have to play 3 months every day and get the money through daily bonuses. However, you are given enough currency at the beginning to buy 1 merc; and every week there are 3 on rotation that you can play as.
As oppose to most shooters, where you buy/unlock guns for each character and kit them out, dirty bomb works through 'loadout cards'. Each character has a default one, then there are 6 tiers: lead, iron, bronze, silver, gold, cobalt. Lead gives you 1 extra passive, iron 2 and bronze-cobalt 3. Silver-cobalt are no stronger than bronze but are essentually the equivilant of getting rare gun/character skins. Each card comes with a primary, secondary and meele weapon (although from what i've played the meele is cosmetic as they all act in the same way).
The gameplay is fun and fast paced. It's easy to get into. Even the snipers have to keep moving to avoid getting shot. The tutorial even discourages scoping/ironsighting unless absoultly necessary. The fast moving objectives and quick descision making makes this game fast and fun.
There are a few problems with the matchmaking system though and don't come in expecting instant matching; the ui sometimes breaks and the game causes other problems. That being said, it's much less broken then most other beta shooters I've played, so don't worry about it causing you computer to brick.
If you're willing to commit the grinding time, and you like fast-paced shooters, this game is a must.

Hard to recommend, which is frustrating, because the strongest element of the game is the most important - the puzzles on the whole are actually pretty decent... But basically everything else is very poor.
Only 30 levels, almost half of which are either tutorial, or could be considered tutorial-level difficulty.
A simple level editor would be a few hours work, and add enormous value through steam workshop levels.
Most controls are keys, but some require mouse.
No key-binding, so you are forced to use the (often weird and unintuitive) default choices.
No zoom out, and no free moving camera options to inspect the levels properly.
No undo button, forcing a complete restart after any mistake.
Ugly, cheap-looking UI. Unskippable, pointless animation at the start of every level.
tldr: frustrating and poor value for money, but worth picking up at heavy discount if you can overlook the problems and appreciate the solid puzzle mechanics.

This a nice puzzle games with interesting ideas, and it's not an easy game, some levels are quite challenging.
Ultimately I sadly cannot recommend this game as the controls and the gameplay are quite bad:
- Each level begins with an animation that is long and unskippable. This is particulary annoying when you have to restart a level, as there is no way to restart without quitting the level and restarting and rewatching the level.
- The game is mostly keyboard driven: you move the blocks using the keyboard and switch blocks using keyboard or the mouse. It feels a bit awkward using the mouse just for that so it's more natural to use only the keyboard. However, the only way to navigate menus is with the mouse. Which means you use the mouse in the menus (to start a level or to quit a level: esc does not work) and the keyboard during the rest of the game, this is painful. Playing with a controller does not solve the problem as it only emulates the keyboard part
- Due to the way the camera is oriented, you don't see everything on the screen, due to blocks being hidden by other blocks. You can only rotate the camera 90 degrees, which doesn't always help. It becomes a problem later on and the developer actually acknowledges it on level 13 when the tutorial even says that sometimes you have to move your blocks just to see what happens !

I ultimately chose against recommendation due to all these technical issues that ruin the game for me. The first two are easily patchable and I might change my review if this changes.

Abyss Odyssey is a fighting game disguised as a beat 'em up/platformer/roguelike. You do the basic things one would expect from those latter 3 genres -- fighting heaps of disposable bad guys, hopping around on moving floors, and crawling through variable dungeons that change with each iteration. But it's the fighting game mechanics that will carry you. Your use of animation cancels, unforgiving parries, launches, juggles, and general purpose combo mastery will carry you.
The better you are at these fighting game mechanics, the faster you'll progress. A solid player can beat the boss within a few hours. There's a lot more to accomplish including fleshing out all the heroes, capturing all the enemies in the cool extra-life soul-stealing system, and multiplayer and nightmare difficulty.
So take this recommendation with a caveat. The price you get Abyss Odyssey at should reflect the extent to which you can explore the game's mechanical depth and it should reflect your willingness to play to completion. If Abyss Odyssey is a one-and-done game to you, wait for a sale that justifies 3 hours of play. If your fighter mechanics are solid and you tend to be a completionist, feel free to pick it up for retail price.

This game is a lovely experience.

The graphics are simple, but absolutely adorable. The characters and their relationships are pretty unique and I quickly became fond of each of them in different ways. And the conversation system, which works in real time, is probably the greatest thing about this game. The writing and voice-acting are also top-notch which quickly adds to immersion since it makes you feel like you are actually talking to real people.
There's a certain replay value due to some consequences of your choices that are mutually exclusive.
All in all, it's the first game in a long time that surprised me with how new and creative it was in many aspects. I don't have to think twice about recommending it!

Since this is a yes-or-no review situation, I'm going with yes. That said, I had some problems with it.
The good here is the artwork, the score, and the 80s-horror vibe. It's a fun, almost Stranger Things-esque story. The bad is that the "choices matter" tag is deceptive. Your choices only matter a little bit at the end. And when I got to the post-game "here's what happened to the characters after this" portion, I found myself going, "Wait, how did my choices lead to that?!" In a game that's supposed to be, to some degree, choice-based, that makes the whole experience feel less satisfying than it otherwise would have. Maybe I said the wrong thing and set off another character accidentally, or somehow said the right thing to a character I didn't even like and ended up becoming besties with them. But the point is, the game would've been better off structuring itself less a choose-your-own-adventure game and more as a solve-the-mystery game.
Still, I had fun playing while I was playing--so consider this a conditional recommendation.

Oxenfree brings to the table some of the things I really love in games. The main draw to Undertale for me was the fact that things in the game change if you go back and play it a second time. I still really love Undertale, but I think Oxenfree surpasses it in that regard. Little details about the game are different the second time you play and some parts of the abandoned island even restore themselves for one moment in a time loop, which really threw me off. I even found myself documenting all the little changes in my game through pictures.
Another unique mechanic in this game is the radio and how you can open it at any time and scroll through the channels. I even found one of the songs from the soundtrack on station 89 while in the woods area one time. This game does not draw you into any cutscenes at any time. Alex can always walk around, ignore questions, or walk away while people are talking. In this way, this game surpasses telltale games as well, because Telltale games are all big cutscenes with some walking around parts and lots of dialogue choices.
I think it's also worth pointing out that this game contains 12,000 different lines of dialogue. I know this from the documentaries you can find in the start menu under options. That's really impressive for such a short game. For someone to put so much care into how these characters interact with each other is really something I admire. Alex can only act how you want her to, so it's your choice to decide what kind of a person she ends up and how she feels about each person on the island with her.
I also admire a good story and boy does this game have that. I am someone who really does not like horror games, but upon reading the reviews for this game and hearing that this game didn't rely on jumpscares for it's horror, I immediately wanted to play it. Subtle horror games like this are defiantly the kind I like.
In conclusion, I got this game on sale for $4 and I defiantly do not regret buying it. It's taken me through it's story twice now, and I still love it and recommend it to those that want a good story and meaningful choices.

DO NOT buy this game, especially for $15.00.  If you get it free, I would still recommend you don't waste your time like I did.  I got it in a bundle and still regret losing an hour and a half of my time.
I loaded up with a friend and jumped right into co-op play, here is the bad:
- You start with two characters.  The girl is okay the guy is an obnoxious character to play as.
- The game doesn't really tell you anything or explain any of the game mechanics to you.
- I am not really into the story of games, but if I was, this game has nothing of interest to offer.
- You go down into the Abyss and as you go down you get gold and buy things from the shops on each floor.  Problem is you don't gain gold at a comparable rate to the item price in shops.  Considering you don't get to keep the items when you die, the system that is in place is atrocious at best.
- Speaking of this, in co-op you don't share loot which makes gold gain even harder.
- During the course of play, they have some weapons laying around for free on the map.  Most of the time it says "not usable by the character you are playing".  So, not very helpful.
- When you play co-op, you have to be on the same screen at all times, so if I drop down a level, I can't see my character.  The camera follows the host.
- Jumping in the game is bad.
- The combat is extremely clunky, even with a controller.  For the most part, it feels like your just mashing buttons when fighting.
- The AI is ridiculous at times.  It's like they anticipate everything you are doing.  I'll throw fireballs at enemies who are fighting my partner and they somehow dodge behind my partner at the last second every time and the fireball hits him.  They feel like they are teleporting all over the screen sometimes.  Sometimes they'll just hold the block button for what seems like forever.
- Speaking of enemies, they have way too much health for just being common enemies.  I don't want to play a game where every enemy feels like an HP sponge.  If your fighting more than 3 at once, good luck not getting stun locked for half your health or more.
- When we loaded up, my friend wanted to turn off friendly fire.  The game said something about not being able to access all areas if you turn it off, so we left it on.  Talk about a terrible experience.  With the combination of having to be on the same small screen, the terrible jumping, the clunky controls and the enemy AI being obnoxious, good luck not hitting your co-op partner for at least a third of their health in each fight.
Here is the good:
- The graphics.
- The music.
tl;dr If all you like in a game is graphics and music, get this game when it's in a bundle for a $1.00.  If you want to have fun, there are 100's of cheaper games that are far less frustrating.

After spending about 45 minutes on The End Is Nigh, I'm forced to ask why McMillen decided it would be a good idea to remake one of his most popular games ages later, but slow it down, make it dull and bland looking, and sell it for 15$. Level design is punishing in a unfair way, such that many levels are impossible to complete on the first try simply because there are little to no clues about what is going to happen (which parts of the level will move, what is passable/unpassable terrain, etc). Trial and error was in meatboy too, but usually because of timing errors or figuring out a new obstacle. Here it is because there is no way to tell what kind of obstacles you are facing before it is too late.
Before finishing the first world I was too bored to care about collecting all the tumors, and the game is a failure if only for that: I stopped caring before I even really got into it.
I was looking forward to this game for weeks, and now I probably won't pick it up again.
Do yourself a favor and just replay Meatboy. It's a better game and you already own it.

There are levels that make you sun-blind which consist only of rich dark shades of red and black. There are levels that blur your vision intentionally. This is the first game that has given me vision issues after playing it, and I have played hundreds of games.
I love Ed McMillen's art, message, and the extremely tight controls of the his games. I only fear I've gotten too old to meet him with my reflexes. I will not be playing this more than once, unlike super meatboy/isaac. It is just too stressful.

Memories of a Vagabond is a very short but impressive rpg. You can complete the game in 3-5 hours and this can turn off some players. If you are a player that have little time but truly enjoy rpgs then this is definitely worth a play through.
You play the role of a hero who is about to ask his girlfriend for her hand in marriage and live a happy life. This all suddenly changes as a demon appears and takes her away and to make matters worse, you die trying to stop it!
This story also leads to the most unique play mechanic of the game and that is when you die, you are granted a new body. A new body is much more then a new look as it's also your way of changing your class. Battles are similar to classic Final Fantasy and the animation for the characters and monsters is decent. Aside from the battles the backgrounds and sprites are nicely done and look very nice. The music is good and fits each scene perfectly though not totally memorable. It also has small sound details like each tile in the game have different footstep sounds and that is very cool!
Outside of fights it's very basic as you buy weapons, armor and level up to learn more skills and for what it's worth it's done right. Many times throughout the game you are offered choices for dialog and it keeps the short and basic story interesting. It has many advanced features not in classic rpgs like quest logs, being able to loot body's and even being able to craft weapons and items! Many side quests are available and it even have a few mini games to distract you from your main quest and that is always welcome in a rpg. Even upon finishing the game you have the option of new game + and that let's you start over with your money and items already earned. Being able to play again with different classes with your current items gives some replay value that most rpgs lack.
This game was made using the rpg maker engine and though a very short game, it has many unique and custom features that are very impressive. I recommend this game to anyone who like classic rpgs or looking to play but short on time.

Since this is a yes-or-no review situation, I'm going with yes. That said, I had some problems with it.
The good here is the artwork, the score, and the 80s-horror vibe. It's a fun, almost Stranger Things-esque story. The bad is that the "choices matter" tag is deceptive. Your choices only matter a little bit at the end. And when I got to the post-game "here's what happened to the characters after this" portion, I found myself going, "Wait, how did my choices lead to that?!" In a game that's supposed to be, to some degree, choice-based, that makes the whole experience feel less satisfying than it otherwise would have. Maybe I said the wrong thing and set off another character accidentally, or somehow said the right thing to a character I didn't even like and ended up becoming besties with them. But the point is, the game would've been better off structuring itself less a choose-your-own-adventure game and more as a solve-the-mystery game.
Still, I had fun playing while I was playing--so consider this a conditional recommendation.

Fair warning: this is more of an Edmund McMillen game than a Tyler Glaiel one. It's also not a Metroidvania, even if it sometimes seems like it wants to be one.
At its core, The End Is Nigh is a twitch platformer in the vein of Super Meat Boy. In most levels, it's not too hard to figure out what you need to do in order to survive. The challenge is pressing and releasing the right controls with a split-second margin of error. Since I have the reflexes of a dying walrus, I was disappointed this isn't more of a puzzle platformer like Closure, but I appreciate that it doesn't try to trick you--if you can scout out a logical path through the level and are dextrous enough to execute it, you generally won't find yourself trapped or die in unfair ways.
Additional collectibles and story information can be found by searching out secret routes to hidden areas. This is where more puzzle aspects come into play, with some clever hiding places that rely on a precise understanding of the game's mechanics. However, this isn't really an "open-world" game, and most side paths will eventually return you to the linear progression of main levels. The limited amount of warp points also makes it something of a chore to go back for collectibles you missed the first time through the level.
At my current point in the game, I can't evaluate the story, but I find it striking that almost all of it so far is in hidden areas. Players who explore will get a very different impression of what's going on than players who stick to the main path. It reminds me of An Untitled Story, a Metroidvania with a similarly obscure approach to its world and characters.
I'm tempted to say that The End Is Nigh isn't really my thing, but the fact that I'm still playing it means it's at least a good game. If you like twitch platformers, you'll enjoy this game quite a bit.

Oxenfree brings to the table some of the things I really love in games. The main draw to Undertale for me was the fact that things in the game change if you go back and play it a second time. I still really love Undertale, but I think Oxenfree surpasses it in that regard. Little details about the game are different the second time you play and some parts of the abandoned island even restore themselves for one moment in a time loop, which really threw me off. I even found myself documenting all the little changes in my game through pictures.
Another unique mechanic in this game is the radio and how you can open it at any time and scroll through the channels. I even found one of the songs from the soundtrack on station 89 while in the woods area one time. This game does not draw you into any cutscenes at any time. Alex can always walk around, ignore questions, or walk away while people are talking. In this way, this game surpasses telltale games as well, because Telltale games are all big cutscenes with some walking around parts and lots of dialogue choices.
I think it's also worth pointing out that this game contains 12,000 different lines of dialogue. I know this from the documentaries you can find in the start menu under options. That's really impressive for such a short game. For someone to put so much care into how these characters interact with each other is really something I admire. Alex can only act how you want her to, so it's your choice to decide what kind of a person she ends up and how she feels about each person on the island with her.
I also admire a good story and boy does this game have that. I am someone who really does not like horror games, but upon reading the reviews for this game and hearing that this game didn't rely on jumpscares for it's horror, I immediately wanted to play it. Subtle horror games like this are defiantly the kind I like.
In conclusion, I got this game on sale for $4 and I defiantly do not regret buying it. It's taken me through it's story twice now, and I still love it and recommend it to those that want a good story and meaningful choices.

Strife is a rather interesting game with lots of classes. You have all the classes from the beginning, which means that you don't have to grind for ages just to get the class that you like. While this game is fun you can't attack enemies while moving, unless your attack makes you move, which means it isn't quite as fast paced as other games. There are also a few classes that are more powerful than others, but generally it is rather balanced. The crafting system is an interesting addition, allowing you to give your hero more powerful attacks, or providing a great escape mechanism. The graphics are rather good and the heroes are very creatively designed. I recommend this game as a good MOBA with interesting mechanics.

Imagine the successor to a good old Worms classic like Armageddon, or its faithful follow-on Worms World Party. Update the graphics, add a few classes, and add dynamic terrain features and water physics! Oh, but the curvy graphics make it hard to play precisely, classes feel more like a restriction than an exciting array of options, the water feels insignificant and flows like treacle, and when the terrain features aren't exploding, they just bounce around like balloons. Then, take away a bunch of the weapons and options, cut it down to 16 worms in a match, remove the ability to add custom content, simplify the missions into a glorified, tedious, unrewarding tutorial, and slow the whole thing to a snail's pace. Finally, replace the glorious ninja rope with a limp noodle.
Now, compared to something like Worms Reloaded, it's fine. Unfortunately, Worms Reloaded was an abortion of a game and fails miserably in comparison to the older titles. While Revolution does add a few features to try to distract from the fact that the last solid Worms game came out in 2001, the core gameplay just isn't good enough. Here's hoping we'll someday see a modern Worms title that actually builds up from the classics, instead of trying to start again.
Oh, but I nearly forgot! You get to put hats on your worms!

This is a welcome addition for every Half-Life fan. The story follows one of the HECU marines that gets rescued by the Black Mesa staff after his aircraft was shot down. The expansion features many new enemies and additional weaponry. You have the Displacer Cannon, which is like the Half-Life variant of the BFG9000 for one enemy, a M249 machine gun, the Shock Roach, which acts as an alien bazooka and much more.
The level design in this game is great, featuring many puzzles and the maps themselves have less overall bugs and issues than the ones in the original Half-Life.
The main issue I have though is that it's short. It took me roughly 3 hours to finish it, so I recommend getting this on a sale.
- Really cheap on a sale (0,99€)
- Improved level design over the original Half-Life
- Some puzzles will make your head spin
- Fast paced action
- Many new enemies and weapons
- Short campaign (~3 hours)
- The soundtrack can get a bit repetitive at times

Let me start off by saying I enjoyed this game at first. The premise of it is super fun; a super mobile, FPS/MOBA blend with objective play, casual matchmaking and a ranked mode. When I first started playing I had a blast, but then as the novelty wore off I noticed many issues. First off, where is this casual matchmaking? I sat in a queue for Objective mode for 30 minutes, and not one person ever entered into the lobby. Why am I forced to go into server browser and play the same game mode repeatedly with no variation?
On the same note, there is no team balancing in this game. Whatsoever. You will go up against teams that have 3 level 150+ players who've played for years while your team is comprised of new-ish players. There is also no option to balance teams it seems, as every time one has been called for it either fails, or doesn't change teams if it succeeds. The only option is to leave, or hope people leave so that the next game that gets made will change the team.
Gun mechanics also are not very consistent at all. I'm not the greatest when it comes to aiming with a mouse, I can admit that. But when my reticule is on someone's head, unless it's Battlefield, my bullet should go into someone's head. Damage on guns also does not seem very consistent. It feels like I have to empty 20+ shots of my 30 round clip to get the person down to 4% health, yet they down me in what feels like 6 shots with no headshots?
Like I said, the game has the potential to be great, but once the novelty wares off of the new shiny game, the glaring issues really start to show through.

Easily the best kart racer of this generation, and probably the best one ever released on PC. It's not a dramatic departure from the formula invented by Mario Kart, but Sonic Transformed tweaks and improves upon that formula in a lot of ways that make it even better than Nintendo's more recent offerings. Weapons are a lot more fair and can be dodged with quick and careful driving. The single-player mode offers up a huge amount of missions with a lot of variety. The graphics are gorgeous. The trick system for earning boosts encourages learning the tracks. The three different vehicle modes all handle very differently. There's a lot of depth here if you want to dive into the time trials.
And if you're into Sega, this has a ridiculous amount of fanservice. From Segata Sanshiro to Burning Rangers to Panzer Dragoon, this is the ultimate tribute to Sega's history.
About the only major flaw is the inability to turn off weapons in online or grand prix play. Some of the single-player missions are weaponless races, and it's a real shame that you can't play like that with friends or in a racing series. But it's telling that I consider that a flaw - that the core racing in a kart racer is so good that I want to enjoy it without the accoutrements normally layered on top of games in the genre.

Nice puzzle game using some basic concept but where it can become very complex to solve some of the puzzle.
It's all about colored block. You have usually 3 moving block of differents colors (Red, Blue and Green) The moving block can only move to another square of the same color or the white square where every color can move. Some of the tile can change the color of the block that move in it. So it add to the challenge even more. You have to do it with a minimal number of move to get the 100% completion on every puzzle.
Some of the puzzle require you to think every move properly, or you can be stuck and need to restart the puzzle if you move to the wrong place. It add some challenge to the difficulty of the game in a nice way.
The only thing I don't like is that you can't zoom out, some of the puzzle are quite large and you don't see everything. This can become REALLY annoying, it add some dificlty to a game already difficult for no obvious reasons. Seriously to plan some of the puzzle accordingly you have to plan many move ahead. This is the main "feature" of the game and it don't allow you to have a good overall view of the puzzle. Maybe it's on purpose, if it is, then it's a bad choice from the devs if you want my opinion.
In the overall, this is a game that will force you to think alot. If you like very challenging puzzles to test your own limits, it's the game you want to try. It start very easy to show you the basic control of the game, but become more and more challenging at every new puzzle.

Original/ TLDR:
Welcome to Super I Wanna Be the Meat Bros <3
Yes, to me it seems like a nice mix of Super Meat Boy, I Wanna Be the Guy, and Super Mario bros 3. It is tough as nails, as well as very rewarding when you finally nail down a room that seemed impossible the first dozen deaths!
I'm three hours in and already have over fifteen hundred deaths...
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Updated: After playing more I will say this game is an 8.5 out of 10 for me so far. It continues to add new elements, and challange the player throughout the chapters progressions. It really reminds me of Super Meat Boy in that design.
The gameplay consists of a wide variety of platforming puzzle rooms, tight controls, and the classic humor you know and love from Edmund. Also a few deaths. Can't forget about those...
Going back to try and find secrets, and more tumors, is in the end fun. That adds a great deal of replayability. The NES era nostalgia that many design elements brings up is heavy and very much welcome. Even the complaint that you have to restart a world from the beginning each time seems to be apart of the triubute to old school gaming that this is. Back then you didn't save your game. If you wanted to play SMB3 you started from the beginning each time.
It isn't perfect though. There are some bugs that are being worked on, although non that will jump out as an evening ruiner. The puzzles at times can feel too obtuse, but again, that just reminds me of old school games where some secrets were rarely found without searching for them.
The biggest complaint to be had with the game is the backtracking. Some rooms can only be 100% done if you make sure to try again from the other direction. Which ones? You won't know... A few times I thought a tumor had to be backtracked, only to find out that the room closes off when you go through it. That means the easy mistake to try a backtrack attempt means that I HAVE to try again later from the beginning of that map/floor.
Not a crazy burden though with the ability to warp to any map/floor from the start menu.

Other than the issue I have with music, from a speedrunning perspective it seems like it's going to be fun. There's very precise movement in some places, which I was I fan of in Meat Boy. If you're thinking of getting this game and you haven't played Super Meat Boy, go play that instead.
If you like Super Meat Boy and want more of the same type of game, this is an amazing game to turn to.

Introduction
Hello, my name is Bleachfx and I have been playing MOBAS for over 8 years (Dota 1 + Dota 2 and a little League of Legends too) and I only recently discovered and fell in love with this game. I was hoping to provide an in depth, longer review of the game, but unfortunately due to Steam's character limit in reviews, I'm forced to present a very summarized version.
Pros
+ Power
+ Split last hit gold
+ Out of combat regeneration
+ Personal Couriers
+ Pets
+ Item Crafting & Creation
+ Map Objectives & Warding
+ Community
+/- Hero selection
Cons
- Matchmaking & Player base
Strife manages to retain the best elements of established MOBAs (like Dota 2 and LoL) and throws in more than enough fresh ideas to provide a wonderfully entertaining game! Strife has the POTENTIAL to be one of the greatest games of the genre and definitely compete with the 2 giants. But only if it manages to fix one major problem, its matchmaking (justified by the game's current small player base and to avoid long queue times).
Strife is easy to learn, fun to master and has the least toxic community of any MOBA I've ever played.
Simply put, I've had more fun with Strife in only 3 months than any other MOBA I've played over the last 8 years.
As testament to this statement, in the 2 years I have spent playing Dota 2, I have purchased roughly 5€ worth of skins/sets whereas Strife has already convinced me to purchase the Collector's Edition (currently valued at 41.39€)!
I highly recommended Strife to all! And I'd give it a 9/10 even though the game is currently in Open Beta or Early Access.
I'd also recommend reading this extremely well written article by Dailure, if you have any questions regarding the game.

It's a 2D Worms game but with a 3D engine, unlike previous Worm games in the past ,objects you see sticking out of the terrain in a map now have physics properties, they can bounc around,crush other worms,explodes,emit poison gas or even throw water around and there's now a seperate water in the game that also has some very nice looking physics to it when it moves around, this water doesn't instant kill your worms like the regular water at the bottom of the map but instead drains 1-3 HP per turn if a worm is submerged in it and everything in it moves slower (both worms and projectiles).

Heavy is the slowest but can take the most abuse
Scout is the fastest,has the highest jumps and can perform some crazy maneuvers while walking thru terrain buuut has the lowest HP and dies the fastest
The Scientist is pretty much a healer, each turn he heals  5hp and that's about it.
However if you don't wanna play with these new classes you can just simply play the Classic mode where every worm is a regular worm like in the older games.
That's pretty much it, everything else is the same, It's the Worms game we all know and love since the 90's.

The Talos Principle is, hands down, one of the most thought-out and creative puzzle games to date. It not only challenges the player’s ability to solve problems, but makes one question what it is to be conscious. The basic premise of the game is as follows: You come into awareness as an advanced humanoid robot tasked with completing puzzles to be rewarded with sigils that unlock other worlds. All these instructions come from a sentient voice who identifies as Elohim.
The game stems from Croteam’s previous game, Serious Sam 4. Croteam wanted to expand on the idea of complex puzzle games. This led to some complicated puzzles that the team was inspired to build upon further as a separate title.
The game starts with some terminal code that suggests the initialization of a child AI being you. So you basically start off as a brand new being and are introduced to Elohim, who describes himself as your creator and goes on to elaborate that you are in his garden that he created for you to learn the true meaning. You are introduced to the games puzzle mechanics by completing a basic by using jammers and logic to disable bots and turrets to complete puzzles and receive sigils, which are said to bring you closer to eternity.
The game has relatively simple mechanics. Basic movement and interaction allow you to move through puzzles and manipulate jammers, boxes, reflectors and fans to complete levels and obtain your sigils, which unlock more levels. The only tool you start off with is the jammer, which disables bots and turrets which kill your bot if you cross their path. As you obtain more sigils, you unlock both levels and more tools like reflectors, boxes and fans. The basic interaction reminds one of portal, the game play is similar but neither game is a blatant copy of one another. This title has stunning graphics for what it is. I often found myself just admiring the scenery and some of the detail in non-vital areas and domains. There are some over worlds that are set outdoors and you are able to see for miles it seems, and the scenery is rendered with great and beautiful detail. The game is far more than just solving puzzles though. A big portion of the game is typing and conversing, yes conversing, with the terminal throughout your quest.
The basic premise of the game is about discovery. Initially, all the player has to worry about is completing the puzzles and progressing through the game. But as you learn more and more about yourself, your surroundings, and Elohim, the player has no choice but to question both the motives of the game and Elohim. A few examples pertaining to Elohim are; 1. As you enter one of the levels, the environment darkens and becomes extremely eerie. Elohim commands the darkness to leave by deleting excess data. And 2. After completing one of the levels, a ‘ghost’ of another robot runs screaming in terror towards you. Elohim banishes the lost soul and warns of what could be if the player doesn’t do as he wishes. As you familiarize with the terminal, you have the opportunity to make an admin account, all you have to do is prove that you’re human. Simple, right? The player is asked questions about liberty and freedom of choice and what it is to be human. On my play through, I was not able to provide sufficient evidence that I was human, so I was granted an account with basic privileges that did not include network access, which is an attractive ability because the database is corrupted and a lot of the files you uncover and partially corrupted, leaving out big chunks of information. You are able to piece together a good amount though. A lot of the texts are references to previous philosophers and their views. An example is a translation and interpretation of one of Osiris’s texts and the 5 elements of humanity.  Later on, you discover quite an impressive tower that Elohim forbids you from entering, claiming that it will void the player’s gift of eternal life. This, and the beginning of the game alludes very strongly to the biblical story of Adam and Eve and the Garden of Eden.
There are no cut scenes, parse, only dialogue from Elohim as you progress through the game. The one-way conversation is extraordinarily deep and encourages the player to progress through the game and find out more about the environment, himself (humanoid robot), and Elohim.
This title has extremely beautiful graphics. You can tell that far more work went into the graphics than is necessary for a puzzle game and its greatly appreciated. The level of immersion is unprecedented for the genre. The sound track is also stunning. It’s both very calming and accurate. There are different environments that are represented audibly accurate. For example, there is a world based in a desert biome that is accompanied by Egyptian themed music.  The graphics and soundtrack along with the encompassing storyline, makes the player feel almost as if he/she is in the game and is discovering this strange and beautiful world for themselves.
I’ve covered the character progression just a little bit. But the whole idea of the game, from what I’ve played, is to make a choice. Either to follow the words of Elohim and attain enlightenment and eternal life, or to explore the great tower, lose your perks, and gain independence and consciousness. The game repeatedly hints to an underlying sinister scheme and tries to simultaneously sway the player to in both directions.
Frankly, I like how deep the game is. It touches base with a very profound and uncomfortable internal conflict I think many people face or avoid facing. It’s very introspective and forces a player to think not only of the game and tasks at hand, but what it is to be human, to be conscious. What value is, or if there is even such a thing. I can’t complain about a single thing, and I know that sounds biased, but there is little to criticize.
I think that this game is one that should be played by most everyone. It forces one to think on his/her values and self-truths. There is little contemplation about things as abstract as the topic this title covers. I’m not saying that people should go out and preach that there’s no such thing as reality or what not, or even think exclusively about the prefaces and problems this games brings forward, but I do feel that there should be more introspective scrutiny on a large scale. I don’t know how this game would affect other people, but to me, it has caused me to question facets which I had previously been oblivious to and reopened contemplation on others I thought I had concluded.

Everything about this game is amazing. The music, the graphics (not just the quality, the details and the design too), the voice acting, the dialogs/texts, the story and, most of all, the puzzles.
You have worlds with rooms that present the main puzzle mechanic: you must grab a tetromino (sigils) that's in an unreachable part to the room, and to get there you use lasers, connectors, jammers, buttons, fans, boxes, enemies, energy fields and even time manipulation to reach that part, with every new item introduced after understanding the previous one. The pacing is really well done. The secondary puzzle mechanic is one where you place the sigils you found in a grid to unlock doors to access new worlds.
But that's not everything, those are the "easy" puzzles, the ones that you have to do to reach some of the endings. There are more puzzles and more mechanics, you'll find axes, you'll steal lasers from rooms, you'll found stars, you'll grab a jetpack...
Every level is really clever and you have a color code for the difficulty, you'll be using every mechanic and device in ways you can't imagine to solve the room puzzles, and in some more ways when you discover the rest of the puzzles outside the rooms.
It's also full of easter eggs. And you can get the Road to Gehenna DLC with more awesomeness, and Sigils of Elohim (free) if you need more "unlock door" puzzles.

The Talos Principle is the most memorable gaming experience I have had in recent memory. It has been almost a year since I originally played Talos Principle and nothing has yet proven to be more engrossing or profound since. The only other game that I can compare Talos Principle to, in terms of atmosphere, gameplay, and impact combined is Antichamber. If you liked Antichamber I'd wager that you'd also enjoy The Talos Principle as well. Functionally the game plays a lot closer to Portal but the atmosphere is completely different.
The Talos Principle, on the surface, is a puzzle game with some exploration thrown in. The puzzles are challenging and, for the most part, quite rewarding. If you are looking for an additional challenge or can't bear the thought of missing completion there are stars scattered throughout the areas that you can collect. Often the stars require you to think out of the box and I've found myself more than once just surveying an area, brow furrowed, while I contemplated ways I might make a puzzle work. The puzzles, however engrossing, are not Talos Principle's strongest asset though.
The game's strongest point is the atmosphere. Your character is born into the world at the same time you start playing, so you essentially know little more than your avatar. I've rarely seen the divide between character and player so blurred. On your first playthrough your motivations are almost completely aligned and the gameplay feels very natural. Much like your character your motivations are to solve puzzles, explore, figure out what is going on, and question everything around you.
The world is vast, beautiful, and stiflingly desolate at times. Yet there is a strange sense of connectedness thanks to the terminals you can access for information and the barcode messages scattered throughout the world. The music is soothing and the scenery of the puzzle locations tranquil, but underneath it all there are unsettling hints that something is terribly wrong. What more the game fosters a grand sense of mystery. Long after you think you've figured out what is actually going on there are still small mysteries and surprising discoveries to assure you that you haven't seen everything yet.
For fair coverage I'll touch briefly on a few negatives, though I didn't find many to be honest. Some areas are exceedingly large so travel can be a bit long and frustrating at times. There also really isn't much more to the game other than puzzles and exploring so if neither of those are your thing you probably aren't going to like this. Additionally, some of the puzzles (usually the optional ones) are exceedingly difficult on your first try. So if you have limited time to play it's something to keep in mind. For a few of the tougher ones (for me) I probably took over an hour and a half between thinking and experimenting. However, I can say that your efforts are ultimately rewarded. On more than one occasion I discovered Easter Eggs in pursuit of stars and it felt amazing. At least until I realized I still hadn't figured out the trick to getting at the star.
The short version: If you like to explore and take puzzles as a challenge rather than a tedium, then this game is incredibly rewarding. The over-arcing story, hidden in snippets from terminals is an excellent driving force for the game, playing off your innate sense of curiousity.
I played this game in the middle of a long Maine winter while my wife was on the other side of the country, smoking way more than I should have and staying up to 2am, thinking my way through the puzzles and pondering the troubling implications of the notes. My personal experience was profound, I don't think a game ever made me think this much before. This game deserves all the accolades it gets. My personal recommendation is to play alone at night for the best results to best capture the intended feel of the game.

I checked Oxenfree because of its theme and atmosphere, but also because it features something that I need in games: short (4-8 hours) but multiple playthroughs. It didn't disappoint on either count, and I had a lot of fun going through three of those so far. A fourth one is in my plans for the foreseeable future.
The game follows Alex, a high school student, on a night trip to Edwards Island with her best friend Ren, her new stepbrother Jonas, and a couple of girls from their school. Of course, "teenagers + island" screams "slasher movie" at first; do not look for ye olde serial killer here, though, for the story is different, and the "typical cliché kids" have to deal with more emotional issues than just who's getting to snog who. Various choices of dialogue bubbles let the player decide which kind of style Alex will follow: very nice girl? Mean? The silent type? A blend of those? And these styles do influence further dialogues, as well as the ending. Not to mention a few decisions to make that will appeal to one's sense of "is the means to an end always the best way?"
The genre is thriller/horror, in a psychological and paranormal way (not much gore here -- it wouldn't work well with the graphic style anyway). Not too many jump scares, but definitely distorted audio that also hints at Easter eggs now and then. The OST lends places and situations a mysterious feeling, and regularly veers on the creepy side.
Conclusion: for fans of paranormal/supernatural mystery with a dash of horror and emotional issues, and who don't necessarily have the time to go through lengthy games.

There are some interesting ideas here in the mechanics: the protagonist is effectively immortal, can change class mid-game, and can hone skills to make them available for all classes.  These aren't orginal ideas, of course -
did all that first - but they're unusal enough that it's nice to see them being used here.  Even so, the class switching and skill honing seem out of place in a game that doesn't last long enough for the player to fully take advantage of them.  Also, the game seems weirdly unbalanced in some ways (maces are OP, and magic is both more costly and weaker than physical attacks, to name a couple).  What really kills it, though, is that the writing is so bad it's almost funny (and peppered with typos).  If I play an RPG, I want to be playing it for the story, and this one was just one big cliche (girlfriend gets abducted - check; demonic big bad - check; nebulous plot for world domination - check... I could go on, but I think that's enough).  Don't let that stop you if you're one of the many people who got it for free - who knows, you might actually enjoy it, and it's only 5 or 6 hours long anyway - but I wouldn't recommend buying it.

Quick review
-Moderate/fast paced precision platforming
-Precise Jumps
-Precise air control
-Good ground movement speed
-Unique ledge grab mechanic - easy to learn, tough to master
-100s of levels! Very content packed
-Donkey Kong Country like collectables and secrets
-Many hazards - stationary and in motion
-Many monsters - varied AI
-Macabre art style - signature Edmund
-Beautifully programmed - Tyler
-Humourous
-Atmospheric, remade public domain classical music
-Forgiving hitboxes
-High production
-Appropriate minimalist macabre story
-Difficult and rewarding - enough content for novices and more for experienced players
-Value for money
-The most fun you can have when you're dead
-The End is Nigh
Long review
I have a bias towards enjoying platformers, certainly more than most, so I'll aim to keep this review as objective as I can -judging it solely as a platformer rather than a new creation from Edmund and Tyler.
For a completely new player to the game, its a precision platformer, all the way through to its core. Think Super Meat Boy, n++, Fenix rage, Life of Pixel, Slime San. It's a difficult game, with trial and error. Extremely suitable for skilled players, speedrunners, average players WITH patience, and fans of 2d platformers. I struggle to objectively recommend this to Edmund fans if you do NOT like platformers. Although, mileage will vary. Edmund fans surely expect challenge, and seem to love being thrown into difficult and atmospheric worlds even in genres they do not typically enjoy. Just look at the number of SMB fans who hate other platformers. Amazing.

Level design...
is varied and challenging. Individual static screens that helps player focus on where they are per screen, no jerky motion of scrolling background. This I cannot emphasise enough as a really important feature - it keeps screen still and allows player to do the movement. N++ does this of course. Player moves screen to screen (by exiting one side) horizontally for the most part, but sometimes downwards and upwards (DKC style). Secret areas are numerous, hidden away sometimes by environments that are queued to destruct based on players actions. Aforementioned destruction of environment is a novel level design feature which resets if player leaves the current screen and returns. This adds a new puzzle element to tricky precision platforming. Without spoiling too much - there is water to swim through, spikes, lots of monsters - sometimes with projectiles to avoid, all with varying AI. Threats can be in motion or staionary. There are more surprises that should really be discovered alone. It's very novel overall and I'd say has more level design surprises in precision platforming than I've ever seen. But do not worry, it's not a convoluted experience, each idea is fully fleshed out over hundreds and hunderds of screens. I'd describe the hazards as tightly packed. Far less width for running wildly. Less horizontality than Meat boy, but still with ample wide leaps that need to be calculated.
Control/mechanics -
move, jump, and the big new move - grabbing ledges.
Movement on ground...
is graceful, predictable. Not jerky - I suspect Ash's ground acceleration builds for a few split seconds before full speed. However it's subtle, not as pronounced as Meat Boy's heavier start, where ground acceleration provided quite a sticky and slower start, appropriate for the skinless boy. Ash has a slower full speed. Perfect for the dense level hazards.
Movement in air...
from jumping is great. Very precise. Can stop air accelaration just like that, fall where you need to. Falls faster than meat boy I think. In air control is tuned well. Jump height variable to jump input time. Also jump distance is larger on the horizontal plane following a ledge grab. This takes a bit of time to adjust but its exciting. NO wall sliding NOR wall jumping. Overall the jumping feel has less of an overall horizontal pull (than meatboy) with more weight in vertical gravity. As mentioned above, falling is faster. Jump height is pretty decent and you can easily learn the limits in the early levels.
Ledge grabbing...
is new, I believe Edmund is very proud of this mechanic. Grab onto either upper wall corners, or little thorn like looking spikes anywhere up a vertical wall side. It feels finicky at first but once you learn why you need it, its really fun. You may also ledge grab upper corners that have hazardous spikes on the top, merely a pixel way. This is extremely tight an execution, but its badass. I like to think of ledge grabbing in the same vein as hanging in the air or wall sliding in Super Meat Boy - both give you neceassry time to breath and adjust to plans in navigating the levels. Once you master it you can hang out on walls and enjoy a split second to then jump again. Its a welcome addition and produces a fluent stop start rhythm that makes sense within tightly woven hazards.
Hitboxes...
are really good for me personally. I tested the waters when i started my game and just walked up to monsters. There is slight and small overlap of pixels (thank goodness) between player and hazards and its makes for a more enjoyable experience. The levels require tight excution therefore a bit of freedom to brush into a hazard goes a long way.
I love the game. I hope this review is helpful for some of you.
PS - As much as I tried to discuss platfoming objectively - Edmund and his previous work was mentioned. This is retrospectively fairgame for me - Super Meat Boy, particularly, set precision platformers to be judged by new standards. Thanks for reading.

A divisive game and it makes sense. The controls are fine with a controller (why fight controllers on PC for games it makes sense? Honestly...) But there is a hitch with the mechanics of the game, which some perceive as unresponsive controls.
The mechanics are slow, plodding and clumsy. This isn't a 2D Devil May Cry game and it's not even a Shinobi or Ninja Gaiden game. It's even more slow. Slow to the point that it should be tactical but it isn't even that. Enemies remain unresponsive for most of the battles. So, your inclination is to just spam attack them and if you do they'll invariably hit you with their own clumsy attack which staggers you and slows everything down immensely. Because there's no obvious skillset or pattern to enemies this can make the game rather random and frustrating.
I can see the appeal to such mechanics if you have the patience for them but I just don't think it's very fun in the end just like hacking and slashing can be very boring. Beautiful art design and music is wasted on a clumsy combat system that never really justifies itself.
It's a shame but there is a chance you'll like it.

I bought Oxenfree as a recommendation for loving Kentucky Route Zero. It's a choice-based game that is a little surreal and very paranormal. I enjoyed the art style a lot; it gave me similar vibes to KRZ, but there was a little more detail in the setting and characters. The characters were all very unique but hard to identify with; they're all teenagers, so that might be why. The story was interesting at first, but the more you uncover, the more confusing and ridiculous it seems to get. But the story isn't bad by any means, it kept me very interested; I just felt frustrated the more I progressed. I only played through it once, so I'm not sure how much impact my choices in the game affected the storyline. I got the feeling that my choices did not, however, at least not until the very end. And the dialogue wasn't really compelling enough where I felt connected to my character and wanted to respond in consitent ways to the other characters.
All in all, I would recommend the game if you like games like KRZ or Life is Strange, and  you find it on sale. I bought it for $5, and I felt that was a fair price for it. You'll likely enjoy it.

I've played dota 2 and LoL, i can tell you that this MOBA is a great and fresh new experience. It combines both positive things from dota and league and add new features which make the game so much more interesting. The first thing which is new and quite awesome is item crafting: you can modify shop items in the main menu so that they adapt to your style of play/a certain hero, completely change it's stat and it's cost.
The second new feature is the pets, which have 2 passive abilities and 1 active. Another great add to our usual MOBA's, once again to tailor the way you play.
Also, they designed the game so that you almost never rage or get mad at anyone. Supports can't steal last hits, because last hits by ANY of your teammate in lane gives gold to both of you. This takes teamplay to a whole new level in matchmaking, and they also removed the 'death' stats when you press tab so you can't blame anyone for feeding, neither can you speak to the other team in chat, which is also great because you can only focus on the game.
Overall, this MOBA is great and i didn't find any negative points, especially because they will add more items/heroes/pets in the future, adding depth to the game.
