Short version:
Pros:
+satisfying combat
+beautiful visuals
+rogue-lite gameplay with some persistent progression
+procedurally generated levels
+unique fighting style for each playable unit
+worthy of multiple playthroughs
+coop
Cons:
-simple goal with little story
-fairly easy if you're good at this kind of side scrolling action
-controls are somewhat clunky at times
-a single play through is relatively short. game designed to be replayed (this can be a pro for some people i guess, since each play through does feel quite unique due to the randomly generated levels)
-no online versus mode
This game's controls feel a little bit clunky, but I don't think that takes away from the gaming experience too much. Once you get used to the controls, the combat system feels quite satisfying. It has enough depth and encourages varying moves. You can perform special cancel to chain up combo, throw enemies who keep on guarding, do a 360 degree attack against those who get behind you etc. Overall, the fighting mechanism actually feels quite like something you'd expect in a fighting game.
Each hero and other unit that you get to control has a unique move set. While some are arguably better than others (when playing as enemy units), They're still all interesting and fun to play as.
Coop is also fun. I always embrace games that include the coop feature. If you have a friend who to play with you, definitely check this out.
Gameplay wise, this game has a lot of rogue-lite elements. Levels are procedurally generated, and they offer a unique experience for every playthrough. Everytime you die, you'd have to restart from the beginning. The entire dungeon has to be cleared in one go and there is no in-dungeon saving. Also, if you die, all the items you're carrying are also gone. However, you do get to keep your levels, gold, and unlocked abilities, so there is a persistent progression. Because of the randomly generated levels and the uniqueness of each character, this game is certainly worthy of multiple playthroughs.
The visuals are beautiful. Backgrounds have an unusal amount of details for any randomly generated level.
However, there isn't a lot of story. the majority of the gameplay centers on combat and platforming with some exploration for hidden rooms and loot. A single playthrough is also relatively short, which is something i don't mind since i can replay it multiple times and still get a different experience in each playthrough. However, if you don't like replaying, then this might something you'd have to think about.
The game has a local versus mode, but puzzlingly it doesn't have online versus (but it does have online coop).
Overall, the game is fun, especially if you have a friend to play it with. Even if not, it is still worth getting for the single player expereince because of the randomly generated levels, which add a lot of replay value.

I personally love this game. I have no previous history with this game [though I've played previous Chris Sawyer products] so nostalgia is not acting as a bias here. However, there is some issues with this game that make it frustrating and leave you wanting more. If you can look past the quirks and prepared to do a little work, you got yourself an amazing game.
Probably the strangest part of this game is the graphics. Don't get me wrong, isometric view has a special place in my heart....but this game came out in 2004, the same year Total War: Rome released. This game was supposed to be the sequel to Transport Tycoon, Chris Sawyers next big game! If I got this in 2004 I would have been disapointed...but the graphics isn't the only ugly thing.
The gameplay, mechanics and literally everything is just like Transport Tycoon. 10 years after Transport Tycoon this game released....10!!! And what was done in those 10 years? Nothing.....So if you played TT or OpenTTD then your getting pretty much the same exact game. Which brings us to....
Ai is dumb. I'm talking building a railroad to nowhere and running a train on it even though it has no stops dumb. Anytime there is other companies trying to compete with me, I just scoff and keep about my buisness. Sometimes they get in my way, but they never pose a threat.
The only real challenge in this game is the objectives each scenario has. Even then some of them are overly easy. Transport 500 passengers is one I will never understand....why put something so trivial in a game about transportation? Luckily you can continue maps even after the completion of the objective.
Remember how this game was released in 2004? In this game there is some annoying mechanics that are 90s quality and not the good kinds. Most annoying is setting automobiles on tracks. Trams is a mode of transport I use often. each track you lay is a double which allow for two trams to go in opposite directions. Placing the tram on a specified side is annoying. You got to either rotate the camera or manage to find the sweet spot after furiously jerking the cursor around.
On top of that there is this bug where drivers won't stop at their specified route locations. I watched a transfer truck drive in circles for three months before correcting. A boat kept slamming into a section of land till it finally decided to take a wider turn to avoid it. It happens all the time....which is why I prefer trams and trains with a one way route.
So after all that you are probably asking me "Dude, then why is it amazing?" Well sit tight, this will be the longest section of the review.
First is the price. I'm getting into industry style of management games for the first time in my life. I always liked combat RTS or Paradox style Grand Strategies. Well when I started playing these type of games I noticed, the new ones are either expensive [like Transport Fever] or just plain bad [like Urban Empire]. So during the summer sale I looked at reviews and prices. This game was a dollar and some change with the negative reviews being mainly geared towards windows performance [NOTE: 9/10 people who tried all fixes got the game to work] I got 20+ hours in this game and only paid a little over a dollar....worth it
Second is the gameplay. Once you look over the dumb AI and working around the quirks becomes autopilot, you begin to recognize that this game is hella fun. The outdated stuff for 2004 almost seems fitting considering this game is 13 years old. Eventually you begin to see it as a charm and catch yourself thinking this game came out in the 90s.
So what is the gameplay? Well each scenario you get a certain amount of money to use. You can take loans to get more money quickly. You build bus, tram, truck, trains, planes and boat routes in towns and between them. You transport passengers, mail, goods etc....the goal of course is to be effective and make bank.
It's such a satisfying experience watching your transport empire function. When your transportation is effective, towns start to grow into massive cities. I watched a 4 building town called "Sulkygate" turn into a few dozen sky scrappers. Since you can play past your objective completion/failure, it's fun to see how far you can push the map. I once, as a sole company, made a huge map full of frontier turn into a cramped, skyscraper jungle.
Another plus, something all games should have, is the scenario editor. You can customize the map or have it randomly generate. I'm currently trying to make the state of NC since I live here, but making a map at an isometric view is difficult. I'll post screens when I'm done.
Lastly if you use third part software such as Hamachi, Tunngle or Evovle if it ever comes back...the two player mode works. Me and a buddy played it quite a bit, it's fun having another human in the world.
All in all, next sale you should totally pick up this game. If I left anything out I'll add it, just let me know.

Dark Messiah of Might and Magic was an attempt to branch out the otherwise stagnant Might & Magic franchise, and it should be remembered as one of the better attempts by all of those that played a little of Might & Magic's foray into the real time strategy genre, now that was a bad idea if I ever saw one. It's a Source engine action RPG. Unlike the usual Might & Magic RPGs it takes a much more mainstream approach to just about everything and anybody that's play even a little of modern RPG's will quickly find themselves at ease with the simplicity of it all.
Gone are the exploration and everything else that made Might & Magic unique. Only the name and some of the lore remains. Not that I am completely opposed to ignore part of the Might & Magic lore, I was never that excited about the whole space aliens bit. Unfortunately this leaves the game feeling shallow. It's a game that saw what everyone else was doing and thought, "Hey, me too!".
In terms of gameplay Dark Messiah is the worlds most premiere kicking simulator. It's an odd thing really, Dark Messiah has weapons, skills and magic but you'll find yourself using nothing but your boot to dispatch the vast majority of foes. The harder the difficulty is turned up the easier and more tempting it becomes to kick your enemies into spikes and off ledges simply because it's an instakill maneuver more often than not and your weapons and magic will never be able to match it for damage except in that extremely rare location where there is no environmental hazards to kick enemies into.
The storyline is fairly decent, a little predictable at times but nothing worth complaining about. There is a pretend storyline choice or two that does have a little impact so that helps greatly.
In terms of graphics and sounds it's the source engine and that all comes down to style and Dark Messiah falls squarely into the "Okay" range. Nothing too impressive but nothing that'll ruin your experience either. You'll never be in awe of it but you'll never get annoyed with it either.
The multi-player component is fairly decent although it was always a graveyard so without friends it was impossible to play.
Besides all the kicking Dark Messiah ranks as a not too bad game. It does nothing stellar, it doesn't even try to, but it does provide a decent enough experience that it's worth it to play through the once. And if you're feeling particularly feisty, you can challenge yourself by making a hard "No-Kicking" playthrough and watch the difficulty skyrocket.

A surprising load of fun. I've always been intimidated by hard-core tactical shooters like ARMA so I was hesitant to give this game a go. But it was on the Steam Autumn Sale so I took the plunge and I'm very surprised. It relies heavily on team work and communication and there's no room for error. You get shot, you die. There's no lone-wolfing on the massive maps, and you MUST play as a team if you want to win. But if you're new to the game, make sure you play on a server that speaks your language, and don't lead a squad until you know what you're doing. There's definitely a learning curve for people who are used to games like Battlefield or Call of Duty - and things don't happen as quickly as they do in BF or CoD (like reviving a team mate, or relaoding your weapon) but that's okay. It adds to the "realism". The community that plays is very cool and accommodating of new players. It's fun without being too serious. One thing that really stands out for me is the quality of the sound effects (the weapons sound real and the sound of bullets whizzing by your head are both scary and exciting). The graphics are good for a game in Alpha. You can see it's not polished like a finished game should be, but the little details like dust and debris when bullets hit the ground around you or when a grenade blows up makes me excited to see the final result. I don't regret buying this game at all.

First thing: Wow. Just...wow. Play this game. Just...play it.
At first, it starts out like a teenager simulator, with dialogue choices affecting your relationships with your small group of "friends"--You've got your new stepbrother, your childhood best friend, a mean chick and her best friend. But an outing to the beach turns out to be so much more. As a supernatural mystery begins to occur, complete with time loops and spooky ghost-like things, the history of the island you're stranded on begins to unfold, as do your relationships with people. One of your main tools is your radio, the tuning of which can make things happen, uncovering collectibles and little snippets of the past and creating supernatural happenings. At the end of the game, similar to Walking Dead and other choice-based adventure games, you get to find out how you did compared to other players, and there are a LOT of changes you can effect based on your choices and even your dialogue options. There's a lot of depth and replayability. The music is great--creepy and atmospheric at times, just nice and soothing other times. Voice acting is excellent, and the art, while simplistic, really creates a mood and atmosphere that's just right.

I have just completed the game and I can definitively say that this game is an epic spiritual successor to Super Meat Boy, from the innocous start to the awesome finale.  Everything you could want in a platformer is present.  The graphics are smooth and well drawn, the art style is a cool take on the well-treaded post-apocolyptic motif.  The animations are snappy and expressive amd lighting is used to create a cool atmosphere.   Musically the game is a winner too, with remixes on classical tunes.  Some hit more than others, but when they do nail it, they nail it.  Got to give a shout out to the chiptune music that plays during the cart levels, such a seamless transition you'd think it was done 30 years ago.  Funny voice acting, when it is utilized.  A well-written but ambigious lore is present, but you will have to work to access some of it.
The ironic thing about this game is that there are Nintendo references all over the place, but this game actually stands toe to toe with anything they have made in a 2-D plane(mainly referring to the DKC reboots).  I've seen nods to Super Metroid, Mario 3, Mario World and others.  If you enjoyed the game Catherine, you'll notice this game takes a couple of design and structural cues from that amazing game as well.
The mechanics and gameplay are just as exacting and devilish as before, this time using compact level screens to propel the game forward.  The worlds all have thier twist on the gameplay, and the way they are able to design challenges down to the pixel is still impressive after Meatboy, because no one else does platforming this precise and distilled.  There is a clear and distinct skill progression, so you will notice yourself breezing through worlds you thought were insurmontable a few hours earlier.  You also can choose the order to play certain areas, which is a nice touch.  The hidden goodies are actually more than just bashing the cracked wall, some of these secrets are actually, well secrets.  Shh, don't tell anyone.   And the mini-games are sweet, though I'm just starting to tackle them after beating the game.  I recommened doing the same, as the skill level you will gain will make them more bearable.  But the puns and old school CRT filter are just oozing with charm.

Overall this is an amazing value, and easily a game of the year canidate.  15 hours to beat a platformer, then add a ton more to get the achievements....buy this game full price and don't look back.

This game is great. At first it can seem pretty difficult, but it's a game that requires some level of mastery. The way the combat system works is very similar to Super Smash Bros. There are shields, rolls, grabs, air dodges, directional attacks and aerial directional attacks. It handles differently though. It might take some time to get used to it even if you are familiar with Smash Bros. The campaign mode is like a randomly generated metroidvania with varying paths, monsters and bosses. There are multiple playable characters with all different skills, weapons, and movesets. You can even capture and switch between playing as your current character and a monster. The only negative things I can say about this game is 1) grabbing ledges is awful. You have to be really specific about how you approach the ledge. In some situations this can cost you a lot of health. 2) Sometimes you can get overwhelmed and wrecked by a group of enemies and/or stage hazards. They'll combo you to death if they attack you at the same time and get the first hit off. 3) Unavoidable hazards. There are some hazards that seemed too long to jump over. At least I couldn't make it with a double jump and dash/airdodge. I had to jump in and get poisoned. That's all the issues worth mentioning though. It's really good overall.

Right here is the thing with Strife I love the look of it and I love the characters but thats it.
Here is my reasoning why it doesn't do it for me.
1. No matter what level I am it just seems like I do no damage even with a full damage build
2. When I get a kill or take a tower it is just not satisfying, something about it just feels like im bashing at a brick wall for what feels like hours, it crumbles then nothing.
3. Team fights last 10 seconds, It all kicks off people die immediately then your back to just killing minions
4. Theres too many minions, It's just a constant influx so you never really get to fight the person on your lane until team fights.
5. The items are somewhat confusing in the sense I can be one part away from an full item and the game suggests I start buying a totally different thing.
6. It feels slow, it feels dragged out when you die you feel so painfully punished because it just takes so long.
7. Past a certain point the game is decided, five people defending 4 attacking at the final obstacle in a base and the defenders have litterally no chance of saving the game, you go in pile in all youve got and your out of mana, out of health and forced back to the fountain to wait whilst till you can go back in, even the teleport back is painfully slow.
8. you can shoot through walls at the camps which means a hunter can farm camps endlessly without taking damage because the camps are confused by the walls which is I imagine they will fix very soon.
9. Items feel like they do nothing - like previously mentioned you never feel like your doing much damage or that you're fully leveled and you can have all the mana items and you still feel like you're going back to base just as much as you had to at the very begining.
10. If you get in a bad situation and run from a fight if someone wants to chase and kill you they will win, there is no movement penalty when attacking so you can run all you want they will always catch and kill you unless you teleport away with what I think is the most valuable item in the game, the boots of teleportation.
11.The camera is screwed, if you're attacking from the bottom left you'll be fine, if you're attacking from the top right your vision is impaired by the overlay at the bottom of the screen with all your items ... I can only suggest they mirror it so everyone has the same experience and view of attacking from the bottom left.
12. The enchanted items is a really cool idea but it unevens the playing field if you have basic items and your opponent has enchanted ones which in a moba can be a deciding factor. This wouldn't be a problem for someone dedicated enough to grind but i still think it puts people at a disadvantage.
Now what I like about the game is its introduction, its simple to understand. For someone who isn't keen on top down its not so bad, it feels somewhat comfortable. The AI is fantastic like you could play a game against bots and it isn't too far off playing against actual people just starting out. I can see why this would appeal but to me its just failing at a lot of things like pace and fun. Also their ward idea with observatories is top notch so it has potential but its definately not for me as it is.
PS. as someone mentioned it feels more RPG than MOBA ... like they took torchlight and tried to make it a something else... I love torchlight and I would have loved this as an RPG :(

The best way of me explaining it is there have been days in smite with new builds where I felt like I was doing no damage it seemed slower and more tiresome (maybe it was a bad day) but I still had 40K damage which was the highest on the team so I was doing damage I just didn’t feel it. That’s how i felt with this, no satisfaction it just happened
The fighting picks up in team fights but to the absolute extreme ... it goes from dull 1v1 to a team wipe out which is just as dissatisfying whatever side you’re on.

What to say about Strife except "Uninstall."
This game doesn't even cater to casuals. It's so mind numbingly boring with very little dept to it. The crafting system is a total joke and makes the person who has recipes for improved in-game items god like where other characters simply can not make these enchanted weapons unless they grind for hours on end or... pay!
The game
Pay 2 Win. The very first line on the store page is a blatant lie: "Strife® is a truly free to play, competitive, online ARTS / MOBA that features non-stop action and engaging combat." It is not "truly free to play." It is not "competitive." It is not "non-stop action." This is a blatant lie. It's the slowest MOBA i've come across. It's slower than League of Legends, it's slower than Infinite Crisis, it's slower than every MOBA title out there and that's reflected by the 50 minutes it will take you to play a match.
"Truly free to play" does not include an out of game crafting system that places custom created weapons you craft in-game. Custom made items and weapons you can "enchant" to get buffs like lifesteal, more health than the item/weapon would give normally, more charges, more damage than normal but for a bit of extra in-game gold(200g more?). Can you craft these freely? Nope. You have to use "Elixirs" which you get VERY few of for each match played. For me it took 4 games to get 36 Elixirs, that was four 40-50minute matches. If you want a permanent recipe it costs you 360 elixirs just for that one item to be in-game enchanted or not. So, doing the math... 4 games gives you 36 elixirs... 36 divided by 360 equals 10. So, 10 by 4 = 40. That's 40 games, close to 40 hours to get a single recipe that you'll find you ABSOLUTELY need. Or, you know, you could simply pay for it to have an edge in-game. That's is, by definition,
You can play the game, but can you be competitive without paying? Absolutely not! Cost to create a permanent recipe? 50 gems. Only option to buy gems? $2.99 for 75. This game is nowhere near a fair game and definitely caters to those who pay over those who do not, giving people who pay a clear advantage in-game.
Each game lasts 40-50 minutes. Yes,
as standard. That's insane! It would be okay if it was actually enjoyable but it is anything but! The map is HUGE by MOBA standards, the turret ranges have massive areas of aggro and turrets are way too close to one another. This is a huge problem of itself but the fact that turrets are so overpowered you simply can not tower dive even if it's to get that last hit on an enemy and then diving back out. Turrets are simply too powerful which makes ranged sitting by turrets an absolute chore to go up against or play as. Literally, sit by your turret and last hit for gold. Turrets also scale up to late game making turret sitting a viable tactic by a losing team which definitely effects the game length.
The "feature" of allowing you to regen health out of combat is a terrible concept altogether. The only reason I feel it's in the game is because mana regen is so poor you have to gain mana faster somehow as more often than not you're out of mana after a single "poke" or engagement(All your abilities used once). It also makes the laning phase so much more tedious than it has to be. It makes poking an enemy pointless or even bringing them to low health. Why does it suck so much? Turrets. Turrets are extremely over powered. The enemy could be sitting in turret range, soaking up experience with 100hp and you could not dive in to take them no matter your level because the turret will kill you from full health regardless of your level.
Turrets are overpowered. It ruins any potential ganks and combined with the regen buffs you get in the game it makes poking or trading absolutely pointless except to deny the enemy a small bit of gold(Last hitting enemies). It's simply not great, they need to be nerfed hard and not scale to late game. Scaling turrets in a MOBA is the most stupidest things to do in a game after a certain point. When it's 50minutes in, everyone is max level and maxed their item slots with nothing but gold adding up and turrets are still hitting like trucks there's something wrong there.
It needs to go or it needs to be seriously nerfed in the price it costs to make recipes. It adds an artificial layer of complexity to the game in the form of "meta" recipes which you really need to be working towards from the start as it costs far too much to craft and takes far too long to craft these recipes.
It's basically just one big laning phase for the reasons i've outlined: Turrets have too high aggro radius, they deal too much damage from the start to the finish of the game and they're far too close to one another making backdoor ganks next to impossible. Did I mention that the map is huge? The map is huge. You have three turrets in each lane with the last tier being like a nexus turret. Each turret is beyond tanky and those nexus turrets have regenerating shield. The turrets range is, from the center, 90% of your screen. Then there's a small gap between each turret's range so they're not overlapping(Half a screen but i'd have to check). Then you have an average to small sized gap between the enemies first turret and your own turret which essentially means ranged can easily run back to their turret and sit under it with not a care in the world. This prolongs the game and makes it an entirely long, boring laning phase with very little action going on.
The heroes are very lackluster. They're quite boring, look very bland and have animations that do not offer much flexibility. For instance if you want to spin your hero around in a circle the hero simply will not do that. It will only look left to right as the command is too fast for the game to allow. Is it a disadvantage in-game? Not really but it makes it feel even more sluggish and boring.
You literally sit in lane and farm gold then at max level(15) go engage enemies. Basically every tank hero is LoL's Nasus, HotS's Arthas/Stitches in Alpha and Dota 2's Str heroes on steroids with max equips.
It's not a good MOBA. It doesn't even look that good and it feels like they seen a lot that was being put into other games and thought it would fit in their game if they mixed it around and tried to make the game more like Heroes of Newerth(Which was a terrible MOBA and is now almost completely dead -- It's the same developers! Look them up, S2Games).
You have a very, very, very bad take on what I could only even try to relate to League of Legend's "Rune" system, a system which can only be purchased with in-game currency by playing games and can't be boosted or bought with real money and doesn't take nearly as long as it does in this game to gain a full rune set as it does to craft a recipe. Then you have the seriously overpowered Turrets and the game lasting 50 minutes and you have what is an afterthought to the Heroes of the Storm system which is shared experience/shared gold gain. It's pretty much the exact same as in LoL and Dota 2 except you only need to be near a hero that is last hitting mobs to get the gold gain: It's a simple patch job to fix "supports" and who gets priority over gold so as not to include GP5 items or whatever else to give you income to buy things.
My advice to the developers would be to get rid of the crafting system entirely as it's a completely broken concept unless it were 100% free, make the map smaller as it's way too big for the speed of the heroes in it and nerf turrets in every area; damage, range, health, scaling, everything!
I just could not recommend this game. It's worse than Dawngate right now and that's saying something.

I've been playing this game since it came out on the Xbox 360 back in 2008, and bought it on Steam a couple years ago to revisit on of my favorite co-op experiences of all time.  Even to this day I enjoy throwing this game on to tear through the story and juggle enemies with my little brothers.
One of the best parts of the game is exploring the world that Behemoth has developed. There are tons of levels that look and play completely differently from one another. With flowery fields, sandy deserts, slippery icy terrains, and high speed rivers, it's clear that every single level was made with passion. And there's never a boring stretch of land, since there's always something interesting on the playing field or in the background making the environment truly come to life.
Choose your favorite character, level them up, and place their stats to whatever fits your play-style.
There's many weapons that can affect your stats in both positive and negative ways. Throughout the game you won't want to stop searching for something that looks even cooler and has better stats, so expect to search through each level closely for some secret gear.
Ohhhhh yes. The cutest things Behemoth has ever created. There's about 30 of these little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s hiding across the map, and of course it's up to you to collect them all. After you catch them you can chose to have them follow you as your companion. Each animal helps you out in different ways; for example, the ram charges into your enemies, the owl brings you food, the tiger increases your agility, and the giraffe allows you to earn more xp.
This is how you do F2P. This is how you do massive battles. This is awesome.

This game is just astonishing. No other game has made me think so hard about moral choices I make, and I was genuinely stuck on quite a number of these choices the game gave me. I was also stumped on many of the actual puzzles, some for quite a few hours!
It's tricky to explain the narrative without giving too much away, but if you're curious, just get the game already! It's seriously worth it.
As far as the actual puzzles go, I found them really quite fun and challenging, and the difficulty scaled really well, introducing new mechanics at the right times. I might have started to hate those stupid recorders at points, but they weren't overused at all. In fact every puzzle seemed to offer a new challenge, though some made you feel stupid for not seeing the solution!
The DLC is actually well worth it too, it adds a large amount of content set in a 'side-story' with a completely different narrative yet again. The hardest puzzles are harder than any in the main game (To get one of the bonus stars took me 5 hours!), but it works well and offers another intriguing story.
Highly recommended!

So if you are thinking: "Ah, sweet childhood memories", think again. There is little of the original worms (or worms 2) to be seen in this game. The worms themselves allow for customization, which would make you believe that you have more control whereas you in fact have less. The quasi 3D enviroment is no match for the old-school bitmap like maps, making it hard to judge where you can stand/walk/jump, and distracting from the game play. The weapons still work in the same way, but the controls are all over the place and judging wind and compensating for new stuff such as water (and whether it will flow or not) is frustrating. The single player campains later on require you to get every shot and movement correct, with little to no margin for error (made more difficult by the graphics).
It is not the worst worms-game I have played (worms: a space oddity for the wii takes that spot), but if you want a blast from the past, I'd suggest going for the versions released for android rather than this.

Arcade controlls, action packed fights, back and forth racing with some luck sprinkled randomly and some really amazing nostlagia filled maps. Developers have fixed many optimization problems and have even personally rewarded people with free DLC for helping out with the bug reports.

This isn't a mario kart clone, its a well-thought and well-made kart racing game that stands on its own merits while using iconic charcters and amazing graphic style to help bring it all together.

===== Not so normal review follows. Skip to the end for a normal review =====
I've achieved 100% on all levels up to 15, without revisiting any of them after beating them It's an extra challenge to get 100%, but that's what took the game from something my kids might struggle with up to something I have to stop and think about for at least a few moments every level. It wasn't that hard to figure out 100% given some thought on how to shave off a few moves somewhere along the line, and while the level designs were engaging, they hadn't been terribly challenging given a sequential approach to the solution. Granted I've had fun along the way, but beyond the initial "aha" moment, it's been more of an "interesting" instead of "challenging" game. Sometimes it would take a few minutes of just staring at the level before it occurred to me, but most of the time all it took was making the wrong move once, then I realized what I should have done instead. Most of my time has been spent staring at the levels and planning out the most efficient route to completely finish the level and put it to bed.
Then I get to Level 15, with it's "oh you want to get red over across the chasm to help his buddies? Great, just leave blue back by his starting slot then. You can't do that and have green move across the chasm? Cry me a river, just for that I'll make you put your cubes in the same unwinnable 'green on the right, blue on the left' condition without realizing it again. Try and recover from that, loser" attitude. Pretty snarky this level 15 was, so of course I have to put it in its proper place with all the others I'd left behind with relative ease.
... Some Time Later ...
After the 42nd similar sequence of events, Level 15 was beyond snark, it had gone beyond the blackest and darkest evil that has ever existed and that music playing in my ears hauntingly regaling me witih the same distorted laserlight carnival tune like it's laughing at my aggravation, telling me I'll never finish this level, and seeming to grow louder and louder as the level bests me yet another time, I pressed Alt+F4 and (uncharactaristically) rage quit entirely out of the application.
It was suddenly, blissfully quiet. 15 had ceased it's biting refrain, and the music had gone dead. The garish out of sorts colors were no longer pressing in on my eyes. I was free of the puzzle that trapped me. Finally, blissfully free. Then I noticed, the garish colors were bright and lively, they fit and made it easier to see problem and solution.
I missed the abrasive colours.
I missed the tune, similarly garish and quirky, it was an urging background theme that asked just one more level before sleep.
I missed the urgency and the triumph of besting another of those levels, designed as they were to add greater and greater complexity with each passing one, while keeping mechanics simple.
I missed being in on the secret of the solution, not because I had been told or guided to the answer, but because a puzzle had been laid out and I had solved it, with that oh so devious combination of movements that moved cubes around to where they seemingly shouldn't be able to travel.
I missed Level 15, with it's quiet urging, it's refusal to reveal it's secrets and allow me through to challenge yet more complex sequences in the attempt to best the pinnacle of them, Level 30, before trying my hand at the time trials that whispered at me from the central menu.
I sat there staring at the Fake Colours banner, wondering if I'll regret in just a few moments what I'm doing. I click the Play button faintly calling to me, and I reenter the puzzle for just one more level before sleep.

This is definately a "completionist" nightmare, in the best ways puzzle games can be. I tend to be the sort of person who wants to complete puzzle games with 100% on each level, yet I struggle with this one by far more than the levels themselves. That being said, I still tagged the game casual, since actually completing a given level tends to be a much simpler affair (early on).
The game's mechanics are simpler than expected, reminiscent of a rubics cube in that individual movement is quite simple yet coordinated movement of each block is key to completing successfully. It builds on simpler mechanics in stair-steps (every few levels it seems), none of them requiring more that a single try to grasp it's utility or challenge.
Screenshots don't do this game justice, it's actually quite beautiful, in a certainly garish color pallete that works exceedingly well for the game's genre. Highly recommend playing fullscreen or you'll miss the full effect. The screenshots also don't fully relate the mechanics, including locations that change the color of blocks and the neccessity of creating "bridges" to span the gap of floor colors in order to complete levels. It later introduces multi-level layouts as difficulty scales appropriately. Through any of this, the usage of previous mechanics becomes more devisive, rather than repeating the same old paradigms you saw on previous levels.
For those gamers who care about the developer beind the game in addition to the game itself, this developer seems to not only have his head on straight, he's active in the steam forums and elsewhere, plugged into the indie scene and has been incredibly helpful around a busy release period, bending over backwards resolving issues that weren't his responsibility related to prior bundle purchasers with issues retrieving keys from a certain bundle site (myself included). This type of developer is why I stay firmly invested in indie games over AAA titles, with a personal touch and displaying a care for his product.
Surprisingly, I haven't yet encountered any issues with this game thus far, even running on Linux and with a tendancy to look unceasingly for potential improvements or annoyances. The only mechanical improvement I found, I asked for a slightly different control scheme (tab vs N to change selected cube). With regard to any game breaking or annoyance factor bugs, I haven't found anything at all, which is rare for someone in the software testing industry. Tabbing away and returning to the game even works without issue, and there doesn't seem to be a way I can cause common freeze/lock issues common to a 3d puzzle game in this vein. Overall, it's got solid code behind it, with a good minimalist design of avoiding superfluous menus and options.
All this being said, I will say the game is now roughly priced at what I would expect (originally it was 2x the price at $19.99). I really enjoy the game, it has 30 levels and I expect to get at least ~6-8 hours of solid enjoyment out of it (without considering time trials section effectively re-playing the levels) given the increasing difficulty and time spent thus far accounting for progress. I would be disappointed if the game were to receive considerably more levels (or steam workshop support) as the level design is part of what makes the game what it is. To be frank, the game strikes me as a solid $9.99-$14.99 game at top end, simply for the length of play and enjoyment I expect to receive out of it.
TL;DR/Overall determination: Recommended at current price, especially if the game ever goes on sale, now that the game is at a substantially lower price point than it was on release. When it was $19.99, I said If it's on a sale for 25-50% off I'd say absolutely snatch it up. Now that it's $9.99 standard price, this is a steal. Great level design, unique artistic balance, simple mechanics and a frustratingly great mastery point make for a recommended title.

Strife compared to DOTA 2 is like Team Fortress 2 VS Counter Strike GO: Just because they're in the same genre, doesn't mean they have to do things the same way. Whilst DOTA 2 is a competitive game that players find fun, Strife is a fun game that players can find competitive: but that's dependant on the player. Casual or hardcore, Strife appeals to fans of MOBAs in general and provides that much-needed alternative to a young genre that hasn't really expanded it's horizons.
Specifically, Strife does away with micomanagement elements and the manipulation of gameplay mechanics, and gives you something straightforward but still competitive. It's not as complex, but everything you want and need is there. Further more, whilst attacks in general feel a little weaker or less game-changing, every hero is capable of impressive feats and contributing equally to a fight. There is way less reason to be angry at your team mates, because the game does not force your rates of survival into your team mates hands - it mearly supports teams of 5 all getting stuck in! It's worth noting though, that as a MOBA-in-development, it's still being balanced out and tweaked often.
Any serious complaints? It has to be said that at times this game is rough around the edges, with minor bugs and some menus not implemented as well as they could be: as to be expected with it's Early Access status. However S2 update regularly and interact consistently with their client base (check out their Reddit page!) and the future looks great for this quirky title! Get on-board ASAP, it's free and it's fun!

is a supernatural coming of age mystery adventure game, the debut title developed and published by Night School Studio. You play as Alex, teenaged girl who brings her new step-brother Jonas along to a night-time party on Edwards Island, an old decommissioned military island. As the night goes on, Alex and her group of friends soon find out not everything on the island is as it seems, and soon things take an ominous turn.
The story is the selling point of the game.
plays out like a cross between
and
, with the eerie atmosphere and tense moments, and the coming of age characters and story of the latter. If you enjoyed any of those two games, you may like this one.
is driven entirely by its story, if you’re not interested in a heavily story based game, this isn’t for you. Indeed, much of the games backstory and lore comes from player exploration. If you’re not actively looking to solve the mystery behind the story being told or paying attention to character dialogue, you’ll likely get lost in what’s happening. With that said, if you enjoy a good mystery adventure game with a teenage cast and creepy atmosphere,
delivers on both those fronts.
The game wears its supernatural thriller inspirations proudly, both the story and dialogue harken back to the 80’s/90’s when teen horror movies were at all-time peak popularity. Not to say
is an outright horror game, far from it. It’s closer to
, with more psychological horror and eerie atmospherics than outright jump scares (though the few are in the game will likely make you jump.) There are some seriously clever “mind screw” moments that reminded me of
, from small things like messing with the interface, to a completely different scene playing on my second playthrough when I chose the exact same dialogue choice on my first playthrough.
Dialogue was a strong point throughout, the conversations between characters never felt unnatural or forced. The characters were believable, even if they were somewhat tropey. You have the protagonist Alex; the carefree teenage girl, Jonas; the introverted shy kid on the block, Ren; the stoner dude, Nona; the smart chick and Clarissa; the popular-at-school but ♥♥♥♥♥y teen girl. The roles of these characters have been done to death a thousand times over, you’ve seen them in just about every coming of age movie. Even though they might not be the most original cast of characters, the banter between them and the developing relationships you have with them throughout the game felt genuine and believable, and it was the interactions and changing relationships with all the different characters that drew me in. All your choices matter, both from the way you talk to certain characters to the major decisions you make throughout, and by the end, your decisions will matter, big or small.
While being a fairly short game at around 6 hours, without mentioning spoilers, there is benefit to be had of a second playthrough, that goes beyond selecting other choices. Honestly, calling it a second playthrough wouldn’t give it justice, there’s so much new content on a second run that it plays like a natural continuation of the story, rather than a rerun of what you’ve already played. I’d highly recommend playing through the game a second time if you enjoyed the game. It’s a short story, but a very compelling one.
Similar to Telltale style games,
dialogue system uses the same point and click styled dialogue choices that are set on a timer. What made
dialogue between the characters so enjoyable was the way it was presented. There are no “cutscenes” or “conversation nodes,” almost all the dialogue between the characters is done while walking from place to place. It feels natural, and the way your dialogue options are presented is one of the games strongest points.
As far as the actual gameplay loop is concerned, it plays much like every other heavily dialogue based story game; you walk from area to area, select highlighted objects for dialogue and puzzle solving, and converse with other characters at the same time. The game doesn’t do anything truly innovative in the gameplay department, but being such a small-scale game and debut title, its fairly understandable.
Your radio is the primary means of puzzle solving throughout the game, and is much more than a problem solving magic wand. Like I mentioned before, much of the lore and backstory of the game is hidden as secrets throughout the island, which you very much should look for if you want to understand the underlying mystery of the plot. The game never forces you to look for these secrets, you’ll most likely want to if you want to understand the hidden backstory. Perhaps it’s somewhat of a negative point that this information is somewhat hidden from the player by default, but if you’re playing for the story, you’d be most likely be the type of gamer looking for secrets and hidden clues anyway.
While remaining fairly minimalist,
is certainly a pretty looking game. It’s art style oozes atmosphere, player immersion plays an important role in the quality of story based games, and Oxenfree very much succeeds in immersing the player in the game. The hand drawn art style graphics of the game is gorgeous and pretty to look at, while still being able to communicate to the player exactly where to go and what objects in the environment are usable. It very much reminded me of
in many ways, with the way the games blended their fantastic artwork into a cohesive gameplay environment. The supernatural effects are fantastic, a lot of work went into making them feel otherworldly and it shows. The game nails the horror/thriller movie atmosphere it was going for, thanks to the excellent art direction.
Like many horror movies and thrillers,
soundtrack mostly comprises of ambient and atmospheric tracks that serve to accompany the eerie ambience of the game. The closest I can describe the music in the game is electronic trance. Oddly calming, the soundtrack makes for a pretty good “study playlist” set of songs, my personal highlights off the soundtrack being
,
and
is a short but compelling story driven experience that plays like a cross between
and
If you liked either of those titles, and/or you enjoy mystery exploration games with a dab of psychological horror and eerie atmospheric gameplay, you may want to give this one a shot. Worth checking out.

This game reels you in with the usual addictive strategy gameplay that we've come to expect from Worms games, but soon enough, I guarantee it will have you howling with frustration and rage, bitterly cursing the day you bought it. The single player campaign is easy enough to play at first, but it quickly turns one-sided. The AI worms are unforgiving, and can always pull off logic-defying, perfect shots that a human player could never hope to calculate. Oh sure, they may occasionally miss a shot, but it's all part of their endgame. You will lose. It doesn't help that the odds are firmly stacked against you at all times - your worms are often placed in the worst possible locations on the map, and the AI team always has more worms than you, often more than double. The Spooky levels are where it really becomes next to impossible. Looking for respite, I turned to the puzzles, but sorry, no rest there! The majority of the puzzles (involving using only the tools available to kill certain worms) require absolute, nitpicky precision, and I was only able to get through the later ones with online help. You will fail and fail again. I also sometimes encountered "glitches" in both modes, varying from random, mine-less explosions under my worms to weapons backfiring. The new "Worm classes" also add little to the game, and the much-touted new physics are of little consequence other than with their forced inclusion in the puzzles. I'm convinced that this game was programmed by Satan. Only buy Worms Revolution if you want your blood pressure to skyrocket and your nerves to fray. You have been warned.

The game does have content problems, as it's corridors and enemies do start to grow stale over time, especially in the layout department. However, combat surprisingly never felt TOO repetitive for me due to its mechanics, and I disagree with a lot of users saying that the controls are bad for the game: they perfectly fit in for what the combat was trying to do. Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed completely outclasses its predecessor, Sonic & SEGA All-Stars Racing, in every way. This game is amazing, and playing split-screen or online multiplayer with friends is a lot of fun. The character selection, course design and gameplay are some of the best in the genre, and the soundtrack is an absolutely incredible selection of remixed classic tunes, to which you can credit Richard Jacques, also known for his work on Sonic R, Sonic 3D Blast Saturn and Metropolis Street Racer, among many other things.
And it's not just a straight console port either! In fact, while this game is great on X360, PS3 and Wii U, the PC version is the definitive version, offering improved textures, resolution and is the only version capable of running in 60fps. The PC exclusive characters leave a lot to be desired though, but their presence doesn't retroactively ruin the game. They're just not a deal-maker over the console editions.
If you're sick of Mario Kart, then this is the best Mario Kart killer since Crash Team Racing. It's a game that is truly full of surprises.

So after a playtime of 4.8 hours to beat the main campaign on a first run, I'm not totally sure how I feel about this one. Not much longer than blue shift, at least for my amount of playtime, it certainly offered much more in trms of story and variety; at least in a mechanical sense. However, my biggest issue with this particular one is that most of the common enemies, especially nearing the end, turned in to massive bullet sponges who pumped out tons of damage. I suppose this was to further encourage more use of the big power weapons (SAW, alien rocket launcher, etc.) and that would be keeping your squads alive but ammo for these weapons was somewhat limited for the amount of enemies there were and the AI for the squadmates is braindead; they sometimes just don't follow you or they run off to fight the enemieson their own, even if mortally wounded, and get themselves killed while you've taken cover and tried to gt your medic to heal you (who has also run off to get himself killed and won't heal you because he's currently running to fight alienes for the sake of freedom). Weapons like the MP5, Spas-12, Glock, and the Deagle (to some extent) quickly became null against the beefy enemies that you'll be constantly assaulted by. Even the humans enemies took way more damage than they really should have (at least 3 shotgun shells point blank) as compared to in the other two titles of the original half-life "trilogy" (Half-life, Half-life: Blue Shift, and Half-Life: Opposing Force). I can't say it's bad, all my complaints are above, and I still think if you liked the original Half-Life that you should give this and the other spin-off title a go just out of respect for the franchise. If I had to give it a score....I'd say something like...7.5 or 8/10.

So pretty much let's think about War simulator games like Battlefield franchise. Now let's make 4 big♥♥♥♥♥maps and make it sandbox. Player controlled (99 percent player controlled) everything. You can spawn tanks, aircrafts, or supporting logisitics to help your faction take bases and mine resources to take a continents and earn special perks (if they're worth a damn).
The fun comes when gaze upon the battlefield and see 100s of players fighting each other over a base, and the players have to work together to do this so you see armor columns form to bombard bases or fight other tanks, air units supporting ground or dogfighting, and infantry engaging each other on the ground trying to take control of point A, B, C, or D (Depending on where the base is), and ultimately the great open battles that happen between bases, trying to gain ground to fully assault a enemy base. These are the real fun things in the game.
But be forewarned, you have to earn guns through certifications and attachments for those guns to make them more useful to you. And the grind could kill ya fun. But don't worry, the starting guns are pretty good starting out since the guns you unlock with certification points are really situational weapons for certain situations. But for your tanks and other logistics, it will be difficult to do anything with them that can be considered useful without certing them out.
Overall Planetside 2 is really fun when you're playing with an outfit or platoon that communicates and has tons of fun, and most of the platoon leads in the game are nice and friendly so you shouldn't have a problem playing in these. If a War game is what you want, Planetside 2 brings it.

Locomotion is a niche title - I think some Roller Coaster Tycoon fans come to this game expecting a similar experience only to be dissapointed. This is a transport sim - you build railways, airports, and roadways to transport passengers and cargo around a series of predesigned or custom scenarios. The mechanics for supply and demand are very simple, which makes the game very simple to learn and play. The city growth mechanics are similarly simple which makes them feel unrealistic, but somewhat easy to deal with. However, some of the scenarios get very challenging with many competitive rivals fighting you for trade and transport superiority.
Pros:
+ Very cheap title that will give you dozens of hours of entertainment. I have purchased this game before, and got it again to have it on steam.
+ A simple, reliable, no nonsense transport sim. If you want to build random railways or tramways, jump right in.
+ Quite frankly, in a similar vein to RCT1, the simple gridded map simply works. Newer titles have developed dynamic curves and city growth but lack the simplicity and reliability of an old fashioned grid.
+ Neat inflation system over time.
+ Soundtrack goes along with the era you are in. Some tracks I like while others are a little irritating.
Neutral:
+ Graphics are nostalgic but may turn some people off. What you see in the images is what you get.
+ Game is great if you love logistics, public transport, company building, and trains. If you don't like these things, you will not like this game.
Cons:
+ Many have pointed out that the game has copied many ideas from similar games. If you have another go to transport sim, this may not give you any additional entertainment. Like I said previously though, it is a cheap title that works.
+ Replacing old vehicles in long games is VERY tedious. Some alternate games in the genre have developed solutions to this problem, but you will find this to be a very unenjoyable experience on maps like the 100 year challenge.
Overall I would recommend this title, particularly if it is on sale, but only to people who like simulation games that don't necessarily appeal to mainstream audiences, like Cities:Skylines.

Just wow is this game a hidden gem. Dark Messiah is about an apprentice to a powerful wizard who finds he's more than just an apprentice. Powered by Source, this game's visuals are amazing for the time it was made.
What really separates this from other RPGs is the physics and controls. Using the source engine, enemies are flung around like ragdolls. There's all kinds of booby traps and other devices to help you fight enemies.
Depending on which buttons you push (forward, back, left, right) determines which way you swing your weapon or which type of attack you use. It comes out so smooth and intuitively it's like you're holding the sword yourself. Because of how well combat is crafted, having good skills means the game rewards you.
There's not much replayability. You can try playing as a mage or thief type character, but there's so much focus on melee and bows you'll end up playing as a warrior anyway. The levels are also too linear.
Overall, 9/10

Everything is great about portal 2. The gameplay, the voice acting (especially Chell), the characters... you name it. The story is good, although nothing too fancy.
But the core of Portal are, of course, the portals. The puzzles can be really challenging and that's what makes this game so good. I love puzzles, and the game forces you to think out of the box. If you like mind-challenging stuff, then buy the game already.
But its brilliance doesn't stop there. Glados (the antagonist) has a lot of personality and really brings life to the game. Her lines are great, and she's gonna make you laugh quite a bit. Another great example of this are the turrets. They're really simple and don't have too many voice lines, but they're full of personality and help shape the game's atmosphere. Besides, they're f***ing cute.
The environment, although very similar most of the time, is dynamically changing so you never get bored.
Perhaps the one thing I didn't like too much was the music, but it's not that big of a deal.
Finally, the game is ridiculously cheap. There really is nothing to think; if you haven't played this game, buy it already!

You could be on a tiny floating chunk of land just big enough to stand on and an AI worm can throw a grenade from across the map, ricochet it off walls and celings and get it to land perfectly on that worm's head without bouncing off. Not only are they unfair, but as you progress, they start to outnumber you more and more. I've gotten to the point where I've started with only 4 worms and the AI has 10. Unless you're the kind of person who enjoys games like Dark Souls, where the challenge is based on how unfair the AI is, I wouldn't touch the singleplayer with a 10 foot pole.
That aside though, this game is clearly meant to be played with friends anyways, and it's definitly worth the buy just for the multiplayer.

Not sure what's up with all the negative reviews on this one
Anyway, this is basically a metroidvania with an actual combat system instead of basic attacks seen in most similar games.
ACE tried to capture the feel of a fighting game with the combat, as can be seen in the fact that literally every character/enemy in the game is playable in one way or another. All and all it feels out of place at first, but it's easy enough to get used to. Speaking of characters, the design of this game is unlike anything I've seen before; many of the monsters the player encounters are very interesting to look at, and often have eerie glowing or melting effects to them. This entire game really looks strange, yet at the same time great.
Other than that this is just an RPG rougelite where dying sends you back to the start without your equipment, but leveling and cash stay with you after death. I'm not the biggest fan of procedurally-generated enviroments, but the dungeon this game takes place in is varied enough to keep my attention.
In the end I have to say that this really is a good game. My only real complaint is that attack inputs often feel wonky or unresponsive since you're probably not going to learn the attacks of all the characters you play as.
Also a lot of people are complaining about co-op and KB/M controls.

Enemies that completely ignore the players hits at times - check (Enemies will sometimes hit you in the middle of you throwing them, which they arent meant to do)
Enemies with spammy and ridiculously oversized hitboxes that extend well beyond their model on both sides - check (this works sometimes with the player as well. But seriously, ♥♥♥♥ those spear birds.)
A block mechanic that works 100% for the AI and quite frequently is completely ignored when the player character uses it - check (Parrying is ♥♥♥♥ing broken too, half the time)
Enemies which can skip entire animations to hit you in the middle of your dodge - Check (why this function even exists is beyond me, its more of a sidestep then anything useful)
Mediocre controls which while passable enough, really show their issues whenever platforming comes into play - check.
Its literally a collection of every single good and bad thing that a Roguelike can do, tbh. It looks nice, plays nice enough, and has decent longevity.... and then it falls flat.
If roguelikes are your thing, and youve grown tired of Binding of Isaac, go ahead and try this. If youre looking for a good roguelike to play, look elsewhere. Im honestly lucky i got this from Humble Bundle or id ask for a refund...

Overall, this game feels much more balanced than Super Meat Boy.
The game is, at first, really accessible to newcomers and people who just want to enjoy a good platformer. The difficulty ramps up slowly, the progression is smoother than SMB for instance, which is a very nice thing.

But what makes this game so good is the fact that you really get a sense of exploration, since a LOT of the content is hidden through secret passages that will really challenge your sense of attention (and your skills).
No matter what type of gamer you are, I think it is safe to say that as long as you are not allergic to platformers, you will not be disapointed.

Abyss Odyssey is a platform based fighting game with a bit of story, a randomized map, and a whole lot of crazy. A major facet of the game is that death is not the end; not necessarily even in each playthough. When the main character, one of either Katrien, a dead dude with hands but no body, or a sea goddess, dies, they are simply replaced by a soldier (still playable, of course) who can revive the main at certain alters. Only when the soldier dies must you restart. However, death only costs you your progress down and your current one items. Level, exp, and gold are kept.
This game has a special mechanic that adds one more layer in. The main can use a special skill and rip the soul from an enemy, gaining the ability to transform into any enemy, including all bosses. Dying as a monster turns you back to the main, adding another layer of life. Which you will need because the monsters are brutally unmercifully good at beating you to a pulp. The AI is intelligent and each monster knows its strengths. If a monster is fast but weak and you shield, it'll wait for a hard hitter to show up and they will tag-team you to death.
The story (for characters, primarily. There isnt much of a plot.) and art of the game are amazing. The story is that a powerful warlock is in a asleep in a coma or something, and his nightmares are materializing in the real world. As one of his dreams, you are trying to stop him. Characters and monster are primarily from old Chilean myth and folklore and also a considerable amount from the Christian bible, plus many from various other worldwide myths, all with the wonderful wackiness of ACE. Plus there is also a crossover character from Zeno Clash now.
Pros:
Great visuals, music and designs.
Every character/enemy is playable.
Either way:
Difficulty. The game is brutal. There is no easy mode or tutorial. Only hard or harder. I like that, but not everyone does.
Enemies are really smart and know you, so you have to know and exploit them. Finding ways to successfully spam attacks is generally rewarded with not dying. You can do it, but so can the enemies, so it could go either way.
Animation cancelling is a major mechanic. This means that learning combos through hard trial and error is the best way and messing one up can mean a lost battle due to long animations. The mechanic is really cool though, so again, either way.
Cons:
Controls can be a tad floaty, but its not that bad.
Soldiers cannot jump as high as other characters, and I am bad at getting places with them. This is far more fruatrating than it sounds.
Verdict:
Excellent game. I really enjoy(ed) it. If you've never played a fighting game, or don't like them, or you're really bad, then this isn't the game for you. However, it is excellent for those who are willing to climb its learning curve.
Notes: This is my first review. My apologies if I've messed absolutely everything up and offended everyone in the general vicinity.

A truly engaging puzzle experience. I bought this game on a whim and abslutely did not regret the decision.
If you don't enjoy reading fairly lengthy walls of text in order to engage with the lore and exposition then the story may not be for you, however the gameplay was some of the most solid intuitive challenges I have ever experienced in a game, it may even top Portal for the way it layers new challenges on previously established systems.
The only issue I had was the bonus challenges. A lot of these puzzles were solved by doing unintuitive things such as breaking the map or stealing items from puzzle rooms, I had no issues with these they are a fairly clever way of getting you to think outside the box. The puzzles I took issue with were ones which would require you to randomly stumble upon them doing things which you would have no reason to do, for instance: there is one item in the game which you can target at other similar items, quite often the slution to a bonus puzzle would come from finding a tiny pinprick/obtusely hidden target. I did not find these puzzles fun, instead of eliciting an "Aha!" they simply brought forth a "Well how was I supposed to work that out!" when I inevitably had to look up the solution.
The core gameplay is brilliant and I would highly recommend the game to anyone who even has a passing interest in puzzle game, just don't frce yourself through the bonus challenges as they could sully your perception of the game overall.

Excellent product though not everybody should use it.
Since it's a monitoring/overclocking utility for gpus one need to have a minimum knowledge on how to. As far as I'm concerned, I finally preferred install non-Steam version since I didn't want to be bothered with Steam login from Windows startup.
- Freeware
- Awesome automatic switch between profiles: are you working on desktop? well, then it switches to gpu power saving and gpu slow pace. Are you launching a game? well, then it switches to high performance settings including higher fan speeds and overclocking if you've set that way. You can configure up to 10 different profiles.
- Nice looking interface with an optional second skin
- Easy to use and parameter with hotkeys availability
- Easily configurable monitoring with(out) saved log option
- Fully configurable On Screen Display
- Handling of multiple gpus
- No info on how to handle overclocking so you need to have a minimum knowledge to use advanced settings (this seems obvious but...)
- Very dangerous KBoost feature which risks should be much more highlighted. KBoost is a feature that aims at forcing graphic cards to run at their maximum capacities constantly. Therefore, if you don't pay attention, as well as greatly overclocking and overvoltaging your gpu, it'll eventually fire it over time!
-Steam rewards: this has already been mentioned by many other users but this is an utilty not a game: no need to include any useless Steam reward to install and use it! Plus it's a freeware!

Remember Remember (the fifth of November?) is a VN based around a SAW like murdergame premise: there's five people in a bunker, captured by a mastermind who puts them through a high stress 'game'. I was drawn to this as a somewhat-fan of 999, I liked the concept of that game and its mechanics, but felt its story was pretty over the top and nonsensical, so an indie take on a similar idea was interesting to me.
My big up front warning with this game: if the concept of having to play a minigame in your VN is a red flag to you, stay away from this title. 'Mask', your captor, has the protagonist play variants of a maze minigame repeatedly to try and get through the plot and discover the truth about the group's past. It's a pretty tough little game too: I took a fair few tries before beating this game, and I'd advocate saving each time Mask calls for a game (He gives a fair amount of warning.)
That said, I enjoyed this game. The voice acting was solid, parts of the plot were quite surprising, the characters were pretty nice and believable, and the did a good job of balancing sympathy for the group and tension of a high stress environment. It's pretty short, even by indie VN standards, but there's replay value for the achievement hunters amongst us, as well as those who like seeing multiple sides of a story/exploring different characters, and I feel a single playthrough will be quite satisfying to those ok with an indie VN being on the short side.
So yeah. Recommended! Though if I see another one of those damned shadow creatures again it'll be too soon.

Strap the f--k in, kids. This game, oh my God, this game.
First of all, let's get some technicals out of the way:
- The voice acting is great. Very natural, very easy. Definitely play this game with headphones on.
- Make sure you pay attention when people are talking. The dialogue options have timers and some are shorter than others.
- The art style for this game is perfect. I'll add to this in a second, but it definitely sets your expectations up a certain way only to run over them.
- My only real criticism? I wish the ending was happier.
Okay, now that that's out of the way, let's do this.
The description of the game and the chosen screenshots don't do a lot of justice to just how nauseatingly frightening this game can be. While it won't ping if you can waltz through Silent Hill, it'll definitely get to you in ways you won't expect. I found myself freaked out a few times, even though the entire game is essentially 2D. It's also pretty easy to find yourself freaked out, in my opinion, because it's very easy to get drawn into what's happening. All the characters interact pretty naturally and Alex's relationship with Jonas builds in a believable way. The only character that may fall a little flat every now and then is Ren, but that may just be my take on things.
As someone who multitasks pretty much constantly, I had to focus entirely on this game about 99% of the time, just to make sure I didn't miss any dialogue options and because I was seriously hoping nothing scary was about to happen.
The story itself probably isn't anything super new - kids stranded on an island that turns out to be chock full of ghosts - but it's executed beautifully. At the very end of the game, players are able to leave behind advice for other people, though it can be hard to tell that this is what's actually happening.
The game has multiple endings, some happier than others, but ultimately only one true 'happy' ending, which is kind of disappointing. I don't want to spoil it for people, so I won't say how it ends, but I definitely feel like that the developers maybe should've put in an ending that wasn't so... well, full of existential despair.
So, all over, probably a 9 or 8 out of 10. Definitely something to get if you love atmosphere, personality, and horror. Just make sure you know where you're going on the map or you'll wind up having to backtrack annoyingly.

This is, to me and many people: The best game of its kind, hands down.
This is a beyond-fun game full of retro (or "ultra retro") references, very fun and unique mechanics, it's VERY challenging if you want to (or if you're a completionist).
The game is not very very long, but the base price is low anyway, and for its price it's a very very good game.
In comparison to the first game: Much MUCH better graphics, actually hard and not quite easy like the first, better and bigger cast overall (although Ryo Hazuki was taken out), much longer too and properly/flawlessly optimized for the PC (no more "cache stutters" like in the first game). The tracks actually have NO LAPS (for the most part) and they're very refreshing, the game is now "Transformed" in which every track has a water and/or air part where your vehicle transforms into a boat or a plane (the gameplay in those parts is different). Both the transforming aspect and the tracks are not repetitive (due to having no laps), it also doesn't feel linear cause there are different routes you can take.
Flaws? Only one. This seems like a new trend, as some modern games like this one HAVE NO TUTORIAL. The first game has a tutorial but this game has the stuff of the first game plus new ones, and only the internet and user-made manuals will help you, it's a must to read a complete guide about basics before playing this game, otherwise you'll have no clue about stunts (and that you can actually pull them), as well as "drift switching" which are very, VERY important aspects in this game as there is very VERY little room for mistake if you're gonna do a race/event on Expert difficulty.
Another flaw (this one is relative) is that it doesn't support 16:10 format resolution, but this game is designed to be played on a HDTV with a controller anyway.
Recommended! This is my fav racing game and again, the best of its kind.
Of course, your performance is also a bit luck-based, but that's a factor belonging in every cart racing game that have random weapon/tool pickups, it's a bit a happy-go-lucky kinda game:)

I really want to recommend this game but there are just enough problems with it that makes it hard to do so.
The premise is really, really cool.  While the overall setting takes heavy inspiration from the Saw films, the central conflict of the story is interesting and unique.  The characters have voice actors, all of whom are surprisingly competent given the indie nature of the game.  They're also reasonably well-written, although I was a little miffed at how wildly inconsistent the main character could be given you control his choices.  All in all, the writing is good enough and this is, after all, a visual novel, so clearly that matters quite a bit.
So why, then, can't I recommend it? There are a few faults with the game.  First, the main "gameplay" element of the game is incredibly poorly optimized.  I have a rig that can run games like For Honor and The Witcher 3 at max settings and the gameplay here chugs along like you're trying to walk through water, and given the nature of the gameplay it actually makes things rather frustrating.  The "fix" the developers suggested - turning the animations off - actually somehow succeeded in making the problem worse, which is quite counter-intuitive.
The length of the game bothered me too.  I haven't even clocked two and a half hours and I've seen and done almost everything.  There are a few more lines of dialogue that I've yet to see but I know all the twists and I know the big revelation at the end.  But none of these things would matter if not for...
...The price tag.  While this isn't No Man's Sky at launch levels, I find it incredibly difficult to justify the $15.99 price, especially in light of the fact that the far, far superior - in both content and story - VA-11 HALL-A is actually a dollar less.
This isn't a bad VN by any means.  But its problems combined with its price tag made me feel like it was not worth the money.  If it drops below $10? Sure, give it a whirl.  But at $16? Pass.  If you have any love for visual novels, put your dollars on VA-11 HALL-A.

If there's one major complaint I have, it's that the map system doesn't handle backtracking for collectables very well. It forces you to start at the beginning of the area whether you want to or not. This hasn't been a gigantic issue for the early areas but I imagine it'll get very frustrating in the harder later ones. Since there's a certain level of connectivity to the levels (although not as much as you might expect), I can understand why they went in this direction but I think the system could be tweaked a bit to cut down on needless padding.
