So far this game has been amazing. I've read the negative comments about the game, and I'm here to tell you why they're wrong. The first point that I want to stress is that NONE of them have even played for two hours. Why are you gonna write a review before even playing most of the game. The first thing pointed out was that they hated precision platforming and that the speed was slow. This is a different seeries to meat boy. They are trying out new things and ideas with every new "character series" that they bring in. They have a different core mechanic in each game that they make. This one so happens to be precision platforming which is one of the things that I love most. (not every platformer they make has to be meat boy). They also don't like the collectibles, while I enjoy them a lot. I like the cartridges a ton because they are just really hard versions of the game. I also like the idea of the tumors being collectibles that you can get at any time, but you just need to know how to get them. I like how they are used in the game. Meat boy had characters, The End is Nigh has harder and cooler levels from the collectibles. The next thing is the color scheme. They say it's bland. I mean if you knew what the game was about you can see why they used the colors they used. It even tells you in the title THE END IS NIGH. For those of you that don't get it, it's a post-apocalyptic world, so the colors are meant to be in a darker mood. I think the colors compliment the game well. The next thing is move restriction and the "speed" of the game. For those that didn't play meat boy, there were mechanics that were in the game, such as wall clinging/sliding/jumping and the "run button". For those of you that did play meat boy, I want you to think to yourself if you ever really found yourself in a position where you weren't holding that "run button" and then tell me that it was completely useless because there was no reason walk. They made is so that you didn't have to constantly hold a button to go at the speed that was meant for the game. I think the character's speed is great for precision platforming. I like this new mechanic of hanging off of certain walls. I felt like the wall clinging in meat boy was a bit wonky, and I enjoy being able to completely control what I hang on to. The next point is that the game is "if you're blind, screw you" which I sort of agree with. There's obviously some stuff that you won't see coming and that you'll have to deal with on your next life. But, get this, you have UNLIMITED lives. They want you to die. Hell, they even have a death counter on your profile screen. They expect you to die thousands of times. Even saying all this, it is definitely possible to beat this deathless from a blind playthrough. It isn't likely, but the♥♥♥♥♥♥they throw at you doesn't come 80 mph. It's reactable. Frame drops are another thing people complain about even though there are settings to turn the shaders down. >:( The final thing I want to talk about is the complaint about no variety. Play for more than one world, and you'll encounter different things. I don't know what else to say. Some of the enemies in the game are amazing. My favorite is probably the better versions of the Oobs. When I first saw them, I thought of how amazing it was to see them correcting the mistakes they did in meat boy. The Oobs were probably one of my least favorite enemies in the game because of they're rapid and, somewhat, unpredictable movement. I'm happy to see that they are looking back at their designs and reworking them. It really gives me hope for their future games. Now you may ask, "Why did you take time out of your day to write this? You dumbass." 1. I don't think the complaints for the game were warranted at all. 2. I have no life to waste. 3. I don't want people to turn their heads from this game because they read all of these bad things about the game and that it wasn't a "continuation of meat boy." 4. I think this game deserves better than what it's getting. It truly is an amazing game that I can see myself playing for 100+ hours.
In all, if you enjoy a challenge (and I mean a REALLY hard challenge) then I advise you to definitely put this at the top of your list of games to play. Even though I like this game, I acknowledge that people don't like games that are difficult and don't have the time/effort to put in to play this game. While it's hard for me to say this, I advise you to stay away from this game unless you, all of a sudden, have changed your mind about it.

Having played League of Legends for about 4 years, I was starting to get tired of it. Wanted  a new moba. This really hit the spot for me.
The balance in the game is genuine and very good. Unlike League, or Dota, it's not the end of the world if one of your teammates goes AFK. I have already carried a game in a 4v5 and we won rather well. The lost teammate only made it slightly more difficult, but not a steam roll like other moba's.
If you like playing supports, this game is very support friendly in lane as well. Just being near the ally who last hits will net you half of the gold, while he takes the other half. This allows the support to harrass or play safe if need be without being completely punished. Additionally if you stay out of combat for a little bit, your hp and mana regen twice as fast. You may think this then turns it into "easy mode and turtle". That's not necessariy the case either, since the tactic simply changes from traditional moba's. Forcing the opponent to have to back to base, since sticking around would be too dangerous.
The real gem of this game though is the crafting. Take any moba you may know, and think of the items. At player level 4, you unlock the ability to customize the in-game items for added benefits and enchantments. You can customize any item in the game with bonus stats or buffs, but at a cost to gems, etc. you get after every game.
As a bonus.. all champions are free to play instantly. No grinding credits like in league of legends. They're all available at level 1. The credits and gems you get ingame go towards buying skins, or customizing an in house item to boost your favorite champ in-game with your personal playstyle.
The developers are being very generous with this game, especially since you can buy any skin ingame just by playing games. You can either purchase the skin for 1 day, or for a higher price permenantly purchase it. However, if you buy it for 1 day for say, 15 Gems, that cost is knocked off of the final price for permenant. How cool is that?
If you're looking for a new moba I'd highly suggest trying this one out.
Update:
I wanted to update this Review slightly and talk about the balance of Strife. I explained it below but it's broken up with other information so I'll explain it more cleanly here.
In League of Legends and Dota they have what you call the "Snow ball" effect. Essentially once you start winning, it gets harder and harder for the other team to stop you, unless you're playing evenly matched teams, and or it's a fair 5v5. In most cases this doesn't happen. As one team is always at some form of disadvantage. Whether it be a troll, afk, disconnect, or some other factor in many cases.
League of Legends "Snow ball" effect is softer than Dota's. In the form of the drake and  baron. Drake giving permenant buffs to the whole team, while baron is the insult to injury final knock out.
The problem with these two monsters is it is very easy to disengange and re engage away from them, the laughably low damage of the drake especially literally allowing the winning team to fight while taking damage from them and still win the team fight against the enemy team.
In Strife, this can't happen. We'll consider the two mobs as the Boss and Super Boss. The Boss in Strife in comparison to the Drake in league. You must kill the Boss 3 times. After 3 kills you get 1 wave of super minions. Unlike League's Drake which buffs the whole team permenantly for a snow ball effect. You do get some global gold for every kill on the Boss, however it is a fair and even amount.
The Super Boss, in comparison to Baron, once you kill it you get an Ape which goes down the lane of your teams choosing. This Ape you must protect as it knocks down turrets and disables them. While it is a very powerful tool there is a catch.
Unlike League where even Baron is rather weak at higher levels, and the team steam rolling can easily fight off the losing team while simultaniously fighting Baron at the same time is far far less likely to happen in Strife. The super Boss and Boss in Strife scale much better than in League of Legends, creating a situatoin where if you even want to kill it at any level you need at least a minimum of 3-4 teammates there. All of them if you want to get out safely, even at max level, unless it's super late game where 3-4 teammates will suffice to safely secure.
This creates a very real possibility that the losing and weaker team can out play the winning team, and take the Super Boss from them. Since the Super Boss will be doing significant damage through all the levels to the entire team fighting it.
Even the way the Super Boss is positioned on the map is far more fair to both teams. Unlike League of Legends where the position of the Drake and Baron are more favorable to one side due to the positioning of the pits. The Super Boss and Boss locations in Strife are positioned in the middle of the map on opposite ends with the open part of the pit facing to the sides of the map, but not at any 1 base. Creating a fair entry point for both teams, without 1 team having to take an extra detour around a wall the other team didn't have to make, or forcing the enemy team needing to use flashes or abilities to jump the wall if they need to contest it quickly.
Dota's Snow ball effect is a much harder one. As you kill players you take a significant amount of their gold and add it to yours. This is a very hard snow ball effect as gold is everything. This is the #1 rule in Moba. GPM is everything to most players and most professionals in Moba. If your gold is literally being stolen at every oppertunity this creates a massive snow ball effect to the winning team as they continue to kill the opposite team and take all the gold. This results later in the game the enemy team not being able to win fights they may have had a chance to win otherwise in a vast majority of cases.
9/10 games in Dota 2 that I've had were a snow ball game, where 1 team got the advantage and steam rolled the other, whether it was my team or the other team. That's my personal experiences in Dota 2, and the logical mechanics of taking gold from the team for kills only supports the fact of the snow ball effect.
This of course as I explained above, doesn't happen in Strife either.
This create a situation in Strife that is both fair and balance through every stage of the game, while still giving boons and rewards to the winning team, but not making it so that it determines the outcome of the game, or makes it nigh impossible for the enemy team to contest you down the road.

I loved this game.  It's basically a moody adventure game with real-time dialogue trees.  The dialogue is strong, the story is engaging, and the atmosphere is at turns funny and scary.
The main character, Alex, is likable and well-acted, but her friends are a mixed bag.  Two of them are likable, while the other two are straight-up unpleasant - one on purpose, the other not.  Ren, her closest friend of the group, is a weird Charlie Bartlett-type that is both cloyingly verbose and a burnout, which is a combination I've seen lots of in 21st-century fiction but (and I realize this is anecdotal) never in life.  I chose not to be around him at every opportunity, with no regrets.  Part of the fault lies in writing, and the other in the performance, which is that sort of mumblecore in which the actor stutters and "um"s and "uh"s intentionally, which I have no inherent problem with, but it has to be done exeptionally well or it feels false.  It felt false with Ren.
The story is a cool combo of horror and sci-fi, but is more moving than it is scary.  It uses the primary conceit, which I won't spoil, to delve into Alex's past, and explore her regrets, along with how those experiences tie into her relationships with the other members of the group.  The ending (the one I chose, anyway, which involved extra legwork) was a little vague and anticlimactic, but at that point it wasn't really about the big mystery any longer for me, so I didn't mind.
Moving past that, I still greatly enjoyed my time in this world, and among these characters, and I want to give credit to the part of this game that really tied the whole experience together: the UI, specifically the dialogue tree.  Letting the dialogue just happen while you go about your adventure game business is brilliant.  Characters will be talking to you, and suddenly you'll have a choice, which will manifest as three dialogue bubbles over Alex's head.  You click the corresponding button on your controller/keyboard (on an XBOX controller, it's X, Y, and B, for the left, center, and right dialogue bubbles) to make a choice, which Alex will respond with at a natural point in the conversation, but you must select it within a short timeframe or Alex will decide for you - or simply say nothing.  This mechanic makes interacting with the conversation while focusing on other tasks extremely intuitive - just as a conversation while walking along a forest trail would actually be.
All in all, I had a great time, and finished the game in one sitting (about 4 hours).  I highly recommend it if this sounds like it's for you.  If it sounds like you'll find it grating, though, I'll be honest: yes, you might.

I've followed Micheala Law's stuff for a long time, and I've been looking forward to this game for months.  All that waiting paid off, and I wasn't disappointed;  another game with fantastic writing, great characters, and a story that keeps you guessing the whole way through and packs a strong emotional punch.  The game's artistic quality is also top-notch:  all of the artwork is gorgeous and detailed, the music and sound design is beautiful and does a great job at setting the right tone, and the voice acting ranges from pretty good to absolutely fantastic.  You can tell that the main actors are giving their all, and boy does it pay off at the right moments - the final act of the game really hits you like a truck because of their performances.
The story had me on the edge of my seat the whole time - the constant tension of trying to figure out who was guilty and who wasn't played a large part in my enjoyment of the game on my first playthrough.  I also had some fun trying to figure out ways they could escape or fight back against the kidnapper, though none of them played out.
Subsequent playthroughs are also worth doing - each character has their own spotlight route, if you choose to focus on them in the cutscenes.  Each one feels pretty unique and it allows for some really nice development of their personalities, backstories, and relationships.  It also unlocks some really nice bonuses in the 'Extras' area, like the kidnapper's journals and some bloopers from the actors.
That being said, the game isn't without some light criticisms.  Particularly the maze portions:  While the puzzles themselves are well thought-out and genuinely challenging, the technical limitations of the Ren'Py engine prevent them from working as well as they should.  The controls lag occasionally, and the block-by-block movement can mess with players' timing when it comes to switching direction.  Another thing to mention is that the maze will change every time you play:  if you fail and reload, you won't get the same layout to navigate as you did before.  While this does add another layer of challenge, it also messed with me quite a bit on my first playthrough;  the Ladybug puzzle in particular took me around two hours to complete because I had no idea which map I would be dealing with and kept mixing them up at critical moments.  Oh, and the game's background music can get a bit loud at times too, but that's hardly worth complaining about when it can easily be fixed by changing the audio settings.
Overall, I would definitely recommend this game for anyone looking for a great thrill ride.  15$ might seem pricey at first, but trust me it's worth every penny and it's going towards supporting a pair of game developers that honestly deserve so much more recognition for what they do.

When i finally got to the gameplay and mazes, I found myself slightly scared, as each is pretty terrifying, but also determined to beat it. On top of that, the voice acting for everyone in the game was almost perfectly done, even for the villain themselves. Whether it was characters breaking down at certain points of the game or
, the voices really got the emotion and intensity of the scene across.
Ultimately, i feel that the game is more of a psychological puzzle game than it is a horror game, but i understand what the creators were going for. I had a very satisfying experience with the game and I highly recommend purchasing it. Solving a mystery and heading through a maze was never so satisfying.

A sharply-written, engrossing and enjoyable tale. I thought initially that the dialogue and voice acting might become grating after a while, but they turned out to be the best part - often funny, occasionally moving and entertaining throughout.
There isn't much challenge in the limited gameplay; the hardest part is choosing dialogue responses in a limited time, especially when those can go on to have big consequences.
A few gripes - dialogue is cut off too frequently, dialogue choice bubbles can on rare occasions fall beyond the edge of the screen and loading times are a bit sluggish (particularly grating when combined with the large areas and slowish walking). This was one of my favorite games growing up, but I'm sorry to say it hasn't aged well at all. I can't recommend this version as-is, although mods and fixes might exist to address some of my complaints. Haven't looked.
Pros:
- ~100 years of transport simulation in North American, British, and Swiss environments.
- Scenario editing with decent customizability. You can't write new victory conditions or do anything too incredible, but it gives you full control over the resources available and the map.
- Tons of pre-built scenarios of varying difficulty.
Cons:
- Very limited simulation. You can't set your own prices, so competition is purely a matter of delivery speed and building stations that receive more of the seemingly arbitrary resource outputs. New resources do not develop over time.
- Dull early game. Small maps, early starts, and small towns leave very few opportunities for profit and often only a single way of exploiting them. It feels like "connect everything to everything" more than anything else.
- Stability. Alt-tabbing once is fine. Alt-tabbing a second game always crashes the game. Crashing on its own is hardly uncommon and there's no autosave.
- Building controls. It's possible to build two pieces of track that overlap perfectly and don't actually connect, and some types of track can't be built from eachother for seemingly no reason.
- Route building controls. Busses and trucks can end up in infinite loops that aren't even logically part of their route. One loop I saw had a bus driving off-road to keep its endless square alive. Trains will ignore stations they've decided are unreachable without telling you.
- Terrible random maps. "North American" climate resulted in an entirely desert map multiple times. There don't seem to be settings between "mostly water" and "all land" unless you want mountains. Industries routinely spawn so far from required resources that they're basically unusable.
Since I got it on sale and had some nostalgia for it, I don't necessarily regret my purchase, but I can't possibly recommend anyone else buy it.

Squad offers an addictive mix of high-octane combat and realistic mechanics that is unlike anything I have ever experienced. No other game captures the sheer chaos of combat like Squad does. Absolutely worthy of the "Whoooaaaaaaa, dude!" Steam Award.
Teamwork is essential to enjoying the game to its fullest, so if you bristle at the thought of following the orders of your squad leader and don't want to lead a squad yourself then this game is likely not for you. The vast majority of people I have come across are very willing to answer questions and explain any orders if asked politely. Most are not military tryhards who will be screaming jargon at you, though you can probably find those people if that's your thing :)
The developers actively communicate with the community and the pace of development feels adequate. The pace seems to be picking up lately as more fundamentals are implemented and progress can be delivered in smaller pieces.
Pros:
-Combat is intense like no other FPS game.
-The sounds are amazing and immersive -- I duck nearly every time a RPG lands nearby or bullets crack the air a few inches from my head.
-Graphics are beautiful and performance is great. (i5 3570K 3.4ghz, GTX 970 4gb, 8gb system RAM)
-In-game voice communications are excellent quality.
-You will learn how to use a map.
Cons:
-Server browser is not ideal and there is no queue for joining, but there have been improvements recently.
-Difficult to overcome instances of severe lack of coordination among squads, but normally there is enough to at least have a good game.
-Somewhat long load times with my HDD.
Overall I absolutely recommend this game to any fans of realistic shooters. Watch some gameplay videos if you are still unsure and want to see the game mechanics in action.

Don't know what to make of this one. On one hand, yeah, you're basically doing everything again, but this time with a green HUD. On the other, this is an extension of an amazing game. So, what's different? Actually a lot.
For one, the tutorial. Actually kind of sets the mood; putting you through boot camp, and full metal jacket boot camp too. And then you actually get into game. You gotta meet officer chunk. The living meme himself, proto-paul blart mall cop. This time he's on your side and he's ready to fight. Of course, after he's done shoving his hand in a vending machine.
Unfortunately, that's where the funhouse ends, and its time to dive face first into what you really came here for: the Black Mesa vent crawling simulator. This one is significantly longer than Blue Shift, and it kind of follows the same structure as the first game, with some welcome deviations, of course. At this point, I feel like I must've explored a million miles of the facility, and that it must be bigger than the entirety of civilization, despite it only having a small lunch area, and one lobby.
If I could point to any game between the three of them as being the weak link, I think it'd be this one. Feels a little less cooked than the others. I don't know. The NPCs are useless, same as before, but the difference is this time instead of just being in your way, they're necessary for progression AND in your way. Woooo! The gun selection is slightly larger this time around, too. You get a few new toys, and a reskin of a toy you already had. (Looking at you, magnum pistol.)
What else is there. Did I mention NPCs are useless? You actually need their help at crucial points in game. No joking. You need everything to fight the new alien super elite. And they're packing heat too; enough to shred you and your fellows like paper. This game gave me the most trouble out of the three. And that's no small feat considering the difficulty curve on the original Half Life. These new aliens are tough.
The cherry on top is the last area leading up to the ending. It's underwhelming. I didn't even know I was walking in on the final boss before he just appeared to challenge me to a dangerous game of Uno. What he didn't count on was me being smart enough to immedietly beat him in two minutes, completely nullifying his presence as a final boss. I prefered giant floating fetus, honestly.
Would I count this as necessary? Not really. It's a Half Life game, so it's still a million times better than any regular FPS though. I'd consider the time well spent, even if this time around I was a little more disillusioned. The memes were spicy. Two thumbs up.

This game had remnants of Bizarre Creations (Project Gotham Racing / Blur) and Black Rock Studios (Split/Second) working on it, and their experiences seem to show through. This is a very fun kart racer that often benefits driving skill more than having the luck of the moment - not that the latter doesn't help.
Focus on the racing line is important (which is reinforced by the brutal World Tour and Time Trial modes), and the items require good senses of aim and timing to use effectively. The tracks are all very fun, with some particularly nasty turns sprinkled here and there to make things interesting (see: Chilly Castle), and the transormation gimmick is used well to create variety within the same track. However, the boat transformations are usually less pleasant to drive through, due to the delayed steering and the risk of losing a lot of momentum very quickly due to one wrong move. There are lots of characters to unlock, and they all have "mods" to unlock that drastically change their handling, so a character you like with base stats you hate can eventually be tweaked to better suit your driving style. The online play is usually smooth, but there are some collision oddities that can result in your vehicle flying across the track due to a light bump with an opponent.
Highly recommended to those who like arcade-style racers.

Huh. I actually don't like it. I've 100%-ed each game by Edmund so I've been a fan for a minute, but End is Nigh came out so quickly that I didn't have any expectations for it. The focus is far more on precision platforming. Meat Boy's charm was it's fluidity, speed, and precision platforming at 100 miles a minute. This is far more methodical and drawn out- not to mention a lot of forced trial and error. Collectables are pretty meh, with cartridges being a big ticket item. However, they're merely more stages in lo-fi graphics. Music is great. There's an odd charm to the fact that 30-50% of the soundrack is public domain music, but remixed with the gothic/rock stylings of Isaac. Animations and graphics are fantastic. Controls are perfect. It's a very self contained game- no map for each stage, no real cutscenes (so yes, you must backtrack through each world in its entirety to search for collectables. Your mileage may very on that one). But with no real charm, a bland color scheme for each world, little variety, and mostly just waiting, jumping in the right spot, and repeat (as opposed to Meat Boy's dynamic levels with far more obstacles and variety from different mechanics and speed that kept things fresh),
End is Nigh is basically Meat Boy distilled down to its main mechanics, remove wall jumping and sprint, and in doing so switch the focus from fluidity to precision platforming over dull stages that never feel like they change and collectables that feel very empty and unrewarding

Just picked this up from the latest Humble Bundle and was pleasantly surprised with how good this game plays. Most of the negative reviews of Abyss Odyssey were that the controls were bad, or weird but I'd only agree with people playing with the keyboard.
this game plays very well and its play style is reminiscent of Castlevania: Symphony of the Night. Granted, the actual story and game progression is different from castlevania, but the many different abilites triggered from different directions of attack gave similar feelings.
I like the idea that the play-throughs are a bit different everytime and things unlock as you play so that there's a want to go back an play again. Definitely worth 2-5 play, and with the 3 hours I've played so far I've beaten the boss 3 times. So overall about an hour of gameplay per playthrough.
I would say I wish the story was a bit grander. The visuals have all these beautiful accents and details that are wonderful, but the story is a bit like "Get to the bottom, you win. Do it again!" There are these journal pages, and they give more insight to what's going on. But they feel more like an explanation of the world rather than key elements to the story that will engage a player.
Overall, as a game it's fun. It's worth a couple of bucks, and will keep you interested for a few hours. Do I see myself going back to it? Probably not for a while. But was it worth the purchase? Yes, this is worth a go.

Half-Life: Opposing Force is an expansion of Half-Life 1. Instead of playing as Gordon Freeman from the normal game, you play as Adrian Shepard, one of the many soldiers invading the Black Mesa base in order to destroy Freeman, and end the alien infestation.
Much like the normal game, this game has no cutscenes, and mostly keeps you in control the whole time. Decisions you make can be based off of what you want to do, not what the game wants you to do.
A lot of the gun fights in this game are intense as hell, so expect a ton of heavy fire from the enemies in this game. Thankfully, this expansion adds a whole cake load of new weaponry that wasn't in the normal game. There are so many weapon choices, you can get overwhelmed sometimes at how much scrolling you'd have to do mid-combat. That's only a minor issue. All of the weapons play beautifully, and are pretty dang creative.
With new weapons also comes new enemies, and this game throws quite a bit of new enemies into the game. You'll only see the enemies from the normal game near the beginning, but later, the newer enemies make more prominent appearances.
This game's tutorial stage is also something really cool. Even if you know how to play an FPS, you should still check out the tutorial. It makes the game's story feel a little more fleshed out.
The few nitpicks I have are the aforementioned over saturation of weapons you get, and I also think that some of the chapters in this game just feel like a repeat of a normal Half-Life chapter, just with different complications and locations. Also, platforming is still an issue, but it shows up much less often than it did in normal-life.
Overall: 8.5/10

More like a rogue-like fighting game than a metroidvania style game, which will probably throw a lot of people off at first.  You're going to need to give the enemies more attention than you're used to, and the controls will not be like those of a platformer.
But if you're willing to put some effort into learning the controls, it can be a very challenging and fun title.
The art style and  atmosphere created make this one of my favorite games.  The enemies are interesting and well scripted, so that you'll need to learn their individual strategies and weaknesses in order to deal with them.  The three main playable characters have very different fighting styles and allow for customization of weapons, accessories and special moves.  These can synergize to give the player much more power when the right combinations are found.
The levels are procedurally generated, so each playthrough you'll want to pay attention to the map layout to find the most desirable route.  The different difficulties make quite a bit of difference in AI ability, and you'll want to stick to the easy levels until you get the hang of it.

Abyss Odyssey is a beautiful game with a nice gameplay and combat mechanics. It focus on the Hero/Soldier duality, when the Hero dies then a Soldier comes to continue it's progress. You have a chance to revive the Hero at an Altar if you make it that far. The Soldiers are weaker but still capable on their own and provide an interesting gameplay ideia: you're forced to do with the Soldiers what you could not do with the Hero.
The art style is incredible, all characters including enemies are very well design and the environments fit well within the game. The combat is varied and allows you to choose between 3 Heros + 3 Soldiers + about 20 different monsters you can summon once in a while. Each one has its own style and unique special abilities.
The game is a bit difficult, to get to the final boss you have to pass through many levels with different difficulties and if both your Hero and Soldier dies you're back to square one. There are checkpoints along the way to save progress but these require tokens which are quite expensive. Any attempt to defeat the final boss is an expedition that requires preparation and nerves of steel.
Pros:
- Amazing art style
- 3 heros to choose + a bunch of other playable characters
- Good combat
- Random generated levels improve replayability
- Made by the Zeno-Clash boys, guaranteed seal of Awesomeness
Cons:

In 1995, Chris Sawyer painstakingly coded Transport Tycoon in assembly. To those of you not familiar with software engineering, programming in assembly is like driving a car by pouring fuel into the engine and turning the wheels yourself, as opposed to Java, which is more like driving a car by letting your cat do it.
Everybody loved Transport Tycoon, mostly because nobody could afford train sets. This is still the case, which is why OpenTTD exists.
Seeing as nobody really cared about the other forms of transport in the game, himself included, Chris Sawyer made a sequel and named it Locomotion to make it abundantly clear that even if you find anything in the game that's not a train, you are strongly urged to ignore it. It's like the man is saying "trust me, you're not really here for the lorries that stop whenever they're being overtaken - I mean, do you even know what a lorry is? Thought so. Also the ships that are even more bland and slow than in the last game? They're that way so you can have the fun of building twisting railway bridges over the ocean because I built the game on the engine of a rollercoaster game I made! The second one! You'll never guess which! Also have fun hammering that left mouse button!"
To be fair, there's still some fun to be had building twisting mountain railroads and even bridges above entire cities using the rollercoaster tycoon 2 building tools. And you have the same degree of freedom, if not more, when digging underground, which is something not many games offer - which is a shame, I mean, if we take the Locomotion system and remove the part where you have to demolish everything on surface before you can edit anything underneath it (which in case of metro systems spells bad news for most of the above city's populace), as well as the part where your index finger and your mouse button partake in an endurance competition when building long stretches of rail, it might just make for fun and challenging railway building.
Of course you'd also have to code an AI that would not cheat in every way imaginable to build hideous twisting skyrails all over the map, covering much of it underneath in some kind of bizarre train fetishist orwellian fantasy, where the lower class lives underneath many layers of railroad bridges as their train overlords stroll on the surface while you and AIs as olympian gods watch from above, with you trying to convince Zeus Transport to stop being a♥♥♥♥♥♥and not take your cargo.
I'm afraid being religious still won't help when all your trains start breaking down every fifth tile of the way, no matter how much you pray for it to stop. Old man Chris would just never admit those were bad design, no, you absolutely have to do nothing but replace trains once you have more than 20 of them, it is so much fun, you see, you just fail to appreciate the genius behind it. You know what else is genius, Chris? Me taking a♥♥♥♥♥♥on your face.
That's not to say Chris Sawyer's Locomotion is a bad game, it just leaves a lot to be desired. It repeats many of the mistakes of Transport Tycoon, but it still improves on the basic formula enough for me to let it slide. In fact, if somebody were to tell me there was a sequel by the man in the works, you can bet I would preorder in an instant, then just copypaste this review over to that game's steam page and it would still be relevant.
Even if it's not perfect, Chris Sawyer's Locomotion is still a Transport Tycoon 2 under a different name, and that means something.

The End Is Nigh is a competent platformer, and a worthy spiritual successor to Super Meat Boy.
Pros:
+The music is incredible. Its some of the best music I've heard in a game in a long time. It's all remixed classical music. Any fan of the genre will smile every time they hear the themes they're so used to hearing come from an orchestra instead come from an assortment of instruments that give the music new life.
+Controls are tight. Most of the time when you die you know it's your fault for missing a button push or being a little slow (I'll touch more on the other part of the time in a minute).
+The art is pretty. It's nothing mind blowingly pretty or anything, but if you've played any of the designers other games like The Binding of Isaac or Super Meat Boy then you know what to expect; high quality illustrations that make the envirornment of the game more enjoyable.
+It's difficult. Every bit of progress you make is hard earned and it's very satisfying to reach a goal you've been working toward after suffering death after death. There's even added difficuly for completionists looking for the challenge in the form of collectibles called tumors that are placed in hard to reach locations.
+The atmosphere is well constructed. The game is funny, but it delves into extremely dark subject matter such as death, an apocalypse, and even subtle notes of necrophelia. The art and music both help to promote this eeriness while not taking itself too seriously by using dark muted colors (primarily grays) and primarily upbeat music that can make you laugh at a death and keep everything lighthearted when you reach your 100th death on a single screen.
+The story is compelling. The "npcs" you meet hint at a future betrayal and some deeper meaning to the death of everyone around you. That's all I can say about it without spoiling anything.
+The game runs well. Programmed by Tyler Glaiel, the program makes excellent use of his own engine, and is able to run on haardware that isn't necessarily suited to gaming while still looking great and maintaining a high frame rate.
Cons:
-It's difficult. I list this twice because there are moments when the challenge can become too much, and you can feel like you're dying for things that aren't really your fault. There is an enemy in the 4th or 5th area (depending on your choice of progression) that moves without much pattern and there's not a whole lot you can do to influence it in a specific direction except for continue to die and restart the level. On several occasions it didn't feel like I was playing a challenging platformer but rather that I was rolling the dice only to come up with snake eyes every time. I have yet to be able to reach that collectible due to the sporadic nature of these foes.
-The music kind of loops a lot. The music is great, and because of my own love for classical music I didn't mind too much, but there were times when I thought to myself that if I hear Hungarian Dance No. 5 one more time I'm going to lose my mind. This is really the only piece I've felt this way with, but it doesn't change the fact that all the others loop a lot as well.
As you can see by the absolute domination of pros compared to cons on the list; I've clearly enjoyed my time with The End Is Nigh. There is plenty of content and it's extremely enjoyable while providing a formiddable challenge to the completionist in me. I highly reccomend this game to anyone who liked the previous king of soul crushing platformers: Super Meat Boy, or really to anyone who enjoys platformers in general. It's exactly the kind of game I've been looking for, and will no doubt go down as a classic with the rest of Edmund McMillen's works.

Memories of a Vagabond is an RPG reminiscent of the old SNES glory days. Battles feature party members opposed to enemies in lines on either side of the screen a la Final Fantasy VI (or III in the US), there is a basic class system offering some versatility for the main character, as well as a few other recruitable allies with various set classes. While the game is an RPG Maker game, the visuals are reasonably good for the style of the game. The music is a noteworthy strength of the game, generally being catchy, exciting, or otherwise appropriate for the given circumstances.
I do not recommend this game however. For all of the things right, there are a number of faults that detract from the overall experience leaving the game, as a whole, lacking. The game is short, at a somewhat methodical pace, trying to collect everything in each level, the game's first playthrough didn't take more than a couple of hours. Most of my time in the game was fooling around with the controller settings in which there were legitimately issues upon release (to the developer's credit, they acted quickly to resolve this, kudos to them for that).
The gameplay seemed somewhat unresponsive, particularly in menus, being an RPG, this wasn't gamebreaking, but still slightly annoying throughout the game. A number of glitches existed and in the short time it took to complete the game, I encountered the screen freezing after a scripted puzzle moved the screen, rain that carried over to other areas (including inside a shop and houses), etc. In combat, most of the abilities felt uninspired and, on normal difficulty setting at least, they could be all but ignored. Attack and/or heal pretty much would win the game if characters were decently equipped. The attacks didn't feel necessary or worthwhile to do. For instance, one of the final abilities I acquired with my assassin class only dealt about 10% more damage than my regular attack on average, for a relatively high SP cost. SP moves felt lackluster as they cost large amounts of SP (particularly for non mage classes), but only boasted marginal damage increases for using them with few added effects that often were unreliable. (It MIGHT apply a status effect. and to this day, I've never sucessfully paralyzed an enemy with the mage's Paralyze spell.)
Story, was rather cliche and didn't feel relevant most of the time (if the gameplay were stronger, it might have been easier to overlook). Dialogue was usually particularly weak, with frequently mispelled words and conversation, at times, so unnatural to the point it was distracting.
Pro's:
+Good soundtrack.
+Pretty visuals.
Con's:
-Very short.
-Weak story/dialogue.
-Combat is not compelling, particularly abilities don't feel useful/necessary.
Fortunately the game's low price point and an available demo do not make this a huge investment and some may find the game worth the time to play it. It does have some redeeming values, The game felt as though it had quite a bit of potential and could have hit the mark, if it were lengthened and given more polish.

Among Gearbox's classics. First played on CD ROM circa 2002, then on Linux Mint 17.3 via Steam. Worth owning.
Half-Life: Opposing Force was created in a time when FPS single player campaigns and expansion packs (now called "DLC") weren't just rackets, and it shows. The opening scene sets up the story with no need for exposition. The environment practically tells the story, a'la Unreal or Quake. The very first area acquaints you with the mechanics just before the real action kicks in. From the use of atmosphere to the fully realized world to tutorial being built into the opening area, Half-Life: Opposing Force feels like a full stand-alone game.
The multiplayer component of Half-Life: Opposing Force is pretty cool, but nothing you haven't seen before. The multiplayer component utilizes the Black Mesa environment as an interesting place to compete with your friends in. Team Fortress and Counter-Strike already do this quite well. Nonetheless, it's pretty cool to have this multiplayer component included.
All-in-all, I enjoyed Half-Life: Opposing Force on my crappy ol' eMachines (566MHz Celeron, 32MB graphics, Windows ME) desktop back in 2002. With Mac and Linux support now available with the Steam release at only $5, I highly recommend it.

Abyss Odyssey is procedurally generated, side scrolling Beat 'em up. The player is tasked with venturing deep into the procedurally generated abyss with the goal of killing a warlock. In order to accomplish their goal, the player must learn the secrets of the abyss through trial and error. failure is common.
Throughout the abyss, the player will battle a multitude of dangerous creatures through melee combat. This combat feels sluggish and stiff initially. Later on however, it becomes much more enjoyable as the player masters the combat system and unlocks more moves. As a result Abyss Odyssey runs the risk of turning new players away before it gets interesting. Players who persevere are rewarded as they learn how best to combo moves and abilities together effectively, yet even in it's later stages, it lacks some of the polish found in other side scrolling Beat 'em ups. I found that using a controller helped a bit with some of the combat's issues, as the game was clearly designed with a gamepad in mind. Altogether the combat is decent, but not great. Little things like not being able to change directions in the middle of a combo and poor aerial combat drag the experience down. Where Abyss Odyssey's combat makes up for it's lack of polish is in variety. The number of playable characters is surprisingly impressive, and while many are not as developed as others, they still help change up the combat occasionally.
I was also pleasantly surprised by Abyss Odyssey's procedurally generated level design. While nothing groundbreaking, the levels it generates feel well constructed and reasonably different. While they still lack the same tightly focused nature of many hand-made levels, they serve as a good backdrop for the game's combat, even mixing in a bit of light platforming to break things up. Throughout these levels Abyss Odyssey offers the player many opportunities to make risk reward based choices which leverage immediate reward against the risk of long term peril. While a nice system, I rarely found any situations where the risks outweighed the benefits, effectively undermining the tension these systems could have created if they were more effectively balanced.
Abyss Odyssey's most notable feature is its art and music. The environments on display are beautiful to look at and manage to help disguise the procedural generation. Character designs are especially good. Each one is reasonably interesting to look at. As a result, I always enjoyed seeing what creature I would stumble upon next. Abyss Odyssey's soundtrack is also fairly good, and manages to capture the mood of the game just right. I especially liked the eerie guitar pieces, which add to the unique atmosphere.
Despite it's numerous flaws, I still believe I can give Abyss Odyssey a cautious recommendation. Anyone interested in a procedurally generated Beat 'em up will likely be satisfied, so long as they can overlook some frustrating design elements.

The AI isn't made of super rubber, there are no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t blue shells, the catch-up item is fair, the selection of characters is diverse and entertaining, the transforming mechanic really shakes up the pace and the tracks are a real step up from the last installment. It also feels more like a SEGA all stars homage then just Sonic & co. with some other peeps. You're really in the SEGA universe thanks to the wide representation of series, the music and the online works. That last isn' really SEGA, but contrary to Mario Kart's online, its a step upwards. I'm fueling a 90s console war debate here and I'm loving it. Great game.

I have played many MOBA games over the past 6 years. This includes HoN, LoL, DotA, DotA 2, Smite, Immortal Arena, HotS, and Prime World. I enjoy the games that had a lot of depth and strategy while being fun to play. And I must say Strife hit that magic point for me - a lot of content and strategy available while being very action packed and fun! never a dull moment.
About me: I am fairy experienced with Strife, have been playing on and off for a while. I just keep coming back because there is no better substitute for a MOBA for me.
Strife is a game that is full of action! I have never seen a game more action packed than Strife. It is not your typical boring farm and carry game. The game is based on ganking and proper team communication/play. There is the concept of "Out of combat regeneration" which triples your regenration of health and mana after roughly 10 seconds of not taking/doing damage. You can be in your lane, give it your all and push it, then while it is pushed up you can sneak to another lane and gank for them, and you will be at almost full HP/MP by the time you roam there. The games typically last 20-30 minutes with some very rare cases of 40+ minutes.
Bosses: The boss content is great! there is a giant monkey you can capture and it will push towers like a BOSS for you! and there is a portal you can spawn in each lane after multiple mini-boss kills that will summon very strong minions for you and they will push like CRAZY!
Roles: Support is not truly support and carrys are not truly carrys. If a team fight is 4v3 or 5v4 it gives your team a huge advantage, numbers DO matter. Of course sometimes a well position carry could kill 2 or 3 players but in no way a 1v5 is possible like in other MOBA games.
Art: At first I really disliked the art because of how cartoonish it was but eventually I realized that the simplicity of it makes the game easy to grasp visually. The character animations are great! I absolutely love them, as well as the taunts! Yes the taunts in Strife are something I have never seen before but I will leave it for you to explore (hint: Ace, Caprice).
Overall I see this game as having the proper content to grow and be a successful game! See you in game :)

Basic movement system of Super Meat Boy minus the ability to wall cling/slide and wall jump.  That mechanic is replaced by a corner hanging mechanic which turns the gameplay into a series of tedious precision jump puzzles.  The movement is so restricted that it takes most of the fun out of the game.  You'd think the ability to wall jump would be a small thing, but it really makes the gameplay trudge to a stop without it.
Since the rooms are so small and self-contained (failure means you respawn at the side of the room you entered), most of the challenge comes from things falling from the ceiling that looked like they were stable, or platforms moving that looked like they were stable.  It exchanges the relatively straightforward and fair difficulty of SMB for "screw you for playing this blind" difficulty, where the first few tries through a room are likely going to fail because of obstacles you couldn't see or account for.  This is compounded by the monochrome color pallete where spikes can sometimes be confusing to pick out from the background.
The addition of a loud, annoying voice for the main character adds nothing, thankfully it only seems to pop up in cutscenes and they're skippable on the first viewing.  Unfortunately, there's no way to turn them off completely.
In conclusion, don't buy this expecting a continuation of Super Meat Boy.  It's not that, and you'll likely be disappointed the same way I was if you go in with that mentality.

The storyline isn't what shines in Wolfenstein: The New Order. It's...okay, I suppose. It's not groundbreaking but it's not terrible. What really shines is the combat. It retains the classic feel of the original Wolfensteins, in terms of combat strategy (none necessary), combat flow (very fluid), and gun handling (nothing special necessary aside from point at bad guy). Yet it has the current gen polish that smooths out what was rough with the genre from it's inception. You don't need to crutch on one or two guns due to limited ammo. The controls offer more depth to position yourself advantageously.  Cover can actually be used, even if it isn't critical if you can hit the A and D keys. And it looks good, both in terms of graphics as well as art style. So buy it. Play it. Love it. I have no doubts about that.

I'm primarily writting to clarify for others.
First off, this is a GPU overclocking software. It is not a game, and shouldn't be treated as such. I've already read reports of users ruining their graphics cards due to chasing achievements associated with this software (a rather silly feature).
Second, many reviews are stating that a con of this particular steam version is that it requires steam to be running simultaneosly with the software. This isn't worded clearly though. Here is a direct quote from the EVGA website, from their FAQ regarding this software:
"Q. Does EVGA Precision X need to be running in the background to set clockspeeds and settings?
A. No, EVGA Precision does not need to be running, just make sure to select the Apply button before exiting."
So, while it's true that steam needs to be running simultaneously in order for the actual software to be running, neither have to be running in order for any changes/tweaks you've made to be in effect.
Overall I don't recommend this product on steam, because it's not user-friendly enough for the people using steam. The achievements should be removed, and the FAQ should be posted in the steam description.

This is a fantastic builder/management sim! It has a simillar look-and-feel to Prison Architect, but the gameplay is much more balanced; Prison architect is very management heavy, whereas Rimworld has a nice balance of building, resource gathering, combat, and storytelling. It's also challenging, you will lose a couple colonies at first, but it's not as demanding as Dwarf Fortress.
Pros:
- Fun to build and grow your colony
- Challenging to keep your colony alive, but not frustrating
- Stable, excellent interface and controls
Cons
- "It's about the journey, not the destination". Gets boring fast if all you want to do is "beat the game".
- You have to challenge yourself, the game will happily allow you to pick the easiest starting location and you can hand pick the best colonists to start with.
- Could use more content, has more than Banished, but less than Terraria/Stardew Valley.

BJ Blazkowicz is very likely the most interesting character that I've played as in a while. He is a total reinvention of his former pixely, stoic self, and the changes are much more than a fresh coat of paint. He's beautifully voiced, all Texas, cigarettes, and whisky add up to an amazing gravel in all the deliveries. He's also beautifully written, he's three dimensional, reacts and observes the world around him. He has become the epitomy of the man who doesn't talk much but thinks at 40 mph. The character of BJ alone is enough to play the 11 odd hours it takes to get through this game. But that's not the only reason you could have, either. The gunplay feels amazing, and it feels absoutely epic to be dual weilding shotguns. All that, alongside the really pretty environments that create pitch perfect atmospheres, add up to an experience that you absolutely deserve to experience.
Thumbs Up!

If you don't like games with a challenge, and if games such as Dark Souls make you whimper in a corner and cry, Abyss Odyssey is not a game for you.
In this game, you need to learn the controls. You need to learn how the enemies fight and you need to build and adjust your characters skills and special attacks in order to progress.
Some have described Abyss Odyssey as a mix of Super Smash Bros. Brawl and Castlevania? That comparision is only partly correct: the gameplay reminds me a bit of Super Smash Bros Brawl, but not Castlevania. Unlike in Castlevania, in this game, you cannot just whip&One-Shot-Kill basic enemies. A mob of low-level enemies can easily hack'n slash you into pieces, if you are not careful. Health vials are scarse, mana-vials are even more rare and good weapons cost a lot of coins. Did I mention there are no free save-points? In order to save progress, you need to grind enough coins, then you need to find a merchant who sells a camp token, and then you need to find an altar to use a camp token to have one or maybe two retries from that particular point.
The game graphics are sounds are awesome, but I am personally more attracted by the fair challenge of this game. The game is quite merciful to some degree: for example, dying does not automatically reset your character experience and it does not strip you from your special attacks you built, only your weapons and items are lost, and you are returned to one of the three starting stages.
I'd say learning to use different attacks and gradually proceeding in this game is the main hook, so for skill-oriented players looking for a bit of a challenge in a game, this is one to pick. The game is also very beautiful, has unique and interesting lore and is flawlessly designed.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game.

Abyss Odyssey
Rating 7/10
Overview: Unique 2D roque-lite
The Good:
+ Unique art style
+ Very creative enemy design. It is always refreshing to play a game that has interesting characters
+ One of the main aspects of the game is that you can collect enemy spirits by filling up your mana bar and then unleashing a devastating area of effect attack. Once you collect an enemy spirit you can then transform into that enemy and play as them. The game has quite a few enemies so capturing and trying out all the different enemies is fun. The only stipulation is that you have to be the same level or higher in order to capture an enemy.
+ The game has 3 main playable characters. You start with one but unlock the other 2 through different means. Each character has their own weapons, attacks and special attacks.

+ As you level up you gain skill points to upgrade your special attacks. You can either make them do more damage, get more mana or provide you with defensive abilities.
+ Soundtrack
The Average:
Given the unique art style, the level design is comparatively bland. This is a 2D roque game so each level is randomized. Although each level is designed differently in some way, every level feels the same. I find games like Spelunky and  even Risk of Rain to be good examples of randomization done right. The levels in those games truly feel different, hazardous and unique as you progress through the levels. Making it through those levels feels like an accomplishment, this game does not. Although there are plenty of environmental hazards to avoid the game is more about combat than navigating the levels.
You will either love or hate the combat. The combat IS good IF you take to the time to master it. The combat is a bit reminiscent of a 2D fighting game and it comes with some pretty advanced techniques to learn if you truly want to get the most out of it. The majority of players will probably just keep spamming their favorite special attacks over and over again.
Gold is useless. When you die you lose all currently equipped items which makes sense given the fact it's a rogue game however you get to retain your gold and experience making subsequent runs through the abyss easier. Many of the items the shopkeepers sell is usually over priced and since you lose your equipment anyways, buying any equipment feels somewhat pointless
Conclusion
It certainly is a very unique game something that I would expect from the developers of Zeno Clash. The combat is good and trying out all the different enemies is awesome the problem is everything else that makes a roque game good is average in this game.  This game certainly has potential to be a great game and a sequel that fleshes out some of the ideas would really help.

Gold earned is split fairly evenly between all heroes, so no player is ever pidgeon-holed into playing a support role and missing out on the action. The game engine is seamless, without any annoying delay in turn rates (dota 2) or creep bounty (LoL), while also boasting a vivid interface.

A pretty simple adventure game. Good enough story and cartoony graphics, characters were varied enough in personality, controls were simple (only directions and one action button).
It's a story about leading a group that was stranded on an island following a plane crash and trying to survive various situations until you're rescued. The story is pretty modular/separated; you just go from one problem/situation to the next and it's not especially connected. I don't remember any real foreshadowing; you deal with whatever is currently facing you, the problem is resolved, and you move on the the next problem. Your decisions determine which situation you face, what characters you bring (and some situations are handled better with certain characters), and who survives. There are fluff decisions and game-changing decisions, you'll just figure out which ones are which by trial and error. Certain decisions are on a timer.
There are some messed up situations but at least the cartoony graphics make it not so dark. Also, things go by really quickly; they never really lingering on a subject. When incredibly bad things happen, it's just a couple sentences and everyone accepts it and moves on. It simplifies a lot of things, keeps things light and moving.
Almost all of the interaction is in the choices. There are things to inspect but they're usually fluff (except things needed to progress the story). Sometimes it's nice background stuff or funny quips though. My least favorite non-dialogue interaction is the 'drag wood' minigame (which is exactly how it sounds). It was okay the first time but a pain to go through on every replay.
It's relatively short for one playthrough but there is enough content for at least three playthroughs where you see enough new situations in each run. Then after that it's about learning from the impact of your decisions to make sure you enter a situation in a certain state to try it in a new way (or by just using a guide to see what you missed).
It's very nice that there's a 'Day Rewind' function after you clear the game. It lets you more easily explore the choices and see the different situations. However, it's too bad that there's only one save slot and you're not allowed to rewind freely (you can only rewind to mornings and can't unrewind to future days after rewinding).
I would be nice to have the standard Visual Novel button to skip text/fast forward until the next decision. It would speed up replays and lower the time wasted. TL;DR
PlanetSide 2 is a great game, but it can be very frustrating for new players. Huge world, open combat with lots of playstyles. Solid 9/10 from me.
The game is dominated by experienced players, and there's a certain lack of direction that will be very annoying to players coming from games like Overwatch or Call of Duty. PlanetSide 2 is NOT a casual game, at least not until you learn how it works. There's no reason to start playing if you aren't prepared to sink some serious hours into it just to learn the basics.
With the disclaimer out of the way, I can talk about the positives :)
The community behind this games is the best I have ever found. They're very easygoing in the open groups, and you can find more serious groups like AoD if you want to have more of a realistic war experience. I've met a lot of my friends in PlanetSide 2, and it's relatively easy to find friends despite how overwhelming the massive world of Auraxis can be.
The weapon unlocking system is fair, but it takes a lot of grinding to unlock ALL the weapons for every character. It's best to start with medic or engineer on one faction and level everything to max before you move on. I say this because medic and engineer can grind "certs" (certification points) quickly by repairing vehicles and healing people. You then use certs to unlock weapons and tools. All the weapons are relatively balanced, they just appeal to different playstyles. The default weapon for each class is very good, if you unlock all the attachments for it and deck it out as best you can. Again, it's best to max out one weapon for one class rather than spreading yourself thin. Within infantry, different classes make an interesting rock-paper-scissors dynamic that requires players to have a good diversity within their ranks to win battles.
When you start the game, you choose between three factions: the Terran Republic (fast firing weapons with large ammo reserves and low damage per bullet), the Vanu Sovereignty (average fire rates and damage, with no bullet drop but slightly slower projectiles), and the New Conglomerate (heavy, slow firing weapons with smaller ammo reserves but stronger damage per shot). The three factions fight each other for map control on each continent, as the take land and lose land in a neverending battle for dominance.
The world is sectioned off into four continents: Indar (mostly desert), Esamir (covered in snow), Amerish (thin chaparral with some grasslands and lots of trees), and Hossin (thick swamp with lots of fog). you get to choose between coninents when you spawn in, although some are always locked (I'll explain why later). Each continent is a massive open map with objectives spaced evenly in "hexes" (tiles centered on bases controlled by one of the three major factions). Each base has capture points that, when your faction holds control of them for a few minutes, will turn the base to your side and allow your troops to spawn there.
It may seem simple at first, but base battles can range from 10v10 skirmishes to huge battles with over a thousand players fighting at once. These battles are the most cinematic and have brought PlanetSide fame, but they're usually not very fun for infantry, That's where vehicles come into play. Vehicles play a very important role in the game, as they are used as backup for infantry. Bus-like Sunderers can create mobile spawnpoints when setup, which allows an entire army to appear out of nowhere. Each faction has a large tank and fighter jet specific to their faction, as well as a multitude of other vehicles that all factions can use (I'd like to talk about all of them, but it would be much easier to just look at them on the wiki!). While you'll find yourself as infantry for most of the game, it's really fun to provide backup for you friends in a Valkerie, or just get together a group and sneak into an enemy base on a bunch of invisible ATVs!
Even with (at the time of writing this) almost 500 hours in the game, I can tell that I've barely scratched the surface of what this game has to offer. If you can make it past the first 10 or so hours of frustration, I promise it's enjoyable. If you aren't willing to put in that kind of time commitment before you even start enjoying it, that's fine and respectable. Just please don't leave an angry review complaining about how terrible the game is when you just aren't willing to commit your time and effort to a free game :)
So, thank you Daybreak. You've made an amazing game, and managed to make it fun for everyone, from free to play to hardcore players. This doesn't feel or look like a game from 2012. It can still actively compete with Overwatch and other FPS titles. That's entirely because of the support from the community and frequent updates and bug fixes from the dev team. Props to you and I look forward to your future endeavors (PlanetSide 3 in a new physics engine maybe?)

Before I start here Dark Messiah suffered bad reviews because of all the terrible bugs that launched with the game. now that 2 1/2 years have passed Dark Messiah's bugs have been pretty much been ironed out and you now have a pretty fun action RPG. Before I start explaining the game DM uses the Half-Life 2 engine so you can expect some wonderful graphics and effects. DM uses the HL2 engine very well, but the engine is a bit supped up so you'll need a fairly beefy rig to run this game. If you computer was being pushed with HL2 then your computer will have a hard time running this game. I also have to mention that DM felt a lot like Oblivion Lite in the sense that it is set in Medieval times, melee combat is first person, and the art style is a little like Oblivion (not as unique of course).
You play as a young protagonist named Sareth and you must stop the evil Arantir from using the Skull Crystal and bringing the Dark Messiah back to life. You have a choice to either stop him yourself or let the Dark Messiah live on. The story is actually fairly interesting and will keep you on the edge throughout this 15-20 hour adventure. Now DM is a linear RPG (it's not free roaming like Oblivion), but makes up for it with a intricate combat system. You have about 30-40 different item slots and you can carry things from health, mana, weapons, magic etc. As you progress through the game you will earn skill points for completing objectives and you can upgrade a variety of things from endurance, health, stealth, archery skill, learn new skills such as heal, fire arrow, freeze, sanctuary etc. There's a lot to learn and you won't upgrade 100% in a play through. You can either concentrate on being a Knight, Mage, or Archer or just go down the middle.
There are a variety of unique weapons you can pick up throughout the adventure such as the awesome rope bow (shoot an arrow at any wood overhanging and a rope will come down), ice staffs, flame swords, poison daggers, and even a cool electricity shield that stuns enemies when they attack you. Now there are no shops where you can buy things so everything has to be picked up throughout the world. This keeps the action constantly going, but will disappoint people who are used to having stores in their RPGs.
Combat consists of left clicking for your basic attack, but if you hold it down you do a Power Strike and whether or not you strafe, move forward, or backward will determine whether it's a side swipe, impale, or overhead strike. This can let you easily dodge attack and quickly strike back. You can use the right mouse button to block (and when you get the ability) left clicking to knock enemies back. Hit enough bad guys and you'll get your adrenaline bar up and this results in a gory slow-mo instant kill. This applies to all weapons and each of them have their own unique advantages to them. You have a kick button and this is great when you are on a ledge so you can just kick them off. Every so often you'll find spike beds on walls you can impale enemies on, also you'll find traps that can be kicked down to crush enemies.
While the combat is really fun and you can do a lot with it; it will get repetitive after about half way through unless you use different weapons and toss things up. Every so often you'll find a blacksmith room where you can add bars of metal and forge your own weapons. Now when it comes to enemies there aren't to many of them (knights, undead, spiders, necromancers, evil demons) and that's about it. They are mixed up a lot, but you still can get bored of them after awhile.
Every so often, though, you will get a great boss fight and these are huge creatures that require key items in the environment to kill them. These are pretty awesome and are very satisfying to take down. My biggest complaint must be the level design. A lot of times you won't find most of the hidden secret areas since they aren't even in places you'd remotely think they'd be in. There will be times you'll wonder around for over 30 minutes in the same place wondering where to go and this has to do with poor level design. The levels are very linear, most of the time dark, and really hard to navigate. Other than this Dark Messiah is a pretty good game, and you can even get it off Steam for $10! I highly recommend Dark Messiah to any action RPG fan.
~Score: 8/10

And it looks good, both in terms of graphics as well as art style. So buy it. Play it. Love it. I have no doubts about that.

This is not necessarily a full review of Abyss Odyssey but more of a response to a number of people saying they found the controls to be "clunky". When I hear clunky I think unresponsive, slow, or even glitched controls. I was initially turned off to buying the game because of this, but got it on sale anyway because it looked cool. I have to say I don't understand the complaints.  If you're looking to mash endlessly with gigantic hitboxes, then yeah you may not like the feel of the combat. Instead you have to consider each of your options and how to string them together to make them effective. It has a 2d fighting gamey feel in that each attack has specific ranges in which they are effective and everything can be special cancelled (up to three times in one combo). As a fan of many fighting games I enjoy this aspect of the game. Seeing what kind of combos you can pull off with each character and enemy soul is pretty fun. It is certainly a unique experience and I look forward to a sequel in the future.

I was intrigued by all the negative reviews mentioning the controls. Seems like everyone agrees something is not right but they can't quite put their fingers on it. "Feels heavy" some say, "jumping is awkward" others say. So I bought it out of curiosity! Before buying the game I even had a theory about the jump profile, but my theory was wrong.
I find the movements ok. Nothing particularly good or bad about it. It's functional. Grabbing ledges can be annoying at times though. The combat, with all honesty, is actually pretty damn good! I was shocked and surprised by it, judging by my low expectations. I am not sure why the poor reviews focus on that aspect. Maybe people went in expecting something alike Dust: An Elysian Tail, which has a very fluid and easy fighting mechanics. You can just mash the buttons in different ways and there's always a new combo there. But Abyss Odyssey is a completely different deal. Combat is extremely tactical, your movements are not instantaneous and you are not invulnerable while attacking, so you have to plan when to attack, watch your timing, be aware of other enemies around you, use defense correctly, use evasion etc etc. It reminds me a lot of Dark Souls actually. Not so unforgiving, fortunately, but the pacing is similar and it also requires focus and skill.
I still haven't finished the game, and some reviews made sure to point out that the game becomes unforgivable during the nightmare modes (each level has a random difficulty level). So I might change my recommendation if these modes are bad enough to make me dislike the game altogether.
So I find the combat good and the controls ok, what else? Yeah, the rest of the game is not successfully engaging me I'm afraid. First time I played I died pretty quickly, but the second time went on forever! I was starting to get tired and I wanted to stop playing the game but I never died, I just kept going and going and going. The environments are all too similar and the gameplay doesn't change in any way. I find the progression very tedious so far. Probably (this is me just guessing now) the game lacks more gameplay elements. There is platforming, but it's trivial challenge, and the controls wouldn't even support more than that. I'm thinking it needs sections with a slower pace, so we can catch our breath, look at the scenery, absorb some of the story, solve a couple of puzzles. I'm digressing now though.
This is my recommendation with a handful of salt (instead of a pinch, get it?). It's an interesting thing this game, I'm glad I bought it, even if I lose interest before finishing it.

I can't recommend this game enough.  All of this studios games so far have been taking conventional gameplay and kinda twisting it.  I'll tell you right now that's why many people like this game, and that's why also there's lots of negative reviews. From the looks of it, this game is a platformer hack and slash, but its a platformer fighter which has caused people disappointment when the game is a lil too clunky or hard.  That's not to discredit legitimate peoples criticism of this game, sometimes you wish you could jump just a lil higher or hit a lil harder or be a lil more responsive. But that doesn't get in the way of enjoying the game if you arent turned off so far.  There's endless replayability here as you have 2 main characters to level up as well as a later unlockable third as you travel down 3 columns of procedurally generated levels. On top of that theres 2 reserver characters that come in if your main dies.  One of the main mechanics is the ability to capture souls, allowing you to switch back and forth between your main and this monster soul.  As far as I know, you can capture every enemy in the game including the last boss, and each one has its own set of moves, though you cannot level them up.   If you like Castlevania but want something a lil different and new, get this.  If you like fighters, get this.  If you like Super Smash Bros., or Rogue-likes then you NEED to get this game.  Throw in an incredible art style, intense music, and a really great Dev team, and you get a wonderfully unique experience of a game.  I honestly believe this to be one of those "gems" that get lost in between the cracks of indie games.  This is worth every penny, especially if you can snag it on sale.

I absolutely LOVE this game! Every play through is so quick and concise, thus making it incredibly replayable. You play as Rita, one of the six survivors of an airplane crash, and getting stuck on an island forces you all to find ways to survive together.
What can I say? Each character is unique and nuanced, and there are tons of different things you can find out about them from subsequent playthroughs. I was pretty surprised by how much I didn't know a character until I went back and talked to them more, as well as get them to tag along for the daily task of survival. This could range from foraging for food, exploring the crash site for supplies, along with several ways to get off the island.
The combination of choices and outcomes seem almost limitless and you will find yourself wanting to explore the differences. And not all of them can be waited on, as there are some choices you need to make under a timer. These of course could mean life or death when your fellow survivors are about to be attacked by the island's wildlife. You'll be weighing your choices on what secret (if any) alliances you'd like to make with one or more survivors, and who to favour in your quest to survive.
What I love about the playthroughs I've done by now is wondering who to save and who to let go of. Sometimes I feel cynical and don't mind if someone dies, but then other times despite how inconvenient they can be, there are certain skills they posess that can help our group progress if I had only let that one person eat!!!
Anyways, I highly suggest this game at either full price or discounted. You can't go wrong with it. If you like choose your own adventure stories, this one has choices that matter and come up frequently!
Random sidenote: the soundtrack is BAWSS!!!
