I started Playing this game when it first started out before steam and have watched it change, pets were able to level and other features have changed as well.
Alright, the game is indeed fun and has a very casual feel to it. Characters are simply to learn and the items are not so abundant to be confusing. The game is planning a campaign or story system which the first chapter is realeased and it is really fun to have lore in a game that is playable.
Con:
The one and only Con that I have with this game that many people will not agree with is that the game has a bit of a play to win feature to it. This is in regards to the crafting system that is in place. The crafting systems allows for reworking on items piece by piece as such you can optimize the weapons and make them what you want and at the end you are able to enchant those items to give them sometimes a big bonus in the end that alter the game rapidly. This process uses in game currency that is earned in small amounts and by level up. It would take on average including quests probably a day or two worth of playing for a single craft. So a casual player that wants one or two games would not have the same ability. This system would not be to big of an issue if you couldn't purchase the crafts by using real money. Also currently these are permanent as well. The Matchmaking system does not take into effect that people may have a bunch of these thanks to money or just playig a ton of the game unlike others that can not. Thus you will get many games where one team will have a full inventory of custom items that boosts their specific style and granting really powerful bonuses while the other team may have one or two. This will begin to lead to a very one sided feel to the game and will create many loses. Until the system can add in the fact peopel have these items it will be unblanaced in that regard.
Now, if you are able to deal with this major flaw and some character that are at time unblanced or useless then go ahead and play. I still enjoy the game ut at times it will be one-sided and i hope the game will take this into effect one day.

The Talos Principle is a first-person puzzler like Portal, but with a more somber, philosophical tone to it. You play as a robot awakened and put to task solving puzzles by a booming voice in the sky known only as "Elohim". In the course of exploring and solving puzzles in Elohim's "garden", you come across fragments of texts and audio recordings that themselves have to be pieced together in order to understand the whole story. The game is concerned with a lot of deep questions regarding the meaning of existence, humanity and civilization, as well as curiousity and free will. The puzzles themselves start off as fairly simple, manipulating switches, boxes and fans, and slowly becoming deviously complex, such as having to creating copies of yourself to "co-op" with. Thankfully, the truly brainbreakingly difficult puzzles were left as bonus puzzles that could be skipped. Overall, a satisfying workout for the brain, in more ways than one

Since years I use Linux and my days are filled with happy computing. Only seldom memories of the dark days haunt my mind, when Windows was the main operating system on my machine. In the last years even gaming became not only a choice, but a pure joy on Linux.
Anyway, in a recent rush of grace I decided to commemorate one of the few positive aspects of these rough Windows-days and bought the HD remake of Age of Empires II. This game was always fun and (according to my believes)  is the sole reason why Microsoft is not on the list of designated terrorist groups. As long as the HD remake is somehow close to the original it cannot really disappoint. That were my thoughts.
Autumn-sales, even cheaper, what could possibly go wrong? A no-brainer! So its time to start up the good old VirtualBox running XP, which allowed me to play similar Windows-only games: Desperados, Diablo2+3, and even AoE3. The installation via Steam is as easy as expected. Right-click, Launch AoE II: HD. My mind was already playing the awesome menu tune tadaaaaa tadadadaaaa..
But instead an error message shows up: "ERROR: The application is not a valid Win32 application". Immediately all my joy was gone and I am in the middle of this sober and dry Windows-world, where the user is confronted with cryptic error messages, left alone in a complete mess of unresolved responsibilities. Reluctantly I start the tedious search for hints, what might be wrong and whose fault it is. And soon it becomes clear: This game requires Windows 7 upwards. I can't believe it. Windows 7. It was my fault, as I did not read the system requirements. Shame on me, ok. But after playing AoE3 and Diablo3 on that exact same machine, it was out of question for me that AoE2 might not run. And even if it is the HD remake, I simply did not expect this issue.
As I categorically refuse to spend any more money on that pile of bananas which Microsoft sells as operating system, I am stuck with a game I cannot play and some memories of good old times. Probably not that bad at all, except the disappointment which stays.
(In the end I had to get the win10 iso to install the game and get 5 minutes playtime to be able to write this review. I start to question life itself)

An artistic fighting game, and a welcome challenge.
A large variety of enemies adds some depth. Some enemies are quick and agile while other are large and slow with powerful or long range attacks. The ability to play as all of them except ghosts encourages you to learn how characters fight and counter them.
No two traps work the same and you are likely to fall for them. Randomly generated areas change the location of terrain, traps, and goodies. But it does not change the difficulty, level type (like ice or jungle) and therefore the enemies you will fight in tha area, or the prescence of a mini-boss, so it is largely predictable.
The combat is exciting yet unforgiving.  The game locks you into enemy encounters with more than one enemy until youve killed some of them, which can lead to one versus four scenarios. In spite of that, enemies tend to engage one at a time unless you have nightmare difficulty turned on, so the challenge is not impossible.
Enemy AI (except in 'easy' areas) knows how to utilize all of their moves and will likely punish you for using the same move twice, staying shielded for too long or shoot projectiles if youre running. Learning how to grab, air dodge, and special cancel is essential to fighting AI opponents.
One simple improvement they could have made is too give more options to getting up. Against humans opponents who can be fooled it wouldn't be a problem but AI opponents know where you will get up and then knock you over again.
The PC version suffers from the game having been developed for console. The controls are hard to get used to, and features like co-op and versus fall short. Co-op online even between two computers in the same room was prone to crash often. And although versus mode is great and you can play bots you probaly wont find games without friends who play it.

For this, a controller is a MUST for this game. If you don't have a controller, don't get this game (or get a controller. Lots of games are better with a controller anyways).
If you see a review complaining about the controls, ignore it.
Now, the game does have some issues, mostly in the tutorial aspect. It has a tutorial, but for things like the menu and the shop, not for some of the important concepts like Cancel Points, capturing creatures and transforming into said creatures. However, I still recommend it.

Oxenfree is the best kind of adventure game. It begins slowly, pulling you in with hints of mystery while you get to know the characters. Then things get weird, and the roller coaster falls over the edge, taking you along for the ride.
The sound and art combine to create a unique atmosphere that's creepy, but not excessively so. The music is a brilliant electronic staccato, percussive and synthetic, just as it should be.
The voice acting is exceptionally good. The characters come to life in a way so few animated ones do because of the voice actors. And this game is further evidence that everything Erin Yvette touches is gold (The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us, Firewatch, etc.).
The game itself is short, and not very challenging, though it can be frustrating if it seems like you can't find the right frequency for the puzzles.
They managed to cram a lot into the little island they created. The collectibles are fun because they're easy to find if you're looking for them, but easy to miss if you're not. And each of the different kinds of collectibles enhance the story in different ways. None of them are superfluous.
Your decisions matter. And the outcome does drastically change based on how you behave. For how much we talk about wanting player agency in modern games, that's still a rare thing to find.
Perhaps the best part of this game is that there's no sequel bait. No cliffhanger. When the story wraps up all the questions have answers - or, at least, some sufficiently satisfactory explanations.
You will want more, because you'll want to see how things change, how the plot can unfold differently. Oxenfree keeps you engaged across multiple playthroughs, and that's another exceptional point in its favor.
If you're a fan of adventure games this is the gold standard for 2016.

The light puzzle solving aspect of Dyscourse's gameplay - while not exceedingly challenging - lends well to the narrative, and in no way trivialises the game's message. Through controlling Rita, players become the unofficial group leader and are often forced to make final decisions about where to go or what to do next, something which presents a rather enlightening commentary on humankind. What do we do when we don't know? What do we do when we are afraid? Alone and marooned on an island, the dichotomy between right and wrong can seem almost negligible. This is what Dyscourse is about. Taking risks. It puts us into situations where we must decide in order to survive, and teaches us that in the face of adversity, trial error is not something that should be feared, but rather, something that should be embraced.
PROS:
+ Strong, polished visual style
+ Beautiful music
+ Good characterisation
+ Well paced
+ Multiple possible endings
CONS
- Puzzles are quite simple
- Short playthrough

Excellent little choose your own adventure style title. The game presents itself as a series of difficult choices. You control the fate of a small group of plane crash survivors, each with their own skills and opinions on the best way to move forward. The art style is excellent, and each character is distinct and interesting in terms of looks and personality. As a sort of de factor leader of the group, you will make decisions about how to proceed that may (and probably will) get people killed. There seems to be a sort of mysterious (possibly fourth wall-breaking) story to it all which will require multiple playthroughs to fully explore.
This is a short game, and may not be for everybody. But if you like the idea of watching a character-oriented story in the vague vein of Lost unfold based on your decisions, this is a great game for you.

+ great brawler gameplay

+ tons of unlockable characters
+ tons of unlockable weapons & animals
+ level design and atmosphere

There are three modes to play - Campaign, Arena and Back Off Barbarian. The Campaign is the main source of fun, the levels are different, the challenges unique and the bosses cool. But they best way to experience this game is not solo (although you can) but through the wonderful co-op. This is where the game shines as you share your adventure with up to three buddies. After you finish the standard campaign Insane mode will unlock with all the New Game+ fun and challenge. The only thing I can point out as glitchy here is that progress updates strangely and sometimes you have to re-do a level because it won't save for your friends (or you, if you are not the server). Arena is fun competitive fighting and Back Off Barbarian is precise button pressing alone or with a friend. Each character has their own save and XP progress. You can unlock lots of character, weapons and tiny animals to help out. Fighting is responsive with options between ranged (archery, magic) and melee. Playing with keyboard is really doable but feels suboptimal. Mainly because your fingers start to hurt real quick. There are a lot of combos and tons of button mashing and a good gamepad helps with this. Behemoth humor and art-style are awesome in all of their games, Castle Crashers are no exception. This makes for a great game and one of the best co-op games currently on Steam for both casual and hardcore gamers. Don't miss out on this great experience!

So I really liked this game. The combat was very easy to control and get used to and yet hard to master as any good fighting game should be. The Abyss that you go into is interesting and there are several characterrs you can meet who are all interesting in their own way. The three playable characters are fun to play as, as well.
One thing I don't like is the levelling up system, but this may only be me. You level up by getting EXP by kiling monsters in the Abyss and for every 3 levels you get a skill point that can be used to upgrade one of your 3 special attacks in 3 different ways. Or you can use it to get a permanent cancel which lets you rapidly use a special or dodge during attacks. This is all the variety you get. I would have enjoyed it better if you had a bigger variety of skills you can upgrade such as your attack or speed or ability to dodge or defense. This to me felt limited.
A funny story though is as soon as I unlocked the second character, The Monk, I decided to play as him. I expected to die pretty quickly because that's what I had been doing with the first character. But as a level 1 character, who eventually reached level 19 by the end, managed to beat the whole Abyss and the last boss in my first try. I hadn't ever played as this character before and I beat the game first try. Whether this is good or bad, is up to you. Personally I think I was just lucky to have found so many health potions in the dungeon. I personally recommend this game as it was the first Rogue-like I actually liked. 4/5

Squad is a rare gem that only comes around every once in a while, the perfect blend of teamwork, communication, and an unforgiving battlefield.
Work together or your squad will fall apart and become easy targets for the enemy.
With vehicles the game flow has improved considerably, partly due to the asymmetrical game design that is consistent throughout the game and compliments the real world settings of Squad.
Vehicles don't feel like an all-powerful ark of protection rather a fragile paper boat that can be destroyed in seconds by a well coordinated ambush attack - which makes driving vehicles tense and rewarding when running supply runs or dropping troops off at the battlefront.
All in all, Squad is a great game and highly recommended if you enjoy tactics, teamwork, and communication.

This game is difficult to give either a negative or positive review for.
It takes your classic worms and gives it a new look and feel with updated graphics, physics objects, an assortment of new weapons and utilities, but still leaves a lot out.
Worms Revolution is both comparable to Worms: Reloaded and Worms: Clan wars but to me, seems to be the best of both worlds.  It's got it's share of bugs, such as when you use the worm swap utility, you may be left with an un-useable worm.
The narration is witty and funny, but can slow the progression of the game down with all of the random banter.
The addition of dynamic water and physics based weapons bring a new spin to the game but it falls flat with the lack of diversity.  Weapons seem to be less powerful as their old counterparts but is offset by the various classes of worms.
If you're looking to play multiplayer, there isn't that big of a community to play with random people; it's a game best played with other friends online or locally.  If you love the social aspect of worms matches, you'd be better off with Worms: Armageddon.  It's still a personal favourite and holds true to the community.
In conclusion, Worms Revolution IS a fun game, and you can spend hours in the single player campaign as well as the multiplayer fun, but you should wait until a good sale comes around.  There are a lot of little, frustrating bugs that happen constantly (like the worm swap bug, or when you stand on another worm and the one being stood on CANNOT MOVE).
All in all, it's still a very fun game that I've invested over 50 hours in (playing locally myself or with others).
All I really have to say is thank you Edmund and Tyler. Thank you

Remember how the great writing and voice acting in Telltale's Walking Dead game really conveyed the tension among a group of strangers trying to work together to survive the zombie apocalypse? Dyscourse is basically a VERY poor imitation of that, with no voice acting and TERRIBLE writing.
The biggest problem is that none of the six characters has any real depth, and two in particular are ridiculous, cartoonish stereotypes. The conspiracy nut's CONSTANT paranoid interpretation of the most innocuous things ("Cats are evil robot spies!") could work in a game with a lighter, silly tone, but people DIE in this game! It also could have worked if the other characters discussed whether this obviously delusional man under extreme stress was a threat to them (like the Wal-Mart worker in Telltale's Walking Dead game), but no, they brush it off. And then there's the GAMER character, who makes Law and Order's episode about Gamergate seem respectful in comparison. He relates EVERYTHING to video games, which again could have worked if he were portrayed as severely autistic, but instead he's as silly as a witness in a Phoenix Wright game, which does NOT fit Dyscourse's tone.
The writing is also frustratingly bad, with characters doing stupid, nonsensical things (when you find a small pond that's your only source of fresh water, one guy inexplicably JUMPS INTO IT and ends up covered in leeches) and seemingly NO ONE in the group has even a basic common sense understanding of how to survive. For example, one character is insistent on the importance of coming up with a way to signal any passing plane or ship. The obvious choice would be to get a signal fire ready, but instead they only make an SOS out of driftwood on the beach, which would only be seen by a plane flying low overhead during the day. Your characters also come across an easy source of meat, but choose to go hungry instead.
The only silver lining to this game is the bonus campaign where a bunch of indie game devs have been stranded on the island. It's actually somewhat funny because it has a silly tone, so all the moronic characters and game references work.

Okay, first off, this is a hard game, especially if you're going to be going for collectibles. The levels get quite unforgiving quite quickly, even in the first area, and the difference in timing between success and failure can sometimes be measured in tenths of seconds. Additionally, the controls are really precise, so when you screw up, you don't have anyone to blame except yourself. Therefore, it's not for everyone.
Second... I like this game. It has its charm, and it has the sort of charm that you'd expect a lovechild of Edmund M (Time ♥♥♥♥, Super Meat Boy, et al.) and Tyler Glaiel (Closure) to have. Invariably, there are going to be comparisons to Super Meat Boy, but this doesn't do either game justice. TEIN is a slower, more precise, and more methodical experience with bursts of intensity throughout. There isn't a timer that you're racing to get A+, there are no alternate characters that are better-suited to certain levels than others, and the obstacles that TEIN offers are different than those in SMB, but not inherently simpler. TEIN's levels are dynamic in a different way than SMB's as entire sections of the map can move and react to the player in a way that didn't happen in SMB. Additionally, TEIN has to be the one modern platformer that doesn't have homing missiles anywhere in the main game. If you're expecting another SMB, this is not it. This is barely even a spiritual successor, and that's okay.
Death is a frequently occuring event but one you recover from quickly. Ash controls very well in the air and doesn't keep his momentum upon releasing a movement key (which may or may not be your thing, but does make landings onto small platforms easier). The individual levels are for the most part short and focus on one idea at a time (though there are plenty of exceptions to both). The areas each have their own distinct styles and mechanics.
The game's tumors are a nice mechanic. They're collectibles that you have to enter a level, collect, and then leave the level by some means other than warping using the map to keep, and they're present in practically every level. For the most part they are gained by taking a harder route through an area, backtracking, or getting in and out of a hidden area (which gives you five at a time). If you lack the skill or patience to get one, you can always skip it any come back to it later. They're optional, although they unlock additional levels for you and become very important in late game (specifically,
).
The game also has its retro levels, and quite a lot of them. Some give you ten lives (nine revives) and a continue to get ten more, some require you to beat the level sequence without dying, and some have progression similar to the main game. Accessing them requires you to get game cartridges, which are usually tucked away in hidden levels and don't require you to leave the level to keep them. As an added incentive to do the retro levels, completing them gives you bonus tumors. The better you do, the more bonus tumors you get.
In terms of performance, the game runs really well at full resolution, even with all the settings turned to max on mid-range current-gen hardware. However, as it is a vector graphics game, lower-end computers may still stuffer while running it (even with Glaiel's tricks).
However, that's not to say the game is without its faults.
While there is a warp system, the warp points only take you to the start of each area and not all of the levels are traversible in the opposite direction, meaning if there's a collectible closer to the end than the beginning, you may have to traverse all the way from the beginning of an area to get it anyway. This leads to a lot of retracing your steps. At least it's practice, right?
It doesn't always feel like the game explores its own mechanics to their potential fullest. I would have preferred if the areas were each 5-10 levels longer to better explore the possibilities that interactions between the different obstacles and mechanics could provide.
The challenge/reward balance is sorely lacking at times. Some individual tumors are obscenely hard to get, while others the game practically gives away for free. The worst offenders are the "locked" levels, which contain some of the most difficult challenges in the game in exchange for a mega tumor, which is the same reward as most other secret areas. There's only one locked level that gives something different/maybe better, and it's markedly easier. Additionally, unlocking those challenges consumes your key and you usually have to go partway through the challenge to get another one, meaning if you accidentally bump into one of the locks with a key (which can happen as several of them have to be jumped over to avoid), in the worst case you'll be barred from progression through the main game (as there is an area that makes heavy use of keys and locks) until you get the key back. Fortunately, there is no way to permanently lock yourself out of the locked areas.
Some of the keyboard controls (none of which are directly gameplay related) are screwy. For instance, many interactions respond to the Up binding as well as Interact. Additionally, warping directly from a warp point allows you to use your Interact keybinding to confirm the warp, but warping from an arbitrary area in the game using the map requires you to use Space instead. Glaiel's twitter implies that the latter is a feature instead of a bug intended to reduce accidental warping, but there are plenty of games that require you to hold down the key to confirm a critical action, and the game is paused while the map is open, meaning I'm not buying this justification.
Finally, Ridiculon's soundtrack hit and miss for me, even with the classical adaptation theme. It's more miss than hit in the beginning (anyone else notice this pattern?), as some of the pieces feel like they're far too upbeat and loud for the game they're in. There is one particularly grevious offender around midgame which I know was supposed to fit with the hectic nature of the area, but actually succeeded in putting me off from the area entirely until I turned the music off (for those curious, it was
). They also missed a glorious opportunity to have an adaptation of Liszt's Totentanz, which doesn't appear anywhere in the game or the OST.
All in all, however, another good hard platformer from Edmund & friends. I know I spent a lot of time writing about the negative points, but I do still seriously enjoy this game. Buy it if you're into hard platformers that require incredibly accurate movements.

Day 1: You think you'd be playing a survival game.
Day 2: You have beaten the game for the first time (after an hour, tops).
Day 3: You realize that survival simply falls into your hands. Gameplay is reduced to a minimum - in reality, Dyscourse is a Telltale adventure light, or a visual novel with the ability to walk around if only to glue it all together instead of adding any meaningful mechanics this way.
Day 4: So, since gameplay takes a backseat in this game, you'd want to play it for the story, right? Too bad you have already beaten it once, with the general setup of the (usually) 10 days you spend on the island staying the same throughout each playthrough. Oh well, there are still locations and major plot parts to discover. So you stick with it a bit more.
Day 5: Plodding through the same lines of dialogue repeatedly becomes a chore, so only the prospect of achievements keep you motivated. However, all of them are hidden without ANY hints given. In addition, they are highly inconsistent. For example you get an achievement for losing an arm to the cold or to a jaguar, so you'd think losing an arm to a shark would reward you with an achievement, right? Unfortunately not. Your survival is made up of a pretty large number of decisions, both small and big, and they lead to all kinds of different outcomes. Some of these have seemingly randomly been chosen to trigger achievements, while others haven't. There is no rhyme or rhythm to this, so you either try out EVERY single possible path to take or resort to a walkthrough, thus killing any sense of exploration a deserted island could possibly hold.
Day 6: You decide to hunt down all the achievements with the help of a guide and yet you still manage to get annoyed by Dyscourse and start cursing at the screen. Text takes far too long to skip. Minor decisions can suddenly (and days later) block you from unlocking an achievement. You can only rewind time by entire days, which is far too wide a timeframe especially in the early days. Big decisions are often made at the end of a day, which is painstakingly bad game design in combination with my previous sentence. Another example for bad design? When making a decision you are often asked again whether you stand by that decision just seconds after, but the order of your options is switched. So for example you are asked if you want to "A: rescue X" or "B: Secure the food". Right after, you are asked again, but this time "A" will let you secure the food and B lets you rescue X. This game just doesn't value your time. You keep trudging through the same lines of dialogue again and again with minor variations you simply don't care about anymore.
Day 7: You die of dysentery.
Dyscourse isn't all bad. Visually and acoustically it's pretty nice and I certainly enjoyed some of the dialogue, but fans of survival games won't find anything to like here and fans of story-driven games are also bound to be disappointed.

From the first moments of waking up in the rusting Aperture Science facility to right before the credits roll, Portal 2 rarely falters. The world is bigger, the story thicker, and the character development more surprising. The mania of GLaDOS, the facility's operator, is molded into unexpected forms alongside a host of brutally funny personalities. The history of the Aperture Science facility is filled in, character origins discussed, and though its pacing suffers as it occasionally strikes a more serious tone, an abundance of cruel jokes and cheerfully sincere death threats prevent it from losing its sarcastic charm. When you're not staring at your screen with wrinkled, pained expression on your face trying to figure out a puzzle, expect to be laughing. You still play as Chell, dragged back into Aperture after the events of the first game. You soon meet Wheatley, a spherical robot, voiced by Stephen Merchant (The Ricky Gervais Show, Extras) who helps you through the early stages. It's difficult to overstate how Merchant's obvious enthusiasm for the role benefits the game. No word Wheatley speaks is without witty inflection, and the consistently clever writing perfectly complements the onscreen action. It's easy to be be just as concerned about missing lines of dialogue as about progressing through the puzzles, especially during Wheatley and GLaDOS' verbal sparring matches.
The attention to detail throughout is nothing short of stunning. The facility is in a state of disrepair at the beginning. Once GLaDOS whirs into action, so does the facility, becoming an extension of her body and personality. When you enter a room mechanized crane arms and wall plates spin and shift with an urgency like you walked in on them with their pants down. As Portal 2 progresses, the environments expand from claustrophobic test chambers to yawning underground chasms. Metal girders and structural supports break and crash into each another, snapping apart in chaotic and natural ways, consistently serving not only to entertain the eye but to expand our understanding of the game's characters. The core appeal of something like Portal will never be the visuals, but it's still impressive how much mileage Valve is getting out of its Source technology first used for Half-Life 2 in 2004. I never really gave Dark Messiah a chance back when it was first released. I bought it, played it for maybe 10 minutes and then closed it. I don't know why, because I started playing this again recently and it was pretty good for a game released in 2006. This is one of those games that needs a 'maybe' rating for the review.
It's a good idea. Plane crashes on desert island, you, the sensible person, have to lead a group of idiots to survival over the course of a few days, while waiting for rescue.
Simple as that. Works rather well too, in the sense that choices certainly do affect the outcome of the story somewhat. But it is rather simple, and figuring out all the different 'pathways' and variations of those pathways can be a fun thing to do. However, it isn't as in-depth as people make it out to be, you can have a husband and wife be rather blase about one or the other committing murder for example, even when their relationship is absolutely rock bottom, where the expectation is for some actual 'reaction' to happen, to push them over the edge.
Where Dyscourse fails is in its characters and the direction the game takes with them. As I mentioned, the idea of the desert island survival story is a sensible one. But the characters are something out of a poor hack's comedy show. There's the husband and wife, who seem relatively normal. The absolute bat-snot insane conspiracy theorist, tin-foil-hat, rage inducing idiot "Teddy" who will spout off all sorts of ridiculous rubbish about THE NANOMACHINES! and the ALIENS!!!!!! And omg the sand has ears... Oh shut up, you delusional nutter.
There's the 'gamer', and I use that term ever so mockingly because apparently gamers IRL would go out in a thunderstorm and suggest a lightning strike means a Black Mage is nearby. Wut? Dude, get a grip.
And then the office jocky, who seems to have an unlimited amount of cigarettes, who mopes like that one friend who tries to find a negative in absolutely everything? "Good morning!" "Nothing good about it, oh woe is me, I wish some rock would casually stone my brains out." "Jesus Christ mate, all I said was good morning!" "And wooooooooe I am still alive, to listen to your mundane voice, please kill me now!"
If you find that sort of thing absolutely, knee slappingly, hilarious, then Dyscourse is right up your alley, a survival game with absolutely "hilarious" characters.
If, like me, you find that sort of thing absolutely moronic, then Dyscourse is probably not quite the game for you, and it is a shame because the idea is a relatively simple, safe one that really should work no matter what, and yet the developers somehow managed to actually make it almost unbearable to get through. (Additionally, turn the 'voice effects' sounds off, it will save your sanity.)
So yeah, get it on sale if you absolutely must. Don't bother if you feel those characters I summed up above are unlikable people, unless you want to buy it just to kill them, which some of you will, so go for it.
(Game rating: Mixed.)

Dyscourse is a game about surviving on a remote island, with a branch of random people from a plane crash. Sound like the interesting concept? Well, this game has ruined it in many ways...
Every character in this game is so annoying! If you really involved in this chaotic situation, then you might expect to find others have a great will to stay alive, or no will to live at all! This game presents you with indecision people who really can't tell whether they want to live or not! If they want to live, why they don't try harder to do things? Or if they think they're doomed, why they still help you out? I think this conflict is the main course that pulls back this game.
The characters are also foolish! Let them live without your guidance and they will do nothing! Find water? No. Gather more food? No. Explore area? No. Defense themselves from animals? No. Salvage goods from a crash site? No. Chitchat at camping area? YES!
It's like they're not in a plane-crash-on-remote-island situation anymore! Everyone seems to think they're on a vacation! Are you a gamer? Please, go ahead and hallucinated yourself that you're actually in a magic dessert. Working for secret government project? It's ok to think aliens shoot down your plane!
These behaviors will develop you, a player, with a perspective toward this game (and maybe toward this kind of situation in a real world): It's OK to be ALONE in order for YOU to stay ALIVE.
And when you realize that, you start playing this game heartless style. Want to get some water from a swamp? Send your least favorite guy to explore that area first. Suspicious about a damaged bridge? Let the heaviest guy try it out.
The saddest part of this game is when someone falls, you feel no sorrow at all. Instead, you just thought "thanks god, that's a less weird guy to annoy me".
I think this experience, for a survival simulation game, is very bad. Take a look at XCOM franchise, if someone dies it's mean a big loss that you might need to restart the whole game. Or at lease, you should be tense all the time like when you play This War of Mine.
Despite this major issue, you may be aware of:
- Art style: Most people like it, but I'm not. Why render everything so rigid and so square? Pentagon frying pan! Square shape airplane body?
- Inhuman speaking: Every character has its own voice, or rather a noise, because you can't understand it! That's hardly developing compassion toward them.
- Joke: I know you can't stress out all the time, but seriously, at this time you still play those lame joke?
- Price: $15 is too much for a very short game. It's true that this game is replayable, but as I said about annoying character design, I hardly find reasons to play it a second time.
By all of these, I can not recommend this game to anyone.

Worms Revolution is a great game that is sure to have friendships on edge as players battle it out with crazy weaponry such as Cluster Bombs, Moles, Super Sheep, and the infamous Holy Hand Grenade. Players can choose between single player campaign, offline skirmishes, or online games with friends so there is never a shortage of carnage.
The campaign isn't very long, with around 32 missions (not including missions added from DLC) but you'll be laughing through-out the entire length of it. The AI isn't a push over either, if you're as bad as I am at least, and will definitely have you hiding in the caves if you're not careful. The narrator of the campaign is a bit...annoying to say the least, but the voices from the worms make up for it in the end.
Worms Revolution brings a new style of gameplay into the mix by adding classes to the classic worms game. Each class has it's own benefits to offer and can be the deciding factor on a major victory....or a horrible loss. The four classes available are Scout, Heavy, Soldier, and Scientist. Some of the benefits the classes offer are increased movement speed, increase jump height/distance, team-wide health regeneration, etc.
Physics objects are also a big game changer in Worms Revolution, adding objects that are highly volatile (more so than the common oil drum), or that contain dynamic liquid that you could use to literally wash away the competition. Unfortunately it seems that some of the classic weapons have been removed from the base game but others are offered in the available DLC.
All in all the game is loads of fun and it never seems to be the same game twice. I definitely recommend this game to anything looking for some casual fun offline, or for those who wish to duke it out with their friends in an epic online war and truly test friendships.

Transformed is not only a trip down memory lane for long-time Sega fans such as myself, but an immensely enjoyable and often times challenging cart racer. The lineup of characters is strong and diverse, although the lack of Shenmue and Virtua Fighter representation keeps it from being perfect. Tracks are well designed, full of set-pieces, and feature some amazing attention to detail when it comes to paying homage to the various Sega franchises. There's a good variety of weapons and powerups, and the "Transformation" mechanic is a neat, fresh twist on the genre. AI is also surprisingly strong at the higher classes. They race smart, take shortcuts and use weapons effectively. Makes for not only a good challenge but some really intense finishes and rewarding victories. There's also a full suite of multiplayer modes as well as local split-screen for up to 4-players, a very welcome addition if you want to hook your PC up to an HDTV.
Sumo Digital did a tremendous job of creating not only a wonderful nostalgia trip for those of us who fell in love with the Genesis/Saturn/Dreamcast, but also a legitimately fun and rich cart racing experience. Absolutely recommended.

Is this game good? Absolutely. Even though there are people who will tell you that it has problems, and in many cases they are right. This game's community has veterans of thousands upon thousands of hours that could summarise game balance, statistics and tactics far better than I ever can, and while some of them are quitting and many of them have quit in the past, there are still many more who still play and more players gaining on their long grind to veterancy everyday, because even if they hate some changes they think that the game is worth something.
Is this game still worth playing now? I have to say yes. I reinstalled the game roughly two weeks ago and found my old server was dead, created a new character and still had a blast. There are still two hundred plus player battles going on every day, just fewer of them - so if you want big fights you can't be as picky about where to go as you used to be able to.
I'm not going to talk about performance since I haven't had huge problems with it (playing on a decent quality, year-old laptop gives me 60fps with roughly medium settings). There are tutorials out there if you need to improve your performance.
Is this game P2W? No. It's pay for efficiency. What that means is that when a new player and a max rank player get into a firefight, the max rank player will be even with the new player, or maybe slightly at a disadvantage depending on their loadout, based on just gear alone. What the old player has that the new player might not, however, are things like restoration kits and extra grenades, so he can be more effective over longer fights and potentially have a higher score per minute - but if a veteran makes a new account and fights a max rank player, there's a high chance that the max rank will lose that fight. Vehicle combat is more difficult for me to judge, because I know little about it, but from what I've seen the effect is similar, and that skill is what makes the big difference between an effective and ineffective vehicle (despite what veterans may tell you about nothing ever dying and positioning having no effect, they can't deny that they'll destroy new players who are trying vehicles for the first time).
Is this game balanced? My unqualified opinion is yes. Look elsewhere before you make a decision.
Is this game friendly to new players? No. It has improved, but your first encounter with an enemy will probably give you a second-long life expectancy. There are a million ways to die on Auraxis, from invisible people with knives to aircraft with strafing missiles to being run over by a friendly tank, and in your time you will experience all of them. But if you're willing to see past the deaths to your improvement, start to anticipate the deaths before they come, and then act to avoid them, you'll soon be fighting with the best. (Until you hop into a vehicle, that's a completely new learning curve...)
This game will make you laugh, get annoyed, get excited, and everything else that a good immersive experience should. There are plenty of times in this game where you just have to stop and take in the sights - a rush of players onto a continent after an alert ends, all hustling into aircraft to get to the front lines. Two columns of tanks firing on each other, with infantry being slaughtered in between. A group of maxes pushing out of a spawn point, explosions everywhere.
This game is five years old now, but if it was released today people would still be surprised by the boundaries it pushes. I have never seen anything quite like it, and I am happy to have spent the time on it that I did - and happy to spend more time on it in future.
(Oh, and all this is without outfit play. That's where the game really gets fun.)

The beginning of the twentieth century saw a new era in world politics. The cornerstone of what Henry
Luce would later dub “The American Century” having been laid with the Spanish–American War in
1898, the United States stood ready to play a more active part in shaping world affairs. Although this
shift in the nation’s approach to the conduct of diplomacy had begun before 1898, it was only in the
early twentieth century that the nation’s policymakers assumed the new responsibility of helping
orchestrate international affairs.
Between 1901 and 1920, the United States increasingly intervened in the affairs of other nations. The
presidents during this period, Theodore Roosevelt, William Taft, and Woodrow Wilson, despite
differences in background and temperament, held similar views regarding the redemptive nature of
United States values and the nation’s obligation to further Western civilization. Each subscribed to the
notion that political advancement and economic progress were two sides of the same coin, that
democracy and republicanism were corollaries of free trade. All three championed policies that, in their
estimation, furthered both.
If their opinions and actions were similar, their effect on long-term policymaking was not. The
administrations of Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson bookend the Progressive Era. They
established the key principles that would animate United States foreign policy for the remainder of the
century and beyond.

In 1999, on this dinosaur of a computer, I played Age of Empires 2 for the first time.
Back then, I was four years old and not the best player, but enjoyed real time strategy games the most. I would do things like make the female villagers get berries, lambs, and farm, and make the males woodcut, get gold, stone, and occasionally mix them up if I thought some of them were getting lonely. Now I realise how much of a waste of time that was, but it's still funny to look back on, and some say there were hidden buffs with those villagers' genders, so maybe I wasn't all wrong.
There's a lot of little nuances that are impressive that many modern games do not take into account. Things like having a defensive boost at the top of a hill, or recreating a civilization from a stockpile of 50 spare food (Ha!), or setting a house on fire with a sword (Ha ha!). It's easier to appreciate now that I'm better at video games, and slightly more masochistic. The campaign level design on the base game alone, which includes Age of Kings and the Conquerors expansion, will give you over a hundred hours of playtime.
The developers give this game a lot of love, and are a nice salute to Ensemble's masterpiece. For instance, in the HD edition, there is better AI that was developed with the Forgotten expansion. The hard AI now actually acts smarter, instead of cheating by getting more resources. So, you can also effectively crush the AI's economy now through raiding and such which was questionable before.
The workshop is also nice. I enjoy the texture mods to make the scenery more beautiful and the fire more realistic. Also more blood, and corpses staying longer. More taunts. Player-made campaigns. A lot of competative players like the "♥♥♥♥♥wood" mod to make the trees tiny.
Overall, I've been impressed with the HD edition, and nominated it for the "Test Of Time" award. What other game on steam still has an underestimated active playerbase of over 5,000 people daily for a game from the 90s? Writing this at 10:10am, there is 7,142 people ingame, and it's peaked to 11,616 in the past 30 days. If you like strategy games, this will be a game you come back to again and again.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a solid entry for a series that went into the FPS genre with Wolfenstein 3D. The game offers much in both story and gameplay.
The story puts players in the shoes of BJ Blazkowicz. While BJ would fight Nazi's in WWII, the story changes the pace in having him fight against Nazi's that rule the world, more or less making BJ and by extension the player not a US soldier but rather a rebel and terrorist fighting against Nazi rule. To add on that, the game shows one just how vile the Nazi's are, with the first segment in the Nazi ruled world showing the brutality that can be witnessed.
The gameplay is more similar to FPS games like Doom but with a twist: you can either kill enemies by stealth in some segments, especially when you have Nazi's that can call for backup should there be trouble or you can kill enemies by going in guns blazing. The aresnal of weapons are more or less the same in that you get a pistol, shotgun, rifle, and other such weapons but what makes it special is the ability to dual-wield any gun that you keep sans special weapons like the laser cutter or the minigun used by Nazi supersoldiers.
In terms of length, the game has enough content to keep one coming back, especially with the fact that there exist two timelines you can play through (both are the same but with some different NPC's).
In all, Wolfenstein: The New Order is a solid title to own that shows how fun it is to kill Nazi scum.

A first-person action/adventure game which eschews player levels for skill points awarded based on progress through the game rather than kills (except bosses). Allows combinations of the three combat styles common in games (warrior, rogue, mage), but the more skillful player will use their environment to greatest advantage.
The world is littered with physics objects which may be used to hurt, disorient, trip, or impale your enemies. Shove your foes into the fire, or use oil to bring the fire to them. If they are foolish enough to wander near a high ledge, give them a kick and let gravity do the work for you. Take advantage of traps or unsafe building equipment, which could hurt them just as well as you.
If you're not the type to get your hands dirty, charm the most powerful foe and watch them fight amongst each other. Or sneak by them, you need not be the grim reaper in this world, as foes are merely obstacles in your path, not the goal.
Would you embrace your destiny or fight it?

Sonic and All Stars Racing Transformed had me at a crossroad, I already owned a Mario Kart type racing game, but this peaked my interest.  On the one hand, it was Sonic and the rest, and spin off racing games that stem from the simple quest of 'It's like Mario Kart' wouldn't normally keep me curious, this did.  Three different modes for the vehicals?  And thus my purchase of Sonic and All-Stars Racing Transformed began.  From the get go I was pleasently surprised, the vehicals felt different in each mode.  Boats felt like boats, cars felt like cars, planes felt like planes...pretty obvious there I suppose.  But the tracks themselves are pretty brilliant.
Now for the online mode, prepare for some pretty hard competition.  While you may just be learning, you can be put against those that have been at it since the games release.  Not to say that's a bad thing, but it can make you feel pretty outclassed, heck, I was happy enough when I hit a second place.  But it was still fun.  Could I recommend this game to others, oh most definitely.  The racing is solid, the unlockable mods let you customize those characters whom you feel most at home with to play just the way you want.  But be warned, you may wanna level up a few characters, as there's no telling if the character you've worked hard on will be taken.

This review leans 40/60 towards not recommended. Don't get me wrong, Dirty Bomb is my favourite game but something has to be done to keep new players away from veterans. [Asia Server] CMM has not been implemented but max lvl _ and min lvl _ servers have been removed.
Stacked teams are somewhat common but there are helpful veterans who would call vote shuffles or switch teams and try to balance etc. Still, there would be situations where there are enough veterans for a vote to go through but they wouldn't press yes because they're stacked and want to♥♥♥♥♥♥newbies. Then probably go whine about how the game isn't growing etc.
DB does have a high skill curve though so I'd suggest you watch some videos every now and then. Also join the adopt a noob group where veterans can help out newbies.

Some stuff you need to know :
1. Team composition : Whether your team needs a Medic, Engineer, Fire support. I'm not going to touch on recon because newbies should stay away from them lol
Medic : Keep your team healed and revive downed teammates.
Engineer : Defuses, plants bombs faster, repairs objectives faster than other mercs.
Fire support : Keeps team's ammo topped up. Some crowd control abilities.
DON'T ever play Assault mercs like Fragger, Thunder, Rhino, Nader and even Javelin (Fire support) unless your team already has the essential roles covered. They don't provide any team utility.
Also don't call for medic when you can obviously see that all you're medics are dead by pressing TAB. It's annoying.
2. Map knowledge/Movement : Watch trick jump videos on youtube and frag movies to some extent. There are many shortcuts and flanking routes.
3. QoL stuff : Turn on reticle when aiming down because some iron sights are actually not centered.
Reload cancelling works in DB, normally done by sprinting.
Turn on press R to cancel reload in settings. So if you have Double Time augment (which allows you to reload whilst sprinting)  : You can cancel reload WHILE sprinting.
You don't need to aim down sights most of the time as the spray is pretty centered, so you can strafe to dodge bullets etc. Aiming down gives more recoil but lesser bullet spread.
Switch to pistol or knife to run faster. It's pretty safe to do so as weapon switching is very fast in DB.
-
Anyway that's all I have to type for now. Feel free to add me if you're a n00b in Asia and I'll support you as a medic or engineer or for whatever other reasons. Not a veteran at level 26 but I'll still try to help anyway.

In 1999, on this dinosaur of a computer, I played Age of Empires 2 for the first time.
Back then, I was four years old and not the best player, but enjoyed real time strategy games the most. I would do things like make the female villagers get berries, lambs, and farm, and make the males woodcut, get gold, stone, and occasionally mix them up if I thought some of them were getting lonely. Now I realise how much of a waste of time that was, but it's still funny to look back on, and some say there were hidden buffs with those villagers' genders, so maybe I wasn't all wrong.
There's a lot of little nuances that are impressive that many modern games do not take into account. Things like having a defensive boost at the top of a hill, or recreating a civilization from a stockpile of 50 spare food (Ha!), or setting a house on fire with a sword (Ha ha!). It's easier to appreciate now that I'm better at video games, and slightly more masochistic. The campaign level design on the base game alone, which includes Age of Kings and the Conquerors expansion, will give you over a hundred hours of playtime.
The developers give this game a lot of love, and are a nice salute to Ensemble's masterpiece. For instance, in the HD edition, there is better AI that was developed with the Forgotten expansion. The hard AI now actually acts smarter, instead of cheating by getting more resources. So, you can also effectively crush the AI's economy now through raiding and such which was questionable before.
The workshop is also nice. I enjoy the texture mods to make the scenery more beautiful and the fire more realistic. Also more blood, and corpses staying longer. More taunts. Player-made campaigns. A lot of competative players like the "♥♥♥♥♥wood" mod to make the trees tiny.
Overall, I've been impressed with the HD edition, and nominated it for the "Test Of Time" award. What other game on steam still has an underestimated active playerbase of over 5,000 people daily for a game from the 90s? Writing this at 10:10am, there is 7,142 people ingame, and it's peaked to 11,616 in the past 30 days. If you like strategy games, this will be a game you come back to again and again.

Its Cheap, its simple, its fun. And theres a two pack. The game is relatively bare bones but its more fun than playing Call Of Duty: WW2 or No Mans Sky for that fact. Yet another zombie defence has to currently have the best name in the gaming universe, I have the strong incline that the Dev's got so fed up with figuring out a name for a zombie defence game and we're just like. "What should we name it?" "I dont know the good names are already taken" "True, we did just make Yet another zombie defense.." "...." "....".
Ill cover the pros and cons and then talk more about this game
Pros: - Smooth progression system
- Four Person online co op
- Two person local co op
- Easy to understand top down controls
- Simple system and mechanics
- Little to no glitches
- Extremely low price tag that drops during sales
- Two pack that makes it lower
- Worth your money
- No loot boxes or microtransactions or add on's, what you pay is what you get
Cons: - Pretty bare bones
- Simple small ish map (its a defence game so meh)
- Could use a bit more character customisation
- If you dont plan your defence right you can get caught out quickly (but this could be because youre an idiot or your younger autisitc cousin is on your team)
- Should mainly be done with friends (requires you to unlock friendship)
Ill now talk a bit more about the game.
So the game is really yet another zombie defence. The mechanics and idea of the game is simple yet the game is ironicly fun. I would recommend playing this with friends and since during any steam sale (summer, autum and winter) the two pack is 0.50 usd for a two pack, spending 1 usd to get four copies means you ensure you get a four man team to play with and your friends get a free game. This is counting that you are willing to spend 1 usd for your friends or if you have friends to begin with. If you dont you are sad and should stop reading this, go outside, and meet people, please shave as well, because if you dont please do not be offended when parents hold onto their children tighter as you walk by.
So the price of the game aside, the actual game is this. Youre a survivor of the zombie plague that is surviving by staying near the worlds only working lamp post, which is the only structure this world has considering the map tileset it grey ground for miles. (We could explain this by saying youre in a salt plain but that still dosent explain the lamp post, but toys have feelings and M.Night Shamalan exists so there are other more pressing questions at large).
The games progression system through the waves comes by you and your rag tag team of friends collecting money from dead zombies, purchasing barricades to hide and cry silently behind or to build chuck norris aproved turrets, which range from simple turrets with Uzi's to top level ones that fire a minturised death star. The progression system is smooth heading up from night one, and once a night is over use the day to collect money and strenghten your lamp post fortification.
Overall its bare bones but the progression system is the best ive seen in any game having little to bias to being a good player or not. The game has no micro transactions so that small price tag is all you pay and its a very very small price tag. No loot boxes or anything and all money is earned in a match that will lead to you buying new weapons to use personally.
Ive had alot of fun with friends in this game and I now hand it out highly recommended to anyone looking for a good cheap game or a gift to get social and to train co operative play with friends!

Here's why you should play strife over dota 2 and league of legends (and yes, I have played it outside of steam) :
-Breath of fresh air. If you've inhaled too much toxicity or have burnt out, strife is something new to try out.
-You pick heroes before being matched. The game will put you with teammates of separate roles that'll likely complement yours. Most characters can play several roles. No need to argue with teammates about hero selection.
-Gold from last hitting is shared with teammates. No need to fight over last hits. No carry killing everything while support stays poor.
-Wards are integrated onto maps. Players tag wards by moving near them. Any player can tag wards. No support playing as ward slave.
-Games last around 20 minutes plus minus. Map is small, action is plenty. No stress from games that drag on too long.
-Everyone gets a personal courier that's invincible. No need to take turns sending items between players and certainly no rage from dead couriers.
-There's a back to base button, but you regenarate out of combat. Allows for fast and aggresive play.
-Fight for objectives as well. Giant monkey can allow for significant push. Games can be dynamic, comebacks are viable.
-Pet and crafting system further customize playstyle. Crafting lets you edit an existing item, eg: remove health component for damage component.

I played this game back when it was in Beta, it was plagued with Hackers and it was really difficult to have fun. It was extremely pay to win and was just generally dissapointing. Recently I Redownloaded it and thought I'd see if they learned anything. For those of you who played before and want some comparisons I'll give a few.
First and the most important is the Pay to Win aspects of the game. Can you buy Power? Yes. Is it to the extent as before? No. You do need a to still unlock mercenaries before you can play them but it's no longer a huge grind. If you play it for a few hours a day you can unlock an average character in 3 days. If you play casually you're looking at more of a week or two.
Can you still buy overpowered cases? Kinda. They still have the premium cases with higher chances for Cobalts and golds, but they give you a medium case every other day. The premium cases are cool but they aren't necessary, I've gotten cobalts off of the daily cases and golds off of them too. It's all RNG.
Are there still hackers? I honestly don't know. I haven't run into a hacker yet, but there are some really good players. The teams can seem stacked at times and there will be times where you get spanked like a little girl who took candy before dinner. There is movement mechanics in this game that are absolutely insane, and there are people how can do them like second nature. These are not hackers, they are just better than you.
Is the game fun at least? Without a doubt. This is the most fun I've had playing a shooter in a long time. There aren't very many games where I can run full speed with a knife out, jump off a wall while switching to shotgun, headshot the player infront of me on my way down, pull out my knife again and impale him as I touch the ground, then turn around to plant the bomb. At the same time there is rarely a game where I am on the other side of that interaction and I don't call hacks. This game is FAST AS F*** BOI. There's little to no recoil, but there is spread. It is a game where you hip fire from 15m and ADS any farther. It is just a very enjoyable game, the closest I can compare it to is that old BRINK feel but improved.
Overall I recomend trying this game, especially if you tried it once before and didn't like the beta because of how pay to win it is. it's definatly improved and it's a whole lot of fun.

I echo the reviews of many here who note that incredible awkwardness and unresponsiveness of the controls -- especially the unreasonable difficulty in simply getting your character to face the right direction while enemies quickly and fluidly move around you.  Animations lock you too easily and quickly.
The game is obtuse and offers almost no guidance on its quirky mechanics.  And I suppose I could handle death penalty if it wasn't so random and out of your control -- sometimes you just get mobbed by 3 fluid, well-aiming enemies who simultaneously kill you very quickly while you struggle with just aiming the right direction.  I don't want to grind for gold to replace expensive weapons so I can continue when that happens.
There are a lot of other minor complaints, like the common problem that it is VERY evident that the game was quickly ported over to PC from consoles with as little change as possible in UI and control scheme.  Hint: ESC should not take you to main game menu from anywhere in the game; it should function as a "back" button when you are in in-game menus.  Do NOT require the player to press the B key to exit a menu on a PC game; we hate stuff like this.  It's more irritating over time than it would first appear.  In the world of PC ergonomics, it's like putting the doorbell button to your house on the mailbox 30 feet away from the door.
Again, like others, I was attracted by the art and music and visually fluid animations, but had enough of the unresponsive controls; and terrible, poorly-ported UI; and the death penalty + death by UI + need for grinding to get equipment again.
Note on hours played: I played a few hours on my son's account, so you can consider me as having about 4 hours in.  If there is indeed a gem buried under the punitive barriers to entry, I couldn't bring myself to play further to see it.  If I hear that these issues have been addressed later, I would be happy to try again and revise my review.

This is legitimately the best game I've played in years. It's rich, deep, complex, clever, and it kept me intrigued and involved from beginning to end. I've always been a sucker for great character development and believe me when I tell you, this game goes beyond great character development. Whereas most games create and build on the characters as the story progresses, this game does something different. This game gives you fully fleshed out and interesting characters from the get go and lets you interact and dynamically evolve and grow with them as you move through the story.
The game's mechanics are simple: You walk, talk, and use a radio to progress certain key points of the story. The mechanics may be simple, but they tie perfectly into the story and the world that the developers have created. The music sets the mood, the art gives depth, and the gameplay allows you to delve deep into the intricate story. I can't say too much about the story without spoiling it, but I can say that it's a ghost story, it’s amazing, and it’s never the same twice. And to give a little insight into how literally I mean it when I say this game’s never the same twice: Most Telltale games have about 2,000 or so lines of dialog, this game has about 12,000. Yeah. Not to mention, it has some of the most real characters that you’ll encounter in a modern game.
Pick it up, you won't regret it.

Don't let my current played time deceive you, I've been playing since closed beta and have logged somewhere around 200 hours in game.
What do I love about Strife?
- Combination of Dota 2 and League mechanics (Dota 2: Couriers, Uphill terrain, LoL:  recalls, bushes)
- Dota 2 style business model (all heroes free, you can even grind free skins since you get 1 unit of free cash currency at the end of game, win or lose)
- Item customization adds depth to item builds while allowing base builds to be simple for new users
- Tutorial story + Adventure mode allow you to actually experience the lore of the game instead of just reading it.
What Could Be Improved:
- Item customization grind could be a bit lessened, its not bad if you only play one hero but builds for a few heroes can take awhile. Same goes for pets.
- The game currently heavily favors tanky builds over all others which leads to very standardized picks
- The lack of ability to see what heroes will be on your team can lead to terrible teams being made by the matchmaker
- Chapter 2 of the story mode has been 'coming soon' for almost a year
All in all a solid MOBA title which is definitely worth your time to check out.

Man, I have been long overdue in writing a review for this game. I've played it maybe four or five times, now, and still haven't found all the little exciting tidbits that really bring it to life. I think it takes me about four hours for a single playthrough, and every time, I find myself playing through the whole game in one sitting. It's an enthralling storyline, with great charaters, and I absolutely adore the concept. I don't get fully invested in games very often, but this is one I think I'll still be playing for a long time to come. The designs are gorgeous, the dialogue is on point, and I still feel immersed in the game every time I play.

I don't know what all the negative reviewers are blabbing about, I think this game is really unique, as a player of HoN (Only a few days...), DoTA (Maybe only a few months?), LoL (Quite some time), I think Strife is as easy as LoL, not easier.
There's also a lot of things in common with DoTA 2 and LoL, they introduce the same things, with a combination of different methods (Baron, Roshan, Cindara), but Strife adds odd things like out of combat regeneration, which I actually think is perfectly fine, all the actual problems lie in normal regeneration.
This game has a LOT of potential if balanced right.
The meta is a bit undeveloped, due to how supports can do around as much damage as the nukers, and mages can build enough tank items to work like one, but it IS unique in the fact that top and middle are duo lanes, while bottom is usually soloed.
The biggest complaint I have, however, is Ray, Strife's Teemo.

The controls take a lil' bit to get used to, in my experience, but it's quite a bit of fun once you're into it. I've only played on... one map, and it was a tad small, but we still had a jolly good time. Definitely going to continue playing this game.

In Dyscourse you've crashed landed on a desert island that is full of dangers. Every choice you make has some repercussion. Be careful in what you do and who you send to do other things, because your fate may ultimately depend on it. You're joined on this quest by a cast of zany survivors with their own quirks that make this a very entertaining story.
Dyscourse is a point and click adventure game with a heavy story influence. Everything you do changes the story in some way. Find and discover all of Dyscourses secrets... if you have the stamina to do so.
Sound: The music in Dyscourse is pretty appropriate and I actually enjoyed it: the first 3 runs through the story. After that it kinda faded out and I didn't really notice it so much anymore. Didn't get annoying, just tuned it out.
Graphics: Honestly, I'm not really a fan of the art style in this game. Don't get me wrong, it's not bad, it's just not my particular taste. Though the longer I played it, the more it grew on me. That being said, it's still done well even if I don't really like it myself. However, it does seem as if it could have come from a mobile platform originally.
Controls: Simple and easy. Point. Click. Repeat.
Gameplay: The gameplay is rather interesting, nothing that is actually difficult. I played many times to see various changes to the story based on what I chose. There are a couple main branches that are interesting to discover. However, the achievement hunting aspect is really kind of annoying. There is no way to fast forward through the text once you've seen it for the umpteenth time. Sure you can click click click, but only as fast as the dialogue boxes complete their animations. So that's kind of frustrating later on.
Overall: 7.1/10 - This game was definitely fun and enjoyable at first. There is a lot of replaybility, but probably better to do it on different days, rather than in one massive sitting. My annoyance level rose for the above reason relating to not being able to speed through text you'd seen multiple times before. That being said, the characters are vastly entertaining and amusing, and you'll have a good time. Price wise? A bit overpriced in my opinion. Get a discount and you'll be pretty happy.

from the creator of super meat boy comes a game that takes everything you know about super meat boy and flips it on it's head.
and it does it beautifully.
at first glance, it seems like this game is very similar to meat boy, but besides the visuals, there's not much of a comparison.
instead of building up momentum, you have one constant horizontal speed, and instead of walljumping, you can hang off of corners instead. the game is structured in such a way that given enough time, you can absolutely destroy the game wtih 100% consistency.
unlike super meat boy, there are, to my knowledge, zero elements of RNG. no cycles to worry about that may screw up a strategy, no enemies with random patterns, and no missiles that decide to just fire whenever they want to.
the game is consistent with tight controls, and even when something seems random, there's usually a way to make it's movements predictable.
the visuals and aesthetics of this game are one of my favorite parts, as the dreary atmosphere of many of the areas are done really well, even though it generally focuses on a minimalistic artstyle. the story of the game is a nice addition, and really works well with the visuals, furthered by rich evans playing ash. the music by ridiculon is probably their best soundtrack yet, remixing classical themes into rock style renditions. it somehow manages to perfectly coincide with all of the games environments, and i love it.
rather than taking a "one level at a time" approach like mario, the game is much more structured like a metroidvania, albeit slightly more linear than other games following that formula, however some of the later areas really do some cool things with how they're structured.
there's a lot more to this game, but frankly saying much more would spoil the experience.
there's a lot of stuff to do in this game, and if you're trying to 100% the game, you will need to develop skills that only the top 0.1% of players are going do develop. in many ways this game seems like super meat boy, but in my eyes, it's more polished, more skill based, and even more difficult.
to my knowledge this is one of the first games that edmund mcmillen never had a set deadline for, and in the end it really shows. here's to hoping the next game mcmillen makes is just as good, if not better.

Okay, it took me about an hour to understand the concept of this game.
First of all, it's in the style of "Castlevania-whatever else games" in that style you know, etc.
Secondly and the most important part of this game is that it's actually based around you dying. Follow me on this:
You're a toy named Brand and every night you come alive and have to fight other toys that are the "Lost Ones" meaning that they don't have an owner anymore, also every night the house changes randomly, heavily RNG based, for example you could find a slot machine in the first room in the first night and it wouldn't be there in the second night, etc.
While the RNG mechanic seems lackluster due to enemies actually happening to get stuck between the RNG'd beams that don't allow them to jump or move anymore, it's actually helpful to you. You have only 6 inventory slots and when you die any cash (nuts) you have and whatever items you grabbed from the other toys to fill those 6 slots are put into your room.
In your room you can craft new weapons if you RNG-find the blueprint or heavily fortify the room with the cash and materials you got from other toys.

Much more than I expected from a game with "Wolfenstein" in the title. There is great action - slightly less hectic than COD, with a functional and simple cover system. Weapons feel great (Do you like duel-wielding? I hope so!). Has stealth elements that are sometimes mandatory, but often can be disregarded with consequences of varying severity (it nicely telegraphs times when stealth is recommended, but optional). One pet peeve of mine: the Metro 2033-style magic throwing knives that can silently kill anyone instantly. Seriously?
What was unexpected was the quality of the narrative. Despite the usual assortment of unlikely plot devices, the strong narrative and dialog kept my attention diverted from the stupidity. The story is both dark and hopeful, and delivered well. There are a few scenes featuring unusually grotesque violence, but these do not feel exploitive. Somehow, the game manages to make you somewhat sympathetic to the even-more-unstoppable-than-usual killing machine of a protagonist. In terms of replay value, a difficult decision early on leads to two alternate "timelines" which, while mostly identical, have a couple different characters, cutscenes, and bonuses which give a bit more replay value than most FPS.
All in all, a very solid game that combines great action with a story that won't leave you feeling like your intelligence is being insulted.

The thing that matters the most is the skill, not the weapon. If you got a weapon but you don't have any skill at using it, you won't able to control the recoil right, you won't know how many ammo you need to take down an enemy, you won't know what is the actual range of your weapon and you won't know how height you must aim to hit a target at distance. Yes this game has physics on bullet, meaning you need to aim higher for a target after a certain range, mainly if you use rifles or snipers, but even tanks, turrets and such like in real life, it would. I was a big fan of the developer's previous free-to-play shooter Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory from back in around 2004. Similarly, this game features objective based gameplay, but instead of classes like soldier, medic, etc., there are several "mercenary" characters that fit the archetype, and similar to MOBAs, the available characters are continually rotating, with two permanently free characters. You earn  (or buy) crates that give you loadout cards for each mercenary (regardless if you own them or not) which offer alternative weapons and special perks.
The most common card is a Lead card which comes with 1 perk, followed by Iron with 2, then Bronze and up have 3. All cards beyond Bronze are simply aesthetic improvements. The ways to get cards are as follows:
1) As drops from crates, which you increasingly better chests throughout the week. They are guaranteed and also occasionally occur just from playing the game. Special events can earn you speciail edition cards with unique aesthetics which is basically just gun skins and camouflage.
2) Buying from the store with in-game currency.
3) Crafting them with fragments (plus in-game currency) which come from recycling unwanted cards. Like opening a crate, this is determined by RNG, but only for the specific character and rarity you are crafting for.
Gameplay wise it's solid. Objectives are similar to WolfET, where the attackers have to do a few different things in one map e.g. blow something up, steal some containers, etc. and the defenders try to prevent them from doing so during the time allotted. Secondary objectives can facilitate/impede the attackers' goal, such as opening or closing a side gate.
Shooting is sort of a throwback to older games like RtcW, it even has hit sounds from Q3 Arena, although obviously no crazy weapons. You can aim down the sights, but the only real benefit is to zoom in. Guns are extremely accurate without ADS. Health is also much higher than games like CS or R6 Siege, so winning in a gunfight is about being able to strafe around and still hit a moving target, rather than just camping and shooting first. I appreciate this because it feels more skillful rather than games where guns automatically lock on and require no targeting, or games where the guns do so much damage that it really matters who saw the other first.
tl;dr:
Good for fans of old Wolf ET
Card drops from opening cases giving better character loadouts and perks
Grind to earn characters is sorta meh unless you buy a starter pack
Shooting is old-school (better not to ADS), trick jumping is a thing
NOT pay to win
