This is a forgotten gem. A first-person perspective action/adventure/RPG game set in the world of Heroes of MIght and Magic, it plays very similar to the old Thief classics. Combat is very difficult and you often have to use the environment to your advantage to survive a battle against more than one enemy. You get skill points for reaching objectives in the game, and you can spend them on combat skills, magic skills or "general" skills (thief, plus stat increases). You to combine powers to create many fun character builds.
If I can find something to criticize it is the 2d female characters. You have one ♥♥♥♥♥♥ temptress, and one saintly good girl, and you get to choose between them. That's it.
The level design is fantastic though. Chasing a fleeing thief across rooftops of a city, moving across crumbling orc huts precariously put at the side of a great mountain. Areas all look great and are fun to explore, and are filled to the brim with secrets.

I'm really enjoying Arelite Core, and that's surprising to me, because I don't generally play games with turn-based combat or those that are party-based. That being said, I think it's a testament to this developer that a gamer like myself could find enjoyment in a game that's not typically in his or her "wheelhouse.'
To begin with, the graphics are really sharp and clear. Though the images I see on my higher end gaming laptop with a GTX 970 aren't quite as vivid as the stills on the Steam page for this game, they come pretty close. The characters are well-defined artistically, and the variety of enemies took some real time to individualize.
In regard to layout, I noted that one reviewer mentioned an RPG Maker-like appearance, and that's partially true. However, I found more diversity in area design and assets the further I progessed in the game.
The soudtrack has a retro vibe to it, but it's very repetitive. I can't say that I heard anything revolutionary or that I would want to invest in the soundtrack. This isn't a soundtrack to jam by, and it's not what I would consider soothing, so I don't see myself listening to it outside of normal gameplay.
The storyline is really quite deep, and this is a much more involved game than I'd originally anticipated. I've noticed a trend in some of the more recent game publications where emphasis is put on blacksmithing, weaponsmithing, or smithing as a crafting skill. It's a trend that's actually appealing to me and should also hit its mark with classic RuneScape players who spent hours mining and smithing to get the perfect armor and weapon set.
As I mentioned above, this is a party-based game with turn-based combat. You'll begin with one main character and add to your party as the game progresses. Each character has its own unique special skills, combat styles, and weaknesses. In this regard, it does require a bit of strategy as the battles gain in complexity. While exploring different areas and completing quest objectives to complete the story, you'll encounter many battle instances, some of which you can see coming by the presence of an enemy you can't avoid, and many you won't see coming at all. During battle, each character rotates and gets a turn whereby you have to decide whether to use a basic attack, special attack, item, or skill. The reverse is also true, because your opponents will essentially be doing the same thing. There is a certain amount of randomness to the battle instances, as you'll see varying types of enemies, number of enemies, hitpoint variations, and a variety of attacks and skills being thrown at you. This fact alone creates some degree of replay value and prevents the game from feeling stale or stagnant.
In addition to combat, there is a looting mechanic, as you'll often obtain currency drops or find items while exploring. Some of these items can be used right away, such as weapons, armor, and gear, while others might not have an apparent use until later in the game. You'll also encounter merchants and shops of varying types from which you can purchase gear or consumables for your party. Talking with NPCs throughout the game can point you in the right direction if you're having difficulty determining what to do or where to find something.
All gamers should be aware that this is a lengthy game, and it feels somewhat slow-moving at times. I've seen projections somewhere in the neighborhood of 20 hours of gameplay; however, with the high degree to which I've been encountering battle instances, it has made storyline progression feel interrupted.
In regard to controller mechanics, the developer has done some really solid work here. I've been playing with a wired XBox 360 controller, and I've not had any issues in regard to controller mechanics or menu navigation. Gamers have the ability to save their game at any time via the menu interface, and that's in addiiton to autosaves along the way. There's no reason why this game can't be played in short durations if time is a factor for you.
Overall, I certainly recommend Arelite Core. It's got a very retro feel to it; in fact, it reminds me a lot of Dungeons & Dragons: Chronicles of Mystara. If you enjoy that style of game, as well as party-based games or those with turn-based combat, you're in luck. Arelite Core is definitely for you. If, however, you're are a gamer like myself who doesn't naturally gravitate to these types of games, but are willing to broaden your horizons a bit and try something new, I'd absolutely recommend that you give it a try. My assessment at this point is that if you try Arelite Core and don't like it, then this genre of game is probably not for you, but if you have a reasonable adaptable gaming acumen, you may just find a new favorite. Achievements and steam cards are included with this game, but at this price point, that's not a deciding factor for purchasing in my opinion. If this sounds like a game for you otherwise, though, then it's worth every penny.

I liked this game a lot more than I thought I would. The gameplay itself is far more appealing than it would first seem. Once you get the double jump, things are a lot better, though combat remains a bit annoying most of the time. It does have a bit of a "hook" to it and a few redeeming qualities, such as being able to upgrade your armor with scrap you find, and the art style of the enemies and backgrounds were really nice.
The game is advertised as being "tough as nails," and I suppose that's true if you count procedurally generated enemy placement in which some enemies are randomly placed in spots that it's impossible to kill them, as well as some enemies that take about 8-10 hits in melee to kill, where there is no block button and one robot enemy has a triple burst shot that takes out more than half your health in one attack that can be difficult to avoid. More of the game's difficulty comes from the procedural generation spawning about five enemies right around you when you enter a room. Each enemy in the game can take off huge chunks of your health, so having five of the jerks surrounding you with melee and ranged attacks against you is pretty lame.
I don't particularly like the offhand/secondary attacks. Granted, I only tried the starting one, which is an axe you hurt in a difficult-to-predict arc, and it costs 2 energy out of your max 10 energy (my max energy never went up despite spending huge amounts of bolts on outfit upgrades, and I believe it says the head governs energy), and your energy does not just regen over time, nor do enemies drop a reliable amount of energy.
In regard to primary weapons, they're all melee weapons. However, the enemies are usually so fast either to move or to attack, so any weapons with a slow attack speed, like heavy weapons, feel like a big waste in investing in. They will get you killed fast. You aquire new weapons by collecting crafting items dropped by enemies, and random blueprints from boxes you open. If you don't have a blueprint, you can't craft the weapon. If you
get the blueprint, it's kinda like Final Fantasy XII's license board, in that you have to unlock each blueprint and weapon in between your "spot" on the board and the blueprint you're going to. So you might have a blueprint located 2 blueprints to the left of your current weapon, so you'll need to get those other blueprints in between and craft those weaposn to be able to make the one you want.
The last thing I covered, crafting weapons, presents my biggest problem with this game: grinding. Your health is super low, so you need to grind for bolts to upgrade your outfit to raise your health and give you double jump, dash, etc. You can spend what seems to be thousands of bolts on this, However, you
have a base to build to protect the kid's bedroom while you're out at night exploring, or else your people/toys get abducted, and the enemy steals significant numbers of your bolts and other crafting materials, which slows you down on crafting more weapons and upgrades for your base. Upgrades for the base cost about 20x or so the early bolt costs of outfit upgades, and you also need some random item drops that seem to be rare.
So after playing for 21 in-game nights, my constant need to upgrade my outfit to keep me from dying and the unreliability of random item drops and nightly enemy raids taking the items I
need for base upgrades if I were to try to save bolts up, kept me from ever getting to build even one base structure. Maybe they're cool? Maybe not? I don't know, and the amount of time needed to juggle building up enough resources to stay alive
afford base upgrades appears to be costly. In short, the game has a grind built into it which, as best I can tell, exists solely to prolong playtime, rather than to make the game a more enjoyable experience.
A game I would recommend which has very similar elements but is pulled off much better in regard to procedural rooms/enemy placement and the grind, is Rogue Legacy. I don't particularly tend to like tough games, but that one had me completely hooked and was a lot of fun, even if I did get my rear handed to me time and again. If you want a true Metroidvania kind of experience (I wouldn't really call Toy Odyssey one, personally), then go with Dust: An Elysian Tale, or Shadow Complex Remastered. They are very good in my opinion.

Tag "Casual" is definitely not suitable for this game. It is a true hardcore old school puzzle with a lot of things to do and plenty of different mechanics to explore and learn. Despite giving it a positive review, I can't recommend Molecats for everyone. If you want to play some mindless nice-looking casual time killer, you should absolutely stay away from this game.
Turning to actual gameplay, it is really difficult to describe it - it would be the best to try it yourself. Several first levels can be deceptively easy, however, difficulty rises really quickly and in no time you start to use levers for rotating tiles, avoid Molecat-eating flowers, use some kinds of multidimensional elevators and so on. In addition, controls are steadily becoming more sophisticated while you progress through the game because of acquiring some additional powers to use.
Finally, be aware of the fact that this game has just recently been released in Early Access. That is why it still has some issues with controls, some hints and indicators can be quite unclear and the game even crashed for me once. Therefore, it can be better to wait for a full release if you want a smooth experience. On the other hand, developers are quite active and responsive. For example, I had some issues with my xbox360 controller, which were solved with a patch in less than a day.
So, does this game worth its price tag? Absolutely!
Is it suitable for everyone? No.
Nonetheless, I totally recommend giving it a try if you like complicated puzzles with unique gameplay.

Wolfenstein the New Order is an expertly crafted first person shooter. Set in a fictional alternate history where the Nazi's won WWII, you help a resistance group to fight back. I don't want to get too much into the story so as to avoid spoilers.
The story itself has some surprising twists that keep it engaging. I found myself becoming invested in the other characters that B.J. Blaskowitz meets. Each have an interesting story to them and have their own reasons and motivations for fighting the Nazi's. These aren't your normal Nazi's though. As can be expected they have some nasty new weapons in the form of armored soldiers wielding things like rocket launchers, flame throwers and yes even lazers and tesla guns. Among the new Nazi arsenal are the mechanized enemies consisting of drones, panzer hunds, and mechanized soldiers that look like they stepped out of James Cameron's Avatar.
The shooting feels tight and responsive. You gain a variety of weapons that mix things up and several of these have alt-fire modes. An assault rifle with a rocket launcher? You got it. Want to wield 2 assault rifles? You can do that too. You also gain access to knives, grenades, a lazer gun, and a sniper rifle.
What surprised me the most is that the game allows for some pretty satisfying stealth play as well. You can stealth kill your way through a few areas if you watch enemy patrol patterns.
The game also has collectibles and enigma codes to find and solve. It adds a bit of replay incentive. On normal the game provides a decent challenge though it never becomes too excessive. The game also taunts you for your choice of difficulty as well as when you exit the game.
Wolfenstein the New Order is just a well made game that serves as a reminder what a good FPS campaign can offer. Its perhaps for the best that the game doesn't have multiplayer. It has been designed as a single player experience which it absolutely nails.

Being a fan of Ace Team's previous games (The Zeno Clash series especially), I was really looking forward to playing this! Even more after seeing the character design, it looked awesome!
Unfortunately, while I enjoyed a some of my time with the game, it simply fails as a whole. It has several things that could have been really interesting, separately, but they just don't fit, and the whole design falls apart.
The game is supposed to be a fighting and roguelite hybrid. And one of the coolest aspect was how the game "evolves" as people beat the final Boss. This turned out to be an artificial evolution: basically just a series of updates with different moves for the Bosses, more bosses, modes, etc.
Sure, it's a cool idea to keep updating a game, but I was expecting something more substancial that would make people want to go back to the game.
If you're experienced in fighting games, you may have an easier time with this title. If not, prepare for a loooot of frustration. The game simply throws you into the Abyss, with a 1minute tutorial on your first minute of playtime. Good luck interiorizing anything worthwhile without context...
Anyway, the game is extremely reliant on mechanics like move cancelling and timed blocked which are never taught in any way. If you already know about it, you may be able to use it. Otherwise, the controls will simply feel really sluggish and unresponsive. When you start a move, you'll have to wait for the animation to completely finish. Unless, you spend
to get cancellation points... Something that isn't wel explained either.
Regardless, after spending a bunch of hours trying to learn the mechanics, I felt pretty satisfied with the combat, in general. However...
The roguelite elements are really bad. Like... the elements just don't connect properly.
So, you have the main character, but you can capture an enemy to switch with. When your main character dies, you'll have a weaker soldier to play with. If you can reach an altar, your main character respawns. This, in theory, would be a reliable way of having a second chance. Great!
But, there's a huge issue with it...
While you run through the Abyss, you find shopkeeper and items (Weapons and Equipment) that are really useful. But, when you die, you lose most of it. As the soldier, you can pick a couple up, but the rest are lost. The choice of the ones destroyed is also
, making it really frustrating to lose an item you wanted to keep.
On shops, you can also buy "camp tokens", which you can use in altars as a checkpoint. Once again, sounds great. But you lose ALL of your items when you respawn. The result is: hey, I'm farther into the dungeon, cool. However, I have absolutely no equipment, so I might as well just kill myself, since all progress is basically lost.
You see this works? This completely defeats the point of these cool little mechanics, since they're all useless.
Ok, let's assume you want to finish the game without items. Sure. That's where the fighting problems come in.
On normal mode, the game is fairly easy. I beat it on my third try. And I've beaten it like... 8 times, or something? Sure, I still died several times, but it wasn't very interesting, with as many victories in such a short time.
So I switched to nightmare mode. ♥♥♥♥ing hell... this is the most frustating experience I've had with a game, lately.
It's not very different than the normal mode, except that every group of enemies is bigger. Bosses now have an elite ally. You'll be faced with groups of 5+ enemies... It's a mess.
In a fighting game, full of stun times after hits, you'll just be juggled by most bosses and even groups of enemies. As soon as you stand up, you'll be hit by another enemy. Then there are projectiles flying in your direction... it's a mess. If you're experienced in fighting games, you may have a chance. Otherwise, you'll have to waste hours and hours to learn how to cope with it. And it's simply not fun. It feels unfair to have such a number of enemies on you. And then, if you die,  the "second chances" are completely useless.
This was a huge disappointment, and it's a shame. The game has lots of different character to learn, and the game could have been really good. Unfortunately, the rogue-lite elements simply don't work, and the game isn't balanced.
No good tutorialization, the story seems really interesting, but ends up unexplored, ... Oh well.
Maybe I was expecting too much out of it, but frustration put me off.
If the respawn/checkpoint system was reworked, I think the game would have benefited a lot. As it is... not so much.
I hope their next game is more balanced, because the talent is clearly there!

Update:  Okay I'm updating my negative review to a positive one because I've finally found a way to play this game.  It's possible to disable the controller completely by manually editing one of the game config files.  I posted an article to the communite page to help other people who run into the same problem.
If this were a five star rating system, I would subtract two stars for not only not supporting a normal controller but also for setting up the controls in such a way that the controller can't be remapped.  However, that said, I'm happy now that I have a work around.  My first 2.6 hours spent "playing" this game were spent trying to fix the controller issue, finally i can start playing.
Update 2:  Thankfully, now that Steam supports native controller customization, this is no longer an issue whatsoever.  Just go to your controller config in Steam, hit Apply Configuration, Browse Configs, go to Templates and then select Gamepad with Camera Controls and then apply changes.  Instant gamepad fix.

Due to how short this game is and how there is not much replay value because once you beat it with two different characters there is just no drive for me to even keep playing. I can't recommend it unless you can get it on sale cheap enough like I did. It was $5 in the 2015 summer sale and I had like $1.25 in my wallet so I got it dirt cheap. Don't pay over $7.50 (50% off) for it because it is only about 3-4 hours long. The problem with buying it cheap is that after the summer sale it will probably never go on sale again less than $7.50, which even seeing that price is rare. The other problem is that once you beat it, there is not very much replay value. I had the game on my steam and
watch lists for several months before it finally went cheap enough. I already knew it was a short game but I thought it might have some replay value. It does a little, but not as much as I was hoping.
At any rate, it is a very enjoyable game for one or two playthroughs, provided you are willing to adapt to its purposely sluggish controls and incredibly cheap enemy combo attacks, even when you are helpless on the ground. When you figure out what moves to spam on what characters to spam combos and knockdowns, do not hesitate to be as cheap as humanly possible to enemies because that is how they are to you. I've seen a lot of reviews complaining about the sluggish controls and how long it takes you to turn around. While not being able to turn around instantly can sometimes lead to you taking a cheap hit, it is easily overcome-able once you get used to the fighting system. The controls for the monk are noticeably more sluggish than the girl's because he has bigger slower attacks with a 2h sword. The girl is fast and can get in and pull off moves quickly enough to wreck groups of enemies. Sometimes enemies can ground combo you several times, making it super cheap, and sometimes the cheap hits can get you in trouble before you can get to the last boss, but overall it was not much of a problem for me. My first time to the boss he crushed me mercilessly because he has some of the most annoying, cheap, unpredictable attacks I've ever seen any enemy have. All bosses in this game do, and some of the enemies as well. The second time I played through the game and got to him I beat him by working him over as much as I could with the girl's spinning attack, working the cheap move option in my favor as much as I possibly could, because if I didn't, he sure would've.
For the first 3 hours the game seemed really hard and a bunch of times I was getting pretty frustrated, but always having fun. When I got the combat down pretty good, hours 3-4 were much easier and I found the game to be considerably much easier than I had first thought.
The graphics are good but the game really shines with its awesome art style, mainly in the design of the characters and enemies. The music and sound effects are done nicely as well. Everything flows really smooth too. Once I got the hang of combat I was using the way the character animations flow to my advantage to look for tells when I could hit and when I should block. Which like I said means jack sh-t though on bosses because they are extraordinarily cheap and unpredictable.
It is too bad it is so short, but that is the fate of most indie games. For what it is worth, catch it on sale for no more than 50% its normal price. The short time you do have with it will be fun, and you might even want to play through it again as a different character. The sluggish combat and cheap enemy attacks, and your own ability to spam cheap hits, makes the game pretty much a one way street. A better more well thought out fighting system may have helped this game to a 7, maybe even 8, out of ten.

An interesting little game *BUT*
Like other Kickstarter projects, this little title has made it's way to Steam.
Gameplay-wise, it's very simplistic. As the main character, you are set in charge as the alpha decision maker for a group of plane crash survivors.
You do this by being presented with a simplistic cost/consequence decision tree that makes it apparent very quickly that no matter your choices, not everyone is going to survive.
However, despite it's indie-artistic charm, that's about where the appeal ends. On my first playthrough, I finished the game in about 30 minutes; taking the time to read each dialogue. My following seassion was pounded out in less than 15 as I found myself skipping through the dialogue simply due to lack of interest and the non-existant story. Your fellow survivors all speak in this mumble language (much like in the Sims) which also became an irritant. If there had been actual voice acting, perhaps that would have been enough to encourage one to listen to the dialogue.
Normally titles like this on Steam I would expect to see in the range of $5 to $10. But at $16.99 CDN there is just simply nothing new or interesting enough here to warrant such a high price. Thankfully I picked this title up during a sale at 80% off, otherwise I would have been looking into the refund process.

A point-and-click shooter that will leave you wondering why Rick Grimes has such a hard time killing zombies.
It's a simple game. You will not need a manual or a tutorial to help you started. You can play three modes: defense, endless match, and deathmatch. You can also play three characters: the guy, the girl, and the swat. Choice of character makes very little difference in the actual gameplay, and other players can choose to be the same character as you if they so desire.
Defense mode is an onslaught of zombies, stage-by-stage, released against you and your teammates. The process of clearing the stage will net you loot such as money or grenades. Once you clear a stage, your team will take a brief break while the leader makes decisions on what to do with the money your team collected. He or she can either purchase defense materials or purchase weapons and ammo; the most you can do if you're not the leader of your team is to  request to purchase certain items otherwise you're pretty much in the hands of the leader. It's important to note that you will share weapons and ammo with your team so the good stuff often never lasts for very long. Endless Night mode is exactly the same except that there is no break between stages, it's just an onslaught of zombies. And Deathmatch mode is your traditional player vs. player mayhem. The mode that I play the most, and the mode that I found others playing the most, was Defense mode. It has a lot of potential and the co-op experience is actually sort of pleasant.
Other than these three modes and the three characters mentioned above, there is little to no variation in the game. Enemies get stronger and receive added bonuses throughout the stages in Defense mode, and likewise, you'll get to choose which perks you'll carry on to the next stage.
Overall, if you're looking to burn some time and not commit to a lengthy game or gaming session, this is the game you need to pick up. Be careful though, the game is much more addicting than you might expect.

TLDR, If you're looking to play InfantrySide 2, go right ahead. If you were interested in the bigger picture, this game has peaked and is on It's way down.
What
great about PlanetSide 2? A mostly spotless record on avoiding P2W. Vast continents with player driven battles and seeing hundreds of soldiers fight for control of a base. If large scale battles are your thing, this is the game that can ruin the rest of the FPS genre for you.
What
great?
Performance. Game is CPU bound for most users. There are lots of tips on how to improve it, but for most systems you'll have to sacrifice a lot to get decent frame rates.
Customer support. Avoid making any accidental purchases in the game, exercise patience when the game goes unresponsive during a transaction, always make sure you use the right currency, avoid misclicking in general to avoid making purchases that don't come with confirmation popups (this isn't an issue with spending real money or anything, just spending the ingame and premium currency). You will never get refunded by DBG's support.
Anticheat. The game isn't running wild with hackers by anymeans, but years back they made their automated system toothless after some individuals made a game of creating false positives by playing on more highly scrutinized fresh accounts.
Why did I qualify it's good record in regards to P2W? A few months back they redesigned the implant system. In the new system, you unlock game altering perks by dumping your ingame or premium currency on RNG crates. Implants are divided into 4 tiers of rarity, with the rarest calculated to take hundreds of hours of grinding to unlock. The real money equivalent is nothing to laugh at either. And all of these unlocks are character specific, you'll be at the mercy of RNG again for every faction you play and every server you play.
What
great? Vehicle combat. On the ground you have tanks, buggies, and busses. In the sky their are fighters, gunships, and dropships. All aircraft have hover capabilities and the dogfights are one of a kind. To get an idea of tank combat imagine battlefield 3, put no restrictions on the amount of vehicles that can be inplay at any given moment, make gunners relevant in tank engagements, remove rocket launchers from the engineers, and remove the ability to steal enemy vehicles. Also add in hover tanks.
What stopped being awesome about the vehicle game? Increased time to kill, slower repairs, lower effective ranges, simplified directional armors (now just "rear" and "not rear"), removal of 1 hit kills. Devs' plans going forward? A few tweaks, instead of rolling back to an enjoyable state. This was 6+ months of development time and they're sticking with it no matter how many playstyles it kills.

Toy Odyssey seems like a game that would be really good, and for short periods of time, it is. Unfortunately, it falls short (but just barely so) on nearly everything. I should also note that about 4-6 hours of gameplay were in offline mode.
The toy designs are all really interesting and the main character is pretty cool. The room design is well thought out and the story seems really good thus far.
I can't exactly say why I noticed this, but the sound effects felt really fitting, given that you are literally a toy. I thought it was amazing that the player "hears" from the perspective of an average-sized human being. Swords won't sound like swords, but like tiny toothpicks being swung. It's probably my favorite part of the game.
Like all rogue-lites, the gameplay is compelling. There's always an urge to go a bit further, especially if there's the possibility of reward.
Cons:
Unfortunately, after a few runs through the house, I began to dread trekking through the first few rooms to get to a new area. Sure, the rat holes offer fast travel, but on some runs they barely appear, or appear in mostly useless places.
The first time I came across a chest and was greeted with a spinning card, I was excited to recieve a new weapon, as I was doing paltry damage to the other toys. Instead I was given a
for a silver sword. I planned to craft it as soon as possible, but was told by the game that I needed to craft every sword
the silver sword before I could make my prized posession. I didn't have a single one of the blueprints for the previous weapons, and I still haven't obtained one, despite getting the blueprint very early in my gameplay.
Normally I wouldn't point this out in its own flaw section, but since it makes up the majority of my deaths, I believe it needs to be addressed. Sometimes I entered a room (usually from below) only to spawn on top of a group of enemies, taking massive damage and getting knocked away from the door. It feels like there is a "anti-spawn radius" next to doors that enter from the side, but some enemies get projectiles or attacks that trigger so fast it seems like it needs to be bigger.
The voice acting for the game is a bit strange. Some characters sound fine, and the base audio quality really shows in these characters, but others, like Brand, sound like they're reading the lines with a gun to their head, as fast as possible. The sound balance is also an issue, as sound effects (like in the baby room for example) are much louder than music and dialogue. This may be a problem with my sound system (as I've noticed it in a few other modern games), so don't take that point as absolute fact. The text, however, is poorly translated in some areas. It isn't a huge problem, and is still readable by all means, which is why I included it with two other minor points, but it is very noticeable.
Overall I wanted to like Toy Odyssey, but it pushed me away with a lot of tiny punches. It was at the top of my wishlist for months, so I was very disappointed to see it fall flat. There is a good chance I will play it more, and will change my review to reflect any changes in my opinion, but for now, I think it would be best to pass on this one.

I don't really think that this game justifies the mediocre scores it achieved. It's not cutting edge - after all it uses the Source engine familiar in many FPS's. But this has got a number of novelties in it - a few extras that make you think the developers thought quite in depth about this hybrid of RPG and FPS.
It's much more action focused than say Oblivion, but in doing so, sacrifices a lot of the depth of that game. Sometimes the controls are a little fiddly and the enemy manages to score hits on you when clearly they didn't. Seemingly difficult situations like a horde of spiders in their lair can simply be defeated by running in circles around them and hacking away.

So what happens when you take Castlevania Symphony of the Night... or more accurately Castlevania Aria / Dawn of Sorrow and combine it with Dark Souls clunk?
Well let me answer that for you... You get a game about travelling in to a procedurally generated abyss delving deeper and deeper to kill some demon warlock Freddy Kruger guy, who's nightmares are your reality. In fact, you're not even real because he dreamt you up... except you want to kill him... that's what kind of game you get... yeah.
So this game tries way too hard to be epic and it just fails on just about every front. The art style is the only thing this game has going for it and it's just a shame it was wasted on such a giant turd like Abyss Odyssey. It's as if all the production value went in to the art style and none of it in to the game development, plot or music because it was all forgettable.
It's nothing new you haven't already seen, the point being is a lot of the game play mechanics are drab, boring and redundant... let me explain:
It's a rouge like game, where no dungeon you enter is ever the same twice... except that's kind of a lie because every area is almost exactly identical to the last, aside from some buzz saws and flowers trying to kill you.
You basically travel down a linear path and encounter a branching point here and there. These branching paths quickly lead to a dead end with a treasure chest or check point of some kind. Usually when there's nothing there I do what any veteran Casltevania player would do and smack the wall. 20% of the time there's a hidden area with a shop keeper or paltry weapon hiding behind it...
No meat though, I probably would of enjoyed a nice Castlevania roast beef here and there but no... it's usually just some crap.
Another thing about this game is how lazy the direction is... I mean, procedurally generated dungeons for a game with this kind of art style?
With all the effort put in to the art direction you figured they would of came up with some cool level designs and boss design concepts and made an actual game... you know, one where the developers have to always be one step ahead of themselves so players can't sequence break the game... either way it's wasted potential.
The game itself gets dull and tired way too quickly. It has unlockable characters and starting points but you need to rely heavily on luck... Okay basically everything resides on your luck, as well as time put in to the game.
I beat the game once, unlocked some floaty chick with a spear who has a jelly fish for a companion (Yeah is this making you cringe yet? I was rolling my eyes the entire time... what pretentious ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t is this any way?)
There's also a heavy weapon user who looks a lot like Tyrael from the Diablo franchise (because THAT was purely a coincidence) and he's randomly unlocked by beating random bosses you encounter... random, random, random ....so have fun with randomly doing that.
Another thing that bothered me was the limited inventory space ... of 4 whole spaces. Enjoy managing poison antidotes, mana potions, health potions and check point tokens when you can basically only carry 1 of each item.
The number one biggest waste of resources though that made up most of the game's mechanics, or should I say gimmick, was the ENTIRE enemy capture system...
I mean WTF is the point of all this? All the enemies I caught were even clunkier and weaker than my main character.... none of them had any really cool abilites and were all difficult to control... It's as if the developers were saying: "Hey switch to this centaur thing if you want to die... like right now... yeah there ya go, you're dead now, hope that helped."
I never understood why the game forced you in to sequences where you had to play as random enemies either, other than to basically get their spirit afterwards... as some kind of reward? Great, thanks for THAT. Most of the time I had something better to do, like NOT playing as a worthless enemy character.
Either way the game's plot and premise is a cryptic mess, just like Dark Souls, so I guess they got the worst possible aspects of that series right...
Clunky gameplay, in order to artificially increase the difficulty of the game; and a cryptic plot so it confuses the player in to thinking their mind has been "blown'.... except... no it hasn't, this game is just stupid and you're trying too hard to make sense of all of it...
It's a 5 out of 10 at best... it tries, it fails... go play Castlevania SotN... It's just a better game as well as the godfather of the genre... When are developers going to learn you can't reinvent perfection?

It still shocks me how few people have played Dark Messiah of Might and Magic.
Dark Messiah of Might and Magic is a first-person fantasy action game built on the Source engine. Think Heretic or Hexen with physics and bloom.
It features full-body awareness (meaning that you can look down and see your body), an RPG leveling system complete with classes andskill trees, which can radically change the way you approach situations, and it's one of those lovely early Source games that takes advantage of physics due to the fact that physics weren't really a thing prior to Source. This means that the level design is full of heavy objects held up by flimsy planks, giant spiked walls, enemies precariously perched on ledges, giant death pits, and other such devices designed solely for you to put boot to orc♥♥♥♥♥to send them into it.
Oh, and it has a button devoted to kicking for that very purpose.
The multiplayer was incredible, too, but it's quite dead by now, which is a shame.

Toy Odyssey is what happens when you put Rogue Legacy and Toy Story together. The game is incredibly well made from the top to the bottom. Character and mob animations and designs are great looking. The soundtrack, ambiance, and sound design are all wonderful. The map generation isn't random and chaotic like many other "Roguelite inspired" titles. And above all else, where it counts, the gameplay and core mechanics are as sound as we've seen in a metroidvania platformer since Ori and the Blind Forest.
You play as Brand, a toy of a child that has been left alone in a part of the house overcome with an unknown darkness. You must venture forth finding familiar friends and fighting toy foes that have been corrupted (prepare to hate spiders and marbles). The RPG elements in the character building are phenomenal. They are incredibly basic simply just paying nuts, the games currency, to upgrade either you weapons or 5 main body parts. Head, Body, Gloves, Cape, and Feet can all be upgraded through a simply yet addicting leveling up process. You just dump money into them for upgrade points worth different amounts of stat increases and passive abilities. For instance if you upgrade you feet enough, you get the beloved double jump.
And that is all without mentioning the base building in the game. While it feels very mobile at first with the amounts of time that each upgrade takes (hours for many of them), they do progressively get easier as you go along. The only major downside with the game from playing is just this. The fact that you have to wait numerous real time hours for an upgrade to finish. The silver lining? It does continue to go with the game closed.
Overall, Toy Odyssey: The Lost and Found is my biggest hidden gem and surprise hit this year. It has easily climbed up onto my Games of the Year list. Not sure where yet  as I need to complete the game first, but after sinking several hours into this delightful game, I needed to let the people of Steam know that it is worth a buy for any fans of Rogue Legacy style games or Metroidvania style games.
Pros:
+ Fantastic art style and animation quality.
+ Sound design is spot on (wear headphones).
+ Addictive and fun gameplay and core elements.
+ Simplistic, yet, comfortable progression system.
+ Well worth the $15 price tag.
Cons:
- Slow base building mechanic initially.
- Few minor bugs (options settings not saving once the game is closed).
- SPIDERS and MARBLES! Ahhh!

Half-Life: Opposing Force is an expansion pack for Valve Software's video game Half-Life. The game was developed by Gearbox Software and Valve Corporation and published by Sierra Entertainment on November 19, 1999. This is the first expansion for Half-Life, Blue Shift beeing the second. Gearbox Software was selected to develope Opposing Force because it impressed Valve and they (Valve) wanted to focus on other projects. Opposing Force returns to the same setting as Half-Life, but instead portrays the events from the perspective of a U.S. Marine, one of the enemy characters in the original game. The player takes control of Adrian Shephard, a U.S. Marine send to neutralize Black Mesa Research Facility but it's then separated from the rest of the soldiers and his goal is to survive and get out of Black Mesa alive. Half-Life: Opposing Force has the same gameplay and graphics with some improvements as the original Half-Life. Do you remember the TV show “LOST”?
It revolved around a group of passengers from a doomed Flight which went down somewhere between Australia and Los Angeles.
Climbing from the wreckage the rag-tag survivors found themselves stranded on a beautiful and terrifying island with mysteries and supernatural encounters lurking around every corner.
Like a lot of people I watched that show every week without a clue as to what was going on, there were polar bears, bunkers and even a black-smoke monster, it was great!
Part sci-fi, part survival and part supernatural, If you’ve never seen the show, think Bear Grylls meets the X-Files and you’re part way there.
It wasn’t just the otherworldly mystery of the Island which made the show riveting either, the disparate mix of characters forced together; each with their own unique personalities and wildly different take on events formed the backbone of the series.
There was Hurley with his “cursed” numbers and Locke with his “blessed” legs.
Sawyer was a conman, Sayid was a torturer and Kate was  a murderer.
Every character had a past and a part to play on the island, but why am I reminiscing about LOST whilst I should be reviewing Dyscourse?
Well, Dyscourse is set on a remote island, it starts just after a plane crash and it revolves around a group of very different characters as they struggle to survive the island and await rescue.
Sounds familiar doesn’t it?
Dyscourse places you in control of Rita, professional coffee maker and amateur plane crash survivor.
She  also seems to have the uncanny ability to convince total strangers to do what she tells them, which is handy as she quickly sets about fulfilling her unspoken Jack Sheppard  fantasies by taking charge of the group of stranded survivors  and bossing them around with varying degrees of success.
You see, with Dyscourse, events almost never turn out the way you expect them too.
The very first decision you're faced with in the game involves two other survivors, some "evil crabs" and (If  you found it in the wreckage) a frying pan.
Which survivor you try to save from the perilous pincers and how you go about your daring rescue is up to you.
If you're armed with the frying pan you have the option of trying to squish the salty nippers into crab pâté, alternatively you could try shouting and waiving your arms around in a fierce display of anti-crab sentiment.
Whoever you try to save and whatever method you choose is going to change how events unfold.
You 're decisions genuinely matter here, every choice you make will push the story in a new direction and the story you forge for yourself is what Dyscourse is all about.
The game itself plays as a pretty simple point and click adventure,  most days begin and end with your band of survivors gathering in your camp to complain about how awful everything is and squabble about  what  the group should do next.
It's these conversations that form the backbone of Dyscourse as you listen to the bickering castaways and decide who to agree with and who, inevitably, to♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
Your input will influence the upcoming events in both obvious and subtle ways, assigning tasks and choosing which errands to help out with yourself can lead to some pretty surprising outcomes creating a very entertaining (if somewhat short) story to enjoy.
You're probably going to get through a single play through of Dyscourse in less than 2 hours, maybe a lot less if you're in a hurry, but don't let that put you off, you will almost certainly play this game again, probably more than once, just to see the vastly different outcomes resulting from your choices.
Different survivors will live and die, you'll explore different areas of the island, you'll discover  more about the insanely quirky characters stranded with you, I'd even go so far as to say you'll find your second play through a deeper, more fulfilling experience than your first.
The graphics are as colourful as the characters and they're perfectly functional in their own stylised way, but they're not going to be to everyone's taste.
Whatever you think of the "zany" cartoon graphics they undeniably fit the mood and feel of the title.
From the very beginning Dyscourse feels like your decisions really matter, events can change so dramatically based on your choices that you'll find yourself trying to anticipate what the possible outcomes might be, you'll also grow to like some characters more than others which is likely to affect your decision making process too.
Don't go into Dyscourse expecting a great character driven piece of narrative though or you'll be disappointed, this is an indie game, it's not a Bioware title, for the most part the characters are two dimensional stereotypes,  you're not going to lose yourself in empathy with your fellow survivors, but there is enough depth there to pull you in a little, just enough to make you care who lives and who dies, and just like the island in the TV show LOST, there are plenty of opportunities in Dyscourse for your new friends to come to a sticky end.
As I wrote earlier, Lost was a mind boggling show, the continual mystery of the bizarre events on the island kept everyone hooked, you had to keep watching to try and figure out what was going?
The sad thing is, it turned out that the writers didn’t know what was going on either; they had no master plan, no outline, and no grand conclusion to tie everything together.
They were just making it up as they went along, which was very evident in the shows final episodes.
The same can be said of my first play through of Dyscourse,  the unexpected events and offbeat characters kept me hooked, I had no idea where it was going to end and as far as my decision making goes, I was definitely making it up as I went along.
However, unlike Lost, which went on for far too long and had a controversial (and arguably disappointing) ending, Dyscourse provides a quick fix of Castaway goodness which never outstays its welcome. As for the ending, well, that’s pretty much up to you.
Don’t like the way it turns out? Play through it again and make some different choices.
It might be a little Island but there’s a world of possibilities waiting for you.

A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame is the imprisoned lightning, and her name Mother of Exiles. With silent lips, "Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, the wretched refuse of your teeming shore. Send these, the homeless, tempest-tossed, to me..."
Wolfenstein: The New Order is a great reboot or soft reboot or whatever; I never quite got what it's place in the Wolfenstein timeline is, but I'd argue it's the best in the series when you consider the writing, the story, the quality of the characters, the level design and audio design. Technologically speaking, of course certain aspects of the game are going to be better than those that are older, but what really stands out in The New Order are the characters. I don't think BJ has had such development as a character, and while he doesn't go through any major arcs, it's the fact that his character actually character that matters. Plus the side characters of Anya, Caroline, depending on your choices, Fergus and Tekla, Set and Bombate, Max and Klaus, they all have to own personality and back story that you can try and delve into in between missions. It just adds something so unique to the atmosphere and world.
The story itself is quite interesting as it doesn't take place in the 1940's like the previous entries. It's set roughly 14 years after the end of WWII, so in this alternate history the game is set in 1960. It starts in 1946, but BJ suffers some serious injuries and is in a coma for 14 years. After the game's introductionary missions set in 1946, you wake up in 1960 as a group of Nazi's are in the midst of shutting down the asylum where he is under a group of doctors and a nurse's care (the nurse is the daughter of the two doctors). Waking up and full of rage, you go on your Nazi killing spree, trying to find the nurse as she was taken away. That nurse is Anya. Basically, that's the start of the epic saga of The New Order as you eventually find your way to the resistance group in Berlin who work with you to try and take down the Nazi regime, or at least part of it. I don't wish to spoil the rest of the story as it really is quite good.
My only complaints really are the incomplete options in advanced settings for changing the graphics.
Overall, great game. 9.3/10

A fun & funny game where your choices really DO matter. Stranded on a desert island following a plane crash, your goal is to help your ragtag band of survivors... well, survive. Virtually every decision you make has its consequences, & you make a LOT of decisions. Friendships are formed & broken, sacrifices are made, people die... people ALWAYS die. But just who, & how many, is entirely in your hands.
No two playthroughs of this game are the same. That's not to say it doesn't sometimes get tedious to replay, but the achievement system in place is a really good motivator to unlock particular paths. Also you can "rewind" to any day in the story instead of having to start fresh every time you want to change something. It even shows you who died or was injured on each available day, making it easier to go back & "save" characters by making a different choice, if you're feeling guilty. I did sometimes find myself wishing for a "fast forward" button for many of the scenes, though -- things get a bit desperate when you're onto those last two or three achievements.
I didn't like the artwork at first, but it grew on me (the backgrounds are great, but the character designs I'm still not fond of -- WHAT is Rita wearing & WHY does she have claws?). The writing is really entertaining; the humorous dialog combined with the cartoonish style definitely help to keep the mood light, even when you're dealing with stuff like murder & cannibalism. The voice acting is... well, it can be turned off, fortunately. As for the DLC story "Indie Island," it was way too meta for me; I only went through it once.
Overall this is a clever, well-made game which really does hide a multitude of secrets. So do yourself a favor & start DYSCovering them today!!! (That was really bad, sorry.)

The Talos Principle is a philosophical puzzle game made by the creators of Serious Sam.
The game has a compelling and philosophical story, told through both the interactions between the player and the two major characters, Elohim and Milton, and through a small number of audio logs. Your choices matter in the game, as they shift what the characters think of you, and can change the ending you get.
The graphics and music are both fantastic. The graphics are bright and colorful, and they help to shape and contrast the different environments. The music is calming and ambient, and helps to add to the atmosphere of the game.
The game also has a variety of interesting and creative puzzles. The puzzles themselves start off easy, but start to get challenging later on. As you progress, different mechanics are added into the puzzles, and are used both on their own, and in conjunction with the other mechanics. One complaint is that the movement mechanics are a bit clunky (most of the jumps are supposed to be performed by pressing space when an icon shows up), although you can still play the game comfortably despite this. Although most puzzles have a set solution, you can find ways to complete them in different and unintended ways.
The game also has a load of easter eggs. Many are hidden out of view, and others require you to go through long processes to reveal them. Despite this, many of the easter eggs are fun to find, and I spent a lot of time trying to find them all.
Overall, the game is worth the price, and I'd recommend it to everyone who enjoys puzzle games.

Well, this is certainly the most impressive use of the Source engine I've ever seen. Pretty cool game. It's not what you think it is. This is not an open-ended adventure game a la Elder Scrolls. This is an "on-rails" first-person hack-and-slash akin to Half Life.
Not to say that's bad; it's just not what I expected. There's not a lot of exploring to do. Some, but not much. There are secret places you might not find, but they rarely contain anything really valuable (just a couple extra potions usually). The graphics are pretty, the combat system is really, really cool.
The one bad thing is that you spend in-game time to perform meta-game tasks. For example, the game doesn't pause while you're in your backpack or re-doing your hotbar. So if you get in a fight and that spell you want isn't already bound, you're taking some damage while you open your backpack and drag the spell's icon onto your hotbar.
Good game, but don't expect Oblivion. It's Half-Life with swords.

Wolfenstein: The New Order is a great reboot or soft reboot or whatever; I never quite got what it's place in the Wolfenstein timeline is, but I'd argue it's the best in the series when you consider the writing, the story, the quality of the characters, the level design and audio design. Technologically speaking, of course certain aspects of the game are going to be better than those that are older, but what really stands out in The New Order are the characters. I don't think BJ has had such development as a character, and while he doesn't go through any major arcs, it's the fact that his character actually character that matters. Plus the side characters of Anya, Caroline, depending on your choices, Fergus and Tekla, Set and Bombate, Max and Klaus, they all have to own personality and back story that you can try and delve into in between missions. It just adds something so unique to the atmosphere and world.
The story itself is quite interesting as it doesn't take place in the 1940's like the previous entries. It's set roughly 14 years after the end of WWII, so in this alternate history the game is set in 1960. It starts in 1946, but BJ suffers some serious injuries and is in a coma for 14 years. After the game's introductionary missions set in 1946, you wake up in 1960 as a group of Nazi's are in the midst of shutting down the asylum where he is under a group of doctors and a nurse's care (the nurse is the daughter of the two doctors). Waking up and full of rage, you go on your Nazi killing spree, trying to find the nurse as she was taken away. That nurse is Anya. Basically, that's the start of the epic saga of The New Order as you eventually find your way to the resistance group in Berlin who work with you to try and take down the Nazi regime, or at least part of it. I don't wish to spoil the rest of the story as it really is quite good.
My only complaints really are the incomplete options in advanced settings for changing the graphics.
Overall, great game. 9.3/10

Abyss Odyssey is an awesome fighting game with some cool rogue-lite elements. There are lots of unlockable characters and every game is a random dungeon. You could say that the game gets repetetive, because it consists of smashing hordes of enemies on your way to the boss fight, but personally I love this game because it consists of smashing hordes of enemies on your way to the boss fight.
As far as the fighting mechanics go, it's a lot like smash bros.  There are no easy combos.  At first a 4 hit combo seems impossible, then you will find a youtube video of an insane 10 hit combo.  This game is sort of an anti-button mashing game.  If you mash, you will be sent to bed without supper.  In my opinion, this makes the game terribly fun to play, as it's all about exploiting the range and timing of attacks.
You can play as any enemy in the game, including the bosses, so there's lots of play time.  I've been playing for about 26 hours and I am still missing about 7 enemies or so.
The art style speaks for itself, as everything is beautiful and weird.  this game is about to go on super monster sale soon, and it would behoove you to buy it.  It is an awesome fighting game, but you have to play by its rules.  Check out some of the combo exhibition videos on youtube.

Castlevania Symphony of the Night, Megaman X and Rogue Legacy walk into a bar, and a baby came out the back door, called...
+Replayability
+Character progression
+Combat
+Variety in gear
+Leading to variety in combat
+And a good variety of enemies
+Aesthetics
+BOOTY AND LOOT! <3
+A story for the Feels
-Grindy in some parts
-Still could use some polish in UI
-Minor and rare bugs
If you have any fond memories of the above, you may enjoy this. There's a steady progression system, some base-building elements and loot extravaganza, in the form of blueprints for weapons, gear, and base-building material. The main appeal would be the combat, which is pretty tight, with the varied weapons having different attacking range, attack speed (in delays and attack rate) and damage. It's definitely not purely aesthetic. In this way, Castlevania SoTN's daddy genes are showing.
At the same time, the movement is heavily inspired by Megaman X. It's responsive, frantic, and mobile, allowing you to juggle yourself in the air with glides, wall hanging, dashes and double-jumps. Combat is pretty fluid, and somewhat strategic, and you'll find yourself dying very easily if you don't know how to abuse your enemy's weakness.
Now comes a minor gripe: enemy AI tends to be quite predictable, but I wouldn't hold it against the game. At the early stages, this means that the fewer enemies you encounter teach you their movement patterns, and you have the luxury of learning; at the later stages, they'll all be on screen at once, so you definitely need to put on your thinking cap or you'll quickly get swamped.
Surprisingly, the story is pretty good, and has some twists. You discover pieces of the story through NPC dialogue, and mainly, the Diary entries. It's like the unveiling of a tragic story, for those of you who like a little drama.
Still, there's something to be said about the way the main quest is done. If you're like me and enjoy a slow walk in the park, this is not bad. However, it's quite hard to speed through the main quest because some of it involves grinding, so you'll probably have to prioritize character growth vs story progression.
And that being said, sometimes the quests can be a little grindy, depending on how often you encounter the enemy you need, and how often they drop what you want. Of course, with procedurally generated dungeons that drop loot you need, this is always an issue. The devs are definitely still working on this though, because the drop rate has been increased as of this review, so it's not unbearable.
That brings us nicely to the end: There definitely are some very minor bugs (non-game-breaking at all) and there needs to be some improvement to the UI (to inform your choice of weapons, for example), but other than that, this game is well polished, the controls are tight, combat is commendable, and is highly replayable. Plus, it's really affordable, compared to other titles.

Are you one of the many players looking for a good rogue-like game on Steam? Do you enjoy fighting games such as SF, MK, KOF, or MvC? Then look no further than Abyss Odyssey, I recently picked up this game, installed and lost myself in it for the next 3 hours.
It's similar in goal to Castlevania(not LoS, more like HoD), plays like a fighting game(dash attacks, dodging, special moves, juggles, etc.), and kicks the crap out of you like Dark Souls. You can play as one of the three characters(I only have two of the three so I can make no comments on the third character), Katrien, the fencer style character, the Ghost Monk, the big sword waving, fireball-tossing, robed badass, and a third character who appears to use a spear/polearm.
Your main goal is to work your way down to the Warlock and defeat him, picking up power ups, weapons, and levels along the way. You can pick up special summons which can be activated by pressing down on the d-pad(Also, definitely should play this with some type of controller), which will turn you into a monster, whether it be a skeleton soldier, a sea witch, or a legless bird masked weirdo. This summon allows you to have essentially two characters, but if you die as your main character(Katrien, Ghost Monk, other lady) you lose the summon and become a soldier. If you die as your summon you become your main character. As the soldier you are slower, a bit weaker, and don't have access to the same amount of mobility or damage as your main character. However, if you make it to an altar or defeat one of the mini-bosses as the soldier you can revive as your main character(missing most of your HP).
Overall, I would definitelly recommend picking up this game if you're looking for a challenging and fun beat 'em up rogue-like. Definitely worth it to buy on sale.

Rimworld is a work in progress, but one that is already very fleshed out. With the developer working hard on updates, this game has yet to reach it's full potential. But the state it is in now shows that it has a lot of potential.
The game puts you in charge of a group of people that need to survive on a hostile planet. Raiders, tribals, mechanoids, animals and the planet itself are all against you. Add to that the personalities and skills of your own colonists and you might understand that survival really means survival in this game.
The game is inspired by Dwarf Fortress and people who love that game or the micromanagement of it, will love this. The basics can be picked up pretty quick thorugh the clean UI and clear messages and explanations, but maintaining your colony for a longer period is something that may take a few tries. The game creates amazing stories just by having the world interact with it's inhabitants, through a choice of three storytellers. Each of these manipulates the world differently and has multiple difficulties to choose from.
The way you play your colony is completely up to you. You choose the storyteller, the starting people and the location on the planet. From there you can choose whatever way you want to make the colony work. This freedom allows you to challenge yourself as much as you like. Or create a relaxing creative experience.
On a final note, the community on reddit is always welcoming newcomers so feel free to drop by there and ask anything you want to know before or after purchasing the game.

The Talos Principle is a great game in my opinion.
The world looks absolutely amazing, but it is also intriguing because it is strangly incoherent, which does however make sense from a lore perspective. Exploring the world will reward you with stars if you manage to find them and a lot of eastereggs, which honestly are way more fun and rewarding.
The puzzles are maybe the weakest part of this (puzzle) game. Not because they are not challenging, the Talos Principle contains some really nice brainteasers, which can take a while to solve, but because of their mechanics. They rely heavily on old video game puzzle stereotypes, such as redirecting laser beams, stacking boxes or using a dublicate of yourself. But again, this is justified by the lore, which is why I mind this fact less.
The aforementioned lore is the strongest part of the Talos Principle. I have never felt so invested in an obviously scripted discussion. The Talos Principle deals with a lot of philosophical topics ranging from the highly philosopical such  religion, inevitability and destiny to more practical topics such as the nature of consciousness, death, the need of an observer and science. While obviously not providing a lot of answers, the game raises questions which still preoccupied me long after I finished the game.
Bear in mind however that nearly all communication in this game is text based, so if you are unwilling to read or if you want to focus purely on the puzzle mechanics, the Talos Principle is not for you.
Everyone else gets a thoughtful puzzle game set in a gorgeous landscape, which I highly recommend (at least to everyone who likes the concepts of a thoughtful puzzle game)

It's cliche, but if you know Choose Your Own Adventure, you know this style of game.  Done well, it can be really engaging, and provide a lot of replay value in going back and finding different outcomes.
Unfortunately, this one didn't really resonate with me.  On a mechanical level, the game is fine, with frequent decisions (some timed) that appear to have a substantial impact on the narrative.  It's the narrative itself I take issue with -- the characterization is very one-dimensional, with each character serving as a simple stereotype.
A bit of personality shorthand is fine for a short game, but these characters are mere caricatures, where every single line is a repeat of their one overriding personality trait.  It makes the game farcical, which removes a lot of (well, all of) the weight from the decisions; when someone gets hurt or killed, it's difficult to sympathize when everything they've said to that point has been the same exaggerated characteristic over and over again.  Couple this with humor that borders on slapstick and emotional responses that seem sociopathic and it's hard to take seriously.
To me, for a game like this to work, the decisions have to be something I care about -- the tension comes from wanting to make the correct decision.  Unfortunately, the relative silliness on display here in combination with the flat characters means that ten minutes in the decisions start feeling fairly arbitrary as I click through for my ending.

I do not know how to adequately express my feeling of dissapointment at the way the creators of this game have gone since I started playing again. Here I go anyways. Off of my memory, I played this game for probably 300+ hours on the non-Steam version around 2-3 years ago. I then logged in about 100 more in the steam version before life forced me to change my scheduling, and thus I dropped the game. I have come back and put about 40 more hours in, and I cannot stand it any longer.
I now come back to find the playerbase has heavily dropped, and a lot of people viewing the game in a negative light. I had hoped that whatever caused such hate for the game I loved to be something I would not care about, but I was wrong. The game had completely changed since I had last played, some of it was for the better, yes, but most of it was for the worse.
I came back to a game where nobody seems to be having fun, and everyone seems to be running the same 'meta' robots. Teams are now only 5 players each, which forces more emphasis on each player more heavily. This means if one person leaves the match or tries to make their bot for fun, you only end up hurting your team. I really do not understand why big teams were a problem for them to remove. Perhaps they had their reasons, but shrinking team size is only going to create problems.
"Well maybe I could manage to squeeze some fun out of this game by making a 'meta' bot." Except I come back to find that instead of making millions or hundreds of thousands of robbits a match, it is all tied to RNG. They replaced such a nice system with a cash-grab crate system that gives you random parts that you probably will not need. But hey, at least I can sell this item worth such a high amount of currency, for barely what it is worth!
To give them credit, they did remove megabots, which before I left was already turning into two giants fighting while a swarm of healers went around them. They also added a lot of cool new movement, special, and weapon items. Too bad I cannot try them out without RNG or grinding in the game more than I ever had before.
I was fine with all the items they added, or so I had thought. They created the hell known as the Ion Distorter. The weapon by itself is alright, it requires the person to be practically hugging you to deal any damage, while also consuming a decent portion of energy and CPU load. However, as I quickly came to notice, this was taken advantage of by creating small fast bots with stealth and/or blink modules that give you no hope of escape. Coupled with the sizeable health pool of the gun, you will be left wishing you were a flying machine.
tl;dr: I've played a lot of this game years ago, and 40 hours coming back. I found a new system of 'earning' currency, which is much worse than it was before. I also came back to smaller teams, and people playing with no fun as a result. I do give them credit for some of the good they've done, but it is in no way enough to sway my opinion. Honestly, the removal of the crate system or a serious overhaul of it is the only thing that can bring me back at this point, as it is the only thing limiting my wish to have fun.

I was just looking through my games list, and the reviews I've done for games, and realized I left out some important ones. I'm in a bit of a chatty mood, so let's do a few, shall we?
HL:OpFor is an expantion pack for Half Life. It was sold along with Blue Shift back when CDs were still a thing. I bought it WAY back when.
Opposing Force puts you into the character of Colonel Sheppard, one of the many Special Forces guys running around in Half Life. Some have argued whether or not Opposing Force(and, by extention, Blue Shift) are "Half Life Canon"... I would say that they are, as they add to the story of Half Life without conflicting with it. The fact that you see Gordon Freeman for a moment puts you right into the original story, even if you're technically walking along side of it.
There isn't much in the way of "new content", but what IS there, works well within the Half Life universe. Your goal is to escape Black Mesa with your life intact, after you've been left behind.
While shorter than the original Half Life, it is still a lot of fun to play, even after several run throughs.

To picture Toy Odyssey all you have to do is imagine a heroic action figure fighting their way through Sid’s room from Toy Story. The game is an indie title featuring all of your favorite new indie game features like procedural generation, stat boosts, and crafting systems. However, the game is firmly rooted in action-style platformers, or the cringe-worthy “MetroidVania” moniker. It’s not a far fetched comparison and it takes a lot of time to build up, but Toy Odyssey still managed to hook me and turn into a time sink.
You'll spend your time crafting new items and trying to travel further in the house. It honestly feels like a reverse spelunky where death isn't as much of a permenent restart.
I know it isn’t perfect, but I’m still totally engaged playing Toy Odyssey. It somehow manages to squeeze every possible drop replayability out of its systems, and even though I have the sneaking suspicion reward systems are a cheap way to get people hooked, I’m still hooked.
There's a lot to say about this. I wrote a longer review here
but honestly if you like games like Spelunky Toy Odyssey is a great way to spend your money.

ACE Team are keen on creating memorable, talked-about games, and their latest creation, Abyss Odyssey, will do just that. In a blend of Metroidvania-esque levels, rogue-like gameplay and setup, and Chilean-inspired themes, settings, and design Abyss Odyssey will test your patience. But like the Souls franchise, you will keep coming back for more and more punishment. Why? Because you will never let a game get the better of you, and as a gamer, you have to see those credits roll. Okay, perhaps Abyss Odyssey isn’t that hardcore, but you get the idea. ACE Team has recaptured an idea that has worked for 20+ years with series like Mega Man, Castlevania, and Metroid. And while it’s not a complete overhaul of the genre, it’s a step in the right direction for the side-scrolling dungeon crawler genre.
Everyone’s game will start the same: you’ll control Katrien, whose Rapier will allow you to make considerable progress through the procedurally generated dungeons on your way to tackle the Warlock in the Abyss. I say considerable due to the fact that it’s unlikely you’ll make it too far before Katrien is defeated and you must then, as a weak soldier, return to a nearby resurrection altar and return her to life, or start over from the beginning. Not all is lost if you die though, as your solider ‘spirit’ (so to speak) isn’t completely useless, but he’s a much weaker competitor than you yourself. Katrien (and your soldier companion) has a bevy of attacks and special moves to accompany you in your journey ranging from arching swipes, to fireballs, and sliding attacks. Utilized in conjunction with one another makes her a satisfying warrior, but the no-so-tight controls and platforming leads level exploration a lot to be desired.
Platforming games have been around for decades, and they aren’t going anywhere, and when I get my hands on one, I’m personally spoiled by them. Having played every Mario game to death, Nintendo has perfected platforming; and with 2D Castlevania and Metroid games helping cement how graceful platformers can be, playing a game that’s a step back is really frustrating. Abyss Odyssey’s isn’t the worst of the genre, but it’s not up there with the best either. Most of the time, you can double jump then dash over crevices, but occasionally you come upon the dreaded ‘ledge’ wherein it’s 90% impossible to overcome unless you’re facing the right direction. Turning to get in the right direction is a bit of a delay, this making even the simplest of things, such as turning your character(s), rather cumbersome. Yes, this sounds almost elementary, but when you’re trying to hurriedly get somewhere and you’re halted in climbing due to such a minor inconvenience, it’s immensely frustrating. Again, it’s not ‘bad’, but it’s unsatisfying when it happens more often than it should.
Another issue with Abyss Odyssey is its lack of real direction in terms of explaining what you can and cannot do. For example, when your mana meter builds, you’re able to unleash an attack that not only deals damage, but allows you to capture the soul of your foe. You’re then able to freely switch between the soul of your newly acquired demon, each with their own set of attacks and moves, to help in the journey. Unfortunately, none if this is really implied or explained. ACE Team has created a world I want to explore, but provides no understanding of the rules or regulations. As far as plot goes (another lacking feature as far as its delivery) comes in the form of pages of the Warlock’s journal that randomly drop from vanquished adversaries. The twenty page journal tells you everything about the Warlock’s beginning, middle, and end, but not much else aside from small bits about the creatures in the Abyss. I’m all for subtlety and minimalism, but at some point explanation and direction is needed, and Abyss Odyssey loses on that front.
What’s found in Abyss Odyssey is a solid exploratory platformer with minor aggravations, but with rich design marred by poor direction and exposition. You will spend hours upon hours collecting enemies, hunting through the various dungeons, and defeating the famed Warlock; and then come back for more. With multiple playable characters, each with their own distinctive characteristics and attacks, there’s enough content to provide second and third playthroughs. And while we were unable to test this while playing pre-embargo, ACE Team promises a ton of continuous changes and additions to the game as more and more people complete the task of defeating the Warlock. Abyss Odyssey holds a world of fun in itself. In the end though, it’s just a shame that what’s here, although it isn’t genre-changing, isn’t enough to pull it from the depths of a dozen of other lookalikes. There’s a bevy of treasures to discover in the great below, however, so don’t pass up the chance to explore it. When Abyss Odyssey stares in to you, smirk and say ‘let’s go’!

This is a game that let's you question every decision for it's psychological effects, because one colonist in a really bad mood  can ruin your whole colony and that is amazing. Every colonists comes to your colony with their unique traits and they develop their skills and relationships with others in their very own way. This game is backed by a fantastic simulation with a huge range of psychological effects as well as medical and management aspects, which beatifully influence each other. This might sound like a box cover text, but it is what makes this game truly special. This is not a game that promises "endless possibilties" and then executes each of them very poorly, quite the opposite. You will get attatched to your colonist very quickly and wether your favorite and fastest worker loses his arm in a gunfight or your cook gets downed by an animal while hunting and you have to put all your effort into his survival, you will appreaciate (and hate) the depth this game provides. How do you manage the expectations of a 10 year old obsessed with roller coasters? He thought this game would be the same as walking around Thorpe Park which he adores.
But on every level this game has exceeded his hopes. He can build dramatic roller coasters with some effortless clicks, he can follow the amazing looking people as they walk around and it's like he's really there.
