If you're like me, you probably heard people raving about Wolfenstein: the New Order as a good game. Then you bought the game, you booted it up and... hmmm...
What's with all this whiny, bleak monologuing from BJ? That's the first sign of worry. But for the first, I'd say, hour and a half or so, all of this pretty much fades. There are nazi robots, you're shooting nazis, there's some banter, a bit of dark stuff, but soon you're on a road trip with Polish Shotgun Grandpa who shoots nazis in the face and then, oh no. A romance subplot(with some really unnecessary and unwanted sex in cutscenes that verge on being outright porn), and the monologue just won't shut up. Ever. Also BJ gets captured and beaten up so many times for no real reason that it starts getting formulaic. There's also the part where you go through four fifths of a level, then a friend shows up in a helicopter(after dropping you up at the start) and goes: "Hey, I can just drop you off at the end!" Why didn't he do that right away? It makes no sense.
And that's also when the gameplay issues start being hard to ignore.
At first, Wolfenstein TNO is a standard, but generally well-executed game where you run, you gun, to take cover, you shoot nazis, you shoot nazi dogs, sometimes you shoot nazi robots, sometimes you shoot nazi robot dogs. Simple but satisfying. Then it starts introducing the "heavy" enemies which are, every single one, incredibly unfun to fight because they're huge bullet sponges with little-to-no indication whether you're hitting any weak spots(do they have any? There's so much dust, explosion and glowing red gunfire hurtling around that I wouldn't be able to tell), doing more or less damage, or what.
The main issue is that the heavy enemies aren't fun, and the farther you get into the game, the more of them TNO throws at you. Usually the fastest way to finish them off quickly is to rush them with dual-wielded shotguns. But then you learn that quite a few of them apparently have instakill attacks at close range. Fun thing to learn the hard way.
Among other issues with the gameplay is a kind of poor control scheme and weird weapon decisions. Why nail a rocket launcher to the assault rifle? Just give me a separate rocket launcher so I don't have to screw around with alternate weapon modes(that I have to switch between, rather than just having an alternate fire button). There's also the laser. It starts out as a tool for solving """puzzles""" by which I mean "shoot the glowing thing with the laser to progress." Or occasionally sawing open crates which always have just a piece of armor inside in an area where you're already drowning in armor.
The laser is then later hyped up as a weapon, but it's a terrible weapon. It has miserable ammo capacity, and recharging the laser(at specific recharge points, not just as a reload...) takes way too long and takes you out of the flow of the game. They try to hype it up more by giving it constant upgrades. Now shots can ricochet off walls! Except the walls and floors are covered in so much junk you'll never have a flat surface to ricochet off, and if you can hit an enemy with a ricochet, you can just shoot them in the face anyway. Now it "blinds" enemies! Except it doesn't actually ever seem to do this. Now it has a scope that autotargets! Which drains the power super fast, even with the upgrade perk(note, all the perks, earned by doing specific annoying things, are either completely useless or absolutely necessary. Upgraded battery power for the laser is VITAL for not making it a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to use), so you pop out, unload at everyone, back in to spend ten seconds recharging. Back out again.
You're stuck using the laser much more than you'd generally ever want to, though, because the game regularly disarms you. Even after such simple things as taking a car ride, BJ has somehow managed to lose all his guns, ammo, armor and sometimes even excess health between the seat cushions. Occasionally it makes narrative sense, such as when you can only smuggle a minimum of weapons on a lunar shuttle(yes, you get to fight nazis on the moon. No, it's a very short sequence that's basically like the rest of the game except the bullets are briefly replaced with lasers so now ALL your weapons are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to recharge! And you barely even get to go on the surface of the moon at all. So you're just in corridors all the time. Like the rest of the game.)
Just to line up the rest of the complaints, the supporting cast is all really dull. They're not even entertaining or memorable stereotypes. The farther I got into the game, the more I found myself skipping conversations, because they'd usually just be BJ railing Anya or BJ having conversations with characters I just wanted to punch for their edgy idiot opinions("THE US SEGREGATED BLACK PEOPLE! THEY'RE JUST AS BAD AS THE NAZIS! THAT'S WHY I REFUSE TO HELP THE RESISTANCE BUT INSTEAD JUST HANG AROUND THEIR HIDEOUT EATING THEIR FOOD AND BEING PROTECTED BY THEM!" Unless playing your guitar for your own entertainment counts as moral support, I guess.).
Oh, yeah, and, there's an ALTERNATE TIMELINE. You get one choice early on that you're supposed to care about(which one of these two annoying NPC's annoys you less, and thus gets to be spared?), supposedly there's literally no actual difference between which one you choose. I confess that I just googled it to find out, because I'm definitely NOT playing this game again, and in fact I'm not even going to bother finishing it. I think I'm... I don't know how long in? I think we're on the fourth or fifth ultimate weapon that'll make the resistance matter and/or finally give us the ability to strike down the Nazis, but we've yet to actually do so, and the prevalence of annoying heavy soldiers is just increasing, the levels are getting more and more similar and I'm so tired of the game trying to tug my heartstrings or have some sort of depth.
There's also both mantling and no mantling. Sometimes BJ will happily leap a waist-high obstacle or slide across it, other times he'll just struggle against it no matter how many times you run against it, jump against it, crouch against it or try to interact with it. Ideally any FPS game would have mantling, but if you're not going to have it everywhere, you should have it nowhere, otherwise it just gets confusing.
Lastly, why the hell cap the FOV at 100? 120 should be the industry standard.
I'm done with this game, you shouldn't even start.
The music's nice at points, though, kind of like a prototype for the amazing game in Doom 2016. Play that instead.

The art bot issue is just a thing of the past. You can't make a competitive MMO game fun for all players if you keep focusing mostly on keeping room for cosmetic bots. The goal of this game is to perform well and win the game, mainly through team play. That's what people enjoy in competitive online gaming. I love building and testing my bots to make them super efficient and still cool looking. Often it requires more time to build and test a robot than to actually play it, but that's what I really like about this game: everyone can build a good bot, but it's up to the players personal skill and play style if you actually win games with it. If you encounter a super epic bot you can find it in the factory and buy one yourself. Customize and improve them as much as you like. Then you realize that in the next battle you find another bot that can actually easily kill you in certain situations, because this game has a whole ecosystem of weapons and hardware to build bots to counter different kinds of strengths. Too many fliers around? Players automatically start equipping their bots with flak guns. Too many ion shotguns in the game? Players automatically build better sniper bots. Etc. It's just like nature itself if you ask me: action becomes reaction and balance is restored quite fast.
I'm curious to see how the game will develop in the future.Looking forward to more maps and different game modes.

Before I give my opinion on The New Order I must admit that I played this story in chronological order (The Old Blood having been bundled with Doom '16 on pre-order) and my outlook on the game is inherently colored by this.
Wolfenstein: The New Order was the first in the recent slew of old id Software titles being given a reworking for modern times, going beyond simple nostalgia-bait and actually trying to explore the possibilities of their premises. Hardly the first time this has happened (Doom 3, literally any Wolfenstein game before this that isn't made of angry pixel art), but probably the most earnest wave of such to date.
It occurs to me as I write this reflection that I'm legitimately unsure just yet whether I would give it a recommendation or not. It's definitely a decent game, fully functional in every respect, but it's certainly not without its flaws and I'm not sure how likely I am to ever play it again. I can say this much, at least, without question: I liked The Old Blood more.
Now obviously comparing something to its immediate follow-up is a bit unfair, at least for the "not-quite-expansion-pack" variety where it's essentially the same game with a few tweaks and a different story. The developers have already done the dance once and have had time to think about what can be done better. But the point stands - I think in almost every respect The Old Blood is just the more solid title.
Putting minor gameplay tweaks aside (the Perks system in Old Blood is significantly less annoying, for example), The New Order's storyline is just a lot messier than TOB's. To start out petty, it has absolutely nothing to do with Castle Wolfenstein so the title's a bit of an artifact. But more importantly the plot lacks flow. The missions are a haphazard series of setpieces that jump around abruptly as the game comes up with another cool setpiece to wreck the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of. One mission in particular might as well have just been titled Destruction Porn, because the 'story' was literally just grabbing some papers off of a dead guy, but the level is a long guided tour of a frankly gratuitous amount of wreckage (which is what makes the second time you use the weapon that caused it such a letdown as all it does is tear up a castle wall).
Because of this, it's hard to feel any sense of progress or purpose to your actions, as there is only minimal continuity between them - sure, the logic always makes sense, but scene changes are so abrupt that they feel like completely seperate episodes of an action-adventure show. As a result, the story's ending - despite being as final a note as can be reasonably expected - is just sort of a dull stop. You did what you set out to do, and the game just sort of ends with little fanfare, because it never really felt like building to anything, just a series of mildly related action scenes and then credits. To spoil a bit, the ending is a guy in a mechsuit who is tougher, but not substantially different, from the dozen or so robots you already blew up throughout the game. And the final plot twist, rather than having any sort of impact, is just kind of a "so that happened" moment.
Which really sums up the whole game, now that I think about it. "So that happened." It's a game so full of ridiculous climaxes that none of them really stand out and you're just sort of left with an impassionate blur. Which might've been the point - BJ's two main emotions throughout the game are obsessive determination and sheer exhaustion. Like he's done the impossible so many times before that he just wants to finish it so he can lay down already. Well done if that's the case, but making your artistic point comes second to your audience caring about what happens.
One final observation to close, which really is what made me start asking myself how much I liked the game, and that is that towards the end the game starts to get really bad about arbitrarily spawning in enemies mid-fight just to screw you over. The most obvious moment of this was on the second-to-last level where I was set with an already-tough fight against two supersoldiers in mid-sized room with no appreciable cover, in which the game spawns half a dozen guards out of a dead-end tunnel (including one armored shotgunner) the moment you break stealth. I wound up actually having to abuse the spawn conditions in order to win, which involved sneaking into the tunnel they spawn out of so they couldn't enter the fight until I was ready for them.
So in conclusion, the game isn't exactly bad so much as basically competent with a few flaws but too difficult to actually get into to really recommend. Pick up The Old Blood instead, which I think is an all-around more solid title, which also mixes in more blatantly supernatural elements to keep things interesting, even if the ending is kind of stupid.

Cons

So, overall, not much more to add than that. Save for these, it's pretty much Half-Life. I personally played it for the story, but for those of you who don't do story, the new enemies should provide sufficient change to justify purchasing.

I was super hyped for this game, i hyped myself with the idea of a beautiful platform figher procedurally generated.
That was until i finally got it and regret.
For easier reading i will try to put this in bullet points:
-Enemies sometimes attack instantly without any kind of telegraph, your health chip down slowly every enemy you fight.
-Enemies also defend attacks instantly, the grab move to break defenses requires proximity but impossible to execute because AI is frantic and react instantly.
-Making my best combat strategy was
on ledges and walls. They cannot execute more than one action sometimes when climbing ledges, and walls prevent knockback so i can attack and stunlock most enemies besides the big ones that are immune to staggering.
-One of the things i most hate on all games is animation locking, every action you start you are locked until it finishes.
-The music, sometimes i hear 2 or 3 musics at the same time, so i stopped to analise and 1 of 3 was actually the skeleton guitar dude. the other 2 was actually only one music, good music but sounds like there are someone completely lost on the music background.

Very similar to The Walking Dead game, but not especially good.
I bought this for $7.50 and found it almost worth that. After the fun first playthrough (about 1 hour), I was not especially excited for a second time through. I did do a second playthrough and feel like I've gotten all I will out of it. So, this is 1-4 hours of gameplay.
The gameplay is some dialog choices along with some very simple puzzle elements. The dialog presents you with some interesting choices. For example, deciding how to divide your party for various tasks or deciding which character to protect from an attacking animal. These choices seem a bit more developed and interesting than The Walking Dead's.
Unfortunately, the results of my choices seemed pretty arbitrary. For example, when I protected one character from an animal attack, the result was that a completely unrelated character got harmed. Similarly, the interpersonal choices had pretty arbitrary and unimportant outcodes. Most of my dialog choices didn't produce any clear effect (something like "Teddy became intimidated" or "Steven suspects that I stole that food"), This made my choices feel nearly meaningless. It didn't  matter whether I was a demanding bully or a selfless enabler, because either way arbitrary things lead to an arbitrary outcome.
I passed an happy hour playing Dyscourse. The game suggests some excellent possibilities for player choice in video games, but it didn't deliver very well on them.

Be prepred for lots and lots of lots of deaths and disappointments -- it will feel like your every choice is doomed to failure, no matter how logical or reasonable or COMMON-SENSICAL it may seem. Eventually, however, you'll learn what the game feels you "should" do and then you'll have some fun, learning about the different characters and the secrets of the island, and maybe even keeping a few of your fellow survivors alive.
Is it rigid? Yes, definitely and to its detriment. Is it short? Yup! I played through it twice in under an hour. But if you think of the game as small puzzle, you can have a good time with it.

After having played the dreadful game that is Motorcycle Club, I decided to play Kylotonn's previous racing game, Truck Racer, that I noticed I also had in my unplayed Steam backlog. Going in with the worst of expectations, I have to admit Truck Racer is actually kinda fun. Take formula truck style racing and give the trucks the ability to drift almost perfectly around every corner, and give them nitrous too because why not? It's hardly realistic, sure, but every racing game doesn't have to be a realistic simulation for me to have fun with it.
Basically, that's what this game is, no absurd switching mid-race mechanic to be seen, like in Motorcycle Club. Speaking of Motorcycle Club, here's a comparison between the two games just to show how much better Truck Racer is, based off the list I came up with for my Motorcycle Club review.

Considering this goes for $9.99 these days and I got it for about 4 bucks, I'd say it's worth it at its current price, yep. It's not amazing and it's way too easy, but Truck Racer feels that much more focused than Motorcycle Club that I can recommend it, especially if you don't mind playing a lower budget arcade racer. Really bad game. Not even "so bad it's fun" or "oh well it was just a dollar", just bad.
I know what you're thinking. "Arcade physics, easy drifting, trucks crashing into each other, mostly positive reviews, how can you go wrong with this?"
First of all, this is probably a bad port or a poorly optimized game, as the framerate is inconsistent even on low settings.
But more importantly, it's just not fun. The overall "feel" or handling of the trucks, is neither realistic nor fun.
There's a boost mechanic, which charges when you grind with other trucks, but that usually gets you stuck and slows you down more than it should.
Also the AI is really bad, and for some reason the 1st truck is always 10+ seconds ahead of the pack, which makes it even harder to catch when you're 2nd since there's no AI around to crash and charge your boost.
There's a fair selection of trucks, but they all feel generic and handle the same.
All the tracks and environments replicate the same assets and look the same.
Oh, and you can't rebind your controller!
It doesn't matter if you've set your expectations low or enjoy trash games, this game doesn't have anything to offer.
Not sure why there's so many positive reviews, but most of them seem to have no more than 10 hours of gameplay, and for good reason.
If you want a great arcade game, with lots of drifting and crashing and hours of fun, get Burnout Paradise instead.
If you want a good truck game, get ETS2, or Formula Truck 2013 (not arcade!) if you want a truck racing game.

Before I give my opinion on The New Order I must admit that I played this story in chronological order (The Old Blood having been bundled with Doom '16 on pre-order) and my outlook on the game is inherently colored by this.
Wolfenstein: The New Order was the first in the recent slew of old id Software titles being given a reworking for modern times, going beyond simple nostalgia-bait and actually trying to explore the possibilities of their premises. Hardly the first time this has happened (Doom 3, literally any Wolfenstein game before this that isn't made of angry pixel art), but probably the most earnest wave of such to date.
It occurs to me as I write this reflection that I'm legitimately unsure just yet whether I would give it a recommendation or not. It's definitely a decent game, fully functional in every respect, but it's certainly not without its flaws and I'm not sure how likely I am to ever play it again. I can say this much, at least, without question: I liked The Old Blood more.
Now obviously comparing something to its immediate follow-up is a bit unfair, at least for the "not-quite-expansion-pack" variety where it's essentially the same game with a few tweaks and a different story. The developers have already done the dance once and have had time to think about what can be done better. But the point stands - I think in almost every respect The Old Blood is just the more solid title.
Putting minor gameplay tweaks aside (the Perks system in Old Blood is significantly less annoying, for example), The New Order's storyline is just a lot messier than TOB's. To start out petty, it has absolutely nothing to do with Castle Wolfenstein so the title's a bit of an artifact. But more importantly the plot lacks flow. The missions are a haphazard series of setpieces that jump around abruptly as the game comes up with another cool setpiece to wreck the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of. One mission in particular might as well have just been titled Destruction Porn, because the 'story' was literally just grabbing some papers off of a dead guy, but the level is a long guided tour of a frankly gratuitous amount of wreckage (which is what makes the second time you use the weapon that caused it such a letdown as all it does is tear up a castle wall).
Because of this, it's hard to feel any sense of progress or purpose to your actions, as there is only minimal continuity between them - sure, the logic always makes sense, but scene changes are so abrupt that they feel like completely seperate episodes of an action-adventure show. As a result, the story's ending - despite being as final a note as can be reasonably expected - is just sort of a dull stop. You did what you set out to do, and the game just sort of ends with little fanfare, because it never really felt like building to anything, just a series of mildly related action scenes and then credits. To spoil a bit, the ending is a guy in a mechsuit who is tougher, but not substantially different, from the dozen or so robots you already blew up throughout the game. And the final plot twist, rather than having any sort of impact, is just kind of a "so that happened" moment.
Which really sums up the whole game, now that I think about it. "So that happened." It's a game so full of ridiculous climaxes that none of them really stand out and you're just sort of left with an impassionate blur. Which might've been the point - BJ's two main emotions throughout the game are obsessive determination and sheer exhaustion. Like he's done the impossible so many times before that he just wants to finish it so he can lay down already. Well done if that's the case, but making your artistic point comes second to your audience caring about what happens.
One final observation to close, which really is what made me start asking myself how much I liked the game, and that is that towards the end the game starts to get really bad about arbitrarily spawning in enemies mid-fight just to screw you over. The most obvious moment of this was on the second-to-last level where I was set with an already-tough fight against two supersoldiers in mid-sized room with no appreciable cover, in which the game spawns half a dozen guards out of a dead-end tunnel (including one armored shotgunner) the moment you break stealth. I wound up actually having to abuse the spawn conditions in order to win, which involved sneaking into the tunnel they spawn out of so they couldn't enter the fight until I was ready for them.
So in conclusion, the game isn't exactly bad so much as basically competent with a few flaws but too difficult to actually get into to really recommend. Pick up The Old Blood instead, which I think is an all-around more solid title, which also mixes in more blatantly supernatural elements to keep things interesting, even if the ending is kind of stupid.

This game took me completely by surprise. While I first expected a mere crossover of the telltale-style "decision"-making and a pretty adventure, it's so much more than that!
While I usually despise everything that borders on the scary (and yes, I'm easily scared) the game pulled me in far too much to shy away from those scenes, especially since the scary elements are not graphics but in the feeling the game manages to convey.
The story itself is brilliant and takes a very unexpected and novel approach at the whole topic, the characters are ... well, kind of realistic for teenagers. Not easily likeable at first, but after a while one starts to understand their motivations and why they act as they do and they grow on you, sometimes especially because one didn't like them at first.
There are three totally different ways to play this game (Nice, Bad and Silent), wich adds a lot of replay value, and the Voice-Acting and the Music is really well done and manages to create a wonderful atmosphere, wich also makes it nice to play it again to sometimes just stop, listen to the music and hear some characters bickering in the background. I also love that the collect-some-stuff-puzzle-elements are completely optional and can be left out when doing a replay.
One thing I'd like to add is that - while usually I see a plot-twist coming - the end took me completely by surprise, and I totally loved it.
So, long story short: It's definitely worth the 20€, but since it's on sale now for 5€ it's a definite must-buy!

Robocraft is a game of grinding.

Premium players receive DOUBLE the items a normal player receives.
Premium players recieve TRIPLE the recycle rate a normal player receives.
Example, NORMAL player opens crate with 8 items. NORMAL player gets 4 of those items, PREMIUM player gets all 8 of those items.
NORMAL player recycles part for 500 Robits, PREMIUM player recycles exact same part for 1500 Robits.
Oh, and don't forget the added XP bonus Premium players recieve as well.
ALL of these added benefits for $1.19 a DAY, up to $28.99 for 3 MONTHS.
OR you can pay $50 for lifetime premium access, you can pay the price of a full game for something that isnt finished or fleshed out in the slightest.
ROBOCRAFT is pay to win, not only that its expensive as hell to do so.
I stopped playing the game because whenever I wanted to try some new strategy, I loss tons of money, and thats because my current bot isnt working, so I cant get any Robits to make up for the huge loss of money recycling gives you, so every time I attempt a new strategy I lose more and more money, eventually getting to the point where I either find a strategy that does work. Or I run out of parts and money completely, the latter happened to me. Because of this its virtually impossible to come back from the defecit of money you're in. Just because you wanted to branch out. If this sort of thing happened to a premium player, they can get out of this defecit much easier than a normal player can. As well, they will likely not end up there in the first place. Not having premium punishes branching out to new strategies. New players to the game have to deal with this kind of thing. Where every strategy needs to be available to really experience the game, find their niche, and actually learn bot building and other gameplay tactics to begin earning money or parts. All of this is a huge turn off to newer players. Or to someone who has played the game since 2015 like me. Where the newer updates are constantly being pushed to something worse and worse. After you get the hang of the game, progressing to the bottom of the dungeon is not particularly difficult, and can be accomplished relatively quickly. at that point of the game, emphasis changes from merely progressing through the dungeon to smaller objectives: collecting all note book peices (items that convey the game's lore) leveling and improving your character's equipment, and collecting all playable enemies.  While its fun, it does become tiresome quickly- the experiance is short but polished enough to reccomend. It helps that the game's art, music, and scant lore are all fantastic.

What do you say about this game? I could tell you that the art style is gorgeous, evoking equal parts the saturated fantastical gloss of Trine and dreamworld fantasy with beautiful, clean Art Noveau.
I could tell you that, mechanically, it's Smash Bros. meets a Roguelite.
I could also tell you that there are technical flaws which harm the game in many ways, that the game is mostly balanced for playing alone and thus making the co-op modes nearly superfluous, not even counting the great technical flaws in the online co-op.
In the end I will say that it is possible to get used to the technical flaws and that there is a great charm in playing what is essentially Smash Bros. with a stamina-based cancelling mechanic in a simple, Roguelite map with fantastic art and presentation. It starts out hard, but gets easier as you get used to the mechanics. If it still doesn't feel quite there, try disabling the V-sync in the options; for some reason, this helps the responsiveness even with a gamepad.

Abyss Odyssey has been a very mixed experience for me.  The art style is gorgeous and the sound track is solid.  The voice acting is pretty good with some well known names and the overall design and aesthetic of the world is very interesting and focuses on mythology seldom seen in other games.
Then there's the combat.  Others may be able to enjoy it, but I have had so many issues with the stiff, frequently unresponsive controls.  The enemy AI is at times deceptively cheap and evil and also at times very thick, with enemies patiently waiting for me to get done with their buddy ten feet away before coming at me.  Maybe this has to do with the controls being based on fighting games, but it feels like a poor man's super smash brothers and the character's movesets are remarkably shallow.
It helps that you can capture and play as almost all the enemies in the game, but their moves are similarly shallow.
I enjoyed this game for a bit, but it requires many play throughs.  I haven't finished them all and I'm not sure I will.  It's worth playing for the experience, but overall, it could have been better. Worms Revolution is one of the best Worms games available today.
I have been playing the Worms series since 1996, starting with Worms 1 on the Sega Saturn, so I am no stranger to this series.
If YOU are new to this series, or curious about the new additions, you are basically controlling a team of 1-8 worms (depending on game settings) in a battle to the death with some of the craziest weapons ever.
Weapons such as the Old Lady, Holy Hand Grenade, Super Sheep, Concrete Donkey, Bazooka,etc will be used as your team fights to the death in a turn-based battle with a time limit per turn and round.
You also get to use a variety of utilities to move around the map such as a Ninja Rope, Jetpack, Teleport, etc.
You have the option of making your own gamestyles with extensive customization settings, and this game also offers you the ability to make your own maps and play them online.
Some new features for this version from other Worms series include dynamic water, new interactive physics objects, and new weapons and utilities. Yes, the rope behaves differently, (think bungee cord) but once you get used to this change you will not want to go back to the stiff rope of past worms versions.
Now let's talk about system performance. Worms Revolution as you may of noticed, wants at least a dual core processor and a good video card. I have used a Pentium 4 3.60 Ghz in the past, and I was getting very playable framrates. A slow dual core seems to run this game very well paired with a good video card.
Yes, there are bugs in this game involving the new physics objects, and possibly annoying aspects relating to controls, but they are mostly minor. Voice Chat works well.
There is an active community online to this day, and adding friends to your friends list who play the game can help ensure full four player games often.
There is A Solo Campaign you need to play to earn coins to buy new classes of Worms. Your scores will also be recorded on Steam Leaderboards. This game has classes for your worms that helps them specialize in certain situations, such as stronger attacks from a Heavy, quicker movements with a Scout, or stronger tools with Scientists.
If you like the Worms series, or if this style of gameplay sounds even slightly interesting, I highly recommend you give this a look.

A game with a self-ironic name,
, or
, I actually had not played any "zombie defense" games like this before.
surprises by being both a good top-down shooter, as well as a proper tower defense at the same time. You (and up to three other people if playing co-op) pick a character (with three variants, no abilities) and start blasting away at zombies.
There are three game modes:
In
zombies come in waves, once every night. Day-time is used to buy and build stuff with the accumulated funds from killing zombies.
Money buys weapons, traps, barriers and turrets. Player count doesn't affect the strength of the horde. However, this matters little because of the:
Interesting concept, all equipment is shared with all players. In more detail, weapons and ammo are shared with both other players and turrets.
Turrets can be equipped to use any ranged weapon in the game and they blast away at the closest zombies with utmost accuracy but without regard to ammo consumption. If the collective ammo runs out, turrets using the particular weapon are useless.
Killing zombies awards money and occasional bonus items, like ammo, power-ups (e.g. invincibility, fast-reload, invisibility...) and extra money, which disappear if not collected soon enough. Money is shared as well, so all players and turrets have to be bought and equipped with the same money pool.
Every day random items have a discount that adds an another strategic element: should I save the dough for another day but in so doing risk dying / losing way more tonight?
All enemies/zombies are ultimately similar. They have speed, toughness and damage.
In the
, the horde becomes stronger by each night (i.e. wave), increasing in both numbers and attributes. Day follows a night, allowing constructing defensive structures and buying weapons/ammo.
While over ten different weapons may keep you entertained for a while, the tougher yet similar enemies render it dull after a while. I did like the AI though: while other zombies chase you, others will try to flank you and cut your escape. Shooting them makes them slow down a bit, giving way for interesting action tactics.
was amusing enough for about 2.5 hours of playing (at which point I had accumulated all Steam achievements). Afterwards, it's got leaderboards to climb for both Survival and Endless modes.
I only saw three other people playing online, so my experience was only from single-player, which I frankly prefer if not playing with friends.
Even SP-only, I feel it's pretty much worth its price ($2). If you wish for a quick action strategy experience and have the bucks to throw away, this is a good game to target. However, check the (slightly pricier) HD version for comparison (

Disclaimer: I bought this game with my own money.  My review is my own opinion and unbiased.
If you've ever played those games on mobile where you tap to moves troops from building to building while carefully managing troop generation within the buildings - this game is basically that at the core.
Where this game differs, however, is the fact that it features both a single player campaign, as well as three (as of now) multiplayer modes, and a skill tree that as you level you invest points in.  You can also use spells in battle to alter structures or give them buffs/debuffs.
I've only played ~1 hour so far, and I played through the first of the 3 campaign "acts", as well as tried out a couple multiplayer matches.  I can't say how their matchmaking performs, I don't know if they have any algorithms to match you with people of a certain level or not.  However, from what it looked like to me, the multiplayer mode is ranked only (i.e. your rank moves up or down depending on wins/losses) so there doesn't seem to be an un-ranked multiplayer mode.
One of the multiplayer modes lets you team up with someone else to defend some buildings against an attacker, which is pretty cool.
This game is fairly fun and simple in terms of core gameplay, but the spells and structure types add a fun layer of depth and strategy.  However on larger maps with a lot of structures, you will need to be REALLY good at multitasking (monitoring structure numbers, buff/debuff generation, clicking/selecting multiple buildings to move troops or collect buffs, watching for incoming enemy advances, etc.).  If you're not a fan of games that require multitasking, I doubt you'll like this very much.
Graphics are simplistic and colorful, the music is cheery (albeit sort of annoying - maybe add some new tracks?  More relaxing stuff maybe?  I doubt everyone wants to listen to the same march-y sounding music all the time.
The price point of $5 (as of 08/25/2017) seems accurate for this game.
OVERALL RATING: 8/10

It's not a terrible game, but Wolfenstein: New Order has some major pacing problems that make the game overstay its welcome. You've probably heard plenty about the concentration camp level. It's the sort of risky centerpiece to a game that could define how people remember it. But you're in and out of it so quickly it scarcely has time to feel difficult, oppressive, or overpowering, which, in turn, makes liberation of the camp a lot less impactful.
That's how a lot of WNO plays out. You spend an inexcusably long amount of time on scenes that could be implied or told by story while these big, ambitious setpieces give you very little time to appreciate them. Would it kill Bethesda to cut a lot of the fluff and let the prison break or concentration camp carry out over a whole act? Would it kill them to make the big sci-fi payoff the actual finale?
Character development. Oh lord. People talk about WNO like it's well written and has fully realized characters. Everyone is a one-dimensional paper cutout, with the protagonist faking depth by periodically monologuing about stuff he remembers. It's a sorry excuse for fleshing out a character. The only person that felt interesting and lifelike exists only in a series of diaries.
This kind of stuff would be easier to let slide if the shooting mechanics were rewarding but all-told, it's a pretty humdrum shooter with guns that lack a visceral punch. With shooting mechanics lacking and storytelling dragging, WNO's ability to throw one spectacle after another wears out and eventually you just want it all to end. After a break of several weeks I finally powered through the last act just to make the game go away. That's not a feeling worth spending 10 hours or 10 dollars on.

Before moving on, there is just one thing I have to say - the only other Wolfenstein game I played is the classic Wolfenstein 3D. I missed all others, so I can't compare this one to them.
Wolfenstein: The New Order is an amazing shooter that looks great and feels great. The story is compelling, the game is intense and the voice acting is superb. With different skills to be unlocked as you play, there are multiple ways to play through the game, allowing the player to go entirely stealthy or full-on guns-blazing to take enemies head-on. The game has a cover system, though it's not at all mandatory to play the game, merely something that the player can take advantage of if they want to. The game is challenging, there are some parts in the game where you're talking to other characters and doing side missions that's a nice change of pace, there are easter eggs to be found (including one secret level) and the boss battles are amazing.
There is one moment in the game where the player has to make a decision and it causes some changes in the story, though nothing major. This game sucks. If you bought it hoping for an action-packed classic-Wolfenstein experience, prepare for disapointment. Even the opening cutscene sucked, because it was at about ten FPS. On a brand new card. Bethesda seems to like cutting backroom deals with Nvidia, because my brand-new AMD card, which can run Fallout 4 max-settings at 60 FPS, can barely handle this game. It's the same thing that happened with RAGE. It was made so it couldn't run on AMD systems, and it happened again here, and then again with Watch_Dogs. The gameplay isn't even all that great either.
It's not that it's bad, just stupid. You have enemies who can barely see you in stealth from about ten feet away, while those same enemies have superhuman reflexes and sight as soon as you break stealth. It's like they couldn't decide whether to make a stealth game or a classic shooter, and they wound up with the worst of each. The first rifle you get can fire semi-automatically and kicks♥♥♥♥♥ while all the 60s era weapons are all-auto-all-the-time, with absolutely no justification whatsoever. Even the pistol is burst fire, but attaching a supressor turns it back. What. Why can't I use that without the supressor?
You keep no gear between levels, again with no justification. You can't even keep your ammo. Good luck playing this game like a real shooter. It's a stealth game advertised as a shooter. Duel-wielding? Forget it, useless. And because of the atrocious performance, forget aiming. In a game with no true semi-auto guns and no way to get rid of the lag, you need something like that.
On top of all that, the controls suck too. Sure, you can remap some of them, but that just makes your control scheme even more inconsistant. The mouse sensitivity is even worse, since your FPS seems to affect that more than usual. The aiming is choppy and inelegant. Sprint-sliding returns you to a standing position, which sucks when you use it to get into cover. The sound design only compounds these issues, as everything but speech sounds distant and washed-out. You can't detect enemies by sound, so you have no way of knowing if you are being flanked
In short, don't even bother unless you've exhausted every other shooter in the universe, because any of them, even Far Cry 4, make more sense than this. And if anyone just says "Git Gud" I am. I play Uber, and it isn't very hard until the game throws a bunch of fake-difficulty at you. If anything, that's another reason not to get it. Not even the hardest difficulty is all that hard, just frustrating. Get Doom 2016 instead. It's actually fun.

I’m going to try and keep this simple... to sum this game up in a few words, I’d have to say, TEAMWORK! lots and lots of TEAMWORK. If you like working as a group, trying to achieve a common goal, with no one player able to be some sort of Rambo that does it all... Get This Game!
Also, Authentic / Realistic, yet still very much Playable as a video game. Essentially the perfect balance which equals an awesome experience.
Lastly, and this is something I feel is missing in modern shooters, Completely Enjoyable, even when you lose a round. As long as you stick with your squad, you will 99% of the time enjoy every round you play, even if your team ends up losing. Minor negatives to some… You WILL need a headset, you Will need to communicate, and you Must have a lot of patients at times while also being able to follow commands if you are Not a squad leader. (Note: all players, from noobs to veterans, may select a squad leader role if one is open, but be advised, these roles are Not easy by Any sense). And lastly, there are still bugs being worked out, most are minor, and don’t hurt gameplay very much, however some can ruin a good round. Don’t flip out over them, the Devs are working nonstop and are very active… this is still an early access game, play it with those expectations.
Ok, so that was a little more than a few words… to end this off, I’ll just states. Get This Game!!!

Well, I haven't seen any of that yet, but Abyss Odyssey is still a damn fine game. The aesthetic is excellent, sucks you right in. The character designs are well thought out, and everything about them and the environment is pretty. What dialogue the game has is minimal, but that's all that's needed to tell the story.
Basically, a Warlock has been sleeping for Christ knows how many years, and his nightmares are leaking into the real world, manifesting as real threats. You can choose from three different characters, but you only start with one, Katrien.  They can be played as interchangably throughout the game.
The game is difficult! There's an optional nightmare mode, which I haven't touched yet, but the default difficulties are either easy, moderate, and hard, and vary depending on which level of the abyss you're in. The easy levels are a tad challenging, but nothing terrible. The hard levels have threats around every corner, and you'll be lucky if you have 1/4 of the health you went into them with by the time you reach the exit.
The controls are fine tuned, as they should be for an action platformer like this. They are strange at first, and might feel wonky, but as you play you pick up how it works. You really feel like it's your fault when you're hit by an enemy, and not the fault of the controls.
I haven't made it very far in this game, maybe four levels down (which isn't far). But it's definitely worth picking up if you like what you see in the videos. It's a unique experience, I've never quite played a game like it before. And for $15 it's worth it.

Rimworld is a work in progress, but one that is already very fleshed out. With the developer working hard on updates, this game has yet to reach it's full potential. But the state it is in now shows that it has a lot of potential.
The game puts you in charge of a group of people that need to survive on a hostile planet. Raiders, tribals, mechanoids, animals and the planet itself are all against you. Add to that the personalities and skills of your own colonists and you might understand that survival really means survival in this game.
The game is inspired by Dwarf Fortress and people who love that game or the micromanagement of it, will love this. The basics can be picked up pretty quick thorugh the clean UI and clear messages and explanations, but maintaining your colony for a longer period is something that may take a few tries. The game creates amazing stories just by having the world interact with it's inhabitants, through a choice of three storytellers. Each of these manipulates the world differently and has multiple difficulties to choose from.
The way you play your colony is completely up to you. You choose the storyteller, the starting people and the location on the planet. From there you can choose whatever way you want to make the colony work. This freedom allows you to challenge yourself as much as you like. Or create a relaxing creative experience.
On a final note, the community on reddit is always welcoming newcomers so feel free to drop by there and ask anything you want to know before or after purchasing the game.

I'm going to write a lot of words about anime tanks because I really like this series and I don't think anyone else knows it exists.  The last game in the series, Limited Operations, has been out for around 9 months and has about a dozen reviews.  Here's a really long one and consider this a review for the series in general.
The War of the Human Tanks series is essentially anime Battleship.  Fights are real time and pause when you click a unit to choose an action.  There's always a large fog of war and most units are of the one hit, one kill variety.  Tanks are of the mass-produced style, outside of a couple of special NPC's, and are permanently destroyed when killed in action.  Tanks can also equip modules that you can create which do things like increase shooting range and area, increase movement and so on.  Limited Operations changes the last few parts up, though.
Unlike in the previous games, Limited Operations, as the title suggests, gives you a set of per-determined tanks for each fight.  You can no longer grind your way to high-level tanks and modules and literally wipe out the battlefield in a few actions.  This may be a turn off for some, but I found the new approach quite refreshing, and it made me use some tank units that I neglected a lot in previous games.  It was nice not to worry about making new tanks and outfitting them with modules and helped prevent the party screen from getting too cluttered.
The biggest increase in usage for me were scout units.  Previously, it just didn't make much sense to use a scout in place of an assault tank, since it was better to have killing power over uncovering the fog of war.  LO doesn't give you many powered-up units, thus scoping out the battlefield and making more strategic use of your scouts in combination with your slow, long-range artillery units become a tactic I used way more than before.  I still don't bother with shock units but I liked the challenge the LO provided and I'd say it's the most finely tuned game in the series difficulty-wise due the nature of the troop dispersal.
Another big aspect of the WotHT games is the story.  There's a lot of talking, like
of talking.  The in-between fight scenes are basically visual novel-type story telling with large-headed characters talking in front of some filtered real-life imagery.  This could be really bad, but I ended up surprisingly enjoying the story parts of the previous games.  LO though is the least compelling of the lot.  The initial story is somewhat confusing and there's a bit too much focus on characters with generic portraits to care about it too much.  It's okay, but I liked the other games story parts more.
Another cool thing WotHT does is provide alternate routes in a cool way.  The first game had branching storylines that changed depending on whether you win or lose certain fights.  It's cool as hell when a game continues in a different manner if you lose rather than just getting a game over, and I didn't expect it when I played the first game.  The sequel doesn't really do this as much, but it has a massive extra dungeon which is way longer than the main game and has its own story and unique tank units.  LO is sort of in between, the game does continue whether you lose or win certain fights, but there's only one fight in particular that will result in a different storyline.  It's still cool and I wish more games did stuff like that.  Like the other games in the series, LO has a bunch of unlockable bonus fights.
The soundtracks for these games is....something else.  There are some eclectic choices to say the least.  It's better to experience it for yourself.
Onward to the negatives.  I said earlier that LO is probably the most challenging game in the series because you can't just grind powerful tanks and modules to bypass strategy, and for the most part that's a good thing.  The problem is that some fights feel a bit more like puzzles than strategy in the sense they feel like they were designed with very specific tactics in mind.  Fights in the series have always had time limits, but they were almost never an issue.  In LO, the clock is definitely something you have to keep an eye on.  I lost a number of fights due to running out of time after it being a near non-issue before.  This is kind of a good and bad thing, but certain fights do feel like they could use a bit more time to them, especially if you're trying to S rank all the missions and clear the action limits.
The other two downsides are kind of minor, but annoying nevertheless.  One is a long-standing problem (since the original game) and it's that the episode intro/outro do not ever play the first time I come across them when I turn on the game.  There's audio but no visual.  This has happened since the first game, I have done everything I can to alleviate the problem and I'm computer literate, but no matter the computer I play it on, they never run right the first time, but will do so every time after.  The second problem is that LO sometimes starts to chug and slow down to an unplayable pace until I quit and restart.  This never happened in the other games but I've run into it a few times in LO.  Oh, and I wish the unit placement screen was combined with you tank roster screen so you could see both at the same time when deploying tanks.
In conclusion,  the WotHT series is a  fun, light strategy set of games that are extremely wordy and feature crazy soundtracks.  It plays relatively fast and has a good bit of content in each game.  I've always liked strategy-rpgs and this series really itched a scratch I've had for moving units around on a grid and killing stuff.  If the simple art-style and wordiness of it doesn't turn you off, it's worth giving the series a chance, especially since the first game has been bundled a dozen times or so and is likely sitting in your game library without you realizing it.

This is the third game in the War of the Human Tanks trilogy, and, as such, this is my third time through the whacky world of adorable chibi girl genocide. It takes place in the ‘fictional’ country of Japon, (which I’ve already made fun of twice so will cut some slack towards today) which is nearing the end of a brutal civil war. It’s just that rather than get their own hands dirty, each side have produced an army of cute robot girls who march out to their deaths in the people’s stead. But they’re robots so that’s okay, right? I mean, sure, they’re technically sentient but they’re usually less intelligent than the average human, so them being blown up in mass numbers isn’t that much of a loss. They’re more like interactive chess pieces, with assault rifles and grenade launchers. That form unique opinions and attachments and smile faintly at you as you order them to their demise.
There’s a lot of text to run through during a Human Tanks game, most of it dealing with the politics of the war mixed in with a healthy dosage of anime tropes, which leaves the creeping feeling of unease commanding a disposable army to grow on you organically. The tanks don’t really mind dying; they were only created to suffer a flashy death on the battlefield, but it’s hard not grow attached or be a little freaked out by their endearing naivety or genuine affection towards you, their commander.
It’s doubly hard to send your Tanks to their doom in Limited Operations which stays true to its byline by limiting the crap out of your forces and giggling behind its hand as it watches you squirm. In the two previous games, grinding your way to victory was a definite possibility. Back then, you could replay old missions as often as you pleased and use the funds gained from your infinite sorties to bolster your ranks with high powered Tanks, or plough resources into research and development to ensure you always had the most advanced army in the fight. Lose that awesome attack tank that could dual wield assault rifles or that scout tank with the insane recon range? Not a problem. You could rebuild them. You could make them stronger. That’s no longer an option.

If you're new to the WotHT series, it's great and I highly recommend it but this is the third game in the series so feel free to check out the previous two games first.
If you're a WotHT veteran, this game plays exactly the same as the previous two but with one major twist in resource management. The "Limited" in the title refers to the fact that you aren't able to collect crates and build units as you please any more. You're given a limited supply of units for each mission. You do have two special units (well, one, really) which are Hotaru, who is played up as a powerful unit by the story but turns out to be a bog standard Command unit, and your actual special unit, a Mihari Scout unit, who has exceptional scouting abilities for the start of the game. Then you're given a handful of other units to choose from to deploy as you see fit.
It doesn't seem to be a perma-death scenario, though. I haven't noticed any correlation between the units left over from the previous mission and the ones I start with on the next mission. Considering you can go back and replay missions without directly continuing from the previous one, I think it's safe to assume that's the case.
I can't really say whether the new resource management is good or bad. On the one hand, I liked building up a super powerful squad and crushing my opponent but, on the other hand, it does take the strategy out of the game when you can simply scount the entire map and then level it all in one turn. It's a matter of balance and this time they balanced it for maximum strategy.
Overall, it's still a great game for fans of the series so definately pick it up.

Dyscourse is an interactive choose your own story. Literally every single choice you make in this game has a consequence, and most of the time, it ends up being a horrific consequence. The main character is a art college graduate, who now works in a coffee shop. You were in a plane crash while traveling to an art event, and you meet five other stranded survivors along the way.
The game play is very point and click adventure, only that you can roam around each scene without being restricted to just clicking on interactive objects. This gives you the opportunity to explore this beautifully crafted stylized world that has been created. Talking with the other survivors broadens your knowledge of the crash and their circumstances, you will form your own personal opinions about them, and your feelings towards them will change as you play through the story.
I wasn't kidding about every choice making a difference in this game, selecting a different choice will result in your ending being different to everyone else's. Some of the responses are timed forcing you to make an instinct decision while others you have the time to ponder your choice.
There is no real difficulty to be seen in Dyscourse, you will finish the game eventually, it's more about playing the game for the store behind it - and it's not just about finishing the game, there are tons of different endings, different story plots to be found in this game. You can play it ten times and still have a completely different story and ending each time. I have only finished one playthrough at the time of writing this review. One run through the story takes about one hour, so given that there are at least another nine to experience, you are looking at at least ten hours of unique content.
Another technically well made game, zero issues running the game. You can choose to lower the graphical options if you desire, but the game could very well be ran on a potato if you wanted.
Now, excuse me while I have another play through this awesome choose your own adventure game!

Yet Another Zombie Defense is a small zombie survival game that I originally played just to get the Steam trading cards for. As cheap indie games go, it’s not terrible and provides some challenge. It also has co-op gameplay so that’s a plus.
The game really has no story other than “kill all the zombies” and it’s played in top down “twin stick shooter” style. This means that you move around with your keyboard and aim/shoot with your mouse. Your goal overall is to survive each night picking up money/ammo from zombies you shoot, then use the money to buy better weapons (including barricades and sentry turrets) between nights.  Every time you play you start from night 1 (nothing but a handgun) and try to survive as many nights as possible with the possibility of other people dropping into your game and helping out.
Honestly the game is like an inferior version of Alien Shooter, Zombie Shooter, Guns N Zombies, etc. (due to lack of story and weak graphics) but I got it for super cheap, it has cards/steam achievements, and I was able to kill an afternoon playing so I give it a thumbs up. You’ll get tired of it pretty quick if you’re just playing by yourself but at least it’s not a complete trash game where the devs made absolutely no effort.

Truck Racer - an unexpected diamond in the rough
Before I downloaded this game, it seemed to scream 'cheap piece of rubbish'. It was in a bundle with a bunch of rubbish games, and what sort of a name is Truck Racer? I was expecting a half-hearted truck simulator with awful physics, ugly graphics and bad controls. Luckily, I was very, very wrong.
If you haven't gathered from the other review, this game is an arcade racer. If you go in expecting a simulator, you'll be disappointed. The trucks seem heavy but agile, and the game's pace is relatively slow; there isn't a real feel of speed, but this acts in the game's advantage, as it is more about staying on the track and smashing your opponents than getting that perfect racing line and improving your PB lap times.
The models are nice with satisfying damage models, the sounds are basic but not awful, the graphical effects are good, if a bit distracting at times, and the menus & UI are beautiful. The trucks have a decent amount of upgrades, but little visual customisation. There are a number of trucks to choose from, but they are all one of two models, with slightly different bodykits. Paint colour can be customised, but that's about it.
Overall, while it may not be the best arcade racer out there, you can tell that Truck Racer has had a lot of time and effort put into it, and I can easily recommend it for some mindless fun.

This certainly stands out in its genre. Puzzles are solid and there's a great deal of deliberation to the world. It toes the line between meta-aware and immersive at the same time, by showing a simplistic narrative with enough going on under the hood to make the world seem plausible. The "Gehenma" DLC in particular makes this one of my favorite games of the year, showing a fascinating and plausible world, and puzzles that the designers clearly thought were too tough to obstruct the main story, but liked enough to make regardless.
One particular note on the gameplay, Talos feels fairly precise for its genre. There's no cube tossing and the platforming (as well as some possible abuse cases that might exist in Portal) are subtly automated. The exceptions to this rule are the "gold stars", which are entirely optional and therefore if you want them you'll have to do every crazy thing the developers could think of. Hunting the stars is quite satisfying, although I'd recommend saving that for last because if you treat it like a requirement to progress, frustration shall abound.

I know it's been said before but, this game is what a Goosebumps episode written by John Green would be like. It's a coming-of-age story with some supernatural spooky stuff going on in the background, but still focusing on the characters and their relationships over the mystery. The cast isn't too clichéd and (for the most part) not overly hipster or obnoxious, (tho the ones that are meant to be are almost too good at it). They do feel fairly realistic and I believe that at least one of the characters will be at least somewhat relatable to most players.
Gameplay wise it's pretty much a "pick a speech bubble" kind of game where everything you say will get a different response but in the long run only a couple big decisions will affect the game's ending. Most of these moments are preceded by a dream/hallucination scene where a different version of the main character tells you something that latter is revealed to be one of the possible choices to make. That different version of the lead is actually a different player who picked these messages at the end of the game to be send to other players. You never know why the player tells you to pick a particular choice so you can always ignore the advice, but it does still create an interesting moment of self-reflection about what you yourself did in the game at the end. Do you think you made all the right decisions and would want others to pick the same? Or would you rather pick differently and try to prevent someone else from making the same errors as you did? etc.
Visually the game has a simple yet appealing style and music elevates the action when needed and blend in perfectly into the background rest of the time. The only issue I have with the audio side is an element of the voice acting. All of the actors did a fine job on their own, but they all sound way too adult for the roles they're in. Except that I could also compline a bit about how easily you can cut the dialog short by accidently walking into the next area or even picking a bubble early, but these are minor nit-picks.
What counts the most in this kind of a game however, is writing and a sense of atmosphere, - at least to me it is -  and these two element are quite fantastic. The story was compelling, mechanics effective, it wasn't manipulative or cheesy at any point and it managed to tell a well-rounded and quite complex story in under 4 hours without feeling rushed at all.
Possibly the biggest prise I can give to this game is that every time a new speech option came up, I picked it instinctively, like I knew exactly what this person would say at every moment. I didn't think about how it would impact the story or my relationship with any character from my perspective, like I tend to do in Telltale's games or did in life is Strange. I got completely lost in the action to such a degree that I forgot I was even playing a game for a moment, and just experienced everything as if it was really happening to me. What caused that feeling? Maybe it was due to the fact that a lot of dialog options shaped your person not by showing how you react to certain thing (like in Telltale's games or Life is Strange) but by actually saying and there for deciding what happened to you in the past, generating a closer connection with the character because, you feel more responsible for what she is like now? Probably, maybe, I don't know, but I don't really care. That magic is probably better left undiscovered. And it is certainly WAY better to experince yourself then read about it in some bearly comprehensible review.

So this is an conversation driven atmospheric horror adventure game... cause that's a thing apparently.  And in this case, it's a thing that works very well.  The voice acting is fantastic.  The characters interesting.  The dialog is totally organic.  I could see myself having conversations like this with my own friends. The story is mostly delivered through conversations, which are happening constantly, and you have to pick and time your responses in real-time.  I'd never quite seen anything like it.
Oxenfree is not action packed.  There is no combat or death.  The pacing is mostly slow.  However it's great at building atmosphere and leverages that to create some remarkably tense moments.  Some have called this game a "walking simulator."  I can see why they would say that, but personally I was never bored while playing this, and started a NG+ playthrough immediately after finishing it the first time.
If you want an interesting, slow-paced, character-driven story that doesn't hold your hand in explaining itself, try Oxenfree out.

War of the Human Tanks – Limited Operations is the third game of the ‘War of the Human Tanks’ series. Developed by Yakiniku Banzai! and published onto steam in English by FruitBat Factory. This is a strategy game where you control Human Tanks – human-shaped tanks – and fight against other Human Tanks on the side of the hostile country.
Seek out, charge and self-destruct to destroy your enemies in this strategy game! Lead your Human Tanks and complete your missions! Scout out the enemy and plan your strategy, but remember that your tanks will go down in one hit and be lost forever.
Before a battle starts you will get to deploy and place your human tanks at spots on the map of course that comes to some planning, clumping them up is s smart choice because a shock tank could kill them all at once if you are not careful. Same as the opposite spread them far apart they will take a long time to move near the enemies and may die to a random blind shot made by the AI which sucks if your key unit gets taken down by a blind shot losing the whole battle instantly.
Some things I would like to note is that sometimes the AI feels a too strong but sometimes the AI feels plain stupid in my experience so far. Lets take for example there are battles where I had and I was standing directly in front of the enemy and they did not attack my unit that was placed in front of them at all, instead they opted to attack a random spot with nothing on it which is kind of weird in my opinion.
But overall gameplay wise it is enjoyable there is strategy which will be used and some luck may be involved like firing a blind shot and killing the opponent and then feeling the sense of saticfication that you just destroyed the opponent by pure luck.

Sometimes, the KISS principle in a strategy game is perfect for engaging gameplay, and the War of the Human Tanks – Limited Operations is a good example of that. While there are a couple of layers, everything comes down to a few basic actions, relying on you to maximize your fighting potential in unit placement and slow but steady actions of taking parts of the enemies field. The game does well in finding a balance in cautious gameplay with having most of your units able to permadie, but also forces you to be aggressive with the smartly placed timer that it's put on top of it. In addition, the game adds a layer on top of the typical strategy genre with having multiple command tanks at times, which directly affects your loss conditions, and forces you to choose if having one less overall unit is worth having a safety line in the game. And surprisingly, the story written here is actually interesting, in particular with the plot about the break down of the human tanks, and them wanting to fight on or find meaning in their existance. Now, by no means is the game perfect: it's very rough around the edges with small issues regarding map layout and not playing to its art styles full potential. But for the 10 dollar price tag, you get a reasonable strategy experience that keeps things simple yet still engaging, and you really can't ask for a lot more at that price. A good way to cap off the series.

A visually beautiful game that doesn't take long to finish, but it has almost infinite replay value thanks to the choose-your-own-adventure format and the huge variety of paths your choices can take you. For such a short game (one playthrough takes an hour), its attention to detail and its ability to successfully flesh out six different characters with very different personalities and with only the most rudimentary voice acting (that's nevertheless really fitting to the whole format) is really, really commendable. is a choose-your-adventure style story told through the medium of a video game (as opposed to the traditional method of a book).  And that is exactly how it plays.  The story is good, but not great; the true identity of the game centers around its quirky nature.
Technically: it is an “adventure game.”  But it doesn’t really have the typical features of an adventure game.  There is no inventory, and there are really no puzzles or minigames to be solved.  The game truly boils down to a quirky narrative, where you make choices via dialogue that then have consequences on the ultimate path of the story.
The depth of gameplay consists of exploring different choices and seeing how they pan out; doing so will allow you unlock all the “stamps,” (read: in-game achievements).  There are various branching-points to the narrative that can be explored; but ultimately nothing drastically different really happens.  The game has a “day-rewind” feature which can be used to rewind the story to certain points and then explore different choices— without having to start the game over entirely.  Nevertheless, you will probably need to restart the story entirely a few times if you want to really see all the different paths and unlock all the achievements.  The feature works well with the quirky nature of the game.  Having said that, I still personally would have rather seen a handful of save slots where you can make your own “rewind” points, rather than being at the mercy of the game’s; but the “day-rewind” feature does help contribute to the overall identity of
.
The peculiar art style, the catchy music, the mumble-language voice acting, the silly dialogue, and the eccentric characters all mesh together and contribute to the quirkiness at the heart of the game.  It is these qualities that make the game enjoyable.  The actual story is pretty bland and played out; but that potential sour point is definitely bailed out by the entertaining style in which it is told.  The idiosyncratic characters and their interesting backstories also contribute positively to the overall experience.
I would say
would mostly appeal to someone who enjoys choose-your-adventure narratives and who will enjoy a quirky experience centered almost entirely around storytelling.  There aren’t really any puzzles to solve, and there isn’t really any thinking required.  If that sounds like your kind of thing: check out
.

Best 3D puzzle game ever! The puzzles are extremely clever and really makes you think out of the box. There are tons of secrets and hidden puzzles. And I've never seen another game with as many hidden easter eggs and references as this one. There's easily over 100 easter eggs and that's excluding the subtle ones. Yet the best part of the game is its deep philosophical discussions. Expect tons and tons of texts in this game (although they are actually completely optional for those only interested in puzzles). The game is not an RPG, yet it managed to have some of the most complicated dialog trees ever appeared in a game, and that’s coming from an RPG fanatic. The game really makes you feel like you are debating with an AI on topics like what is a person (and you will be debating a lot of things with it in this game). The story is superb, and there is actually a really mind-blowing plot twist near the end of the game if you pay attention to the QR codes scattered around the game world – actually one of the best plot twists I’ve ever seen in a game, or movie, or whatever. The DLC Road To Gehenna is just as brilliant as the main game, with even harder puzzles and even more walls of texts than the main game. It managed to present a vivid view of a community/society of a couple prisoners that cannot even see each other and could only communicate through text-based computer network. Even in this small society, there is politics. There are artists, writers, philosophers, even game developers (and you can play their games, all text based choose your own adventure type games - there are quite a lot of these mini text games in the DLC). This is truly a masterpiece of a puzzle game, but it is also more than a puzzle game. This is a game that needs time and a thoughtful mind to truly appreciate.

With the recent wave of rebooted franchises, this game could have been anywhere in the spectrum. The original was part of the initial wave of innovation that set the standard for FPS mechanics, and this one followed on the heels of the abomination that is the over saturation of the genre caused by CoD4: Modern Warfare.
And oh boy did this game ever deliver.
Wolfenstein: The New Order turned an old, rehashed genre into something fun and gripping to play. I got to run, gun, slide,  knife, nade, and laser beam the ever loving crap out of the Nazi hordes, the true Wolfenstein experience.
What's that you say? I can sneak around as well? And it can have a meaningful impact on how I approach a level? Fantastic! I can just toss knives at some baddies, pop a few in the head with my silenced pistol, and then swing up with my dual wielded shotguns and blast this UberSoldat in the face until he kneels before my glorious American♥♥♥♥♥
Now you're telling me that there is a meaningful progression tree that requires you to explore all of the mechanics presented, without feeling overbearing and forcing you into a play style? Yes, please! Numerous secrets as well, with a useful menu that allows me to search for them without consulting a 3rd party guide. And, on top of everything, an interesting story that separates The New Order from its predecessors while still fulfilling that "kill all the Nazis" itch. I honestly wasn't expecting anything in the story department, but it was quite solid. B.J. Blazkowicz is a bit more than your cliche massively muscled "I'm going to rip your arms off and shove them down your throat" protagonist, but not by leaps and bounds. The story is more interesting than expected, but the focus is still firmly set on gunning down Nazis at all costs.
This game renewed my interest in First Person Shooters. I didn't expect there to be any kind of innovation, but The New Order came out as an interesting game with fun mechanics, a simple but engaging story, and good level design with multiple possible plans of attack. Not everything was perfect, though; the parts where you don't have access to a gun are confusing as the enemy will just casually walk at you with a baton and gladly get their faces beaten in when they see you.  The giant Panzerhund parts are a huuuuuuuuuge pain in the butt, and almost every area where stealth can be extremely useful have something that forces you to brawl, most of the time including the elite level of enemies spawning. Overall though, the game was a joy to play. I give it a 9/10.

It's a linear, first-person action RPG. No linear leveling system but linear progression through levels. Combat feels more responsive than Oblivion, and you have the mighty kick of ragdolling foes or off ledges, into traps, etc. Magic is super empowering and I had a blast freezing the floor, watching enemies slip and then stabbing them while they were downed. From the developers of Arx Fatalis, who later went on to develop Dishonored, this first person, medieval fantasy is incredibly overlooked and I do not understand any hate that people give it. Sure it's not something that's particularly amazing, and it's way too linear to have an incredible time. But you get to make choices that matter. You make a choice, your ending is going to be changed. You even get the power of adrenaline to automatically behead an enemy or use magic that is more powerful. IE: Shrunken enemies stay shrunk, fireballs are more powerful and explode enemies, ice permanently freezes foes, and more. Not only that but you can turn into a freaking DEMON and that's fun as HELL.
